events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: Strong, gusty north winds rapidly developed behind a cold front the evening of February 17th. The rapid onset of winds capsized a 16 foot Jon Boat near Port Mansfield in the Laguna Madre. Three people were found drowned, one was found onshore just before Midnight the evening of February 17th and the other 2 were found the morning of February 18th. Three people were injured, with one person passing away from injuries on Tuesday, February 22nd. One person was still missing and presumed perished. F29BO. UBO. UBO. UBO. UBO. UBO.

The event known as the Oak Mott Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 1:00PM CST about 7 miles north of San Perlita, TX along the border of Kenedy and Willacy Counties. It burned until the afternoon of the 3rd when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 2:00PM CST. This wildfire consumed a total of 873 acres, of which approximately 800 acres burned in Inland Kenedy County. A Spot Request submitted by the US Fish and Wildlife Service on March 2nd and the GOES-16 Day Land Cloud Fire RGB channel were used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

The event known as the Oak Mott Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 1:00PM CST about 7 miles north of San Perlita, TX along the border of Kenedy and Willacy Counties. It burned until the afternoon of the 3rd when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 2:00PM CST. This wildfire consumed a total of 873 acres, a total of about 73 acres occurred in Willacy County. A Spot Request submitted by the US Fish and Wildlife Service on March 2nd and the GOES-16 Day Land Cloud Fire RGB channel were used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

The event known as the Miller Fire was estimated to have started around 2:30PM CST near the Brooks County Rest Area just south of Falfurrias. The fire started because of a car running into a tree along US-281, where it then burst into flames. Strong and gusty south to southeast winds then pushed the wildfire from the west side of US-281 north to Baluarte Creek Road and County Road 303, where it eventually damaged or destroyed six homes along Sunrise Road. There were also at least ten cars either damaged or destroyed due to the fire. This wildfire consumed a total of 271 acres and was contained at 7:54PM CST. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Fire Service on March 4th and social media pictures from a US Border Patrol Chief were used as a guide for the ignition time and very rapid spread that followed. Dollar damages are estimated.

Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the northwestern portions of Zapata County on March 1st and expanded southeastward on March 8th due to lack of significant rainfall and low humidity. Extreme Drought then expanded to include the northwestern half of the county on March 15th. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded southeastward on March 8th to include virtually the whole county. Severe Drought expanded across the whole county on March 15th.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across the northwestern half of Jim Hogg County on March 8th and expanded to include the northwestern half of the county on March 15th. Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include the entire county on March 22nd due to the lack of significant rainfall.

Freezing rain likely fell for a brief period between 3:55AM CST and 5:55AM CST near Falfurrias in Brooks County. This is inferred due to the Brooks County Airport (KBKS) reporting a temperature of 30.7 degrees with accumulating precipitation with radar returns overhead.

Gusty south winds to an estimated 40 knots occurred in the Rio Grande Valley of Deep South Texas. An UPS truck traveling eastbound on Texas HWY 48 rolled over shortly before 11:30AM CDT due to the strong, gusty winds. The driver suffered minor injuries during the accident.  Damage to the vehicle is estimated.
Severe (D2) drought developed across the northwestern corner of Brooks County in mid-March. The lack of persistent rain and drier than normal conditions led to the expansion.

Severe (D2) drought developed across the western portion of Starr on March 15th and expanded to include areas west of FM 755 on March 22nd. The lack of persistent rain and drier than normal conditions led to the expansion through the whole month.

Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the northwestern sliver of Jim Hogg County, northwest of the intersection of FM 3073 and FM 649 on March 15th. It continued to expand southeastward on March 22nd to include Hebbronville and along TX-16 into Zapata County.

South winds gusting to a measured 57 knots (66 mph) at the Rio Grande Valley International Airport (KHRL) and a measured 52 knots (60 mph) at the Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport (KBRO) for about 4.5 hours. The public reported several downed tree limbs, fences, and a few power poles. There were also reports of some roofing shingles pulled back in the San Benito area and car port roofs peeled back in the Harlingen area.

South winds gusting to a measured 51 knots (59 mph) at the Port Isabel-Cameron County Airport (KPIL) for about 4.5 hours. The public reported a snapped large tree limb on healthy avocado tree in the Port Isabel area.
South winds gusting to a measured 50 knots (58 mph) at the Miller International Airport (KMFE) for about 4.5 hours. The roof of a mobile home was torn off due to the wind in Pharr.

The event known as the El Negro Ranch brushfire was estimated to have initiated around 3:30PM CDT about 6 miles west of the intersection of Ranch Road 2294 and FM 755 in Starr County. It burned until the morning of March 15th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 8:25AM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 463 acres. An Incident Report from the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the ignition time.

The event known as the La Grulla Fire was estimated to have initiated around 5:00PM CDT about one and a half miles south of La Grulla, TX near the border of the United States and Mexico. It burned until the morning of March 14th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 9:30AM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 578 acres. An Incident Report from the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the ignition time.

The event known as the La Paloma Fire started around 10:50AM CDT near the La Paloma Subdivision in southeastern Starr County due to a trash burn getting out of control. Local media reported that one unoccupied home and a storage shed were lost to the fire. It burned until the afternoon of March 21st when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 4:52PM CDT. An Incident Report by the Texas A&M Forest Service and a report by local media were used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

The AWOS at the South Texas International Airport, 11 miles north-northeast of Edinburg, reported 32 degrees shortly after sunrise.  Proxy observations from western Willacy County and Brooks County support additional freezing conditions, most likely in northeast Hidalgo County, during this time.

The event known as the Wingtip Fire started as the result of a police chase ending in a car accident about 10 miles north of Edinburgh. The combination of cured fuels, very low relative humidity, and gusty winds allowed the fire to spread rapidly. The fire started around 6:30PM CDT on March 30th and ended March 31st at 3:56AM CDT. A spot request from the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the fire's start time. The fire consumed a total of 446 acres.

The event known as the Vib wildfire started on private property about 2 miles northeast of the town of Encino, TX. The fire quickly spread to the southeast on the heels of strong northwest winds and threatened property throughout the control efforts. One unoccupied outbuilding was destroyed as a result of the fire. The fire started around 2:30PMCDT on March 30th and continued until around 11:10PM CDT on March 31st. The start time is estimated based on the GOES Day Land Cloud Fire RGB channel and a Spot Request by the Texas A&M Forest Service around 3:30PM CDT. The fire consumed a total of 9,424 acres.

The event known as the Borrega Wildfire started in Kleberg County around 3:00PM CDT according to the GOES-16 Day Land Cloud Fires RGB channel about 10 miles west of Kingsville, TX. The fire rapidly spread throughout the afternoon and evening before entering the northeastern portion of Brooks County around 12:00AM CDT on March 31st. This did prompt voluntary evacuations for those east of Falfurrias as the fire continued to spread. The fire continued to burn until 6:00PM CDT on April 3rd and consumed a total of 51,566 acres. Approximately 568 of those acres burned in Brooks County north of TX-285 in the northeastern portion of the county.

The event known as the Hayfield South Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 1:45PM CDT about 10 miles north of San Perlita, TX. It burned until the afternoon of March 28th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 6:38PM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 11,128 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Forest Service on March 24th and the GOES-16 Day Land Cloud Fire RGB channel were used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

The event known as the Miller Fire in Jim Hogg County was estimated to have initiated around 4:00PM CDT on March 24th about 20 miles south-southeast of Hebbronville. It burned until 11:07PM CDT March 24th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained. This wildfire consumed a total of 1058 acres. A Spot Request by the Texas A&M Forest Service on March 24th and the GOES-16 Day Land Cloud Fire RGB channel were used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.
Severe (D2) Drought expanded across virtually all of Zapata County on March 8th and expanded to include all of the county on March 15th.

Persistent dry conditions led to worsening drought conditions. Extreme (D3) Drought developed over a portion of northern Jim Hogg County, which included Hebbronville. Severe Drought (D2) also expanded eastward to include all but the extreme southeast tip of the county.
Lack of rain and several dry cold fronts throughout March led to the expansion of the severe (D2) drought to include the northwestern third of Brooks County.

Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the northwestern third of Jim Hogg County due to lack of any significant rain and several dry cold fronts that led to a number of days with relative humidity values less than 30 percent. Severe (D2) drought continues to cover all but the southeastern tip of the county.

Extreme (D3) Drought spread from the northwestern third of Zapata County to all but the southeastern quarter of the county, which remained in Severe (D2) Drought, due to lack of any significant rain and several dry cold fronts that led to a number of days with relative humidity values less than 25 percent.
Lack of rain and several dry cold fronts throughout March led to the continuation of Severe (D2) Drought across the northwestern third of Brooks County through the first third of April.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued across the northwestern third of Jim Hogg County due to lack of any significant rain and several dry cold fronts that led to a number of days with relative humidity values less than 30 percent, to begin April. Severe (D2) drought continued to cover all but the southwestern tip of the county.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued across the northern two-thirds of Zapata County with Severe (D2) Drought across the southern third to begin April, due to lack of any significant rain and several dry cold fronts that led to a number of days with relative humidity values less than 25 percent.
Persistent dry weather in Starr County maintained an area of Severe (D2) Drought across western Starr County for the first third of April.

Extreme (D3) Drought expanded across northern Jim Hogg County during the second week of April due to lack of rainfall and the passage of another dry front that led to a number of days with very low relative humidity values.

The event known as the Gun Smoke Wildfire was estimated to have ignited around 6:00PM CDT on the western side North FM 649 in Starr County about 5 miles south of the Starr and Jim Hogg County line. It burned until later in the evening on April 2nd when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 11:30PM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 425 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the ignition time and spread that followed.

The event known as the Borrega Wildfire  continued to burn until 6:00PM CDT on April 3rd and consumed a total of 51,566 acres. Approximately 560 of those acres burned in Brooks County north of TX-285 in the northeastern portion of the county.
Very dry conditions and several dry cold fronts allowed Exceptional (D4) Drought to enter the western half of Zapata County.

Severe (D2) Drought entered Inland Kenedy County due to very dry conditions and several dry cold fronts to end March and begin April. Thunderstorm clusters late on the 25th and early on the 26th dropped between 1 and 3 inches in western Kenedy, which improved conditions back to moderate levels on the 26th.

Very dry conditions, hot temperatures, and several dry cold fronts allowed Severe (D2) Drought to enter much of Northern Hidalgo County.  Thunderstorm clusters late on the 25th and early on the 26th dropped between 1 and 3 inches of rain, and helped improve conditions back to moderate (D1) on the 26th.

Very dry conditions, hot temperatures, and several dry cold fronts to end March and begin April allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to expand into western Hidalgo County, west of Mission, TX, until late on April 25th and early on April 26th, when thunderstorm clusters dropped generally 1 to 2 inches of rain and improved conditions back to Moderate (D1).

Extreme (D3) expanded eastward into Brooks County due to very dry conditions, hot temperatures, and several dry cold fronts to end March and begin April. The extreme drought covered the northwest portion of the county from approx. 3 miles west of Falfurrias to approx. 8 miles north of the Starr/Brooks/Jim Hogg County line. Severe (D2) drought covered the rest of the county.||Heavy rainfall from thunderstorm clusters late on April 25th and early on April 26th, generally between 2 and 5 inches, would improve conditions across the county on April 26th.

Very dry conditions, hot temperatures, and several dry cold fronts into mid April allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to expand into western Starr County. The extreme drought extended from approx. 7 miles of FM 1017 to approx. 4 miles east of Roma, TX on April 12th.||Torrential rains from thunderstorm clusters late on April 25th and early on April 26th, with general totals of 2 to more than 4 inches, would improve drought conditions on April 26th.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued to expand across most of Jim Hogg County during the middle of April, covering all but the far southeastern part of the county near the border of Starr and Brooks Counties. Very dry conditions, hot temperatures, and several dry cold fronts to end March and begin April led to the expansion.

Lack of significant rainfall, dry cold fronts, low humidity, and warmer than normal temperatures has led to the expansion of Exceptional (D4) drought into northwestern portions of Jim Hogg County. The areas impacted include areas west of a line from approximately 3.5 miles northwest of Hebbronville along FM 359 in the northwester portion of the County south to approximately 4 miles north of the Jim Hogg/Starr/Zapata County line.

Lack of significant rainfall, dry cold fronts, very low relative humidity, and warmer than normal temperatures has led to the expansion of the Exceptional (D4) drought to now include all but the southern 3 to 4 miles of Zapata County.

Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to include all of Zapata County in early April due to lack of rainfall and the passage of several cold fronts that led to a number of days with very low relative humidity values.

Thunderstorm winds estimated at 50 knots blew over a carport and blew it across the street. Additionally, part of the awning and roof of Rigo's Tire Shop and Road Service was torn off and tossed approximately 100 feet down the road. Radar velocity from the Corpus Christi radar indicated winds of 58 knots about 4,000 feet in elevation between 7:15PM CDT and 7:20PM CDT, which was used to estimate the timing of the event.
Thunderstorm winds estimated at 50 knots peeled the roof off of a mobile home and blew debris several feet along La Sagunada Road in Starr County west of FM755.

Thunderstorm winds estimated at 50 knots downed several large tree limbs between Cenizo Street and the intersection of E Eisenhower St and FM755 in Rio Grande City. Additionally, one set of traffic lights were left dangling at the intersection of E Eisenhower St and FM755. The public also shared pictures of numerous trampolines that were blown down the street.

The event known as the San Ygnacio fire burned along the riverbanks of the Rio Grande River approximately 1 mile south of San Ygnacio. The Zapata County Fire Department stated the first started the afternoon of April 2nd and continued to burn until the afternoon of April 4th. The fire consumed a total of approximately 1000 acres.

This event is based largely on observed heat index values across Zapata County, the which saw heat indices top out at 114 degrees. Given the higher heat index values in Zapata counties, it is inferred that Starr County also experienced heat index values in excess of 111 degrees for at least two hours. The Falcon Lake RAWS site recorded values technically reaching Excessive Heat criteria, but this observation site has a history of running notably higher than surrounding areas. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

The Zapata Airport AWOS site first recorded heat index values reaching or exceeding 111 degrees around 1:55 PM CDT. Heat index values then remained above 111 degrees through 6:45 PM, topping out around 114 degrees at 3:35PM CDT. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

Extreme (D3) Drought expanded into all of northern Zapata, and Severe (D2) Drought expanded to cover the remainder of the county, as rain-free conditions, low humidity, and increasingly warm conditions dominated the last half of March.

Persistent dry conditions led to worsening drought conditions. Severe Drought (D2) developed eastward and encompassed the western half of Starr County.  These conditions would continue until the end of the month.

Hail the size of a penny, or 0.75, was reported by the Zapata County Emergency Manager near the Siesta Shores Subdivision at 11:43AM CDT. Law enforcement reported hail the size of nickels, or 0.88, at the Falcon Lake Estates subdivision at 11:49AM CDT.
Law enforcement reported minor street flooding due to very heavy rain near the Medina Subdivision near Zapata County High School.
Exceptionally heavy rain led to street flooding at the intersection of Highway 83 and 9th Avenue in Zapata County.
The Zapata County Fire Department reported hail the size of a quarter, or 1.0, in Zapata at 8:20PM CDT.

A homeowner interviewed by a local television station reported ping pong to golf ball sized hail, which damaged his roof and several of his windows. He also reported severe damage to trees, shingles, and a destroyed wooden playground due to very gusty winds.

A homeowner interviewed by a local television station reported severe damage to trees, shingles, and a destroyed wooden playground due to very gusty winds. He also reported ping pong to golf ball sized hail, which damaged his roof and several of his windows.  Radar indicated this storm strengthening with the potential for even higher wind gusts as it moved into extreme eastern Starr County, but there were not additional corroborating reports as of this writing.

A manufactured home resting on cinder blocks was blown off of the cinder blocks. The metal roof of another manufactured home was completely lifted up and torn off. Another manufactured home was flipped over on its side. Large branches of several trees were broken. Fencing was knocked down next to manufactured home blown off the cinder blocks.  Several other homes in the neighborhood, known locally as a colonia, had minor roof and siding damage.  Two persons were injured at one of the homes, one whose hand was injured by corrugated siding that had blown between two sections of the structure.

The metal roof of the Segovia State Prison Unit was peeled back. A large metal shipping container next to the Lopez State Prison Unit was rolled several times due to the wind. Several trees with large branches were broken. A large tree was uprooted in front of the Lopez State Prison Unit.
Power lines and crop damage (light to severe) were reported by the COOP observer in McCook. He also reported pea to nickel sized hail as the storms rolled through.
Additional pictures of tree damage was shared by the public near the intersection of Interstate 69C and Davis Road in Hidalgo County.

Video on social media shows several feet of fast moving water near Medina Street - a flood-prone area known as Medina Addition - with two SUVs that had been swept off the road and into a ditch. Video later shows the vehicles getting dragged out of the ditch by a tow truck. Based on the during and after videos, it is estimated that 3 to 4 feet of fast flowing water was moving across the road at the height of the flash flooding. Additional video shows people having to abandon homes during the height of the flooding and the water coming up to their waists, which supports the 3 to 4 foot estimates of fast moving water. A report of 8 of rain came in from just northwest of Zapata from this storm. The local newspaper in Zapata County later reported that at least 15 homes were affected with many of them losing their furniture, clothing, and household items.

Social media reports of quarter to ping pong sized hail fell on the Palmview area in southwestern Hidalgo County around 4:22AM CDT on May 24th. There were additional areas of hail of pea to dime sized hail in La Joya and the Mission area around the same times.

Social media pictures showed several submerged cars that were being removed from flood waters from the heavy rain the night before. Flood depth of 3 to 4 feet is estimated due to how high the water was on the cars.
Downed healthy tree in the middle of the road with 6-8 inch diameter trunk near Los Fresnos/Laureles on Kretz Road between FM803 and FM1575.
The ASOS station at the Rio Grande Valley International Airport (KHRL) recorded a wind gust of 58 knots, or 67 mph, at 6:20AM CDT.
The ASOS station at Port Isabel-Cameron County Airport (KPIL) recorded a gust of 50 knots, or 58 mph, at 6:29AM CDT with the squall line that came through Cameron County.

The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at SPI Brazos Santiago, right near the entrance to Port of Brownsville at the southern tip of South Padre Island, recorded a wind gust of 61 knots, or 70 mph.

The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station recorded a wind gust of 54 knots, or 62 mph. This site is on the western side of South Padre Island, about 0.3 miles west of the entrance to Isla Blanca State Park.
Social media report from SpaceX says their weather station recorded a wind gust of 63 knots, or 73 mph. This site is located approximately 1 mile west of Boca Chica Beach.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX OUT 20 NM
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the morning of May 24th. It is reasonable to assume that the coastal waters out 20 nautical miles between Port Mansfield and Baffin Bay experienced Marine Thunderstorm Wind Gusts due to the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2), which is 1 mile from the coastal waters, began gusting over 34 knots at 9:54AM CDT and continued until 10:18AM CDT. The highest gust recorded was 39 knots.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the morning of May 24th. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) began gusting over 34 knots at 9:54AM CDT and continued until 10:18AM CDT. The highest gust recorded was 39 knots.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the morning of May 24th. The Texas Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula (RLIT2) began gusting above 34 knots at 2:30AM CDT and continued until 3:12AM CDT and recorded a peak gust of 47 knots at 2:42AM CDT. Additionally, the same line of thunderstorms brought a wind gust of 40 knots to the TCOON site at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station (PCGT2) at 3:18AM CDT.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the morning of May 24th. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at SPI Brazos Santiago (BZST2) recorded wind gusts over 34 knots from 3:48AM CDT through 4:48AM CDT with the highest wind gust observed of 39 knots.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the morning of May 24th. The line finally arrived at the National Data Buoy Center Buoy 42020 at 10:50AM CDT and brought gusts above 34 knots until 11:40AM CDT. The highest measured gust was 37 knots at 11:00AM CDT.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: A late-May cold front brought a strong line of showers and thunderstorms along with it. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) suddenly gusted to 40 knots at 5:00AM CDT and remained above 34 knots through 6:06AM CDT. The highest measured gust was 45 knots at 5:36AM CDT.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX OUT 20 NM
events.event_narrative: A late-May cold front brought a strong line of showers and thunderstorms along with it. The line was fairly strong and was oriented west to east as it pushed south. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that the coastal waters out to 20 nautical miles between Baffin Bay and Port Mansfield also experienced Marine Thunderstorm winds based on the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) gusting to 40 knots at 5:00AM CDT and remained above 34 knots through 6:06AM CDT. As well as Buoy 42020 gusting above 34 knots from 5:30AM CDT through 7:00AM CDT. The highest measured gust was 45 knots at 5:36AM CDT for RSJT2 and 51 knots at 6:00AM CDT for Buoy 42020.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: A late-May cold front brought a strong line of showers and thunderstorms along with it. The National Data Buoy Center Buoy 42020 recorded gusts above 34 knots starting at 5:30AM CDT and remained above 34 knots through 7:00AM CDT. The strongest gust recorded was 51 knots at 6:00AM CDT.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A late-May cold front brought a strong line of showers and thunderstorms along with it. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Center (TCOON) site at SPI Brazos Santiago (BZST2) recorded wind gusts in excess of 34 knots from 6:48AM CDT through 8:42AM CDT, with the peak gust of 61 knots observed at 6:48AM CDT.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A late-May cold front brought a strong line of showers and thunderstorms along with it. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula (RLIT2) began gusting over 34 knots at 6:24AM CDT with the highest observed gust of 48 knots at 6:36AM CDT. The TCOON site at SPI Coast Guard (PCGT2) observed a peak gust of 43 knots at 7:30AM CDT. Meanwhile, the strongest gust was recorded at NOAA's National Ocean Service Site at Port Isabel (PTIT2), which recorded a gust of 52 knots at 6:54AM CDT.

The Mansfield 2022 Wildfire started on the morning of April 7th across the southern tip of Padre Island, near the cut for Port Mansfield. It burned 438 acres and was contained the evening of April 7th.

Severe (D2) Drought continued to start the month of May. However, some widespread rain fell over the region in late April, which allowed the Severe (D2) Drought to be taken out of Brooks County early in the month.

Severe (D2) Drought continued to start the month of May. However, some widespread rain fell over the region in late April, which allowed the Severe (D2) Drought to be taken out of Starr County early in the month.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued to start the month of May across most of Zapata County with only a tiny portion of southern Zapata County in the Severe (D2) Drought category. Subsequent updates throughout the month remained largely unchanged until a couple rounds of showers and storms, some of which dropped over 5 to 8 across portions of Zapata County from May 22nd through early on May 24th, essentially wiped out the drought conditions across most of Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued to start the month of May across northwestern Jim Hogg County with the rest of Jim Hogg County in the Severe (D2) Drought category. A large portion of the Severe (D2) Drought was removed by May 2nd due to rainfall that occurred in late April. Subsequent updates throughout the month remained largely unchanged until a couple rounds of showers and storms, some of which dropped over 1 to 4 across portions of Jim Hogg County on May 23rd, essentially wiped out the drought conditions across most of Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley.

Power lines down, and power outages, were reported across a large part of Starr County as a developing line of severe thunderstorms moved through.  One of the strongest cells likely produced some of these power outages between Viboras and La Gloria along Farm-to-Market road 2686.

Rainfall ranging from 2 to more than 5 inches in most of Brooks County from late April 25th through early April 26th improved drought conditions.  Severe (D2) Drought remained only across the northwest quarter of the county following the rain.

Rainfall of generally 1 to 2 inches late on April 25th through early April 26th across Jim Hogg County reduced drought levels in response, with the northwest corner improving from D4 (Exceptional) to D3 (Extreme) and most of the remainder of the county improving from D3 to D2 (Severe).

Locally heavy rainfall of 0.5 to nearly 2 inches across Zapata County from late April 25th through early April 26th was enough to improve drought conditions by one category, from Exceptional (D4) and Extreme (D3) to Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2). By the 26th, most of Zapata had reverted to D3, with the southern fifth of the county improved to D2.

Torrential rains of generally 2 to more than 4 inches from late April 25th through early April 26th across Starr County helped improve drought conditions by one category.  Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) conditions improved to Severe (D2) across the western half of the county, and Moderate (D1) across the eastern half of the county, to close out the month.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020, approximately 54 miles northeast of Port Mansfield, recorded a peak gust to 35 knots on June 29th at 8:30AM CDT due to a line of showers and thunderstorms spinning around an area of low pressure in the western Gulf of Mexico.

The very northern part of Jim Hogg County, which missed out on the heavier rain events in late May, saw Severe (D2) Drought return in mid-June. This includes areas northwest of the Hebbronville Border Patrol Station and does include much of the town of Hebbronville.

The event known as the Blanket Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 2:41PM CDT on July 9th about 12 miles northwest of Encino, Texas. It burned until 9:13PM CDT on July 14th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained. This wildfire consumed a total of 5900 acres. A Spot Request by the Texas A&M Forest Service on July 9th and the GOES-16 Visible satellite channel were used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

The event known as the Deer Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 1:21PM CDT about 9 miles northwest of Armstrong, TX, on or near the Encino Division of the King Ranch. It burned until July 9th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 9:52AM CDT. This wildfire consumed 1,062 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

The McAllen Airport ASOS site first recorded heat index values reaching or exceeding 111 degrees around 1:30PM CDT. Heat index values then remained above 111 degrees through 4:30PM CDT, topping out around 116 degrees at 2:53PM CDT. Edinburg International Airport also observed heat index values of 111 degrees from 1:55PM CDT through 5:15PM CDT and briefly topped out at 113 degrees at 3:35PM CDT. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

The Zapata Airport AWOS site first recorded heat index values reaching or exceeding 111 degrees around 2:55PM CDT. Heat index values then remained above 111 degrees through 7:55PM CDT, topping out around 115 degrees at 6:35PM CDT. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

This event is based largely on observed heat index values across Southern Hidalgo County and Zapata County. Both counties saw heat indices top out above 111 degrees for several hours. Given the higher heat index values in both Hidalgo and Zapata Counties, it is inferred that Starr County also experienced heat indices in excess of 111 degrees for at least two hours. The Falcon Lake RAWS site recorded values technically reaching Excessive Heat criteria, but this observation site has a history of running notably higher than surrounding areas. Additionally, the Texas Mesonet site in La Gloria recorded a heat index of 111 between 3:50PM CDT and 4:20PM CDT. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

The Linn-San Manuel Texas Mesonet site (LSRT2) first recorded heat index values reaching or exceeding 111 degrees around 2:46PM CDT. Heat index values then remained above 111 degrees through 4:46PM CDT, topping out around 112 degrees during this time. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

The event known as the Laguna Seca Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 3:06PM CDT about 1.5 miles from intersection of US-281 and FM 490 in Hidalgo County. It burned until the evening of July 25th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 7:34PM CDT. The fire consumed a total of 415 acres. An Incident Report from the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the ignition time.

The event known as the El Pasture Fire was estimated to have initiated around 5:27PM CDT on July 26th along Highway 285 about 7 miles east of Hebbronville. It burned until the evening of July 27th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 6:38PM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 394 acres. An Incident Report from the Texas A&M Forest Service along with a Facebook post by the Jim Hogg County Emergency Management was used a guide for the ignition time.

A very electric storm over the Harlingen and La Feria area of Cameron County on July 27th produced a lightning strike that struck powerlines just outside of the KVEO news studio. Those powerlines then fell onto Interstate 2, which initially caused a backup on the interstate. Crews worked to clear the lines quickly, but had to close the interstate again that evening to repair the lines. Timing was based on radar, National Lightning Detection Network (NDLN), and a broadcast media report. No injuries, or car accidents were reported as a result of the downed powerlines.

Cameron County Beach Patrol responded to a call regarding two possible drowning victims, which came in around 7:10PM CDT on July 2nd. Witnesses suggested the fatality was rip/longshore current related, and an off-duty NWS employee vouched for the dangerous rip current/longshore current potential during the entire weekend (July 2-4).  ||A 37-year old tourist swimming in the Gulf of Mexico off South Padre Island, about 2.5 miles north of Cameron County Beach Access #5, drowned in the current. A child, age unknown, was also rescued from the water by bystanders before the Beach Patrol arrived.

The very northern part of Jim Hogg County, which missed out on the heavier rain events in late May, saw Severe (D2) Drought return in mid-June and continue through the month of July. This includes area northwest of the Hebbronville Border Patrol Station and does include much of the town of Hebbronville.

The very northern part of Jim Hogg County saw Extreme (D3) Drought return in mid-July. This includes the northern half of the town of Hebbronville. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded southward in mid-July.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include much of the northern part of the county. It stretched from approximately 1.5 miles south of Texas Highway 16 along the Jim Hogg and Zapata County border to 19 miles due south of Hebbronville to the northwestern cutout of Brooks County 2.3 miles south of TX-285.

Severe (D2) Drought returned to the northern third of Zapata County in late-July due to the lack of significant rain, hot to very hot temperatures, and low relative humidity values in the afternoon. The drought extended from approximately 1.5 miles south of Texas Highway 16 along the Zapata and Jim Hogg County line westward to 9 miles south of the Zapata and Webb County along US-83.

The event known as the Las Brisas Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 3:30PM CDT about 8 miles northeast of Rio Grande City along Farm to Market Road 755, FM755 in Starr County. It burned until the evening of August 6th when it was announced to be 100 contained at 9:44PM CDT. The fire consumed a total of 400 acres. An incident report from the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the ignition time.

A strong storm developed in southern Hidalgo County and sagged to the southwest the evening of August 11th. At 7:08PM CDT, a member of the public began a Facebook Live that showed a funnel cloud dropping out of the storm. Radar analysis showed some mid-level rotation with the storm to corroborate the video and its timing. It dissipated by the end of the 2 minutes video, so around 7:10PM CDT.

A pulse-severe thunderstorm produced a microburst with winds estimated at 65 mph across the northeast side of Weslaco.  Along its 2.3 mile track, damage included blown in siding at hangars at the airportand peeled back a metal roof on one of them.  Other damage included a small outbuilding that was flipped over, bent in fences, and a trampoline lifted and flung. The Mid Valley Airport ASOS in Weslaco officially recorded a 56 mph wind gust, but missed the core being about 300 meters west of the downburst.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: Buoy 42020 recorded a measured wind gust of 37 knots the morning of August 14th as a thunderstorm associated with a trough of tropical low pressure moving ashore along trhe Coastal Bend south of Corpus Christi.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: A member of the public reported a waterspout near Port Mansfield. This was associated with a trough of low pressure that moved ashore over the Coastal Bend south of Corpus Christi on August 14th.

Severe (D2) Drought returned to the northern third of Zapata County in late-July due to the lack of significant rain, hot to very hot temperatures, and low relative humidity values in the afternoon. The drought extended from approximately 1.5 miles south of Texas highway 16 along the Zapata and Jim Hogg County line westward to 9 miles south of the Zapata and Webb County line along US-83.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued in far northwestern Jim Hogg County, including the Jim Hogg County Airport. Severe (D2) Drought continued to include much of the northern part of the county. It stretched from approximately 1.5 miles south of Texas Highway 16 along the Jim Hogg and Zapata County line to 19 miles due south of Hebbronville to the northwestern cutout of Brooks County 2.3 miles south of TX-285.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include northwestern Brooks County. The eastern extent was US-281 from just west of Falfurrias to approximately 10 miles north of Encino before dipping southwest to the Jim Hogg County approximately 11 miles north of the Starr/Jim Hogg/Brooks County lines. On August 9th, Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include all but the southwestern portion of Brooks County. Abundant rainfall fell across the region as an area of low pressure swirled inland from the Gulf of Mexico the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th and allowed drought to exit all of Brooks County with the August 16th update.

Severe (D2) Drought entered Kenedy County to start the month of August. It stretched from approximately 2.7 miles west of Brooks County south to approximately 5 miles north of Armstrong and eastward to the coast. The drought then expanded to include much of western Inland Kenedy County, west of US-77, on August 9th. Abundant rainfall from an area of low pressure moving inland from the Gulf of Mexico over the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th, allowed Severe (D2) drought to be taken out of Kenedy County with the August 16th update.

Severe (D2) Drought entered Coastal Kenedy County in early August. It covered the northern half of the zone. Abundant rainfall from an area of low pressure moving inland from the Gulf of Mexico over the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th, allowed Severe (D2) drought to be taken out of Coastal Kenedy County with the August 16th update.

Severe (D2) Drought entered Kenedy Island in early August. It covered the northern half of the zone. Abundant rainfall from an area of low pressure moving inland from the Gulf of Mexico over the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th, allowed Severe (D2) drought to be taken out of Coastal Kenedy County with the August 16th update.

Severe (D2) Drought continued to expand south to start August in Jim Hogg County. It covered all but the southeastern part of the county, or a line from 22 miles west of the southeastern corner of the county to 11 miles north. Abundant rainfall from an area of low pressure moving inland from the Gulf of Mexico over the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th, allowed Severe (D2) drought to be taken out of Jim Hogg County with the August 16th update.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include all of Zapata County on August 2nd as the lack of rain began leading to water conservation efforts in Zapata as Falcon Lake dipped to its lowest levels (Texas share) on record and the lowest since 2002 for combined U.S. and Mexico water storage levels.

Severe (D2) Drought entered the northwestern tip of Starr County in early August as the drought continued to worsen across Deep South Texas. It stretched from approximately 12 miles west of the Starr/Zapata County line due southwest to just south of New Falcon, TX. The drought would increase into the western third of the county by the 9th.

Lack of rainfall, very hot temperatures, and low relative humidity in the afternoons led to the development of Extreme (D3) drought in the western two thirds of Zapata County. Rainfall on August 14th and 15th allowed the northern portion of the Extreme (D3) drought to be downgraded to Severe (D2) Drought, and trim the area of Severe (D2) Drought to all but the eastern fifth of the county on the 16th. Reservoir levels at Falcon reached the lowest levels (Texas share) on record between the 13th and 15th, and were at their lowest levels since 2002 during this time.  Torrential rains of 6 to more than 8 inches late on the 15th over and just north of the lake along the Rio Grande would bring a flood wave into the reservoir, starting a rise that would bring water storage levels above the new Texas share record and similar total share values from 2002.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include the northeastern portion of Northern Hidalgo County on August 9th. Abundant rainfall of 3 to 7 inches fell across the region as an area of low pressure swirled inland from the Gulf of Mexico the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th and allowed drought to exit all of Northern Hidalgo County with the August 16th update.

Extreme (D3) Drought entered southwestern Starr County, near Falcon Lake, on August 9th. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded across western Starr County to Rio Grande City on August 9th.  Abundant rainfall fell across the region as an area of low pressure swirled inland from the Gulf of Mexico the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th and allowed the much of the Severe (D2) drought to exit all by the far southwestern portion of Starr County with the August 16th update.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: Three brief waterspouts were spotted about 7 miles east of South Padre Island. The distance was estimated based on radar. A member of the public shared the images on a Facebook group.

Rainfall on August 14th and 15th would reach eastern and northern Zapata County, trimming Severe (D2) and Extreme (D3) Drought to cover the western four-fifths of Zapata County, with D3 conditions across Falcon Reservoir, Zapata City, extending to just north of the Falcon State Park.  Additional rainfall after August 23 would further trim the D2 area to just the central and southern portions of the county, with D3 remaining in the same areas to close the month.

Rainfall on August 14th and 15th would reach much of Starr County, improving drought for all but the southwestern corner of the county where the rain largely missed the area.  Severe (D2) Drought covered an area from Roma to the Zapata County line, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) Drought along the Rio Grande near the Zapata County line by Falcon Dam and Falcon State Park.  ||Additional rains in western Starr County would further trim the D2 area to north of Roma and just east of Falcon State Park/Falcon Dam; D3 remained through the end of the month in those areas.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A waterspout was sighted approximately 1 to 2 nautical miles southeast of Boca Chica Beach on the morning of September 23rd. A meteorologist for SpaceX shared the pictures. Timing was based off their observation along with radar.

Severe (D2) and Extreme (D3) drought remained over the central and southern portions of Zapata County to start the month. An additional 0.5 to 3 of rain over Labor Day weekend (September 2nd/3rd/4th) was enough to trim both Severe (D2) and Extreme (D3) drought out of the county by September 5th.

Severe (D2) and Extreme (D3) remained in extreme western Starr County near Falcon Lake State Park/Falcon Dam to start the month. An additional 0.5 to 3 of rain over Labor Day weekend (September 2nd/3rd/4th) eased drought levels below Severe (D2) by September 5th.

A 17-year old man drowned in a rip current at approximately 4 PM CDT on Wednesday, October 12th, in the surf at Cameron County Public Access #5. The teen was with a group of peers but entered the surf on his own and, according to the witnesses, disappeared into the waves. According to USCG, witnesses reported the swimmer began demonstrating signs of distress, and the currents soon overpowered him before he submerged. A 9-1-1 call from the peer group was related to USCG Corpus Christi, where air assets were deployed, along with water assets from USCG South Padre Island to assist with SAR. Cameron County Beach Patrol, Cameron County Emergency Management, and South Padre island Fire Department assisted in the SAR. The swimmer was recovered a day later (October 13), 8 miles north of the entry point, by Cameron Co. Park Rangers after fishers discovered the floating body and called 9-1-1.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A member of the public shared a waterspout picture with a broadcast meteorologist, who then relayed it to the National Weather Service Office in Brownsville. The picture was taken early Monday morning just before 9AM CDT and didn't last terribly long. In the picture, a well defined funnel cloud was observed along with water spray at the surface. This waterspout likely formed due to a weak boundary collision about 7.5 miles east of South Padre Island.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX OUT 20 NM
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) reported a measured gust of 34 knots at 4:18AM CDT. The proximity to the coastal waters from Baffin Bay to Port Mansfield out 20 nautical miles coupled with additional wind gusts over 34 knots reported at Buoy 42020 later in the hour leads credence to the fact this area experienced Marine Thunderstorm Wind gusts as well.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: Buoy 42020 of the National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) reported wind gusts above 34 knots associated with a cold front producing a broken line of showers and storms starting at 4:50AM CDT and lasting until 5:10AM CDT. The highest gust was 37 knots recorded at 4:50AM CDT.
