events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at SPI Brazos Santiago (BZST2) reported wind gusts above 34 knots associated with a cold front producing a broken line of showers and thunderstorms starting at 5:54AM CDT and lasting through 6:36AM CDT. The highest gust recorded was measured at 37 knots at 6:00AM CDT and again at 6:12AM CDT.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) reported wind gusts measured at 34 knots associated with a cold front producing a broken line of showers and thunderstorms at 4:18AM CDT.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula (RLIT2) reported wind gusts above 34 knots associated with a cold front producing a broken line of showers and thunderstorms starting at 5:12AM CDT and lasting through 5:36AM CDT. The highest gust recorded was measured at 39 knots at 5:12AM CDT. Additionally, the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at South Padre Island Coast Guard Station (PCGT2) recorded a wind gust of 35 knots at 5:48 AM CDT.

A sliver of Severe (D2) Drought continued from the end of July through the first of August in extreme northwest Brooks County, just a couple miles east of the Jim Hogg County line and south of the Duval County line.

Torrential rainfall, with local estimates of 2 or more inches per hour for two hours, produced street flooding from San Benito through La Tina Ranch, including along city and rural roads, with 1 to 2 feet of water on roads where the heaviest rainfall fell.  There were no reports of flooding of structures in these areas, and flood receded quickly after the slow moving band ended.

The ASOS station at McAllen International Airport (KMFE) recorded a 59 mph wind gust at 10:28PM CST. This was caused by a mini supercell that developed along a cold front trudging through Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley. There were also a few public reports of dime to penny sized hail in the Mission area.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 11:55PM CST on December 22nd and did not rise above freezing until 7:55PM CST on December 23rd. The Brooks County Airport (KBKS) observed a low of 25 degrees.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 10:55PM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 11:35AM CST on December 24th. The Brooks County Airport (KBKS) observed a low of 27 degrees.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 7:35PM CST on December 24th and did not rise above freezing until 8:15PM CST on December 25th. The Brooks County Airport (KBKS) observed a low of 26 degrees.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 11:35PM CST on December 25th and did not rise above freezing until 3:15AM CST on December 26th. The Brooks County Airport (KBKS) observed a low of 29 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 11:15PM CST on December 22nd and did not rise above freezing until 10:55AM CST on December 24th. The Jim Hogg County Airport (KHBV) observed a low of 24 degrees during the stretch.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 8:15PM CST on December 24th and did not rise above freezing until 8:35AM CST on December 25th. The Jim Hogg County Airport (KHBV) observed a low of 25 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 12:55AM CST on December 26th and did not rise above freezing until 3:55AM CST on December 26th. The Jim Hogg County Airport (KHBV) observed a low of 30 degrees.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 2:35AM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 11:35AM CST on December 23rd. The Zapata County Airport (KAPY) observed a low of 29 degrees.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 5:55AM CST on December 24th and did not rise above freezing until 8:35AM CST on December 24th. The Zapata County Airport (KAPY) observed a low of 32 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 9:15PM CST on December 24th and did not rise above freezing until 8:55AM CST on December 25th. The Zapata County Airport (KAPY) observed a low of 21 degrees the morning of Christmas, which was the coldest report during this cold spell.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 9:55PM CST on December 25th and did not rise above freezing until 4:35AM CST on December 26th. The Zapata County Airport (KAPY) observed a low of 28 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 1:00AM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 10:10AM CST on December 24th, or a stretch of 33 hours. The Texas Mesonet site at the Texas Water Board site near La Gloria (TBW26) observed a low of 27 degrees during this stretch. The coldest observed low at Falcon Lake (FART2) was 29 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 6:50PM CST on December 24th and did not rise above freezing until 2:50AM CST on December 25th. The Texas Mesonet site at the Texas Water Board site near La Gloria (TBW26) observed a low of 23 degrees. The coldest observed low at Falcon Lake (FART2) was 29 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 1:46AM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 8:46AM CST on December 24th, or a stretch of 31 hours. The Texas Mesonet site at Linn-San Manuel (LSRT2) observed a low of 28 degrees during this stretch.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 8:46PM CST on December 25th and did not rise above freezing until 1:46AM CST on December 26th. The Texas Mesonet site at Linn-San Manuel (LSRT2) observed a low of 28 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 2:15AM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 9:35AM CST on December 24th, or a stretch of 31 hours. The Edinburg International Airport (KEBG) AWOS was used for the timing of this event. The AWOS at the Mid Valley Airport (KTXW) in Weslaco also experienced a similar freeze duration between 3:15AM CST December 23rd to 9:15AM CST with only two observations at 33 degrees. Similar duration and temperatures were also recorded at the Texas Water Board site near La Villa (TBW67). The observed low at both KEBG and KTXW was 28 degrees with TBW67 recording a low of 27. ||Miller International Airport (KMFE) in the more populated portion of southern Hidalgo County experienced at or below freezing temperatures between 3:53AM CST December 23rd through 12:53PM CST with an observed low of 30 degrees.||According to the Texas International Produce Association, there was notable damage to herbaceous crops such as cilantro, dill, and parsley across fields near Edinburg, Alamo, and Mission.  Other crops, including leafy and in-ground vegetables did better.  Citrus escaped all but minor damage to remaining fruit on trees.  Dollar damages will be included in this report at a later date once they are received.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 11:00PM CST on December 22nd and did not rise above freezing until 1:33PM CST on December 24th, or a stretch of 38.5 hours. The mesonet site at the Union Pacific Railroad site (UR074) in central Kenedy County recorded a low of 23 degrees during the morning of December 23rd.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 12:11AM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 2:04PM CST on December 24th, or a stretch of 38 hours. The mesonet site at the Union Pacific Railroad site (UR295) in northern Willacy County recorded a low of 24 degrees during the morning of December 23rd. Additional reports of subfreezing temperatures reported in southern Hidalgo and northern Cameron County support the duration of the freeze for all of inland Willacy County.||There was likely an unknown amount of damage to herbaceous crops, such as dill, cilantro, and parsley.  Leafy vegetables and cabbage fared better, and there were no reports of significant impacts to citrus (fruit) where grown in the county.  Details, when available, will be provided in this report at a later date.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 1:12AM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 2:48PM CST on December 24th, or a stretch of almost 38 hours. A low of 25 degrees was observed at the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2).

Temperatures fell below freezing around 1:12AM CST on December 23rd and did not rise above freezing until 2:48PM CST on December 24th, or a stretch of almost 38 hours.  These times are estimates based on observations in Inland Kenedy and Coastal Kenedy. A low of 25 degrees was observed at the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2).

Temperatures fell below freezing around 4:00AM CST on December 23rd and remained below freezing until 8:00PM CST. The Yturria Union Pacific Railroad mesonet site (UR295) in northern Willacy County recorded a minimum temperature of 23 degrees; the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose recorded a minimum temperature of 25 degrees; the TCOON site at Realitos recorded a minimum temperature of 27 degrees. Given low temperatures in the middle to upper 20s observed in adjacent Willacy County and Coastal Kenedy and Coastal Cameron County, it is implied that temperatures across much of Coastal Willacy County were also in the middle to upper 20s. Times are estimated.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 4:00AM CST on December 23rd and remained below freezing until 8:00PM CST. The Yturria Union Pacific Railroad mesonet site (UR295) in northern Willacy County recorded a minimum temperature of 23 degrees; the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose recorded a minimum temperature of 25 degrees; the TCOON site at Realitos recorded a minimum temperature of 27 degrees. Given low temperatures in the middle to upper 20s observed in adjacent Willacy County and Island Kenedy and Island Cameron County, it is implied that temperatures across much of Coastal Willacy County were also in the middle to upper 20s. Times are estimated.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 8:00AM CST on December 23rd and remained below freezing until 4:30PM CST. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station recorded a minimum temperature of 29 degrees. According to Sea Turtle Inc., over 160 cold stunned sea turtles were rescued during this cold spell.  As of this writing, there were no known sea turtle losses.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 7:24AM CST on December 24th and remained below freezing until 10:12PM CST on December 24th. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station recorded a minimum temperature of 32 degrees. According to Sea Turtle Inc., over 160 cold stunned sea turtles were rescued during this cold spell.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 3:30AM CST on December 23rd and remained below freezing until 10:15PM CST on December 23rd. The ASOS station at the Port Isabel-Cameron County Airport (KPIL) recorded a low of 28 degrees during this time. Several other stations also reported 28 degrees including the Water Level Observation Network (WLON) site at Port Isabel (PTIT2) and a personal weather station in Laguna Vista. Timing was based primarily on KPIL's data.||There was likely an unknown amount of damage to herbaceous crops, such as dill, cilantro, and parsley - mainly around the Bayview/east Los Fresnos area.  Leafy vegetables and cabbage fared better, and there were no reports of significant impacts to citrus (fruit) where grown in the county.  Details, when available, will be provided in this report at a later date.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 2:15AM CST on December 23rd and remained below freezing until 11:53PM CST on December 23rd. The ASOS stations at the Valley International Airport (KHRL) and Brownsville/South Padre International Airport (KBRO) both recorded a low of 27 degrees during this time. Several other personal weather stations also recorded lows between 26 to 28 degrees during the day on December 23rd.||There was likely an unknown amount of damage to herbaceous crops, such as dill, cilantro, and parsley.  Leafy vegetables and cabbage fared better, and there were no reports of significant impacts to citrus (fruit) where grown in the county.  Details, when available, will be provided in this report at a later date.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 2:53AM CST on December 24th and remained below freezing until 8:53AM CST on December 24th. The ASOS stations at the Valley International Airport (KHRL) and Brownsville/South Padre International Airport (KBRO) both recorded a low of 30 degrees during this time. Several other personal weather stations also recorded lows between 29 to 31 degrees the morning of December 24th.

A 1.6 foot storm tide, as observed by the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at South Padre Island Brazos Santiago (BZST2), affected South Padre Island the weekend of November 19th and 20th. The storm tide remained between 1.25-foot and 1.6-foot the entire time. This led to the closer of area beaches the weekend before Thanksgiving and also caused significant beach erosion. Pictures shared with an NWS Employee from the Cameron County Beach Patrol showed water covering the northern portions of Highway 100, which is beyond the dunes. Additional beach erosion was observed November 21st through November 24th, but no water on the roadways or road closures due to water were reported.

A 2.1-foot storm tide, as observed by NOAA's National Ocean Service site at Port Isabel (PTIT2), affected Coastal Cameron County from November 18th through very early in the morning on November 21st. The storm tide remained between 1.25-foot and 2.1-foot the entire time. A picture from social media also showed water overtopping Highway 4 out to Boca Chica Beach the morning of November 20th when the storm tide was running between 1.8-foot and 2.0-foot.

The event known as the Quail Lease Fire was estimated to have initiated around 1:00PM CST on January 4th east of Hebbronville along State Highway (SH) 285. It burned until 7:00PM CST on January 4th when it was announced it was 100 percent contained. This wildfire consumed a total of 321 acres. Facebook posts by Jim Hogg Emergency Management were used as a guide for the ignition and end times.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across the eastern quarter of Jim Hogg County on January 10th. Severe (D2) Drought stretched from 3.75 miles south of State Highway 285 to 10.6 miles north of the Jim Hogg/Starr County line and extended west from the Jim Hogg/Brooks County line about 10.5 miles.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across much of Brooks County, between Falfurrias and Encino, on January 10th and expanded across much of the county on January 17th due to lack of significant rainfall.||Severe (D2) Drought developed across much of Brooks County on January 10th. It stretched from the Brooks/Hidalgo/Kenedy County lines northwest to about 10.5 miles north of the Brooks/Jim Hogg/Starr County line on the southern side and stretched north to about 3.5 miles south of Falfurrias. ||Severe (D2) Drought developed a little more north in Brooks County on January 17th with drought conditions now only 1 mile south of Falfurrias and stretched to include the northwestern portion of the county.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across western inland Kenedy County, between HWY-285 and the southern Kenedy/Brooks County border eastward to US-77 near the Border Patrol Checkpoint, on January 10th and expanded across much of the county on January 17th due to lack of significant rainfall.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to expand across most of Jim Hogg County. This includes all but the northern portion of Jim Hogg County, including the northwestern portion of Hebbronville, and the southern quarter of the county. On January 24th, Severe (D2) Drought expanded across the southwestern portion of the county with all but the southeastern and northern parts of the county under severe drought.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across much of Zapata County on January 17th. This includes area from near the Zapata/Webb County line south to about 4.5 miles north of the Jim Hogg/Starr/Zapata County line westward to about 6 miles south of the town of Zapata and 24 miles to the north-northwest of Zapata. On January 24th, Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include all but the very northwestern tip of the county.

Strong winds caused a light pole to fall and land on a parked vehicle at a Walmart in Port Isabel. No injuries were reported, but the vehicle was damaged. Timing was approximated based on the strongest wind gust at the Port Isabel-Cameron County Airport ASOS station (KPIL), which recorded a measured wind gust of 51 mph.

The ASOS station at the Brownsville-South Padre International Airport (KBRO) recorded a measured wind gust of 58 mph at 11:36AM CST. An NWS Employee also reported a fireworks stand that sustained significant damage just across from the street from KBRO.
The ASOS station at the Valley International Airport (KHRL) recorded a measured wind gust of 62 mph at 11:50AM CST.

Strong winds caused the unanchored roof of a mobile home to be blown off, which subsequently damaged other portions of the mobile home in the Santa Rosa area of Cameron County. The timing and wind gust estimates were based off the recorded wind gust of 62 mph at the Valley International Airport (KHRL) at 11:50AM CST.

Severe (D2) Drought continued into February for much of Brooks County due to lack of significant rainfall. Only the northeastern and southwestern portions of the county remain below Severe Drought the first half of February. The southwestern portion of Brooks County was included in Severe (D2) Drought on February 21st.

Severe (D2) Drought continued into February for most of Jim Hogg County. Lack of significant rainfall allowed for the continuation of drought conditions for all but the southeastern and very northern portions, including Hebbronville, of the county the first half of February. The entire county was in Severe (D2) Drought conditions by February 21st.

Severe (D2) Drought continued into February for virtually all of Zapata County. Lack of persistent rainfall led to Severe Drought continuing for all except the northern mile or two of Zapata County the first half of February. The last bit of northern Zapata County was included in Severe (D2) Drought on February 21st.

Severe (D2) Drought continued into February for western portions of Inland Kenedy County. Lack of persistent rainfall led to the continuation of Severe Drought for areas west of US-77 in Kenedy County the first half of February. The entirety of Inland Kenedy County was included in Severe (D2) Drought on February 28th.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to develop across much of Starr County. This includes areas north and west of a line from 2.6 miles south of FM 1017 along the Hidalgo County line to 1 miles east of Rio Grande City.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to develop across all but the northeastern and southwestern corners of Brooks County. This includes areas southwest of a line from 9 miles south of the Kleberg/Brooks County line to 7 miles west of the Duval/Brooks County line, which does not include Falfurrias. The southern extent of the extreme (D3) drought extends north from a line 0.6 miles north of the Hidalgo/Brooks/Kenedy line to 8 miles north of the Brooks/Starr County line.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to develop across west-central Kenedy County. It extends from 0.6 miles north of the Brooks/Kenedy/Hidalgo County line to 5.5 miles south of the Kenedy/Kleberg/Brooks County line and east to US-77 near Armstrong and the Border Patrol Checkpoint.
Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to develop across all but the northwestern and southeastern portions of Jim Hogg County.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to develop across the southern two thirds of Zapata County. The extent of the drought goes from 10.5 miles northwest of Zapata along US-83 to 5 miles south of the Webb/Zapata/Jim Hogg County line.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to develop across the northwestern portion of Starr County. The drought covers areas from the southern part of Falcon Lake to 12.2 miles west of the Starr/Zapata/Jim Hogg County line.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to develop across the northern half of Northern Hidalgo County. The drought starts 4.3 miles northwest of McCook to 2.2 miles north of Linn-San Manuel to 0.6 miles north of the corner of Kenedy County.
Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to develop across the southern half of southern Coastal Kenedy County.

The Spark Fire in Brooks County burned 932 acres. A Spot Request was received at 1:47 PM CST and satellite data was used to estimate the start time of the fire at 10:31 AM CST. It was contained at 9:57 AM CST.||The event known as the Spark Fire was estimated to have ignited around 10:31 AM CST about 16 miles northwest of Encino, TX near the border of Jim Hogg and Brooks County. It burned until the morning of March 6th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 9:57 AM CST. This wildfire consumed a total of 932 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Forest Service on March 4th and the GOES-16 Natural Fire RGB channel were used as a guide for ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue across all but the northeastern and southwestern corners of Brooks County to start March. This includes areas southwest of a line from 9 miles south of the Kleberg/Brooks County line to 7 miles west of the Duval/Brooks County line, which does not include Falfurrias. The southern extent of the Extreme (D3) drought extends north from a line 0.6 miles north of the Hidalgo/Brooks/Kenedy line to 8 miles north of the Brooks/Starr County line. The extreme drought, combined with windy and hot conditions, helped spread one large wildfire in southwest Brooks County on March 4th.||Severe Drought (D2) continued elsewhere in Brooks County.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue across west-central Kenedy County to start March. It extends from 0.6 miles north of the Brooks/Kenedy/Hidalgo County line to 5.5 miles south of the Kenedy/Kleberg/Brooks County line and east to US-77 near Armstrong and the Border Patrol Checkpoint.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue across all but the northwestern and southeastern portions of Jim Hogg County to start March. D2 (Severe) Drought continued elsewhere through March 6th.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue across the southern two thirds of Zapata County to start March. The extent of the drought goes from 10.5 miles northwest of Zapata along US-83 to 5 miles south of the Webb/Zapata/Jim Hogg County line. Severe (D2) Drought continued elsewhere.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue across the northwestern portion of Starr County to start March. The drought covers areas from the southern part of Falcon Lake to 12.2 miles west of the Starr/Zapata/Jim Hogg County line. Severe (D2) Drought continued elsewhere through Rio Grande City and northeast to the Hidalgo County line west of McCook, with Moderate (D1) Drought in the southeast corner of the county.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to continue across the northern half of Northern Hidalgo County to start March. The drought starts 4.3 miles northwest of McCook to 2.2 miles north of Linn-San Manuel to 0.6 miles north of the corner of Kenedy County.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to continue across the southern half of southern Coastal Kenedy County to start March. Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include most of Coastal Kenedy County on March 7th with all of Coastal Kenedy under Severe (D2) Drought conditions by March 14th.
Lack of persistent rainfall coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to develop across all of inland Cameron County in mid-March.
Lack of persistent rainfall coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to develop across all of southern Hidalgo County in mid-March.
Lack of persistent rainfall coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to develop across all of inland Willacy County in mid-March.

Lack of persistent rainfall coupled with dry to very dry conditions led to the development of Extreme (D3) Drought across the across the northern couple of miles of northern Hidalgo County in mid-March. It expanded slightly to the south on March 14th.
Lack of persistent rainfall coupled with dry to very dry conditions led to the development of Extreme (D3) Drought across the western half of Coastal Kenedy County in mid-March.
Lack of persistent rainfall coupled with dry to very dry conditions led to the development of Severe (D2) Drought across all of Kenedy Island in mid-March.

Nickel to quarter sized hail was reported by the public around 9:25PM CDT a little over 2 miles southwest of Hebbronville along Texas Highway 16 near the intersection of Farm to Market 3073. Additional reports of penny to quarter sized hail were reported by the public from the same storm in and around the town of Hebbronville between 9:30PM CDT and 9:50PM CDT.
A storm chaser reported hail up to one inch in diameter at 3:34PM CDT until 3:45PM CDT  April 21st approximately 7 miles west of La Gloria, TX.
Several reports of quarter to half dollar sized hail in northwestern Cameron County from 5 miles west of Harlingen to near Santa Rosa and La Feria.
Several reports from social media of ping pong ball to hen egg, or two inch, hail just south of the Lyford area to the Cameron/Willacy County line.

Up to an hour of continuous hail fell across the southern half of Hidalgo County, with the Pe��itas to La Joya to Mission area being hit exceptionally hard with several reports from social media of golf ball to baseball sized hail. There were a few reports of holes through windshields of cars in the Pe��itas area along with several dented cars. See the separate report for Penitas between 1537 and 1637 CST for details and localized dollar damage.

The ASOS station at McAllen-Miller International Airport (KMFE) recorded a wind gust of 62 mph at 4:40PM CDT the afternoon of April 21st. There was also some damage to a warehouse a few miles south of the airport with a garage door blown inward.

Powerlines and traffic lights were downed at the intersection of Highway 100 and Padre Blvd on South Padre Island. Additional images from social media show the sign for the Coral Reef Lounge that had fallen on top of a Camaro. Time approximated based on radar and time report was received.
The McAllen-Miller International Airport (KMFE) ASOS recorded a wind gust of 59 knots, or 68 mph, at 1:02PM CDT.
The ASOS at Valley International Airport (KHRL) in Harlingen recorded a wind gust of 53 knots, or 61 mph, at 1:02PM CDT.
The ASOS at Brownsville-South Padre Island International Airport (KBRO) recorded a wind gust of 51 knots, or 59 mph, at 1:47PM CDT.
The ASOS at Port Isabel-Cameron County Airport (KPIL) recorded at wind gust of 59 knots, or 68 mph, at 1:38PM CDT.

An NWS Employee reported two power poles blown over along Ruben Torres Blvd, just west of Oscar Dancy, across the street from Bella Vista Apartments. Time estimated by report of power outage by another NWS employee and radar.

Several members of the public posted images of Padre Blvd on South Padre Island covered in one to two feet of water. One picture showed the water halfway up the wheels of a car near the Grapevine Cafe. The cause of this was the squall line that moved through early in the afternoon of April 23rd.

A palm tree was blown down in front of the Port Isabel Lighthouse and fell across Highway 100, blocking most of the west bound lanes. Time was estimated by radar and the 57 mph gust at Port Isabel's NOAA National Ocean Service site (PTIT2) about 0.6 miles away.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX OUT 20 NM
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) reported a measured gust of 49 knots at 12:30PM CDT. The proximity to the coastal waters from Baffin Bay to Port Mansfield out 20 nautical miles coupled with additional wind gusts over 34 knots reported at Buoy 42020 an hour later leads credence to the fact this area experienced Marine Thunderstorm Wind gusts as well.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) reported wind gusts above 34 knots associated with a squall line starting at 12:18PM CDT and lasting until 1:00PM CDT. The highest gust was measured at 49 knots at 12:30PM CDT. Additional gusts over 34 knots were observed until 4:18PM CDT as a wake low developed behind the squall line.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: Buoy 42020 of the National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) reported wind gusts above 34 knots associated with a squall line starting at 1:20PM CDT and lasting until 2:00PM CDT. The highest gust was 51 knots recorded at 1:50PM CDT. Additional gusts of 34 knots or greater were experienced until 6:10PM CDT as a wake low set up behind the squall line.

A storm survey conducted by NWS personal found wind damage consistent with wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Several softwood trees were found with broke branches from Rio Hondo to about 1.5 miles east of Rio Hondo along General Brant Road. There were also several buildings with damage, including loss of wood or metal roof panels on some outbuildings and mobile homes. This includes most of an aluminum roofing covering two adjacent single-wide mobile homes blew off. At least two of these pieces were blown across adjacent State Highway 106.

An NWS Storm Survey conducted the evening of April 23rd found wind damage consistent with 65 to 75 mph wind gusts between Los Fresnos to Bayview along and north of Old Port Road. Some of the strongest winds were found near along Calle Hermosa where a large pine tree trunk was split. Also, a metal roof of the parish hall at St. Cecilia Church in Los Fresnos was blown off a strewn across W Ocean Blvd. Another cluster of wind damage was reported in and around Bayview with several tree limbs down along North San Roman Road. A large tree was uprooted on South San Roman n Road at the intersection of E Toronja Road. Several other tree limbs were downed along North San Roman Road up to Schafer Road.

Pictures from the Raymondville area of Willacy County showed damage from a line from south of HWY 186 and S 1st Street to a quarter mile north of the Raymondville Country Club along S 7th Street. Some of the pictures included a part of a wood roof peeled back from a porch on W Gem Street and some gate and metal roof damage to a garage along S 7th Street. There was also a video shared from the Holiday Inn Express near the intersection of US-77/I-69E and HWY 186 looking to the southwest showing a large gust front blowing through Raymondville in the areas mentioned above. A closer inspection of the video shows some debris lofted into the air and was used a guide for the estimated 70 mph wind gusts. The time is based on the video and radar.

High northeasterly winds, associated with a wake low developing behind a thunderstorm complex, contributed to enhanced northeasterly swell which led to coastal flooding across portions of Coastal Cameron County on the afternoon of April 23rd. Water levels topped out at 2.68ft above normally dry ground around 2:30PM CDT in the Port Isabel area. Other high water levels measured included 2.32ft above normally dry ground at SPI Brazos Santiago, and 2.32ft above normally high ground at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station. These highest levels occurred generally between 2PM CDT and 6:00PM CDT.  Several docks and a boat sustained damage from the Gale-force to Storm-force wind gusts and pounding waves associated with the event.  Dollar damages for boats are estimated and provided in a separate episode for Marine High Wind.

High northeasterly winds, associated with a wake low developing behind a thunderstorm complex, contributed to enhanced northeasterly swell which led to coastal flooding across portions of Coastal Willacy County on the afternoon of April 23rd. Water levels topped out at 2.38ft above mean sea level (an estimated for water levels above normally dry ground) around 2:12PM CDT in the Port Mansfield area. Pictures from the Emergency Manager in Port Mansfield shows portions of docks damaged or washed away.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the afternoon of April 23rd. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at SPI Brazos Santiago (BZST2) recorded wind gusts over 34 knots from 1:18PM CDT through 2:30PM CDT with the highest wind gust observed of 57 knots.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the afternoon of April 23rd. The Texas Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula (RLIT2) began gusting above 34 knots at 1:18PM CDT and continued until 2:00PM CDT and recorded a peak gust of 42 knots at 1:24PM CDT. Additionally, the same line of thunderstorms brought a wind gust of 48 knots to the NOAA's National Ocean Service (NOS) site at Port Isabel (PCGT2) at 1:42PM CDT.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The public shared video of one unmanned pontoon boat break loose in the Laguna Madre due to high marine winds during the wake low that developed following a line of thunderstorms in the early afternoon of April 23rd. There was also another picture of one unmanned fishing boat that broke loose and capsized near Pirates Landing near the Queen Isabella Causeway. Time estimated based on wind observations nearby. Damage estimates are estimated as well.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: The Emergency Manager from Port Mansfield shared pictures and videos showing high winds and very rough waters on the Laguna Madre near the docks. Several of the pictures show damage to the docks, including missing sections, along with debris being washed ashore by the strong northeasterly winds that developed behind the line of thunderstorms early in the afternoon of April 23rd. Time and winds are based on nearby observations.

The proximity to the coastal waters from Baffin Bay to Port Mansfield out 20 nautical miles coupled with additional wind gusts over 34 knots reported at Buoy 42020 leads credence to the fact this area experienced Marine Thunderstorm Wind gusts as well.

events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2) reported wind gusts above 34 knots associated with a line of storms starting at 12:54AM CDT and lasting until 1:18AM CDT. The highest gust was measured at 43 knots at 1:00AM CDT.

events.event_narrative: Buoy 42020 of the National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) reported wind gusts above 34 knots associated with a line of thunderstorms starting at 11:10PM CDT and lasting until 11:40PM CDT. The highest gust was 43 knots recorded at 11:20PM CDT.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the late in the evening of April 28th into the early morning hours of April 29th. The Texas Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula (RLIT2) began gusting above 34 knots at 1:30AM CDT and continued until 1:36AM CDT and recorded a peak gust of 52 knots at 1:30AM CDT. Additionally, the same line of thunderstorms brought a wind gust of 41 knots to the NOAA's National Ocean Service (NOS) site at Port Isabel (PCGT2) at 1:42AM CDT and a wind gust of 49 knots to the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station (PCGT2) TCOON site at 1:42AM CDT.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A line of thunderstorms pushed off the coast and over the Laguna Madre and Coastal Waters the evening of April 28th. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at SPI Brazos Santiago (BZST2) recorded wind gusts over 34 knots from 1:42AM CDT through 1:48AM CDT with the highest wind gust observed of 42 knots at 1:42AM CDT.

Member of the public shared a picture of a hail stone that was estimated to be about the size of a quarter in the Hebbronville area at 9:10AM CDT. The post was made at 9:14AM CDT and radar corroborated the report.
Zapata County Sheriff's Office reported a car swerving off the road in Morales-Sanchez due to hail the size of golf balls.
Employee at the Falcon Heights Motel and RV Park reported hail the size of quarters.
Roma Police Department reported hail the size of golf balls in the city of Roma.
Member of the public shared a picture of hail estimated to be about the size of a quarter.
McDonalds in Roma at 104 East Grant Street reported hail the size of quarters.
Member of the public shared pictures of half dollar to ping pong ball hail along Suntex Road in Starr County. Hail sizes are estimated based off pictures. Time estimated by radar.

Report via social media of damage to trees, billboards, and utility poles in the city of Roma that occurred between 11:10PM CDT and 11:35PM CDT. Damage confirmed by phone call to Roma Police Department.
Video on social media shows a tree down near the intersection of Suntex Road and HWY 83 in Starr County. Timing based on radar.

Member of the public shared a picture of a large tree limb, the base of which was approximated 6 to 8 inches in diameter, from a Mesquite tree blown across FM2360 near La Victoria in Starr County. Time is estimated based on radar.
The Hebbronville RAWS site recorded a wind gust of 54 knots at 9:46PM CDT.

The ASOS station at McAllen-Miller International Airport observed winds equaling or exceeding 50 knots between 12:20AM CDT and 12:40AM CDT before briefly losing power shortly thereafter. The strongest wind gust of 64 knots was recorded at 12:34AM CDT. There was significant damage in and around the airport, including a Cessna that had been flipped and a Gulfstream aircraft that had been moved.  Damage at the airport is listed in a later report from the NWS Storm Survey.
The ASOS station at the Mid Valley Airport (KTXW) recorded a wind gust of 50 knots at 12:55AM CDT.
The ASOS station at Valley International Airport in Harlingen recorded a wind gust of 53 knots at 1:14AM CDT. Additional wind gusts over 50 knots were recorded between 1:14AM CDT and 1:22AM CDT.
The ASOS at Cameron County Airport recorded wind gusts of 54 knots between 1:33AM CDT and 1:38AM CDT.
The ASOS at the Brownsville/SPI International Airport (KBRO) recorded a wind gust of 53 knots at 1:41AM CDT.
Video shared by a member of the public shows several large trees down along El Pinto Road near Rosendo Benavides Elementary School. Time estimated by radar.
Member of the publics shows several mesquite trees down along Garza Avenue north of Military road. Time estimated by radar.
Video from the public shows the metal roof of a carport peeled back near the intersection of Mile 3 Road and Tom Gill Road. Time estimated by radar.
Broadcast media shared a picture of a few food trucks and trailers flipped over near the intersection of Bryan Road and Business 83 near Mission City Hall. Time estimated by radar.
Member of the public shared pictures of damage to several large oak trees, including several large branches about 8 to 12 inches in diameter, that had snapped. Timing estimated by radar.

The canopy over the gas pumps at the Exxon Gas station at the corner of Lark and N 23rd Street was blown over and pushed partially across the road. An official NWS Storm Survey team looked at the poles to the canopy and found that several of them had rust, which led to a slightly lower wind rating. Timing based on radar.
Weslaco Fire Marshal reported damage to four to five trees in his neighborhood in Mission.
Member of the public called in to report several trees that were uprooted along with several others that lost tree limbs. Timing based on their report and radar.
An official NWS Survey found several sections of netting ripped at the Topgolf in Pharr. Timing estimated by radar.
Member of the public shared an image of the roof blown off the Car Check Auto Service and Ultimate Dental Care building at the corner of N Cage Blvd and W Clark Ave. Timing estimated by radar.

The Fire Chief for Weslaco called and reported several business signs either damaged or blown down along Business 83. The largest sign blown down was an 8 foot tall Long John Silvers sign. An NWS Survey found there to be rust at the bottom of the sign, which kept wind estimates from being higher.
Several citizens reported several large trees and traffic signs down along with stop signs pulled out of the ground along Highway 495 and Sugar Road. Timing estimated by radar.
Member of the public shared two large trees either uprooted or snapped near the base of the tree near the intersection of Del Mar and Russell Avenue. Timing based on radar.
Member of the public shared a picture of several large trees down at the corner of Ruben Torres and Hudson Blvd, or near the Walmart. Timing estimated by radar.

An official with the Brownsville-South Padre Island International Airport reported some minor damage to a few hangers on the property. A portion of the roof of a hanger on the northeastern side of the property caved in slightly, allowing water to enter the hanger. The garage door on the northwest side of the property had a garage door blown in. They also reported minor flooding to the terminal, which was likely caused by wind driven rain. The ASOS at the airport was used as a guide for timing and strength of the wind.

An NWS Storm Survey found roofing material still in plastic along with pull back of cinder block cladding near the intersection of S Bryan Road and W Frontage Road. A little ways east, a large billboard and pole fell onto vehicles. Pole was anchored into dirt, but sitting on high water from recent rains and uprooted. Lower wind speeds used based on poor anchoring and lack of surrounding damage.

An NWS Storm Survey found extensive damage along W Business 83 in McAllen. A poorly constructed roof and cinderblock wall with no bond beam caused a portion of the roof to collapse; the wall was about 35 feet high and fully exposed. A decently constructed metal roof system was partially torn off along with a garage door partially caved in at the intersection of N 22nd St and Beech Ave.  The Linares Auto Center sign was also blown over at the corner of Business 83 and S 21st Street. The sign was mounted in concrete with some rust. It also fell on at least 3 cars in the parking lot. ||The strongest wind indicator was along S 20th St just south of Business 83 where wooden poles were bent or snapped along with several large tree limbs down.

An NWS Storm Survey found more than 50 percent of shingles off on a two story building with full exposure to the west-northwest along S 29th St in McAllen. To the southeast of there, a tin roof and over a dozen trusses and rafters were taken off a lumber store and blown across the road. Additionally, the parapet roof over the Ross Department store was partially blown off. The roof was approximately 50 feet off the ground.

An NWS Storm Survey in and around the McAllen-Miller International Airport found a Cessna had been flipped onto its roof and a Gulfstream jet turned and pushed into the grass by strong thunderstorm winds. The McAllen-Miller International Airport ASOS (KMFE) officially recorded a wind gust of 74 mph before losing power. Wind estimates were closer to 74 knots, or 85 mph, due to the flipping of the Cessna. Additional damage was found downstream, or east, of the airport with large oak tree branches having been snapped and one oak tree snapped near its base at the McAllen Country Club. The roof of the Radisson Hotel McAllen Airport (0.5-1 mile east-southeast of the airport) was partially blown off and fell onto cars in the parking lot. The survey crew was told the roof was 3 years old with the building older than that. Decking was estimated to have been 55 feet above ground level and was fully exposed from the west. While winds are estimated to have been 74 knots, or 85 mph, it is possible higher winds were experienced at the roofline. Timing based on KMFE wind gusts before losing power.

An NWS Storm Survey found a McAllen Public Works truck impaled with 2x4s that were lofted into the front passengers side near the intersection of Nolana Ave W and N Bensten Road. The 2x4s was pulled from a weakly constructed wood scaffold nearby. Additional reports of semi-trucks turned over were reported by the broadcast media in the Walmart parking a few blocks east along Nolana Loop. Additional damage was found along N 23rd St with columns, which were rusted, of a gas station canopy bent near the base at the corner of N 23rd Street and Daffodil Ave. There was also minor metal damage to the roof of an abandoned car wash along N 23rd St across from McAllen High School.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue into April. Abundant rainfall of 0.50 to 4 across the county on April 7th allowed all of the county to exit Extreme (D3) Drought and drop to Moderate (D1) Drought. Severe (D2) Drought lingered for the very southeastern part of the county until the drought monitor update on April 18th.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to continue into April. Abundant rainfall of 0.25 to 3 across the county on March 28th and 29th allowed most of the county to exit Severe (D2) drought for all except the northern portion of it near Sebastian. Additional rain on April 7th allowed Severe (D2) drought to exit the rest of the county.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue into April. Around 0.25 of rain on March 28th and 29th allowed Extreme (D3) to be maintained into early April. More widespread and abundant rainfall of 1.5 to 4 across Coastal Kenedy on April 7th allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to exit the county and drop below Severe (D2) Drought as well.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue into April. Around 0.25 of rain on March 28th and 29th allowed Extreme (D3) to be maintained into early April. More widespread and abundant rainfall of 0.75 to 3 across Inland Kenedy on April 7th allowed Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought to be reduced to Moderate (D1) Drought for all but the western portion of the county. Additional rain the morning of April 11th allowed the western portion of the county to exit Severe (D2) Drought.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue into April. Around 1 of rain west of Hebbronville allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to leave the northwestern tip of the county for the April 4th update. Significant rain on the order of 0.5 to 4 of rain fell across the county on April 6th and 7th, which allowed Extreme (D3) to leave the entire county and be reduced to Moderate (D1) Drought for the April 11th update. A small sliver of the southwestern portion of the county remained in Severe (D2) Drought through the end of the month.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to continue into April. Abundant rain, on the order of 1.5 to 3, fell on April 6th and 7th and allowed Severe (D2) Drought to exit Kenedy Island on the April 11th Drought update.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought to continue for the northern and southern portions, respectively, of northern Hidalgo County into April. While some rain fell across the southern portion of northern Hidalgo County on March 28th and 29th, it wasn't enough to take that part of the county out of Severe (D2) Drought. More significant rain, on the order of 1 to 2, fell on April 7th and allowed both Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought to exit the county for the April 11th Drought Monitor Update.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to continue for southern Hidalgo County into April. Significant rain, on the order of 1.5 to 4, fell across the southern portions of the county on March 28th and 29th, which allowed all but the northern portion of southern Hidalgo County exit Severe (D2) Drought. Additional rain, on the order of 1.5 to 3.0, on April 7th allowed Severe (D2) Drought to fully exit the county by the April 11th Drought Monitor Update.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought to continue for northwestern and southeastern, respectively, Starr County into April. Significant rain, on the order of 0.2 to 3.5, fell across the county on March 28th and 29th, with most of it falling in the southeastern portion of the county. This allowed Severe (D2) Drought to exit the southeastern tip of the county. More significant rain, on the order of 0.25 to 3, fell on April 7th and allowed for Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought to both exit most of the county. A small sliver of Severe (D2) Drought held onto northwestern Starr County through the end of April.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought to continue for Inland Willacy County into April. Significant rain, on the order of 0.75 to 1.4, fell across the county on March 28th and 29th. This maintained Severe (D2) Drought through the April 4th Drought Monitor Update. Additional rains of 1.5 to 2 fell on April 7th and allowed for Severe (D2) Drought to exit the county on the April 11th Drought Monitor Update.

Lack of persistent rain coupled with dry to very dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to continue for Zapata County into April. Light rain on March 28th and 29th allowed for a continuation of Extreme (D3) Drought into early April. Significant rainfall, on the order of 0.75 to 3, fell on April 6th and 7th and allowed Extreme (D3) Drought to be reduced to Moderate (D1) Drought by the April 11th Drought Monitor Update.

The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at SPI Brazos Santiago (BZST2) recorded wind gusts over 34 knots from 1:42AM CDT through 2:24AM CDT with the highest wind gust observed of 73 knots at 1:54AM CDT.

A rapidly-developing mini-supercell formed ahead of an approaching squall line near the Lower Texas coast just before 4 AM Saturday, May 13. The supercell spawned a quick spin-up tornado that struck the town of Laguna Heights, Texas, over a two-minute period before the circulation moved over Laguna Madre Bay and rapidly dissipated. The tornado tracked to the east-northeast after the circulation was impacted by the approaching squall line, creating a boomerang effect since the original motion of the radar couplet was to the north-northwest prior to touchdown. Winds may have reached 110 mph, the top of the EF1 scale, in a few locations ��� but the very poor quality of construction suggests 105 mph is a better estimate.||The strongest portion of the tornado, rated EF1, flattened at least six poorly built mobile home structures, removed part of the second story of a local business, and removed the majority of roof decking on at least ten other residences and buildings. At least a half dozen ash and mesquite trees were snapped or uprooted and two wooden power poles were bent. Casualties were found in several of the demolished mobile homes. A man in his forties was killed when the home collapsed on him. Five others were injured in the same cluster of damaged homes, and two more were injured in a flattened mobile home near the shoreline of Laguna Madre Bay. Two of the injuries, in the home along the bayfront, required extended hospitalizations. Thirty-eight additional residents were displaced by the tornado and were housed at the local events center with American Red Cross assistance. In all, there was the one fatality and eleven injuries, of which two were critical head injuries. Surrounding the EF1 area, portions of roofs and shingles were removed from residences, large limbs were broken, and fences were knocked down.

An NWS Storm Survey was conducted on South Padre Island and found several areas of damage along South Padre Island. The survey found a couple of downed fences in the Isla Blanca area on the southern side of the island along with a couple of flipped recreational vehicles (RVs) that were exposed to the wind but only anchored by unfastened scissor jacks. The flipped RVs were initially reported by a member of the public shortly after the storms moved offshore. Winds here were measured at the Brazos Santiago (BZST2) Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network site (TCOON) to be near 84 mph. A little farther north along the island, the metal roof at Longboards was peeled back along with a canvas type material that was blown onto the second story balcony of an older apartment complex along W Palm Street. Some of the most extensive damage was witnessed at the El Castile Condo at the corner of W Polaris Dr and Laguna Blvd, which lost its roof and roof decking and exposed at least two dozen units to the elements during the storm. Lastly, the South Padre Island Convention Center's Main Exposition hall lost a significant portion of its roof along with a snapped ash tree nearby, suggesting wind speeds remaining near 85 to 90 mph. Additionally, South Padre Island Police Department reported multiple powerlines down across the island immediately after the event.||Note:  times listed are based on the survey results. All severe criteria (58 mph or greater wind gusts) occurred between 148 and 206 AM based on reports from various platforms in the area.

An NWS Storm Survey conducted in the Laguna Heights area found several damaged trees, which supports wind gusts estimated at 75 mph. A large ash tree had its trunk snapped in two places near the intersection of Van Buren Street and Harding Street. A manufactured home lost some shingles and uplifted a portion of metal roof covering along Harding Street between Van Buren Street and Jackson Avenue. Along Madison Street, several large tree branches were broken. Finally, a poorly anchored wooden real estate sign was uprooted near the intersection of N Roosevelt Street and HWY 100.

Hot, windy, and dry weather in early March coupled with long term rainfall deficits pushed Extreme Drought (D3) across all of Brooks County by March 7th.  These conditions would prevail through the end of the month; areas of rain would arrive during the last few days of the month, beginning weekly improvements in April that spread from the Lower Valley through the Brush Country and Coastal Plains.

Hot, windy, and dry weather in early March coupled with long term rainfall deficits pushed Extreme Drought (D3) across all of Jim Hogg County by March 7th.  These conditions would prevail through the end of the month; areas of rain would arrive during the last few days of the month, beginning weekly improvements in April that spread from the Lower Valley through the Brush Country and Coastal Plains.

Hot and very dry weather in early March coupled with long term rainfall deficits pushed Extreme Drought (D3) across all of Zapata County by March 7th.  These conditions would prevail through the end of the month; some rain would arrive during the last few days of the month, beginning weekly improvements in April that spread from the Lower Valley through the Brush Country and Rio Grande Plains.

Continuation of hot, dry, and breezy to windy conditions expanded Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought across Starr County on March 7, which would continue through the end of the month.  D3 conditions covered the western third of the county, from the four corners location along the Brooks, Hidalgo, and Jim Hogg County lines southwest to near Roma, with Severe (D2) conditions to the east and southeast of this line. ||The first torrential rains of the spring would arrive on March 28th across the southern third of the county, which would begin a steady improvement in April.

The Jennings Fire in Zapata County burned 3,506 acres. A Spot Request was received at 2:19 PM CDT and an article from the Zapata County News was used to estimate the start time of the fire at around 10:31AM CDT on August 7th. It was contained at 12:17 PM CDT on August 10th. The event known as the Jennings Fire was estimated to have ignited around 10:31AM CDT about 15 miles northwest of Zapata, TX on August 7th along Texas Highway 16. It burned until the afternoon of August 9th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 6:00PM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 3,506 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Forest Service on August 7th and the Zapata County News were used as a guide for ignition time and rapid spread that followed. The Zapata County News reported that it was started by a vehicle fire along Texas Highway 16 that rapidly spread to 10 acres by the time the Zapata County Fire Department was able to arrive on scene. Several brush trucks were getting stuck in the sandy soil, which hindered suppression activities at the start of the fire. The Texas Forest Service arrived on scene at 2:11PM CDT, with a SPOT requested shortly thereafter at 2:19PM CDT.

The Granjeno Fire in southern Hidalgo County burned 970 acres. A Spot Request was received at 8:10 AM CDT on August 10th. It was contained at 12:17 PM CDT on August 11th. The event known as the Granjeno Fire was estimated to have ignited around 8:00 AM CDT about 1 mile south of Granjeno, TX on August 10th. It burned until the afternoon of August 11th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 12:17 PM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 970 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the US Fish and Wildlife Service on August 10th was used as a guide for ignition time. The worst of the spread was experienced the afternoon of August 10th when the sea breeze came through southern Hidalgo County and the fire was clearly visible on the GOES-16 Natural Fire RGB channel.

This wildfire consumed a total of 1,456 acres between US HWY-281 on the eastern flank and County Road 304 on the northern flank. events.event_narrative: As Tropical Storm Harold passed over the Lower Texas coastal waters on August 22nd, this portion of the Laguna Madre saw tropical storm-force winds between 10:24AM CDT and 10:36AM CDT, the time-frame captured by the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (RSJT2).

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: As Tropical Storm Harold passed over the Lower Texas Coastal waters on August 22nd, Buoy 42020 reported sustained winds and frequent gusts to tropical storm-force for a period of nearly 3 hours between 6:50AM CDT and 9:50AM CDT. The max reported gust was recorded at 51 knots at 8:00AM CDT and 8:20AM CDT.

events.event_narrative: As Tropical Storm Harold passed over the Lower Texas Coastal waters on August 22nd, this portion of the Gulf waters saw tropical storm-force winds between 8:00AM CDT and 10:30AM CDT. While there are no observations in this portion of waters, both Buoy 42020 and TCOON RSJT2 reported sustained wind and frequent gusts to tropical storm-force, and these station surround this coastal zone.

The event known as the Gunsmoke Wildfire in northwestern Starr County started on the afternoon of September 11th, when it was first discovered, and burned until the evening of September 12th, when it was announced to be contained. It burned a total of 447 acres.

The Valley International Airport ASOS in Harlingen recorded two wind gusts in excess of 70 mph the afternoon of September 16th in association with a downburst. The first gust over 70 mph occurred at 4:08PM CDT with a wind direction from the northwest. The second gust of 74 mph happened 11 minutes later from the east-southeast, indicating the downburst moved southeast over the ASOS. There were a few reports of a few downed tree limbs and a fence that was partially blown down.

A member of the public shared video of a landspout just east of La Villa. This landspout formed along the leading edge of an outflow boundary that raced through the Lower Rio Grande Valley the afternoon of September 16th. According to the member of the public who shared video of the event, it only last a minute or so and didn't appear to cause any damage as it was near the levee just east of La Villa.

A complex of showers and storms moved through Jim Hogg County the evening of September 15th into the very early morning hours of September 16th. According to utility companies, over half of their customers lost power during the event. Unfortunately, this led to the AWOS in Hebbronville to stop reporting shortly before the worst of the storm arrived. Before it went offline, the AWOS station recorded a gust of 38 mph. The combination of the number of power outages coupled with radar data was used a guide for this event.

Severe (D2) Drought Continued across the southern half of Cameron County, south of a line from Santa Rosa through Harlingen to Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge, through the middle of September as the typically welcome rainfall failed to arrive in a significant way, while record heat continued from August into September.

Severe (D2) Drought Continued across the southern half of Coastal Cameron County, south of a line from Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge, through the middle of September as the typically welcome rainfall failed to arrive in a significant way, while record heat continued from August into September.

Severe (D2) Drought Continued across the Cameron County barrier island to include all of the City of South Padre Island through Boca Chica Beach, through the middle of September as the typically welcome rainfall failed to arrive in a significant way.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted across the western half of Northern Hidalgo County through September 25th, mainly along and west of Interstate 69C, as the typically wet conditions in September failed to materialize, while temperatures remained at or near record levels for the month and the astronomical summer (June 21 to September 22) overall. The Severe Drought area would expand eastward to cover all of northern Hidalgo County by September 26th. Impacts to livestock continued to be felt, with dollar damages not yet known as of late November.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted across southwest Brooks County through September 25th, before expanding east to cover all but the northern fifth of the county from the 26th through month's end.  Lack of seasonal rainfall for the wettest month of the calendar year, and continued record to near-record heat were the primary reasons for the deteriorating conditions.  No financial data were available for livestock impacts, though there were known issues due to paltry water supplies.

Extreme (D3) Drought dominated September across most of Zapata County, as rainfall was limited to patches of the county (mainly the northern tier) after mid month.  At the start of the month, a sliver of Severe (D2) Drought existed near the Starr County and Webb County lines (south and north); these were eliminated by continued searing heat and lack of rainfall by September 5th, and the entire county was at Extreme levels until the aforementioned rainfall across the extreme northern tier mid-month helped knock down the drought level one category, to Severe (D2) once again from San Ygnacio northeast to the Jim Hogg line on September 19, about 5 miles south of the Webb County line. Livestock were impacted by the conditions, though there were not specific loss values available at the time of this writing (late November).

Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions dominated Jim Hogg County through September, as searing, record to near record heat continued and rainfall was limited to local heavy rain in thunderstorms, mainly in northern portions of the county, during the middle of the month (September 15), when more than 4 inches fell near Hebbronville.  Farther south, lack of sufficient rainfall kept conditions unchanged for the month.  ||For the county overall, Extreme conditions held across the western third to half of the county, with Severe conditions elsewhere until the September 19th monitor, when the aforementioned rains allowed minor improvement from Severe to Moderate (D1) in the northeast fifth of the county, including Hebbronville.||Livestock were impacted by the combination of searing heat and lack of significant rainfall. Dollar damage impacts were not known as of this writing (late November).

Severe (D2) Drought continued from late August into early September across all but the far northwest corner of the county (immediate border with Zapata and Jim Hogg) where Extreme (D3) Drought was in place.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted from late August into early September across southern Hidalgo County (generally defined as locations south of FM 490), and mainly west of the Hargill/Monte Alto area (which were at Moderate, or D1, Drought).

Extreme (D3) Drought replaced Severe (D2) Drought for all but the northeast fifth of Starr County beginning on September 5th, continuing through the end of the month.  Record heat and low rainfall in Rio Grande City were contributors.  There were impacts on livestock in the county, but dollar damages/losses were unknown as of this writing in late November.

Extreme (D3) Drought developed in southwest portions of Hidalgo County, from the McAllen metro area west through the county line (Sullivan City) to about 10-12 miles north along the Starr County line.  Severe (D2) Drought continued elsewhere in southern Hidalgo County through the 19th.  Lack of seasonal rainfall combined with record, searing heat, allowed Extreme conditions to expand eastward along and south of Interstate Highway 2 from McAllen to Mercedes on the 19th; the Extreme Drought area would creep northward on the 26th to include the Edinburg/Elsa/Edcouch area.||The lack of necessary rainfall and record heat heavily impacted dryland crops and livestock across southern Hidalgo County.  Specific dollar damages/losses were not known as of this writing (late November).

Extreme (D3) Drought crept into southern Cameron County, from La Feria through Los Fresnos south to Brownsville and the Rio Grande, beginning on September 19th, while the stripe of Severe (D2) Drought continued in south-central Cameron from Santa Rosa to just north of Bayview - a result of around 5% of the monthly average rainfall and record to near-record heat. On the 26th, the continuation of the dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) conditions to nudge northward to the Santa Rosa-Harlingen-Laguna Atascosa line, with Severe (D2) conditions nosing northward to all but the northern one-eighth of the county.||Dryland and limited-irrigation crops, and livestock, sustained damages/losses that were unknown as of this writing (late November).

Extreme (D3) Drought crept into southern coastal Cameron County, to include Port Isabel and the Brownsville Ship Channel, beginning on September 19th, while the stripe of Severe (D2) Drought continued in south-central Cameron from Bayview/Laguna Vista  to Laguna Atascosa- a result of around 5% of the monthly average rainfall and record to near-record heat. On the 26th, the continuation of the dry conditions allowed Extreme (D3) conditions to include all of Laguna Atascosa, with Severe (D2) Conditions reaching Arroyo City.||Dryland and limited-irrigation crops, and livestock, sustained damages/losses that were unknown as of this writing (late November).

Extreme (D3) Drought crept into the Boca Chica area on September 19th, then expanded north to include all of the City of South Padre Island with Severe (D2) conditions expanding northward to include the public access portion of South Padre Island south of the Willacy/Cameron County line on the 26th.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in Willacy County on the 26th of September, as positive effects from 1 to nearly 3 inches of rainfall associated with Tropical Storm Harold dried up in the record heat and low monthly rainfall (10-25 percent of average). Conditions covered all of western Willacy, and the northern third, including Raymondville, La Sara, and San Perlita.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in northern Coastal Willacy County on the 26th of September, as positive effects from 1 to nearly 3 inches of rainfall associated with Tropical Storm Harold dried up in the record heat and low monthly rainfall (10-25 percent of average).

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in northern portion of the Willacy County barrier island on the 26th of September, as positive effects from 1 to nearly 3 inches of rainfall associated with Tropical Storm Harold dried up in the record heat and low monthly rainfall (10-25 percent of average).

Beneficial rainfall from Tropical Storm Harold, which tracked through Kenedy County on August 22 and dropped between 1 and 3 inches of rainfall, was all dried up by the end of September. By the 26th, Severe (D2) Drought had covered all but the northwest sliver of the county, courtesy of 10-25% of rainfall in the wettest month of the year, and record to near-record searing heat.
