By the 26th, Severe (D2) Drought had covered all of the barrier island, courtesy of 10-25% of rainfall in the wettest month of the year, and record to near-record searing heat.

Extreme (D3) Drought would cover Cameron County from Santa Rosa through Harlingen and Lozano south to the Rio Grande through October 9, before the area of Extreme Drought was trimmed back to a sliver over the southwest portion of the county (Santa Rosa, La Feria, to the Rio Grande) with Severe Drought maintaining elsewhere through October 16. The improvement occurred in areas where 3 to 4 inches of rain fell during the afternoon on October 5th.

Extreme (D3) Drought would cover Cameron Island from roughly the Public Access Point 3 through Boca Chica Beach through October 9, before the area of Extreme Drought was trimmed back Severe Drought on the 10th, due to afternoon rains on October 5th.

Extreme (D3) Drought would cover Coastal Cameron County from Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge south to the Rio Grande through October 9, before the area of Extreme Drought was trimmed back Severe Drought on the 10th, due to sufficient afternoon rains on October 5th.

Severe (D2) Drought continued across the northern half of Willacy County until October 9th, before the area would be sharply trimmed back to just a sliver of the far western portion of the county near the Hidalgo and Kenedy County line on the 10th.  The trim-back was courtesy of torrential thunderstorm rains that dropped an estimated 3 to 5 inches of rainfall over farmland east of Raymondville and Lyford during the afternoon of October 5th.

Severe (D2) Drought continued across the northern third of coastal Willacy County, including Port Mansfield, through October 9th.  Drought improved to Moderate (D1) levels on the 10th courtesy of thunderstorm rains that dropped an estimated 1 to 3 inches of rainfall across these areas during the afternoon of October 5th.

Severe (D2) Drought continued across the northern third of the Willacy barrier island, including the Port Mansfield fishing channel and jetties.  Drought improved to Moderate (D1) levels on the 10th courtesy of thunderstorm rains that dropped an estimated 1 to 2 inches of rainfall across these areas during the afternoon of October 5th.

Extreme (D3) Drought prevailed in southern Hidalgo, generally from the Rio Grande to 15-17 miles north of the river, bounded by Citrus City through south Edinburg to 5-8 miles north of Donna/Weslaco/Mercedes, with Severe (D2) Drought elsewhere, through October 16th.  A broad area of 1 to 1.5 inches of rain on October 10 was sufficient to reduce Extreme Drought to Severe (D2) Drought in these areas.

Severe Drought (D2) prevailed across all of Northern Hidalgo County through October 9th. Locally heavy rainfall across the eastern half of this area following locally heavy rainfall of 1 to 1.5 inches would improve conditions in these areas beginning on October 10th.

Extreme Drought (D3) prevailed across all but the northeast quarter of Starr County through October 10th, with Severe (D2) Drought elsewhere. ||Heavy rains during the afternoon and evening of October 5th across the western two-thirds of the county would help improve from Extreme to Severe across all but the southeast quarter of Starr County on October 10th, before additional improvements arrived by the 17th - courtesy of additional rainfall on the 10th.  Severe Drought would be trimmed across western Starr and Extreme Drought eliminated in southeast Starr on that date.

Extreme Drought (D3) prevailed across all but the northern fifth of Zapata County, from San Ygnacio north to the Webb County line and northeast to Jim Hogg County just five miles south of the Webb County line, through October 9th.  Broad rainfall of 1 to more than 2 inches during the evening of October 5th would improve conditions to Severe (D2) across nearly all of the county on October 10th.

Extreme Drought (D3) prevailed across most of the western half of Jim Hogg County until October 9th, with Severe (D2) drought across east-central Jim Hogg south of Hebbronville and the SR 285/359 area.  An estimated 0.5 to 1.5 inches of rain fell during the late afternoon and evening of October 5th, which would remove Extreme conditions across western portions of the county.

Severe (D2) Drought would begin October across all but the northern fifth of Jim Hogg County, before an area of 0.75 to 1.5 inches of rain fell on the 10th across the portions of the county.  By October 17th, Severe Drought was limited to the south and southeast portion of the county, with Moderate (D1) conditions expanding across the northwest portion and a very small sliver along the Hidalgo and Kenedy County line.

Severe (D2) Drought covered all but a very small sliver of northwest Kenedy County from through October 9th, with the area shrinking to cover most of inland Kenedy County except the southeast corner (and the remaining northwest corner, each at Moderate, D1, levels) due to a thin area of 1 to more than 2 inches of rain during the afternoon of October 5th in southeast inland Kenedy County. Additional improvements would be realized by October 17th, courtesy of 0.75 to 1.5 inches in southern Kenedy County on October 10th.

Severe (D2) Drought covered all of coastal Kenedy County from through October 9th, with the area shrinking to cover the northern half of coastal Kenedy County with the southern half improving to Moderate (D1, levels) due to 0.25 to 0.75 inches during the afternoon of October 5th.

Severe (D2) Drought covered all of the Kenedy County barrier island through October 9th, with the area shrinking to cover the northern half of the Kenedy County barrier island with the southern half improving to Moderate (D1, levels) due to 0.25 to 0.75 inches during the afternoon of October 5th.

Rainfall estimated and measured at 0.5 to 1 inch along the Cameron County barrier island knocked down drought levels from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) along and south of Public Access #3 southward to Boca Chica Beach.

Rainfall estimated and measured at 0.5 to 1.5 inches along and just west of Laguna Madre on the afternoon of October 5th drought levels from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) along and south of Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge south to the Rio Grande, including Bayview and Port Isabel.

Rainfall estimated and measured at 1 to 5 inches across nearly all of inland Willacy County during the afternoon or October 5th sharply reduced drought levels from Severe (D2) to Abnormally Dry/Moderate Drought (D0 and D1).  A small sliver of Severe (D2) remained within a mile or two of the Hidalgo/Kenedy line for the October 10th, 2023 Drought Monitor.  Another event on the 10th and early 11th, combined with soil moisture absorption from the 5th, would end Severe Drought by the 17th. ||With the drought ended, dollar damage estimates to citrus were provided by Texas Citrus Mutual for the entire growing season.  Those values are posted in this entry.  Based on an estimate of 10 percent of citrus field in the county, and based on an estimate of a 50 percent loss of all citrus crop across the Rio Grande Valley in 2023, a value of $12.35 million in loss was applied.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across all of northern Hidalgo County from the 10th through the 16th (with a very slight improvement along the Willacy County line after 0.5 to 0.75 of rain fell during the afternoon of October 5th there. An area of less intense but quite welcome rain fell late on October 10th through early October 11th, dropping 1 to 1.5 across the area and nudging the Severe (D2) area farther west to only cover the western half of the area, mainly west of IH-69C.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions replaced Extreme (D3) Drought conditions across all but far northern Zapata County, following widespread 1 to 1.5 inches, locally 2 inches, of rainfall associated with showers and thunderstorms along the season's first cold front during the late afternoon and evening of October 5th. These conditions would prevail until the October 17th update, as another 0.5 to more than 2 inches fell across the county late on October 10th and early on October 11th.  Conditions would improve to Moderate (D1) with Abnormally Dry (D0) along the Webb County line near the Rio Grande.

Late afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms associated with the season's first notable cold front dropped measured and estimated 1 to 2 of rain across western Jim Hogg County on October 5th, improving Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought in these areas.  Severe Drought would continue elsewhere, except in the northeast corner of the county (mainly along/north of SR 285/359 including Hebbronville, which held at Moderate (D1), as rainfall was below 0.5 with the same event.

A sliver of western Cameron, including Santa Rosa and La Feria, remained in Severe (D2) Drought for the second half of October, as additional helpful rains did not fall after the events of October 5th and October 10th/11th.  Elsewhere, Moderate (D1) conditions prevailed, with a sliver of Abnormally Dry (D0) near the Willacy line.

The combination of pockets of heavy rainfall (0.5 to 1 inch) during the afternoon of October 5th, along with a more widespread area of 0.75 to 1 from late October 10 through early October 11, allowed drought improvement from D3 (Extreme) to D2 (Severe) across much of southern Hidalgo County, mainly along/south of the IH-2 corridor, beginning on October 17th and continuing through month's end.

Measured and estimated rainfall of 0.75 to nearly 2 across Starr County late on October 10th through early October 11th was sufficient to knock drought down further across the county, with Severe (D2) from the Garceno area (between Rio Grande City and Roma) north through El Sauz and points east along FM 649, with Moderate (D1) to the west.  These conditions would prevail through the month's end.

The combination of soil moisture increases from late afternoon/early evening rainfall on October 5th, with another round of 0.75 to locally 1 inch or more from late October 10th through early October 11th continued drought improvement.  By the 17th, just a sliver of Severe (D2) remained across the far southeast corner of the county, which continued through month's end.

The combination of soil moisture increases from afternoon rainfall on October 5th, with another round of 0.75 to more than 1 inch or more from late October 10th through early October 11th across southern Kenedy County continued drought improvement.  By the 17th, Severe (D2) was limited to a stripe from west-central Kenedy County to northeast sections of the inland portion of the county. These conditions continued through month's end.

General rains of 0.5 to 0.75 inches across coastal Kenedy County from late October 10th through early October 11th was enough to knock down drought conditions from Severe (D2) to Moderate (D1) or Abnormally Dry (D0) across the southern three-quarters of the area, with Severe conditions holding across the northeast corner of the area west of Laguna Madre through month's end.

General rains of 0.5 to 0.75 inches across the Kenedy County barrier island from late October 10th through early October 11th was enough to knock down drought conditions from Severe (D2) to Moderate (D1) or Abnormally Dry (D0) across the southern three-quarters of the area, with Severe conditions holding across the northern corner (quarter) of the barrier island through month's end.

The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) at Brownsville and Harlingen generally reported 2 to 2.5 hours of heat index of 111 or higher, peaking just below 113 degrees just before 3 PM Central Daylight Time.  By proxy, and based on maximum temperatures of 99 degrees at Raymondville (maximum at Harlingen and Brownsville were 97 degrees each), it can be assumed that similar apparent temperatures occurred in Willacy County around the same time.

Torrential rains of nearly 4 inches in an hour (2 to 3 PM CST; 3 to 4 PM CDT) fell across west Brownsville as a strong cluster of thunderstorms eased through the city. More than 3 feet of water piled up near the B&M Bridge along Mexico Blvd. near the bridge (and in the C and D street vicinity.  Several cars were submerged up to the hoods. A CoCoRaHS observer in the Los Ebanos community, 2 miles northeast of the worst flooding, recorded 3.7 inches of rain.

Torrential rainfall in a little more than an hour dropped between 2 and 2.7 inches of rain from east of downtown Brownsville into residential and commercial areas to the north, including known flood-prone areas along SR-4 (Boca Chica Blvd.), IH-69E frontage between Boca Chica and Morrison Blvd., and eastward to Paredes Line road.  Street flooding was most common in these areas, with water levels below 2 feet.

Despite some locally heavy rains early during the week of April 21st and more widespread lighter rains on the 27th and 28th, Jim Hogg County continued in extreme (D3) Drought, but had fallen below Exceptional (D4) which was the case until the end of April.

Despite some widespread light to moderate rains on the 27th and 28th, all but the southeast corner of Starr County continued in extreme (D3) Drought; northern portions of the county had fallen below Exceptional (D4) which was the case until the end of April.

Some light to moderate rains in Starr County on April 27th and 28th helped bring the southeast corner down to severe (D2) Drought, falling below the extreme (D3) level which was the case until the end of April.

Some light to moderate rains in Brooks County on April 27th and 28th, as well as some leftover rains from thunderstorms around the 21st of April, helped bring the western half down to extreme (D3) Drought, falling below the exceptional (D4) level which had been the case until the end of April.

Some locally heavy rainfall in Brooks County on April 27th and 28th, as well as some leftover rains from thunderstorms around the 21st of April, helped bring the eastern half down to severe (D2) Drought, falling below the extreme (D3) level which had been the case until the end of April.

Some locally heavy rainfall in Hidalgo County on April 27th and 28th,  helped bring the Drought level down from extreme(D3) to severe(D2),  which had been the case until the end of April.  Conditions would improve further by May 20th across the southeast third of the county, after additional rainfall from May 11th to 17th was incorporated into the Drought Monitor.

Despite locally torrential rains in southern portions of the county on April 28th, most of Kenedy County remained in Severe(D2) Drought into the middle of May, with only the northeast corner falling back into moderate(D1) Drought status.||Conditions would improve further by the 20th, a result of more rainfall which fell generally between the 11th and 17th.

Torrential rains of between 3 and 5 inches on April 27th and 28th put a temporary dent into the drought across much of Cameron County by the end of April, as the once Extreme Drought(D3) levels of mid April across the far western portion were replaced by severe(D2) across the entire western third of the county to begin May.  Locations near the coast dropped back to moderate(D1) Drought.||Conditions would improve further by May 20th, after rainfall that fell between the 11th and 17th was incorporated into the Drought Monitor.

Locally heavy rainfall of between 1 and 2 inches on April 27th and 28th put a slight dent into the drought across much of Willacy County by the end of April, as the once Extreme Drought(D3) levels of mid April across the far west were replaced by severe(D2) across the western third of the county to begin May.  Locations near the coast dropped back to moderate(D1) Drought.||Conditions would improve further by the 20th, a result of more rainfall which fell generally between the 11th and 17th.

The continuation of additive effects from locally heavy rainfall between May 14th and 17th continued to alleviate drought somewhat, if temporarily, in Zapata County.  All but the northeast third of the county reverted back to moderate (D1) drought conditions; these conditions would continue until the end of the month.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across southern Brooks County to start November.  Rainfall of 3 to 6 inches between November 10 and 13 in this area would improve conditions to Moderate (D1) on the 14th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across northern Hidalgo County, mainly west of Interstate 69C.  Rainfall of 3 to 5 inches between November 10th and 13th in this area would improve conditions to Moderate (D1) on the 14th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across the western two-thirds of southern Hidalgo County, from near Progresso northwest through Donna to San Carlos (4 miles east of Edinburg).  Rainfall of 3 to 5 inches between November 10th and 13th in this area would improve conditions to Moderate (D1) on the 14th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across the eastern two-thirds of Starr County, from Roma to just east of Agua Nueva.  Rainfall of 4 to more than 7 inches inches between November 10 and 13 in this area would improve conditions to Moderate (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0) on the 14th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across the southeastern corner of Jim Hogg County, from east of Agua Nueva to the Brooks County line.  Rainfall of 4 to more than 6 inches inches between November 10th and 13th in this area would improve conditions to Abnormally Dry (D0) on the 14th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across a portion of western and north-central Kenedy County encompassing an area from Armstrong to the county line north of Sarita but not the northwestern sliver of the County.  Rainfall of 3 to more than 7 inches between the 10th and 13th would improve conditions to Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) on the 14th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across the northern portions of coastal Kenedy County. Residual moisture from prior late October rains would improve conditions to Moderate (D1) Drought on the 7th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted into early November across the northern portions of the Kenedy County barrier island. Residual moisture from prior late October rains would improve conditions to Moderate (D1) Drought on the 7th.

A peak gust of 51 knots (59 mph) was reported at the Harlingen/Valley International Airport.

Large restaurant sign was uprooted and fell onto a vehicle at Camelot Rd. at the             intersection of 77 Sunshine Strip (US 77 Business). The Brownsville/South Padre Island ASOS recorded a peak wind of 57 mph at 214 PM on November 30th.

Traffic light was blown down at Indiana and Boca Chica in Brownsville. Wind gusts from the Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) at the Brownsville/South Padre International Airport, just one mile southwest of the damage, at the approximate time of the downed light, was 71 mph.

Hurricane force wind gust of 74 mph was reported at Brownsville/SPI International Airport. At around the same time, a container ship's mooring lines snapped near the Port of Brownsville's turning  basin (approximately 3.4 miles northeast of the airport), sending the ship drifting into nearby towing vessels and causing an estimated $500 thousand in property damage.  There was a sign blown down along Boca Chica and International and a tree onto a fence at an unknown location between 12:30pm and 1pm CST. During the windiest period, over 1,000 customers in Cameron were without power.

A grass/brush fire of unknown causes began during the mid-afternoon February 4th along Old Highway 83 (south of US 83) west of FM 649 on the east side of Escobares, and spread rapidly southeast along Old 83 into Garceno, eventually covering 80 acres before more than 60 firefighters from multiple local, state, and federal agencies contained and controlled the blaze in the early evening. The wildfire destroyed one single-family home, a Utility Terrain Vehicle, and a trailer.  ||The wildfire occurred on a Red Flag day, with a combination of winds from the northwest gusting over 40 mph, relative humidity falling to or just below 15 percent, freeze-cured grasses and brush, and warm temperatures (around 80 degrees) .  It took nearly six hours to control, then contain, the wildfire - but embers continued to burn in dry conditions into February 5th.

The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) platform at the Brooks County Airport east of Falfurrias recorded 11 hours of freezing temperatures (32 degrees or lower) from the pre-dawn hours of January 15th, 2024, through mid afternoon.  A Hard Freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees for 2 or more hours, occurred from 655 AM through 1115 AM.  Minimum temperatures fell to 26 degrees, and light precipitation joined the cold air for a little while just after daybreak.

A combination of mesonet stations between the Yturria Ranch (southern Kenedy) and Sarita (northern Kenedy) reported up to 31 hours of temperatures at or below 32 degrees from the pre-dawn hours of January 15th through the late morning of January 16th, 2024.  Hard freezes (temperatures below 28 degrees for 2 or more hours) occurred each morning.  On the 15th, the Hard Freeze lasted for 4.5 to 5.5 hours, beginning between 620 and 728 AM and continuing through around noon; on the 16th, the Hard Freeze lasted for 9 to more than 10 hours, beginning between 1215 AM and 120 AM and continuing through 10 to 1030 AM.  ||Impacts to livestock in inland Kenedy County was unknown as of this writing.

Observations on Laguna Madre, a close proxy to both coastal Kenedy County and the Kenedy Island, fell to or below freezing between 524 and 7 AM on the 15th, with freezing temperatures persisting until late afternoon (mid-Kenedy coast) and just after sunset (along the Kenedy/Kleberg County line).  Time shown in this listing includes the Baffin Bay later end time. A Hard Freeze (temperatures below 28 degrees for 2 or more hours) was observed at Baffin Bay between 8 AM and 118 PM. Minimum temperatures fell to between 25.7 and 28 degrees across the area.

Minor winter crop damage was likely across the county, but dollar values were not known as of this writing.

The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON)/C-MAN platform at Brazos Santiago, along the Isla Blanca jetty just inshore from the beachfront, recorded a prolonged period of much higher than predicted tides, with departures generally 2 feet or more above predicted through the period.  Astronomical tides were generally low, and this likely reduced the potential for property damage beyond severe and extensive beach erosion.  The time period selected combined the above predicted tides with long-period swells and high waves, each which increased both run-up and wave set-up to cause erosion, which peaked at high tide but also occurred between high and low tide cycles.||Damage from calving of the dunes, both in the city of South Padre and along the narrower beaches northward to Port Mansfield was unknown but likely in the several millions of dollars for full renourishment.||Peak surge values - the difference between observed and predicted tides - were as follows:|Brazos Santiago:  3.19 feet at 818 PM CDT on June 19th and 3.14 feet at 336 PM CDT on June 20th. |Coast Guard Station South Padre:  3.17 feet at 912 PM on June 19th and 3.08 feet at 342 PM on June 20th. ||Peak total water levels above normally dry ground, which during periods of lower astronomical (seasonal) tides can have a negative value (meaning the water is farther out and the beaches wider) were as follows:||Brazos Santiago:  2.5 feet at 5 AM June 20th. |Coast Guard Station South Padre Island:  2.73 feet at 554 AM June 20th.  ||The peak total water level at Port Isabel (west side of Laguna Madre) reached 2.87 feet at 606 AM June 20th, which was the fourth highest on record, behind only Hurricane Allen (1980), Hurricane Beulah (1967), and Hurricane Carla (1961).

Severe (D2) Drought conditions began the month of July, and would continue through the 24th, when Hurricane Dolly put a final nail into the severe conditions, which gradually were trimmed back prior to Dolly, courtesy of gradually increasing coverage of showers and thunderstorms, especially during the first eight days of the month.

Extreme (D3) Drought began July in Jim Hogg County, but increasing coverage of showers and thunderstorms during the first week of the month would knock levels down one category, to Severe (D2) by the eighth.

Extreme (D3) Drought began July in Brooks County, but increasing coverage of showers and thunderstorms during the first week of the month would knock levels down one category, to Severe (D2) by the 8th.

Extreme (D3) Drought began July in Kenedy County, but increasing coverage of showers and thunderstorms during the first week of the month would knock levels down one to two categories, to Severe (D2) across the northern half of the county by the 8th, and only moderate across the southern half by the 8th.

Numerous roads in typically poor drainage locations sustained minor flooding in Harlingen when persistent bands of torrential rains moved through the western half of Cameron County during the morning and early afternoon of July 7th.  In general, rainfall between 2 and 3 inches fell during this time period, near the end of a weeklong welcome drenching that  that dropped between 6 and 9 inches, perhaps higher in a few spots, across the more populated areas of the Lower Rio Grande Valley.| |Extensive street flooding was reported in Harlingen and San Benito.  This included the Fair Park area of Harlingen, First Street in Harlingen, particularly near the Highway 83 and 77 interchange near downtown. Numerous streets also experienced minor flooding in San Benito, and heavy rains affected construction sites in La Feria near the Hidalgo County line. ||Brownsville had more nuisance problems with widespread ponding in poor drainage locations, such as those on Boca Chica Boulevard between McDavitt and Security Drive.  In all cases, structures were not threatened, and there were no casualties.  ||The rains ended before mid afternoon on the 7th, and minor street flooding subsided.

Jim Hogg County Sheriff's Department reported the southbound lane of Route 16 experienced nuisance flooding, with one half to one inch of water covering the road for a distance of approximately 3 miles, approximately 13 miles southwest of Hebbronville.

Radar estimates of 4 to 6 inches of rainfall fell over a 3 hour period. Flooding was reported with high water as high as 2 feet flowing over Highway 16 in the city of Zapata. Water was reported in a home in the Medina Addition.
City of Combes shared a picture of a landspout northeast of Woods Road just before 3 PM CDT. Radar estimated time and location.

The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) sensor at Valley International Airport in Harlingen (KHRL) reported 5 hours of heat index of 111F or higher, peaking at 114 at 1 to 2 PM CST.  The ASOS sensor at Brownsville/South Padre International Airport (KBRO) had an estimated 1.75 hours of similar conditions, peaking at 115F at around the same time.

The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) sensor near Bayview (KPIL) recorded a peak heat index of 115F at around 1 PM CST, with around 2 hours at or above 111F between roughly 1230 and 230 PM CST.

The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) sensor at McAllen (KMFE) recorded a little more than 2 hours total of heat index values of 111F or higher between 2 PM and  530 PM CST, though the period was broken by a short break right around 4 PM (values just below 111F).  Peak heat index reached just below 112F during this window.

Heat index values reached 111 or higher at McAllen/Miller International Airport (KMFE) for several hours. Values occurred between 1130 AM and 130 PM CST, and again from 330 to 5 PM CST.  Peak values reached 114 at 1153 AM CST.

A resident of central Harlingen reported a direct lightning strike to the home.  Approximate time is based on the report, which noted that the strike came just before torrential rains that were also reported at nearby Valley International Airport (2.4 miles to the east-northeast). Damage included roof and decking blown out and underlaying PVC pipe damage.  No fire was reported.

Torrential rain, with measured an estimated totals of 3.5 to more than 5 inches mainly from downtown across the north and west portions of Brownsville, created numerous instances of flooding and flash flooding. Standing water was reported on the intersection of Pablo Kisel Blvd and Morrison Road. Roadway was nearly impassable. Additional reports from Cameron Co. and Brownsville Emergency Management included:  water covering roads at IH-69E Frontage and Alton Gloor, Old Alice/Barnard/Price.  A water rescue was reported downtown on 11th and Elizabeth.  Water levels in harder hit areas were between 2 and 3 feet (standing).||Damage estimates were unknown as of this writing.
There was an undetermined amount of water flowing over State Highway 4 near Boca Chica Village and the SpaceX/Starbase area during the early morning hours.
Cameron County Parks Department reported photographic evidence of 1 to 2 feet of standing water along Park Road 100 north of the City of South Padre Island during the morning of September 10th.
Roadways were flooded on Ruben M Torres Blvd near N Central Avenue with an estimated 1 to 2 feet of water depth in spots.

San Benito PD reported various levels of flooding across town.  The following reports were received:  One foot of flowing water down Brooks Avenue at around 445 PM CDT; additional flooding on Franklin Road, Woodford Street, and Bowie Street.  Water reportedly entered homes on Bowie Street with one rescue required; water was reportedly at least knee deep in some locations (2 to 3 feet).

Harlingen PD received numerous reports of flooded roads during the mid to late afternoon.  These included:  Fair Park Blvd, the intersection of 7th and M St, Spur 5             and Frontage, Eye St, intersection of J St and Fair Park Blvd, Bowie Ave and 25th St,             Frontage Rd. at Primera Rd exit to Wilson Rd, Le Moyne Garden, and Emerald Lake Dr. Texas Department of Transportation was notified and road closures began during the event, with water reported halfway up cars in some spots.

Torrential rainfall, as much as 5.48 inches of rain having fallen in 90 minutes in Rancho Viejo, left pockets of flash flooding during the late afternoon between San Pedro and Olmito, including Rancho Viejo. Reports of high water into structures and vehicle rescues were reported during and after the peak of the downpour. Vehicle rescues were reported in Olmito and near Rancho Viejo; water was reportedly entering homes on Melva Court in San Pedro, and Burr Oak Loop and Agave avenue just south of IH-169 in east Olmito. ||Damage values estimated based on the reports received. || Damage information was unknown at the time of this writing.
Heat index values reached 111 or higher at McAllen/Miller International Airport (KMFE) for a couple hours. Values occurred between 1:53 PM and 3:53 PM CDT.

There were several reports of flash flooding in the city of Brownsville, mainly bracketed by Price Road and Expressway IH-69E on the west, Price Road and State Highway 48 on the east, extending to the Southmost neighborhood on the south side of the city. Reports included: Multiple intersections along Boca Chica Blvd impassable due to flooded roadways between McDavitt Blvd and  Kings Hwy and Boca Chica was nearly impassable, as well as the intersection known as Four Corners at State Highway 4; flooding extending along State Highway 4 to Southmost Blvd., and flooding along and near the frontage road at Price Road and IH-69E, extending to Barnard Road, and to nearby apartment complexes and shopping centers in this area.||While all locations inside the ascribed polygon may not have reached flash flood levels - 3 feet or higher of ponded water - the reports of impassible roads and photographic evidence suggesting pockets of this level of water depth made the case for a flash flood event in these areas.||Damage to any property was unknown as of this writing.

Emergency Managers provided several photos of flood waters on Padre Blvd extending as far north as the intersection of Padre Blvd and Dolphin Street.  Poor drainage in the area likely contributed to water depth between 2 and 3 feet along the highway.  Damage was unknown as of this writing.

A pocket of torrential rainfall from a nearly stationary isolated thunderstorm, with measured and estimated rainfall between 3 and 4 inches in a very small area around downtown Edinburg, left 3 feet of water in roads around the Courthouse building, some of which entered structures of estimated depths of 1 to 1.5 feet.  Damage was unknown at the time of this writing.

Emergency Management in Cameron County reported flooding in neighborhoods between Los Fresnos and Laureles due to runoff. There were reports of water depth of 3 feet in some areas. Two-day rainfall in the area ranged from 3.5 inches to nearly 6 inches.

A man ventured into rough and confused surf after completing his shift at the Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) factory just west of Boca Chica Beach.  The rough surf, which included intense rip currents and surf waves higher than four feet, took the man quickly offshore, where he was unable to return back and disappeared into the sea, according to Cameron County sheriff deputies on-scene. Another man who accompanied the deceased attempted to rescue him, but could not.  Multiple local, state, and federal agencies assisted in the initial search, and the U.S. Coast Guard took over later that day.  A search was called off by the U.S. Coast Guard the following morning due to rough seas.||The body of the deceased was found on Boca Chica Beach nearly 36 hours later.

Emergency manager reported water being pumped out of a house due to flash flooding. The same emergency manager reported a stranded vehicle in east Brownsville due to flash flooding. Water levels of 2 feet or higher spread along parts of FM 511 near the Port of Brownsville, which is a typically poor-drainage location, impacting several low-wheel-base vehicles.

Torrential rainfall with estimated totals ranging from 6 to 12 inches affected southern/southwestern Willacy County during the mid to late evening of March 27, with several water rescues reported in Sebastian along the Cameron County line.  Additional flooding with water depths on roads likely at or near 3 feet occurred northward to Lyford and perhaps the outskirts of Raymondville, and also east to FM 1420 between Santa Monica and Willamar. ||An unknown number of structures had some flooding.  Countywide damage statistics will be available later in 2025.

Torrential rains progressed from Hidalgo into Cameron County during the evening of March 27th, with multiple repeating rounds creating rapid onset flash flooding.  The multiple rounds of rainfall in western Cameron County added up to more than 10 inches for the period, with some areas likely receiving 9 or more inches in just three hours.  Widespread flooding was reported between Santa Rosa, Combes, Palm Valley, and La Feria, with nighttime swift water rescues reported in La Feria and Santa Rosa.  The final band of torrential rain (along with strong wind) whipped through just after midnight CST (1 AM CDT) March 28th. ||The IH-2 frontage road was littered with stalled vehicles, and dozens more were removed and placed along the shoulders in each direction.  High water continued well after the rains ended, into March 29th. ||It is likely that dozens, if not over 100, structures were impacted to various degrees ranging from affected to major damage, with several likely considered destroyed. Full damage data will be available in later 2025.

Texas Department of Transportation reported water of unknown depth was reported in an elementary school.  Photos suggested the water depth was 2 feet outside the building, and up to 1 foot inside.  Damage estimates were unknown at the time of this writing.
Two to three feet of water and flooding was reported on FM 755 in northeast Starr County near Santa Elena.

Significant to locally devastating flash flooding began in the McAllen/Mission metropolitan area during mid-afternoon.  Rainfall rates of at least 3 in 30 minutes were too much for the city's drainage infrastructure to handle, and soon after, city fire/rescue/police reported  more than two dozen roads closed citywide and up to forty homes with an unknown amount of water depth inside, to the Emergency Management Coordinator. ||It was likely that several hundred homes had incident flooding, from affected to major damage - most concentrated in the south side of the city.  The frontage roads on IH2 (Mission/McAllen) and IH-69C (Pharr/Edinburg) flooded with varying amounts of water, and hundreds of vehicles were stranded.  The highest water was at least four feet in spots along the frontage south of the McAllen Convention Center. Rainfall rates were historic for the season, ranging from 1/100 to 1/200 probability events (annual return frequency) over a 2-hour period. McAllen/Miller Airport, located just south of IH-2 and just west of 10th Street, recorded 6.25 in two hours.  ||Additional reports of 2 to 3 feet of water were received from the City of Pharr, with two to three feet of water depth at the intersection of N. Cage Blvd. and E. Ferguson Ave., along/near the IH-69C frontage.  Additional, faster moving/impacting rain bands occurred during the late evening, with the final potent band (with wind) racing through just after 11 PM CST (midnight CDT March 28th).  Residual urban flooding and high water would continue into March 28th and beyond in some areas.||As of early July, a county-wide estimate of Public Assistance (PA) and Individual Assistance (IA) damage was $52 million in Hidalgo County. The data were applied to this entry, since the combination of heavy rainfall and infrastructure was highest in this area at this time. More accurate damage reports for the City, and Hidalgo County overall, will be provided toward the end of 2025 or early 2026.

A small tornado briefly touched down about 1.5 |miles east of Edcouch, lifting the sheet metal roof of a warehouse|belonging to a crop dusting company. Pieces of the roof were |blown to the northeast along the 0.25 mile path, landing in open |fields on the north and south side of SH-107. The debris was |scattered in varying directions along the path. Partial metal wall|failure was also noted to the building, which was a total loss. A|metal building structure (MBS) hangar that sheltered one of the |crop-dusting aircraft was also damaged, with a small portion of |the roof lifted off and the garage door bent inward, toward the |center of the circulation. The aircraft inside was also impacted, |with an estimated $500 thousand in damage to it. Each structure |was old with generally poor connectors and rusted metal parts, |each built more than 80 years ago, according to the owner.||Other damage included parts of an unanchored fence blown down at |a drive-through convenience store, several large mesquite limbs |snapped off in open areas along the track, one rotting and unused |telephone pole snapped, and another one bent. ||A resident of a manufactured home who witnessed the event noted a|swirling column of rain as the tornado passed by, indicating that|the tornado was likely rain-wrapped.

A Severe (D2) Drought was designated for Zapata County on March 4, which continued through March 17, 2025, as a combination of very dry air, repeated dry fronts that produced northerly winds, and warmer than average temperatures created a flash drought condition.

Severe (D2) Drought was designated for all but southeastern Jim Hogg County on March 4, which continued through March 17, 2025, as a combination of very dry air, repeated dry fronts that produced northerly winds, and warmer than average temperatures created a flash drought condition.  The drought expanded to include all of the county on March 11th.

Severe (D2) Drought spread to all of Starr County on March 11th, and continued through March 17th before worsening thereafter as the combination of heat, wind, very dry air, and increasing sun angle/evaporation rates contributed to the onset of a flash drought.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the northwest tip of Starr County following weeks of very dry, breezy, and warmer than average temperatures.  The drought would expand to cover all of the county on March 11th.

Severe (D2) Drought developed in all of Brooks County on March 11th, and continued through the end of the month.  Note that locally heavy rainfall between March 26 and early March 28 would reduce drought levels in the county, but these would be shown on the April 1 monitor.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across most of northern Hidalgo County on March 11th, which would expand to the eastern sliver of the zone on the 18th and continue through the end of the month. Increasing stressors were noted in agriculture, with emerging spring crops showing signs of moisture stress. Water hauling and supplemental feeding was in full swing for cattle herds, which continued to be culled. Note that locally heavy rainfall between March 26 and early March 28 would reduce drought levels in the county, but these would be shown on the April 1 monitor.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across the western half of southern Hidalgo County on March 11th, which would expand to the entire zone on the 18th and continue through the rest of the month. Increasing stressors were noted in agriculture, with emerging spring crops showing signs of moisture stress. Water hauling and supplemental feeding was in full swing for cattle herds, which continued to be culled. Note that locally heavy rainfall between March 26 and early March 28 would reduce drought levels in the county, but these would be shown on the April 1 monitor.

Severe (D2) Drought would spread into northwestern through southwestern Kenedy County on March 11th, and continue through March 17th before marching across most of the county during the next ten days. Note that heavy rainfall on March 27-28, which would improve conditions, was not registered on the Drought Monitor until April 1.

The combination of humidity averaging near 10 percent each afternoon for a week (March 9-17), occasional heat spikes, and gusty winds moved conditions into flash drought territory, and the drought monitor was adjusted to Extreme (D3) on the 18th. These conditions would continue until March 26th, before heavy rains arrived and ultimately improved drought somewhat but not until April 1. Detailed agricultural (ranch/livestock) impact was not known, but pastures were completely brittle and overall cattle herds were culled, with water hauling likely in the Deep South Texas ranch country.

The combination of humidity averaging 10-15 percent each afternoon for a week (March 9-17), occasional heat spikes, and gusty winds moved conditions into flash drought territory, and the drought monitor was adjusted to Extreme (D3) on the 18th for all but the eastern one-fifth of Jim Hogg County. These conditions would continue until March 26th, before heavy rains arrived and ultimately improved drought somewhat but not until April 1. Detailed agricultural (ranch/livestock) impact was not known, but pastures were completely brittle and overall cattle herds were culled, with water hauling likely in the Deep South Texas ranch country.

The combination of humidity averaging 10-15 percent each afternoon for a week (March 9-17), occasional heat spikes, and gusty winds moved conditions into flash drought territory, and the drought monitor was adjusted to Extreme (D3) on the 18th for all but the eastern one-tenth of Starr County. These conditions would continue until March 26th, before heavy rains and local flash flooding arrived and ultimately improved drought somewhat but not until April 1. Detailed agricultural (ranch/livestock) impact was not known, but pastures were completely brittle and overall cattle herds were culled, with water hauling likely in the Starr County brush country.

Severe (D2) level drought expanded to most of inland Kenedy County on March 18th, and would further expand to all but a sliver of (southeast) inland Kenedy County on March 25.  These conditions continuing until March 26th before heavy rains put a dent into the drought - with the change noted on April 1st.  ||Between March 10-17, relative humidity averaged around 20 percent during the afternoon. Prior to the rains, flash drought conditions were in full swing.  Agricultural impacts were unknown, but dry rangeland extended into this region, though not quite as parched as locations in the Brush Country and mid/upper Rio Grande Valley.

Severe (D2) level drought expanded to cover all of southern Hidalgo County on March 18th, with these conditions continuing until March 26th before heavy rains put a notable dent into the drought.  Between March 10-17, relative humidity averaged around 15 percent during the afternoon. Prior to the rains, flash drought conditions were in full swing.  Dry rangeland/pastures were common during this period, and newly planted spring row crops were showing early-season stress with water shortages worsening.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded into western Willacy County on March 18th, courtesy of very dry conditions (afternoon humidity averaging around 20 percent from the 10th-17th), persistent breezes, periodic hot temperatures, and increasing evaporation.  The drought area would expand into central Willacy County on the 25th.  Torrential rains and local flash flooding on the 27th would improve conditions by April 1st.  ||Texas Agrilife reported that south Texas row crops - a staple of Willacy County agriculture - suffered early-season stress with water shortages prior to March 27th becoming critical.  Rangeland/pastures became very dry, peaking around March 25th.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded into a sliver of western Cameron County, including Santa Rosa and La Feria, on March 18th, with the area nudging slightly eastward on the 25th.  Torrential, historic rainfall induced widespread flash flooding on the 27th which would improve conditions by April 1st.  ||Texas Agrilife reported that south Texas row crops  suffered early-season stress with water shortages prior to March 27th becoming critical.  Rangeland/pastures became very dry, peaking around March 25th.

Severe (D2) level drought expanded to cover the northern two-thirds of coastal Kenedy County on March 25th, courtesy of breezy to windy, generally dry (low humidity) days, and above average day/night temperatures with no wetting dew.  Conditions would improve soon after rains on March 27-28, but the improvements were not recognized until the April 1st Drought Monitor update.||Unknown was impact to livestock (mainly cattle) in these areas.

Severe (D2) level drought expanded to cover the northern two-thirds of Kenedy County's barrier island (Padre Island National Seashore) on March 25th, courtesy of breezy to windy, generally dry (low humidity) days, and above average day/night temperatures with no wetting dew.  Conditions would improve soon after rains on March 27-28, but the improvements were not recognized until the April 1st Drought Monitor update.||Unknown was impact to livestock (mainly cattle) in these areas.

Local law enforcmement and state emergency management personnel, along with the Texas A&M Forest Service, reported a 130 acre wildfire along the Rio Grande 7 miles south-southeast of Donna, or immediately east of the Lower Rio Grande Wildlife Refuge at Santa Ana. The wildfire consumed a shed, but no other property damage was reported in the rural area.

Emergency manager reported a closed road due to urban flooding in Palm Valley near the intersection of Queens Sago Dr and Stuart Place Rd.  Time of event estimated by radar and duration of estimated rainfall of 3 to 4 inches in two hours.

Torrential rains moved out from the McAllen/metro into the mid-Valley section of Hidalgo County, to include locations east of Edinburg, including Elsa/Edcouch, then south through San Juan, Alamo, and Donna, extending south to around Military Highway (US 281) east of Pharr and near the Rio Grande.||Poor drainage locations flooded with at least 3 feet of water depth, and nearly the entire IH-2 frontage road had 2 to 3 or more feet of water depth, with dozens of vehicles stranded and at least one hundred more removed from the floodwaters. A number of farm-to-market and state highways had pockets of flood waters, forcing closures that lasted into March 28th. ||In this flood area, there were three known drownings when vehicles became submerged in deeper waters in canals/drainage areas during encounters with law enforcement.  One drowning was a juvenile who was unable to be rescued from a vehicle that submerged near Edcouch.||Damage details and further information will be available later in 2025 from these areas.

Torrential rains that previously affected the McAllen/Edinburg metro area reached southeast Hidalgo County, from south of Weslaco to Edcouch and east to the Hidalgo/Cameron line, then south along the Mercedes/La Feria line and all the way to between Progreso and just west of Santa Maria. Similar to the situation in the Donna-Weslaco area, the IH-2 frontage road was littered with flooded vehicles, with rescued vehicles along the side of the elevated expressway.  An estimated 3 or more feet of water was on the frontage roads.||The rain in this area came in multiple rounds.  A first round occurred between 430 and 6 PM, with additional rounds between 7 and 8 PM and again fro 930 to around 11 PM,and a final windy round around midnight March 28th CST (1 AM CDT). Water rescues were first reported in Mercedes at around 7 PM CST (8 PM CDT).  As of this writing, damage was unknown but hundreds of structures likely had varying degrees, ranging from affected to major damage.   ||High water would continue well into March 28th and beyond; the flood control system (floodway) had up to 20% capacity due to spillage and pumping of urban flood areas into it. ||Full damage statistics will be available later in 2025.

Some of the heaviest rainfall associated with the historic rainfall of March 26-28 fell in Harlingen.  In total, nearly 19 inches was measured by trusted sources, with radar estimates up to 20.5 inches.  During the peak of the multiple bands from early evening through just after midnight on the 28th, estimated rainfall rates were at least 3 per hour for at least 3 hours, including at Harlingen/Valley International Airport, where 5 fell in just 90 minutes before the power went out due to lightning strikes.||Hundreds, if not a thousand, structures had flood damage ranging from affected to destroyed. Damage details will be available for this part of Cameron County, which stretches from Harlingen through Rio Hondo and southwest to San Benito, at a later date in 2025.  Harder hit areas reported up to 4 feet of water, including the IH-2 and IH-69E frontage roads in these areas. For several areas, this event ranked as a 1/100 to 1/200 annual return frequency probability event, with perhaps up to a 1/500 event in a few spots. High water would continue in several hours for a few more days, though rapid runoff allowed for relatively quick recovery.||As of July 1, a preliminary estimate of $105 million was derived from Public Assistance (PA) and Individual Assistance (IA) reports, based on applying two-thirds of the values from the number of structures that were impacted with varying levels of damage in Cameron County. The damage was applied to this entry, since much was triggered by the rainfall and rainfall rates in these areas at these times. Full damage statistics will be available by the end of 2025 or start of 2026.

The Cameron County Office of Emergency Management reported a trailer home struck by lightning with the entire building consumed by the flames after the pre-dawn strike. Two residents inside were killed by the ensuing fire.
Several trees were reported down and power outages in the town of Penitas.
The Cameron County Office of Emergency Management reported a small shed blown down by strong thunderstorms winds in Santa Rosa.

The manager and security officer of the Long Island Village (Port Isabel) swing bridge reported damage from a likely small and brief tornado that crossed the bridge just after 1 AM CST (2 AM CDT) on March 28th.  Dollar value of the damage is estimated.

The Texas Department of Transportation, along with local law enforcement and the public, noted a continuation of high water along the IH-2 frontage roads between Mission and Alamo from just before midnight (standard time) on March 27th through mid to late afternoon on the 28th, as water was slow but steady to drain out of the area despite fair weather for most of the period.

The Texas Department of Transportation, along with local law enforcement, the public, and emergency management, reported high standing water of 2 to 3 feet in several poor drainage locations of southeastern Hidalgo County that persisted for two more days following historic seasonal rainfall/rainfall rates.  ||This included much of the IH-2 frontage road from east Alamo through the Cameron County line (Mercedes/La Feria), as well as several Farm-to-Market roads which remained impassible for all or part of this time. Overwhelmed drainage systems took time for the water to run out completely, and the Flood Control Project (Main and North Floodways in southeastern Hidalgo County between Weslaco and Mercedes, extending north to La Villa and east to the Willacy County line near Santa Rosa) continued with up to an estimated 20% of freeboard (capacity).||An unknown number of homes in southeast Hidalgo County had at least 1 foot in them, especially in the poorest draining locations where at least 10 inches of rain fell on the 27th into very early on the 28th. ||Damage estimates will be included with the initial flash flood entries from March 27th.

The Texas Department of Transportation, along with Cameron County and local city emergency management between La Feria and Rio Hondo, and other law enforcement, and neighborhood groups reported a continuation of 2 to 3 feet of water depth (higher in a few locations) well into March 28th, with only a slow recession on the 29th and 30th before the water drained out for all but a few locations. Flood related impacts continued as follows:||*Much of the IH-2 frontage between La Feria and Harlingen, and the IH-69E frontage from the Willacy County line through San Benito, was under 2 to 3 feet of water.|*The Arroyo Colorado gauge in Harlingen recorded a record high level of 30.44 feet at 7 AM on March 28th. While some of the record water levels were due to slow flows due to a need for dredging of sediment and other debris, locations inside the levee saw water levels greater than those seen from all but Hurricane Beulah, and low water crossings in western Cameron County were under at least 2-3 feet of water depth.|*State and Farm-to-Market roads between Harlingen and Rio Hondo remained closed from at least 2 feet of water depth well into the 28th.  |*Numerous homes, vehicles, and more remained under water in Palmview, Combes, Rio Hondo, Harlingen, and Primera.  The community of Green Valley was especially hard hit.  |*The duration of high water was partly driven by drainage backups and fill-ups in the Flood Control project of canals, ditches, and conveyance through-ways between Hidalgo, Cameron, and Willacy - with northern Cameron County communities bearing the brunt due to their location having the heaviest rainfall totals, which extended into southeast Hidalgo County. ||Water finally drained out except for a few locations by March 30th.  Final damage statistics will be included in the Flash Flood entry that includes the Harlingen/Rio Hondo/San Benito area.

The Texas Department of Transportation continued to report flooding along the frontage road near Sebastian well into March 28th, with additional flooding noted by emergency management/law enforcement along Farm-to-Market and County roads in the southern portion of the county.  Flooding continued at homes in the Sebastian area where drainage backups remained.||There was an unknown amount of water remaining in the North Floodway of the International Boundary and Water Commission's Flood Control Project.  Further details for Willacy County flooding well after the rains ended will be provided through updates.

Due to the continued combination of dry and hot conditions with a strong sun angle and evaporation rates, Severe (D2) Drought continued across Zapata County to begin May.  A band of thunderstorms with more than 2 inches (estimated) of rain on May 2nd covered southern Zapata, reducing the drought coverage to the northern two-thirds of the county for the May 6th monitor.

Following locally heavy rainfall before daybreak on May 7th, and again during the afternoon no May 8th, which dropped pockets of 2-4+ inches of rain across much of Zapata and western/southern Jim Hogg County, Drought Improved to Moderate (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0) across all but the northern quarter of the County, including Hebbronville, for the May 13th Drought Monitor.  This area received much less rainfall - around 0.5 inches - insufficient for improvement there.  Limited rainfall for the remainder of May allowed D2 conditions to hold in northern Jim Hogg.

Due to the continued combination of dry and hot conditions with a strong sun angle and evaporation rates, Severe (D2) Drought continued across either a large portion of Zapata County, including the cities/towns of Zapata and San Ygnacio through the month of April, from April 1st to April 30th.

Due to the continued combination of dry and hot conditions with a strong sun angle and evaporation rates, Severe (D2) Drought continued across either a large portion of Jim Hogg County, including the city of Hebbronville through the month of April, from April 1st to April 30th.

Severe (D2) Drought continued from March through all of April across the northwestern fifth of Starr County, as very little rain fell during the month.  Modest temperatures and wetting dew through mid-month were sufficient to keep conditions from worsening.
Dry weather through April was sufficient to extend Severe (D2) Drought farther east in the South Texas Brush Country, clipping the northwest corner of Brooks County by the 29th.

Due to the continued combination of dry and hot conditions with a strong sun angle and evaporation rates, Severe (D2) Drought continued across northern and western Jim Hogg County to begin May.  A band of thunderstorms with 1 to 2 inches (estimated) of rain on May 2nd covered extreme southwest Jim Hogg County, reducing the drought coverage to the remove that sliver for the May 6th monitor.

Due to the continued combination of dry and hot conditions with a strong sun angle and evaporation rates, Severe (D2) Drought continued across far northwestern Starr County to begin May.  A band of thunderstorms with 1.5 to 2 inches (estimated) of rain on May 2nd covered much of northwestern Starr County, reducing the drought coverage to the remove the county for the May 6th drought monitor.

Following locally heavy rainfall before daybreak on May 7th, and again during the afternoon no May 8th, which dropped pockets of 2-4+ inches of rain across much of Zapata County, Drought Improved to Moderate (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0) across all but the extreme northwestern portion of the County for the May 13th Drought Monitor.  This area received closer to 2 inches - insufficient for improvement there considering antecedent dry conditions through much of March and April.  Limited rainfall for the remainder of May allowed D2 conditions to hold in extreme northwest Zapata County.

Altogether, the damage locations were along a northwest to southeast oriented line with six of the seven surveyed locations north of Expressway 83/east of Interstate 69C (beginning near the Muniz/North Alamo city line) and the 7th spot of Expressway 83 in Donna.  For most of the damage path, estimated wind speeds ranged from 75 to 85 mph.||Detailed damage along the track included:|*Partial collapse of a single family home under construction at El Dora Road near N. Tower Road in north Alama (65 mph)|*Blown roof off of a single family poorly constructed home along Roman Circle, just north of Owassa Road in Muniz (sheet metal, manufactured-style) (80 mph)|*A metal structure thrown an unknown distance from a farm, landing along Val Verde Road in north Alamo (78 mph)|*Damaged traffic lights next to a collapsed building along El Dora Road in north Donna (70 mph)|*Fifteen power poles were blown down in a row along El Dora Road near N. Val Verde Road in north Donna (80 to 85 mph)|*Downed fence and a flipped trailer along Wood Ave. in Donna (80 mph).|*Flipped trailer blown onto Val Verde road near Donna North High School, which included minor fence damage.  This was also near the report of the bent free-standing tower (80 to 85 mph)||The most notable damage was to a metal stand alone tower nearby the Donna North High School, which was bent perpendicular to the tower's base and rated at 90 mph.
