A wildfire, initially observed by 3.9 micrometer resolution infrared satellite images and NWS Doppler Radar (as smoke), spread to an estimated 300 acres along and east of Federal Highway 77 in Kenedy County, roughly 17 miles from the Willacy County line or about 6 miles south of Armstrong.  The fire was likely driven by gusty north winds 15 to 20 mph and afternoon humidity falling to between 10 and 15 percent.  It was not known if the highway was closed at any time during or after the fire.

A wild fire grew rapidly during the afternoon across the King Ranch near Norias, approximately 70 miles south of Kingsville.  The fire, known as the Stillman S #14 fire, grew to 1,500 acres and may not have been totally contained until the next day.  There were some unconfirmed reports of Federal Highway 77 being closed near Norias.   The Texas Forest Service responded with an Air Attack (aircraft), two engines, and two dozers. Raymondville and King Ranch Fire Department responded to the blaze.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, including southern Kenedy County. Extreme drought conditions (D3) developed over northern Kenedy County. The drought conditions continue to mainly affect agricultural interests, including crops, pastures and grasslands on the King Ranch.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, including southern Brooks County. Extreme drought conditions (D3) developed over northern Brooks County. The drought conditions continued to affect agriculture, including crops, pastures and grasslands on the west section of the King Ranch in Brooks County.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching most of Jim Hogg County by month's end.  Extreme drought conditions (D3) developed over north eastern tip of Jim Hogg County. The drought conditions continued to mainly affect agriculture, including crops, pastures and grasslands across Jim Hogg County.||Dry conditions persisted across Deep South Texas during the past 6 months. Precipitation continued below normal and temperatures above normal during the month of March. Soil moisture became abnormally to excessively dry and the drought conditions over the region continued to worsen. Severe drought conditions (D2) have now extended into much of Deep South Texas, with extreme drought conditions (D3) over the extreme northern sections of Brooks and Kenedy counties. The drought conditions continue to mainly affect agricultural interests, including crops, pastures and grasslands. D3 drought conditions occurred across the north eastern tip of Jim Hogg County.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching into the Lower Rio Grande Valley by month's end.  Severe drought conditions (D2) spread into Cameron County, affecting agriculture, including crops, pastures and grasslands.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching into the Lower Rio Grande Valley by month's end.  Severe drought conditions (D2) spread into Willacy County, affecting agriculture, including crops, pastures and grasslands.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching into the Lower Rio Grande Valley by month's end.  Severe drought conditions (D2) spread into all of Hidalgo County, affecting agriculture, including crops, pastures, grasslands, and rangeland.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching into the middle and upper Rio Grande Valley by month's end.  Severe drought conditions (D2) spread across all of Starr County, affecting agriculture, including crops, pastures, grasslands, and rangeland.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching into the middle and upper Rio Grande Valley and Rio Grande Plains of Zapata County by month's end.  Severe drought conditions (D2) spread across all of Zapata County, affecting agriculture, including  pastures and rangeland.

In Kenedy County, virtually no rain fell during the entire month of April, with the sole exception of a spot of rain near the coast on the 3rd, and again on the 17th. The dry weather, combined with increasing sun angle and persistent winds, brought extreme drought (D3) into the northern half of the county through April 13th, which spread across the entire county thereafter and continued through the end of the month.|||Precipitation continued below normal and temperatures persisted above normal across Deep South Texas during the first half of April. The extremely dry conditions continued through the middle of April. Deep South Texas experienced above normal temperatures and below normal rainfall during the last 6 months. Soil moisture continued abnormally to excessively dry resulting in a continued deterioration in the drought conditions over the region. The United States drought|Monitor reported that drought conditions intensified to extreme (D3) over the northern half of Kenedy County and that (D2) drought conditions occurred over the southern half of Kenedy County.

Drought conditions settled in at severe levels (D2) for Zapata County to begin April. These conditions would continue through the entire month, as a mid-month thunderstorm and locally heavy rainfall event would combine with the typically drier climate of the Rio Grande Plains to maintain D2 conditions through the entire month.

Lack of any measurable rainfall, combined with warm, dry, and breezy conditions, further intensified the drought in Jim Hogg County. The United States drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported that conditions have intensified to extreme (D3) over the northeastern tip of Jim Hogg County and that (D2) drought conditions occurred across the remainder of Jim Hogg County from the end of March through April 13th.

Virtually no rain fell in Hidalgo County through the first half of April. The lack of rain, combined with persistent wind and above average temperatures maintained notable drought conditions.  The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported that (D2) drought conditions continued over the all of Hidalgo County from the end of March through April 13th.

No rain falling in Brooks County through the first half of April resulted in persistent, yet deteriorating, drought conditions. The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported that drought conditions intensified to extreme (D3) over the northern half of Brooks County and that (D2) drought conditions occurred over the southern half of the county.

Drought conditions settled in at severe levels (D2) for Starr County to begin April. These conditions would continue through the entire month, as a mid-month thunderstorm and locally heavy rainfall event would combine with the typically drier climate of the middle Rio Grande Valley of Texas, as well as the Rio Grande Plains, to maintain D2 conditions through the entire month.

No rain in the Willacy County portion of the Lower Rio Grande Valley through the first half of April, combined with persistent winds and above average temperatures, allowed drought conditions to persist and deteriorate.  The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported that severe (D2) drought conditions occurred over the all of the county through April 13th.

Virtually no rainfall in the Cameron County portion of the Lower Rio Grande Valley through the first half of April, combined with persistent winds and above average temperatures, allowed drought conditions to persist and deteriorate.  The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported that severe (D2) drought conditions occurred over all of the county through April 13th.

While some other locations in Deep South Texas experienced brief drought relief in the form of thunderstorms on the 17th and 18th, Brooks County largely missed the action, and the combination of continued above average temperatures, gusty winds, no rain, and low humidity pushed extreme (D3) to exceptional (D4) drought conditions across the county, with the exceptional conditions covering the north half.  These conditions would continue through the end of the month.

In Jim Hogg County, drought conditions deteriorated through mid April, continuing through the end of the month, the result of little appreciable rainfall.  Weakening thunderstorms moving out of Zapata County on April 17th and 18th helped reduce the acceleration of drought conditions.  ||The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, showed drought conditions had intensified to extreme (D3) drought conditions across the northeastern half of Jim Hogg County and that severe (D2) drought conditions was now occurring across all of southwestern half of Jim Hogg County on April 14th.  A sliver of exceptional drought (D4) nudged across the border of Jim Hogg and Brooks County on the 21st of the month.

With virtually no rain falling across Willacy County through the remainder of April, drought conditions deteriorated further after mid month.||The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported conditions had intensified across all of Willacy County to extreme (D3) drought level by April 14th; these conditions would continue through the end of the month.

With virtually no rain falling across nearly all of Cameron County through the remainder of April, drought conditions deteriorated further after mid month.||The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported conditions had intensified across all but the southern tip of Cameron County to extreme (D3) drought level by April 14th; extreme conditions would continue through the end of the month across all but locations along the Rio Grande, including the City of Brownsville, which remained at severe (D2) drought level.

Drought persisted, and eventually intensified, across Hidalgo County during the second half of April. Rapid deterioration of drought conditions may have been held up by local rains on April 18th, but the overall pattern of heat, wind, and low to moderate humidity returned soon after.||The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported drought conditions had intensified to extreme (D3) across the northeast and eastern portions of Hidalgo County with the remainder western three quarters of Hidalgo County continuing under severe (D2) drought conditions.

Torrential rains fed by continuing outflows from storms along the Sierra Madre Oriental blitzed the west half of Zapata County during hte mid evening.  The Zapata County Sheriff���s Office reported minor flooding along Federal Highway 83 in the San Ygnacio area north of the City of Zapata toward the Webb County line.  The flooding was reported between Corralitos and the La Perla Ranch, Lake #4, area. ||The Manager of the Zapata County Airport recorded 3.75 inches of rain, in addition to the fairly long duration of quarter size hail. Radar rainfall estimates were over 7 inches, but likely contaminated by the prodigious hail. Still, it is conceivable that more than 4 inches fell in a few spots, leading to enough water flowing across roads to consider the event a Flash Flood.

Hail fell for more than 15 minutes near Zapata County during the mid evening.  The Zapata County Emergency Management Coordinator received a report of quarter size hail in the Las Palmas subdivision, about 4 miles northeast of the City of Zapata.  The Manager of the Zapata County Airport noted quarter size hail as well, which cause indentations in some vehicles' hoods. Some larger stones of unknown size were embedded with the quarter sized hail field.
Quarter size hail was reported near El Sauz.
Penny sized hail was reported near the intersection of Farm to Market Roads 755 and 490.

The Hidalgo County Fire Department reported marble to nickel size hail fell approximately 2 miles east of McCook on Farm to Market Road 681.  The hail core intensified briefly as the parent thunderstorm moved east-southeast toward Highway 281.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the exceptional (D4) drought conditions across the northern half of Brooks County and the extreme (D3) drought conditions across the southern half of Brooks County.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the exceptional (D4) drought conditions across the northwestern tip of Kenedy County and the extreme (D3) drought conditions across the all of Kenedy County with the exception of the northwestern tip.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the exceptional (D4) drought conditions across the northeastern tip of Jim Hogg County and the extreme (D3) drought conditions across the northeastern half of Jim Hogg County with the exception of the northeastern tip and severe (D2) drought conditions across the southwestern half of Jim Hogg County.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the extreme (D3) drought conditions across the northern three quarters of Cameron County and the severe (D2) drought conditions across the southern one quarter of Cameron County.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the extreme (D3) drought conditions across all of Willacy County.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the extreme (D3) drought conditions across the northeast and eastern one quarter of Hidalgo County and the severe (D2) drought conditions across the western three quarters of Hidalgo County.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the severe (D2) drought conditions across all of Starr County.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the severe (D2) drought conditions across all of Zapata County.
A cooperative observer reported 3.18 inches of rain in less than an hour near La Joya from a thunderstorm moving quickly through. The public reported localized minor flooding in this area.

A cooperative observer in Edinburg reported 2.05 inches of rain in less than an hour with a fast moving strong thunderstorm.  The rain caused brief, minor street flooding during the late afternoon but no observable damage.
The Remote Automated Weather System (RAWS) location at Falcon Lake reported 2.29 inches of rain from two separate thunderstorms, one during the mid afternoon and one during the evening of May 16th.

A CO-OP observer in McCook reported heavy rainfall from a severe thunderstorms which produced wind gusts a little above 50 mph.  A few minutes later, the same observer reported winds estimated near 60 mph, along with very heavy rainfall and frequent lightning.

A 17 year old boy drowned less than a mile north of Beach Access #6 late Wednesday afternoon May 6. The young man entered the water around 4 pm with two friends. The man was caught in an undertow which pulled him out to sea. The friends attempted to swim out to him but were unable to reach the victim. The victim disappeared under the water about 15 minutes after the failed rescue attempt. His body was recovered about 6 pm approximately 2 miles north of where he was swimming.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching into the Lower Rio Grande Valley by month's end.  Severe drought conditions (D2) even reached coastal Cameron County, affecting agriculture, including crops and pastures.

Severe drought conditions (D2) extended into much of Deep South Texas, reaching into the Lower Rio Grande Valley by month's end.  Severe drought conditions (D2) even reached coastal Willacy County, affecting agriculture, including crops and pastures.

A small trash fire near Edinburg, at the intersection of Miller Rd. and Federal Highway 281, quickly burned out of control during the early afternoon of March 5th, aided by wind gusts of 25 to 30 mph and humidity falling toward the critical value of 35 per cent in the area. ||The Miller Fire eventually covered 1,650 acres. Sixty-five homes were threatened, and one was destroyed. Most of the homes were in or near the Colonia Muniz. A shelter was opened at the Brewster Elementary School, and housed up to 45 people before being closed during the evening. The Texas Forest Service and several local agencies responded. The fire was contained by late afternoon.

A wildfire spread rapidly across grass and ranchland near San Ygnacio in northwestern Zapata County before being contained during the evening.  A reported 500 acres burned in the Barrocita Fire during the afternoon of March 7th.

A small fire rapidly spread to at least 1500 acres on the Armstrong Ranch. While nearly all of Kenedy County is dominated by King Ranch rangeland, this fire affected Federal Highway 77, the only coastal thoroughfare connecting the Lower Rio Grande Valley with the Coastal Bend.  The highway was reported closed for a time on the 28th due to severe smoke, in an area south of Sarita near Armstrong.  ||Firefighters and other first responders from Raymondville, Kleberg County, Willacy EMS, Kenedy County Sheriff's Office, Texas Department of Transportation, and the Texas Forest Service responded to the blaze, which became known as the San Carlos Fire. At this writing, no structural damage had been reported.||A second, much smaller fire (40 acres) would develop a bit farther south, but also along Federal Highway 77, near Armstrong.  This secondary fire, known as the Cross Timbers Fire, was quickly contained but required help once again from Raymondville, Willacy County, and the Kenedy County Volunteer Fire Department.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move portions of Deep South Texas into a higher level of drought intensity.  All but the far southwest corner of Jim Hogg County moved to Exceptional (D4) Drought nto the middle of May 2009.  Some rains on the 16th and 17th would help pull the county back to Extreme Drought by the 19th.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move portions of Deep South Texas into a higher level of drought intensity.  Starr County moved to Extreme (D3) Drought for the middle of May 2009.  These values would hold despite some welcome rains on the 16th, which dropped 2 to 3 inches in several locations, based on radar and ground truth.  It is possible that some areas reduced below Extreme Drought prior to the 25th, even though the change is not listed here.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move portions of Deep South Texas into a higher level of drought intensity.  Western Hidalgo County moved to Extreme (D3) Drought for the middle of May 2009, remaining there until the final week of the month despite a one day break in the generally dry and breezy to windy pattern on the 16th, when locally heavy rains fell.

Rainfall on the 16th of May would reduce drought intensity in Jim Hogg County from Exceptional (D4) to Extreme (D3) by the 18th. Additional scattered storms between May 24th and 28th would maintain the Extreme level through the end of the month.
A trained spotter reported they had estimated a wind gust up to approximately 60 miles per hour during a thunderstorm approximately 5 miles southwest of the Harlingen Airport.
An emergency manager reported that lightning struck a home in Weslaco during an early morning thunderstorm. A fire engulfed the home which was completed destroyed. There were no injuries reported.

Measured winds of 53 mph were recorded at the Isla Grande Resort on the south side of the Town of South Padre Island as a strong thunderstorm swept through.  Awnings blew down nearby at Isla Blanca park, where winds may have been a bit higher in the exposed area.
A trained spotter reported that half-dollar size hail fell in Weslaco during a thunderstorm that moved through Hidalgo County.

A Raymondville Volunteer Fire Department employee reported penny size hail fell in the city of Raymondville during a thunderstorm that moved through Willacy County. The Willacy County Emergency Manager also reported penny size hail had fallen in the city of Raymondville during this thunderstorm.

A microburst from a cluster of thunderstorms moving through Raymondville toward Lyford rolled a new but unsecured mobile home just west of Raymondville. Nearby, several fences were blown down, and the door to an industrial building was blown in.  Farther south, at about the same time, an amateur radio operator reported |estimated wind gusts of 50 mph or higher occurred just north of Lyford.
The manager of the Port of Brownsville reported golf ball size hail on the grounds as a severe thunderstorm moved slowly through.
Family of a National Weather Service Employee reported hail up to golf ball size|during an intense thunderstorm just northwest of the center of Los Fresnos.
The Jim Hogg Sheriff���s Department reported golf ball size hail fell on Highway 16 approximately 10 miles south of the city of Hebbronville as a severe thunderstorm  moved through the area.

While locally heavy rains fell in portions of Deep South Texas at the end of May and early June, much of Kenedy County escaped with very little rainfall, except for the western third of the County.  Since Kenedy, a coastal county, tends to receive more rain than locations farther west on average, the departure from normal continued to grow, and exceptional (D4) drought continued across all but the southwest corner, where extreme (D3) drought persisted.  ||The increasing dearth of cattle feed was causing some producers to liquidate their herds by month's end.  As of this writing, no dollar values had been received for damages through June.

While locally heavy rains fell in portions of the Lower Rio Grande Valley at the end of May and early June, the eastern third of Willacy County escaped with very little rainfall, while the central and western sections only received some needed rainfall on June 1st.  Since Willacy, a coastal county, tends to receive more rain on average than counties farther west, the departure from normal continued to grow, and exceptional (D4) drought held across the northeastern portion through the entire month.  The needed rainfall, mainly along and west of Federal Highway 77, cut drought values to extreme (D3), with a sliver of reduced drought to severe (D2) in far west Willacy County near the Hidalgo County line from June 9th through the 29th.||The increasing dearth of cattle feed was causing some producers to liquidate their herds by month's end.  In addition, dryland crops were beginning to wither from the combination of drought, heat, wind, and sun angle; irrigation was allowing them to hold on but damages were likely underway. As of this writing, no dollar values had been received for damages through June.

Drought index calculations carrying over from late May before rains after Memorial Day maintained a mix of extreme (west portion) to exceptional (east portion) drought across Cameron County on the first of June.

While locally heavy rains fell in portions of Deep South Texas at the end of May and early June, much of Brooks County escaped with very little rainfall, except for the western and southern portion of the County, mainly on June 3rd.  Through June 29th, the northern half of the county remained in exceptional (D4) drought, while the southern half remained in extreme (D3) drought, as rangelands dried up under increasing heat, continued daytime breezes, low humidity, and high sun angle. By the 30th, exceptional drought expanded to cover all but the extreme southern sliver of the county. ||The increasing dearth of cattle feed was causing some producers to liquidate their herds by month's end from South Texas into Deep South Texas.  As of this writing, no dollar values had been received for damages through June.

Jim Hogg County, benefiting from a band of heavy rainfall early on May 28th, saw its drought level drop across the western half from extreme (D3) to moderate to severe (D1 and D2) from the 2nd through the 29th.  Elsewhere, a relative lack of rainfall compared to average allowed extreme drought to hold through most of the month.||By month's end, cattle herds were being sold in portions of Deep South Texas as necessary feed supplies dwindled.  No damage estimates were available as of this writing from Jim Hogg County.

The western portion of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (Hidalgo, Starr Counties) on into the Rio Grande Plains of Zapata County received enough relief from late May and early June rainfall to begin a gradual, though temporary, improvement in drought conditions from severe (D2) to extreme (D3) down below critical levels, reaching moderate (D1) intensity by the 9th.  In Starr County, conditions improved from severe to moderate by June 9th. Much of the improvement is due to observed rainfall compared with long term averages, which are drier than locations farther east.

The western portion of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (Hidalgo, Starr Counties) on into the Rio Grande Plains of Zapata County received enough relief from late May and early June rainfall to begin a gradual, though temporary, improvement in drought conditions from severe (D2) to extreme (D3) down below critical levels, reaching moderate (D1) intensity by the 9th.  In Hidalgo County, conditions improved from severe (all but extreme north and east which was extreme through June 1st) to moderate by June 9th. Much of the improvement is due to observed rainfall compared with long term averages, which are a bit drier than locations farther east.

According to the National Drought Monitor, the drought level was extreme (D3) across nearly all of Cameron County until June 30th, when rains from the previous week along and west of Federal Highway 77 improved conditions from Brownsville to Harlingen to the Hidalgo County line to severe (D2).

Virtually no rainfall in coastal Cameron County through the first half of April, combined with persistent winds and above average temperatures, allowed drought conditions to persist and deteriorate.  The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported that severe (D2) drought conditions occurred over all of the county through April 13th.

No rain in coastal Willacy County through the first half of April, combined with persistent winds and above average temperatures, allowed drought conditions to persist and deteriorate.  The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported that severe (D2) drought conditions occurred over all of the county through April 13th.

With virtually no rain falling across coastal sections of Cameron County through the remainder of April, drought conditions continued to deteriorate after mid month.||The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported conditions had intensified across all of coastal Cameron County to extreme (D3) drought level by April 14th; these conditions would continue through the end of the month.

With no rain falling across coastal sections of Willacy County through the remainder of April, drought conditions continued to deteriorate after mid month.||The United States Drought Monitor, Texas sector, reported conditions had intensified across all of coastal Willacy County to extreme (D3) drought level by April 14th; these conditions would continue through the end of the month.

A wild fire rapidly spread out of control near Randado, between State Highway 16 and Farm-to-Market Road 649. The fire, which spread to 500 acres, was eventually contained. Assistance in fighting the blaze was provided by Texas Forest Service, Helo-Tanker, Air Strike Team, U.S. Parks and Wildlife; Jim Hogg, Zapata, and Starr County Fire Deparments responded, as did the Roma Volunteer Fire Department (Starr). Texas Forest Service sent four bulldozers to help put out the fire.

Dry conditions continued across Hidalgo County the 3rd week of June resulting in an intensification of the drought conditions across portions of the County. Drought conditions intensified to Severe (D2) conditions across the eastern quarter of Hidalgo County on June 23rd, and further intensified to Extreme (D3) across the northeast sliver of the county by June 30th.

Drought conditions intensified across potions of Jim Hogg County the end of June.  A continued lack of rainfall over most of Jim Hogg County resulted in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions spreading across the eastern quarter of the county with Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailing across the central quarter of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions developing across the northwestern and south central quarter of the County the end of the month.
The public reported strong winds occurred during thunderstorms and blew down trees just south of Sebastian in extreme northern Cameron County.

Clusters of thunderstorms dumped heavy rainfall across western Cameron County during the mid to late afternoon on June 1st.  Measured rainfall between 2 and more than 4 inches fell at several locations, including 2.03 inches in Palm Valley and 2.33 inches near Harlingen.  An unconfirmed report of nearly 4 1/2 inches was reported by local media near Santa Rosa, and 4 to 5 inches of standing water were reported along Harrison and Tyler in downtown Harlingen.
The Hidalgo County Emergency Manager reported penny to nickel size hail fell along East Wisconsin Road during another severe thunderstorm on June 1.

Hidalgo County and McAllen City officials each reported penny size hail in southern Hidalgo County.  The initial report, estimated around 225 PM CDT, was in the City of Hidalgo near the Rio Grande River; the second was near the McAllen/Miller Airport between 235 and 240 PM.  The same cell produced a 52 mph (45 knot) wind gust at McAllen/Miller airport at 237 PM CDT.||Pea to dime size hail would continue in the vicinity of the McAllen Country Club, less than 2 miles east of Miller Airport, through at least 250 PM and perhaps until 300 PM as the parent thunderstorm stretched out along and just south of Federal Highway 83.
The public reported three quarters inch hail occurred during a rapidly developing thunderstorm during the early evening, just east of Weslaco.
A trained spotter reported hail up to golf ball size in diameter during a thunderstorm which moved north between Raymondville and Perlita during the afternoon of June first.
A border patrol reported nickel size hail one mile east of Falfurrias.

Minor flooding, with up to a foot of standing water, was reported by the Brooks County Emergency Management Coordinator during a slow moving thunderstorm that dumped torrential rain and large hail.  The NWS Cooperative observer at the Hollywood Hunting Camp, just west of Falfurrias, reported 2.52 inches of rain with the storm.
The Brooks County Emergency Manager reported a roof blown off a house located approximately 5 miles east of Falfurrias from severe thunderstorm winds.

The Edinburg Police Department reported that there were numerous reports from the public of funnel clouds from residents near Edinburg.  Several photographs of shelf and mammatus clouds were sent to the NWS office, including an apparent wall cloud looking west from Edinburg.

Channel 12 (McAllen Cable Access Television) reported quarter size and perhaps larger hail fell during a thunderstorm in the city of Mission during the evening. Nickel size hail was reported a bit earlier by a resident 1 mile north of Palmview, as well as several large limbs being knocked down.  The mini supercell raced south southeast, likely producing additional hail southeast of Mission.  Most reports were received between 927 and 930 PM CDT.
The public reported hail of approximately one inch in diameter continued falling as a severe thunderstorm raced through western Hidalgo County.
A Hidalgo County official reported a roof blow off a small home at the intersection of 9 Mile Road and Moorefield Drive. Several Trees and power lines were down in the same area.

The public reported two separate wind gusts of 52 and 54 knots when a mini supercell raced south southeast through the Palmhurst/Mission/Sharyland area during the evening of June 3rd.  The wind gusts knocked down numerous live oak and other trees and large limbs as the storm passed through.

The Starr County Emergency Manager reported seeing a funnel cloud touchdown briefly near the intersection of 755 and 490 just east of 755 and approximately 1/4 mile north of 490 near the city of Rincon. The Emergency Manager estimated the tornado was approximately 100 feet wide and touched down in the open on ranch land. No damages occurred during this event.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move portions of Deep South Texas into a higher level of drought intensity.  Brooks County moved to Exceptional (D4) Drought for the middle of May 2009.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move portions of Deep South Texas into a higher level of drought intensity.  Kenedy County moved to Exceptional (D4) Drought for the middle of May 2009.  Scattered storms during the last week of May were not enough to reduce intensity below Exceptional, which was the case elsewhere in Deep South Texas.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move most of the Lower Rio Grande Valley into a higher level of drought intensity.  Willacy County moved from Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought for the middle of May 2009.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move most of the Lower Rio Grande Valley into a higher level of drought intensity.  All of Willacy County, including locations near the coast, moved from Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought for the middle of May 2009.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move most of the Lower Rio Grande Valley into a higher level of drought intensity.  All of Cameron County, including locations near the coast, moved from Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought for the middle of May 2009.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move most of the Lower Rio Grande Valley into a higher level of drought intensity.  Cameron County moved from Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought for the middle of May 2009.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move most of the Lower Rio Grande Valley into a higher level of drought intensity.  The north and east portion of Hidalgo County moved from Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought for the middle of May 2009.

Hot, windy, dry weather combined with ample late spring sunshine to quickly move portions of Deep South Texas into a higher level of drought intensity.  Zapata County moved to Extreme (D3) Drought for the middle of May 2009.  These values would hold despite some welcome rains on the 16th, which dropped 1 to 2 inches in several locations in the east and south portions of the county, based on radar and ground truth.  It is possible that some areas reduced below Extreme Drought prior to the 25th, even though the change is not listed here.

Scattered thunderstorms on May 16th would help alleviate the Extreme drought conditions in the western Rio Grande Valley and Rio Grande Plains by the final week of the month.  Additional, more numerous storms on May 28th would ensure that conditions would remain in the Severe (D2) drought category into early June.

Scattered to numerous thunderstorms on May 16th, some which dropped more than 2 inches across a good part of Starr County, would help alleviate the Extreme drought conditions in the western Rio Grande Valley and Rio Grande Plains by the final week of the month.  Additional, more numerous storms on May 28th would ensure that conditions would remain in the Severe (D2) drought category across Starr County into early June.

Scattered on May 16th, some which dropped more than 2 inches across a western Hidalgo County, would help alleviate the Extreme drought conditions in western part of the Lower Rio Grande Valley by the final week of the month.  Other rounds of storms on the 24th, 27th, and 28th would help keep drought conditions under some control to close out the month. Conditions dropped to Severe (D2) across all but the extreme eastern portion of Hidalgo County, where levels remained Extreme (D3).

Scattered thunderstorms on May 16th, some which dropped more than 2 inches across southern Brooks County, would help alleviate the Exceptional drought conditions in this area by the final week of the month.  Other rounds of storms on the 24th and 28th would help keep drought conditions under some control to close out the month. Still, antecedent bone dry soil values maintained Exceptional (D4) conditions across the north half of the county, with the south half dropping back to  Extreme (D3).

Extreme to Exceptional Drought conditions continued across the eastern half of the Lower Rio Grande Valley into the end of May, despite pockets of torrential rains that helped alleviate extremely dry soil moisture values in some areas.  The additional rains did help reduce the drought intensity from Exceptional (D4) to Extreme (D3) across the western third of Willacy County, but Exceptional conditions continued elsewhere through the end of the month.

Extreme to Exceptional Drought conditions continued across the eastern half of the Lower Rio Grande Valley into the end of May, despite pockets of torrential rains that helped alleviate extremely dry soil moisture values in some areas.  The additional rains did help reduce the drought intensity from Exceptional (D4) to Extreme (D3) across the western third of Cameron County, but Exceptional conditions continued elsewhere through the end of the month.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions were noted on the Drought Monitor to close the end of May.  However, there was notable relief in the form of two significant thunderstorm clusters, one on the morning of May 17th and another during the early morning of May 24th, each which affected the Port Isabel through South Padre Island and Boca Chica area.  Additional rains reached the coastal zone on May 27th, mainly away from the barrier island.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions were noted on the Drought Monitor to close the end of May.  Notable relief that moved across coastal Cameron County did not stretch into Willacy County, on the mornings of May 17th and May 24th.  Some rain did fall during the afternoon of May 27th, but not enough to put any appreciable dent into the Exceptional conditions.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: Outflow from a strong thunderstorm complex sweeping across the Lower Texas coast produced a wind gust of more than 34 knots at NOAA C-MAN site of Port Isabel.  47 mph wind gusts would soon sink five small boats moored in the Laguna Madre near the Town of South Padre Island.
A trained spotter reported nickel size hail fell in Donna during a thunderstorm that moved through Hidalgo County.

Quarter size hail fell along Milagros Road between Donna and Weslaco during a thunderstorm that moved through Hidalgo County.  A news reporter from KRGV-TV-5 reported nickel size hail in the vicinity at around the same time.

The business manager of a ship breaking and metal processing firm at the Port of Brownsville reported a bolted down radio tower was blown down by microburst winds associated with a severe thunderstorm, which produced golf ball sized hail nearby.

The Jim Hogg Sheriff's Department reported water along and over State Highway 16 near the city of Randado during and a little after a thunderstorm moved through the area with locally heavy rainfall, estimated by radar to be more than 2 inches. The water depth on Highway 16 was estimated to be in inches, and the road was still passable.

Frequent cloud to ground lightning strikes, associated with continuing strong storms which had earlier produced locally heavy rains and large hail across portions of Jim Hogg, Starr, and Zapata County, moved across the McAllen/Edinburg area during the pre-dawn hours.  One of these strikes started a roof fire by igniting shingles at an estate home.  Within an hour, the blaze had engulfed the entire roof; residents were able to escape unharmed.  Video showed the house, as well as a vehicle, to be a total loss, with replacement estimated to be near $1 million.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: The Harbormaster at Port Mansfield reported a gust of 51 mph as outflow from strong thunderstorms moved south and west through the community.  The location is within a mile of the bay; this value is assumed to extrapolate into the frictionless waters nearby.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the County Warning Area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the extreme (D3) drought conditions across the northern three quarters of Cameron County and the severe (D2) drought conditions across the southern one quarter of Cameron County. This also included coastal portions of the county.

Precipitation remained below normal and temperatures continued above normal across Deep South Texas the first few weeks of May. Deep South Texas continued to experience abnormally to excessively dry soil moisture across the area.  The dry conditions resulted in the continuation of the extreme (D3) drought conditions across coastal portions of Willacy County.

Lack of significant rainfall along the Willacy County coastline, even during the eleven day period between May 24th and June 3rd, held drought conditions at exceptional (D4) through the entire month of June, 2009.
Some welcome rains during the final week of May allowed the drought index to relax in early June, but not after holding at exceptional (D4) levels to begin the month near the coast of Cameron County.
According to the National Drought Monitor, the drought level was extreme (D3)  across coastal Cameron County until June 30th.

A man was found dead in a parking lot near a restaurant in downtown Harlingen during the afternoon of June 12th.  Residents believed the man to be homeless, and the suspected cause of death was heat stroke.  The man was pronounced dead at 5:50 PM CDT but may have died a few hours earlier during the peak of the heat.  Heat index values at the Harlingen/Valley International Airport peaked at 107 during the afternoon, and at 112 at McAllen/Miller Airport in Hidalgo County.  It is quite possible that where the fatality occurred, in a more urban setting, heat index values could have been at or very near local advisory criteria, which is 111 during the afternoon.

Locally heavy rainfall overnight on May 27th into the early morning of May 28th was absorbed into the drought monitor statistics during the first week of June.  Until June 2nd, however, conditions remained at severe (D2) levels before returning to moderate (D1) levels.  Levels would remain unchanged through June despite little or no rainfall, due to low monthly climatological averages in the Rio Grande Plains for June.

Light rainfall that occurred on July 11th was nowhere near enough to reduce the exceptional drought which had dominated the King Ranch since June.  Exceptional (D4) drought conditions began taking a toll on cattle, cotton, and corn on the Ranch in July, and would continue through the entire month.

Virtually no rainfall during the entire month ensured nearly all of Brooks County, including the western portion of the King Ranch, would remain in exceptional (D4) drought for July.  Only the extreme southern portion of the county would remain in slightly better (extreme, D3) conditions until the last few days, when these areas also slipped into exceptional conditions.  Cattle in the area had to be sold as water stocks dried up; cotton and corn began withering heavily in the hot, breezy weather.

Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions prevailed across Willacy County through July, as limited rainfall on the 11th was not enough to bring appreciable moisture to crops and livestock.  Fields of cotton and corn began withering in the strong July sunshine, frequent gusty winds, record heat, and frequently lower than average humidity.  Exceptional Drought prevailed across the northeast half of the county, with Extreme Drought elsewhere.

Drought conditions continued across Jim Hogg County the first three weeks of July.  Exceptional (D4) conditions prevailed over the eastern third of the county, dropping sharply to Severe (D2) across the western third, with Extreme (D3) in the central third.  A spell of locally heavy rainfall with thunderstorms on the 7th would help slow the worsening drought, but Extreme to Exceptional conditions would spread westward later in the month.  Cattle herds' water stock began drying up, and some sales began as the heat and wind took their toll.

Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across Cameron County through July, as rainfall on the 11th combined with prior rains in June and slightly lower temperatures in some areas kept drought from worsening too fast.  However, the continuation of above average temperatures with frequently gusty winds began taking a toll on crops and livestock.  Fields of cotton and corn began withering in the strong July sunshine, as well as gusty winds and frequently lower than average humidity, particularly toward the Hidalgo County line.  Extreme Drought prevailed mainly east of Highway 77, with Severe Drought elsewhere.

Drought conditions continued across portions of Hidalgo County the first two weeks of July. Extreme (D3) drought conditions occurred across the northeastern tip of Hidalgo County and Severe (D2) drought conditions across the north and central quarter of the Hidalgo County the first two weeks of July.

Drought conditions worsened across Hidalgo County during the middle of July, and would continue through the end of the month. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed in the northeast portion of the County by the 14th, and would cover all but the southeast third of the County by month's end.  Severe (D2) drought covered the southwest portion of the County by the 14th, and would remain only over the areas mainly east of Highway 281 and south of Highway 83 by month's end.||Dryland crops began to wither under the very hot temperatures, gusty winds, and many afternoons with frequently low humidity.  Irrigable crops were able to survive as stores of water from up river were used to maintain growth for a suitable harvest.

Despite some welcome rains from thunderstorms on the 7th, Drought conditions gradually worsened in Starr County during the first two weeks of July, moving from moderate (D1) to severe (D2) by the 14th.  Several days of very hot temperatures and occasionally gusty winds under full July sunshine brought increased drying and the continuation of trouble for cattle ranchers as water stocks began to dry up.

Drought conditions gradually intensified across Zapata County by the middle of July as very hot temperatures, occasionally gusty winds, and low humidity easily overcame one day of welcome rains on the 7th.  By the 14th, severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed, and these conditions would last through the end of the month, with extreme (D3) conditions edging across the county line by month's end.

Drought conditions intensified across Starr County the last two weeks of July with above normal temperatures and dry conditions prevailing across the county. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions developed across the extreme north eastern tip of the county and Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across the rest of the county on the 21st, continuing through the end of the month.  Dryland crops continued to wither and cattle ranchers were continuing to sell some of their herds early due to a lack of sufficient water supply.

Several wild fires broke out in Starr County during the afternoon of July 20th.  The most critical fire, burning 40 acres in the northwest portion of Rio Grande City, caused an unknown amount of damage to an unoccupied home on a vacant lot.  This same fire threatened 100 homes, but they were saved by control and containment operations.  Two other small blazes burned several acres near La Casita and San Isidro.  A larger fire scorched 200 acres near La Gloria; this fire did not threaten any structures and was brought under control with assistance from the City of McAllen (Hidalgo County) Public Works Department.

Surface observations generally along and south of Federal Highway 83, including the McAllen/Mission area, indicated several hours of daytime heat index at or above 111F and early morning low temperatures remaining above 80F.  Near the Rio Grande, observations indicated between 2 and 5 hours of high heat index values each afternoon; values peaked at 115 at the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge along the southwest Cameron County/southeast Hidalgo County line on the 7th, and 116 at the McAllen/Miller Airport, around 4 PM CDT.  Record high temperatures were tied on the 6th and set on the 7th through 9th. As of this writing, there were no known fatalities in Hidalgo County during this event.

Surface observations and extrapolated data generally along and south of Federal Highway 83 west of Harlingen and Brownsville, indicated several hours of daytime heat index at or above 111F and early morning low temperatures remaining above 80F.  Near the Rio Grande, observations indicated between 2 and 5 hours of high heat index values each afternoon; values peaked at 115 at the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge along the southwest Cameron County/southeast Hidalgo County line on the 7th at around 4 PM CDT.  As of this writing, there were no known fatalities in Cameron County during this event.

Surface observations and extrapolated data generally in and near the populated portion of Starr County (along Highway 83) indicated several hours of daytime heat index at or above 111F and early morning low temperatures remaining above 80F.  Near the Rio Grande, observations indicated between 3 and 6 hours of high heat index values each afternoon; values peaked between 115 and 120F at the Falcon Lake Real-time Observation Monitor and Analysis Network site near the Starr/Zapata County line.  Peak values generally occurred between 3 and 5 PM CDT. As of this writing, there were no known fatalities in Starr County during this event.

Surface observations and extrapolated data generally along and near the Rio Grande in southwestern Starr County, generally along and west of Highway 83 south of the City of Zapata, indicated several hours of daytime heat index at or above 111F and early morning low temperatures remaining above 80F.  Observations indicated between 3 and 6 hours of high heat index values each afternoon; values peaked between 115 and 120F at the Falcon Lake Real-time Observation Monitor and Analysis Network site near the Starr/Zapata County line.  Peak values generally occurred between 3 and 5 PM CDT. As of this writing, there were no known fatalities in Zapata County during this event.

Heat index values, which commonly held between 103 and 108 for most July days in the Rio Grande Valley between Cameron and Zapata County, nudged upward above critical values beginning on the 30th and ending before sunset on the 31st.  At McAllen/Miller airport, peak heat index reached 114 on the 30th.  New record highs were set at the airport on each day (106 degrees).  At the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge along the extreme southeast Hidalgo and southwest Cameron County line, heat index peaked at 117 between 3 and 4 pm CDT. Critical heat index values lasted 2 to 4 hours each afternoon; overnight temperatures remained near or above 80 degrees. ||As of this writing, there were no known fatalities or injuries from the high heat in Hidalgo County during this period.

Heat index values, which commonly held between 103 and 108 for most July days in the Rio Grande Valley between Cameron and Zapata County, nudged upward above critical values beginning on the 30th and ending before sunset on the 31st across Cameron County mainly west of Federal Highway 77 and along and south of Federal Highway 83.  At the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge along the extreme southeast Hidalgo and southwest Cameron County line, heat index peaked at 117 between 3 and 4 pm CDT.  Duration of the critical heat index was from 2 to 4 hours each afternoon; overnight temperatures largely remained near or above 80.  ||As of this writing, there were no known fatalities or injuries from the high heat in Cameron County during this period.

Heat index values, which commonly held between 103 and 108 for most July days in the Rio Grande Valley between Cameron and Zapata County, nudged upward above critical values beginning on the 30th and ending before sunset on the 31st across Starr County mostly near the Rio Grande River, along and south of Federal Highway 83.  At the Falcon Lake Real-Time Observation Monitor and Analysis Network site along the Starr/Zapata County line, heat index peaked at 117 between 3 and 4 pm CDT on July 30th.  Conditions lasted 2 to 4 hours each afternoon; overnight lows did not fall below 80 in the affected area. ||As of this writing, there were no known fatalities or injuries from the high heat in Starr County during this period.

Heat index values, which commonly held between 103 and 108 for most July days in the Rio Grande Valley between Cameron and Zapata County, nudged upward above critical values beginning on the 30th and ending before sunset on the 31st across Zapata County mainly near the Rio Grande River, generally south of the City of Zapata.  At the Falcon Lake Real-Time Observation Monitor and Analysis Network site along the Starr/Zapata County line, heat index peaked at 117 between 3 and 4 pm CDT on July 30th.  Conditions lasted 2 to 4 hours each afternoon; overnight lows did not fall below 80 in the affected area. ||As of this writing, there were no known fatalities or injuries from the high heat in Zapata County during this period.

Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions prevailed across coastal Willacy County through July, as limited rainfall on the 11th was not enough to bring appreciable moisture to crops and livestock.  Fields of cotton and corn began withering in the strong July sunshine, frequent gusty winds, record heat, and frequently lower than average humidity.  Exceptional Drought prevailed across the north half of the coastal zone, including Port Mansfield, with Extreme Drought elsewhere.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across Coastal Cameron County through July, as rainfall on the 11th missed the area from South Padre Island through Port Isabel, Bayview, and Arroyo City. Lower temperatures in some areas may have kept drought from worsening.  However, the continuation of above average temperatures with frequently gusty winds began taking a toll on crops and livestock.  Fields of cotton and corn began withering in the strong July sunshine, as well as gusty winds.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions spread west across the eastern half of Jim Hogg County for the final ten days of July, with Extreme (D3) conditions covering the rest of the County, as hot temperatures, gusty winds, low humidity, and no rain continued to take a toll on cattle and other livestock to close out the month with water supplies rapidly dwindling.

Extremely dry conditions, caused by record to near record heat, gustier than average winds, and unusually low humidity for late summer, maintained exceptional (D4) drought conditions across all of Brooks County through August. By the end of the month, damage to usable pastureland, livestock and dryland crops was likely to be in the millions of dollars. A specific value will be provided when data are received from the USDA Farm Service Agency office in Falfurrias.

Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions continued across Jim Hogg County through all of August.  The combination of record to near record heat, periods of unusually gusty winds, and very low humidity maintained extreme conditions across the west half of the county, and exceptional (D4) across the east half until just before the end of the month, when some welcome rains helped bring the entire county down to extreme levels to start September.  ||The persisting drought left its toll on pastureland, livestock and any dryland crops grown in the county; the USDA Farm Service Agency in Falfurrias (serving Brooks nd Jim Hogg Counties) has likely recorded crop and related livestock damage in the millions of dollars.

Extreme (D3) Drought held across southern Willacy County, with Exceptional (D4) Drought maintaining across the northern half of the county, through mid August before conditions worsened county-wide to exceptional (D4) to close the month.  The continued rain free, record to near record hot, and frequently windy weather contributed to the severity of the drought, which began to break at the very end of the month.  The rains were too little, too late for most dryland crops, pastureland, and some livestock.  Dollar damages will be reported in the D4 countywide entry between August 18 and 31.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions dominated nearly all of Starr County for all of August, with Exceptional (D4) drought conditions nosing across the extreme northeast portion of the county and a brief period of severe (D2) Drought conditions through the 3rd near the Zapata County line before being erased by the 4th.  Record to near record heat, frequently gusty winds, no rainfall for nearly the entire month, and very low humidity for August guaranteed a significant loss of pastureland, dryland crop, and some livestock by month's end.  The USDA Farm Service Agency office that serves Starr and Zapata County would likely report damage in the millions of dollars, and a final estimate will be available soon.

Drought conditions continued across Cameron County, at the same intensity levels as the end of July, the first few days of August. Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued across the eastern and south central half of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across the western half of Cameron County the first few days of August.  These conditions would worsen quickly with continued dry, windy, and record to near record heat through the month.

Drought conditions continued across Hidalgo County at the same levels as the end of July the first few days of August. Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued across the west and northern two thirds of Hidalgo County and Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across the southeastern one third of the County the first few days of August.  These conditions would soon worsen across all of the county for the remainder of August.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions continued across Zapata County the first few days of August at the same intensity levels as the end of July as above normal temperatures and dry conditions continued across the county. Conditions would soon worsen to Extreme (D3) within the first week of the month and continue through month's end.

Drought conditions intensified across Cameron County the first week of August. Extreme (D3) drought conditions spread across the western half of Cameron County. Therefore the entire county was engulfed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions from the 4th through the 17th.

Drought conditions intensified across Hidalgo County the first week of August. Extreme (D3) drought conditions spread across the southeastern portions of Hidalgo County. Therefore the entire county was engulfed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions from the 4th through 17th.

A continued lack of rainfall over most of Willacy County intensified the drought conditions the middle of August. The Exceptional (D4) drought spread across the remainder of Willacy County the middle of the month.  The Exceptional (D4) drought encompassed the entire county the middle of August through the end of the month.  Massive dryland crop, pastureland, and some livestock damage was reported by the USDA Farm Service Agency in Raymondville which serves Willacy County.  Final estimates, likely to be well into the millions of dollars, will be available soon.

A continued lack of rainfall over most of Cameron County intensified the drought conditions the middle of August. The Exceptional (D4) drought spread across the remainder of Cameron County the middle of the month.  The long duration extreme to exceptional drought, which prevailed for most of July and August, resulted in massive dryland crop and pastureland losses for the entire event.  The USDA Farm Service Agency in San Benito reported at the end of August, prior to the September 1 plowing date, was more than $20 million in damage to cotton, corn, sorghum, sugar cane, and pastureland, county-wide.

Drought conditions intensified across portions of Hidalgo County the middle of August.  A continued lack of rainfall over most of Hidalgo County resulted in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions across the eastern one third of the county and Extreme (D3) drought conditions across the western and southern two thirds of the county the middle of August through the end of the month.  The persistence of extreme to exceptional drought for much of July and August cost tens of millions of dollars in dryland crop, pastureland, and some livestock damage and loss.  A final estimate will be available from the USDA Farm Service Agency in McAllen/Weslaco soon.
Two transformers were struck by lightning in the city of Hebbronville, reported by the  Jim Hogg County Sheriff Department.

Dry conditions continued across Brooks County in early September. However a few showers allowed some improvement across portions of the county. The Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across the north and east one third of the county and extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the west and central two thirds of the county.
Dry conditions continued across Kenedy County in early September. The Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across the entire county.

Dry conditions continued across Willacy County in early September. However a few showers allowed some improvement across portions of the county. The Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across the north and east three quarters of the county and extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the west one quarter of the county.

Dry conditions continued across Jim Hogg County in early September. A few showers moved across portions of the county in early September allowing conditions to improve slightly in some areas. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the entire county.

Dry conditions continued across Cameron County in early September. However a few showers allowed some improvement across portions of the county. The Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across the east two thirds of the county and extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the west one third of the county.

Dry conditions continued across Hidalgo County in early September. However a few showers allowed conditions to improve across portions of the county. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the entire county.
Dry conditions continued across Zapata County in early September. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the entire county.
Dry conditions continued across Starr County in early September. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the entire county.

Dry conditions continued across Cameron County in early September. However a few showers allowed some improvement across portions of the county. The Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across the east two thirds of the county and extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the west one third of the county.

A few showers moved across portions of Hidalgo County the first week of September resulting in a slight improvement in some areas. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the north three quarters of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the southern one quarter of the county.

A few showers moved across portions of Starr County the first week of September resulting in a slight improvement in some areas. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the north three quarters of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the southern one quarter of the county.

A few showers moved across portions of Zapata County the first week of September resulting in a slight improvement in some areas. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the east one third of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the western two thirds of the county.

The drought improved across Kenedy County the middle of September as beneficial rains fell across portions of the county. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the northern one quarter of the county with Severe (D2) drought conditions occurring across the central half of the county.

The drought improved across Brooks County the middle of September as beneficial rains fell across portions of the county. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the northern one third of the county with Severe (D2) drought conditions occurring across the southern two thirds of the county.

The drought improved across Jim Hogg County the middle of September as beneficial rains fell across portions of the county. The Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the northern one quarter of the county with Severe (D2) drought conditions occurring across the central half of the county.

The drought improved across Zapata County the middle of September as beneficial rains fell across portions of the county. Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the northeastern corner of the county.

Beneficial rains moving across portions of Jim Hogg County improved the drought conditions at the end of the month. Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the northern half of the county at the end of September.

Beneficial rains moving across portions of Brooks County improved the drought conditions at the end of the month. Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the northern three quarters of the county at the end of September.

Beneficial rains moving across portions of Kenedy County improved the drought conditions at the end of the month. Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the northern one quarter of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the central one quarter of the county at the end of September.

Extremely dry conditions, caused by record to near record heat, gustier than average winds, and unusually low humidity for late summer, maintained exceptional (D4) drought conditions across all of Kenedy County through August. By the end of the month, damage to usable pastureland, livestock, and any dryland crops was likely to be in the millions of dollars. A specific value will be provided when data are received from the USDA Farm Service Agency office in Kingsville, serving Kleberg and Kenedy County.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across Coastal Cameron County, at the same intensity levels as the end of July, through the first half of August before deteriorating further for the last half of the month. The worsening conditions would be the result of continued dry, windy, and record to near record heat through the month.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions continued across Coastal Willacy County right through August, the result of continued dry, windy, and record to near record heat through the month.  The USDA Farm Service Agency would report significant damage to dryland crops, pastureland, and some livestock across the entire county.  Specific estimates will be available soon and listed in the Willacy County entry including August 31 2009.

A continued lack of rainfall over most of Cameron County intensified the drought conditions the middle of August. The Exceptional (D4) drought spread across the remainder of Cameron County the middle of the month.  The long duration extreme to exceptional drought, which prevailed for most of July and August, resulted in massive dryland crop and pastureland losses for the entire event.  The USDA Farm Service Agency in San Benito reported at the end of August, prior to the September 1 plowing date, was more than $20 million in damage to cotton, corn, sorghum, sugar cane, and pastureland, county-wide.  These damages are reported for the Cameron County listing; please refer to them there.

Drought worsened from severe (D2) to extreme (D3) in normally dry Zapata County on the 4th of August; these conditions would continue through the end of the month.  Some damage to pastureland, and some losses to livestock, were noted by the USDA Farm Service Agency in Rio Grande City, which serves Zapata and Starr County.  Loss value estimated will be reported very soon.

The 2 meter observation platform at the Santa Ana (Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge) location carried heat index at or above 111 for three hours during the afternoon of the 20th, peaking at 116 at 3 PM local time before gradually falling back.  Overnight lows by the 21st remained above 80, but heat index values fell just shy of the local advisory criteria (111) during the afternoon of the 21st.

The 2 meter observation platform at the Santa Ana (Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge) location along the Hidalgo/Cameron County line carried heat index at or above 111 for three hours during the afternoon of the 20th, peaking at 116 at 3 PM local time before gradually falling back.  Values at the Linn/San Manuel Lower RGV NWR refuge in north central Hidalgo County peaked at 114 during the period. Overnight lows by the 21st remained above 80, but heat index values fell just shy of the local advisory criteria (111) during the afternoon of the 21st.

The 2 meter observation platform at the Falcon Lake Mesowest location near the Starr/Zapata County line carried heat index at or above 111 for nearly five hours during the afternoon of the 20th, peaking at 115 at 3 PM local time before gradually falling back.  Overnight lows by the 21st remained above 80, but heat index only briefly touched 111 for about an hour during the afternoon of the 21st.

The 2 meter observation platform at the Falcon Lake Mesowest location near the Starr/Zapata County line carried heat index at or above 111 for nearly five hours during the afternoon of the 20th, peaking at 115 at 3 PM local time before gradually falling back.  Overnight lows by the 21st remained above 80, but heat index only briefly touched 111 for about an hour during the afternoon of the 21st.
More than 2.7 inches of rain fell during a two to three hour period at the cooperative observing site in Hebbronville during the late evening of August 28th.

CoCoRaHS observers reported between 2.5 and 3 inches of rain in both Palm Valley (about 2.2 miles west of Harlingen) and Rancho Viejo from a small thunderstorm complex which moved from Port Isabel west and developed stronger in west central Cameron County during the early afternoon of the 30th. Some poor draining streets had nuisance flooding, but most locations soaked up the rainfall, which was the first of significance during the entire month and going back to July 11th for most in the area.

A very small but intense thunderstorm complex which was nearly stationary produced heavy rains near Falcon Dam along the Starr Zapata county line during the evening of September 9th. The Falcon Dam CO-OP observer reported a 24 hour rainfall of 7.70 inches.

Locally heavy rains fell across portions of Deep South Texas during the day September 10th. An upper level disturbance which moved through the County Warning Area during the day triggering showers and thunderstorms which produced locally heavy rains through the day. One observer reported 3.92 inches of rainfall during the afternoon in Cameron County two miles west of Brownsville which caused a lot of street flooding in the area. Several other observers in Cameron County reported rainfall ranging from 2.22 inches northeast of Los Fresnos to 2.78 inches three miles north of Brownsville.

The ASOS at Brownsville reported 2.72 inches of rain fell during a thunderstorm which moved through Brownsville around midnight, triggered by a weak upper level disturbance which produced locally heavy rainfall across portions of Deep South Texas during the day of September 10th.
A CO-OP observer reported 2.41 inches of rain fell during a thunderstorm which moved through the Sarita area during the early afternoon Sunday September 11th.
A National Weather service Employee reported hail up to three quarters of an inch in size fell at the Sunrise Mall in Brownsville during a thunderstorm.
The public reported hail up to three quarters of an inch in size fell during a thunderstorm. The hail was observed near the intersection of Elizabeth Street and Central Boulevard.
A trained spotter reported hail up to one inch in size fell for about 5 minutes near La Feria during a thunderstorm which moved through the area.

The public reported quarter size hail up to one inch in size fell during a thunderstorm which moved through La Feria. The hail was observed near the intersection of North Parker Road and Expressway 83 in La Feria.
The Roma Police Department in Starr County reported hail up to one inch in size fell in the city of Roma during a thunderstorm which moved through the area.
The La Feria Police Department reported winds gusts estimated to be approximately 60 miles per hour occurred during a thunderstorm which also produced pea size hail at their office.

The Roma Police Department in Starr County reported heavy rains fell during a thunderstorm which moved through the area. The rainfall produced street flooding.  Some streets were closed due to one foot of water standing in some areas.

The public reported Heavy rainfall in a thunderstorm which produced flooding on Business Highway 83 between Airport Drive and Texas. Some homes in the area were reported to have water up to the door steps. Major flooding was reported in nearby streets. Six inches of rain was estimated to have fallen during the thunderstorm. The Hidalgo County Emergency Manager reported thirteen intersections were closed due to the flooding and several cars were totaled due to the flood waters.
ASOS reported wind gusts to 60 miles per hour during a thunderstorm that moved through Cameron County.
KRGV Television station reported that the public had reported a brief touchdown of a tornado near the town of Willamar. No damage was reported and there weren���t any homes in the area.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall across the Weslaco and Mercedes areas September 22. The Emergency Manager for Weslaco reported the area near Texas and Business highway 83 had three feet of water due to the heavy rains which occurred during the afternoon.  He also reported four feet of water along the south side of Business Highway 83 from Oregon west to Westgate Drive. Other areas to the north of Business Highway 83 had widespread flooding with minor damages to some homes.

Beneficial rains which moved across Kenedy County the end of September resulted in an improvement in the drought conditions in October. Still, the long term drought which began in mid 2007 and was largely uninterrupted through 2008 as the area missed soaking rains from Dolly and other events, exceptional (D4) conditions held on near the Kleberg County line toward Baffin Bay, extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the northern one quarter of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the north central one quarter of the county through the 26th.||A frontal system dumping locally heavy rains in Kenedy County on the 26th helped to remove exceptional conditions from the northern tip of the county, with severe to extreme conditions isolated to the northern third of the County at month's end.

Beneficial rains which moved across Jim Hogg County the end of September resulted in an improvement in the drought conditions in October. Rainfall of around an inch or less across the northern third of the county maintained Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the northern half of the county, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) conditions from just south of Hebbronville east to the Brooks County line.

Beneficial rains which moved across Brooks County the end of September resulted in an improvement in the drought conditions in October. However, rainfall of generally less than an inch across the northern half of the county held Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the northern two thirds of the county, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) conditions along and north of State Highway 285 through the month.

The Port Mansfield Harbor Master reported wind gusts up to 60 miles per hour were measured during a strong thunderstorm which moved through Port Mansfield in the early afternoon.  Duration of gusts estimated by proxy with similar conditions as the line passed Laguna Madre-side locations farther north.

The Rincon Del San Jose TCOON site reported a wind gusts to 66 miles per hour during a thunderstorm which moved through the coastal areas early in the afternoon.  Note:  This location is immediately east of the Kenedy County Laguna Madre coastline and is used as a proxy to estimate winds over this area.

A Texas Coastal and Ocean Observing Network site at Baffin Bay, just a few miles northeast of Kenedy County, recorded wind gusts up to 65 mile per hour when line of strong to severe thunderstorms rapidly developed in western Kenedy County and raced east.
