Wind gusts at or above 60 mph continued until 1236 PM.  Note:  Wind gust value is used as a proxy to estimated value on the nearby promontory of northeast Kenedy County.

An amateur radio operator reported that the Isla Grande Resort weatherbug station recorded a peak wind gust of 59 miles per hour when a thunderstorm moved through the resort during the passage of a cold front.

November began warm and largely rain free across Jim Hogg County.  A cool front, with a wave of energy along it, would bring pockets of moderate rainfall to central and northern Jim Hogg County on the 19th and 20th, but the rains were not enough to allow any improvement; in fact, conditions would deteriorate one category for the final week of the month.  Severe (D2) conditions maintained across the central portion of the county, with Extreme (D3) conditions across the northern tip, including Hebbronville.

November began warm and largely rain free across Brooks County.  A cool front, with a wave of energy along it, would bring locally heavy rainfall to central and northern Brooks County on the 19th and 20th, holding the Severe (D2) drought conditions  across the north and northwestern third of Brooks County through the end of the month.  Moderate, soaking rains on November 30th and December 1st would begin to end the severe drought in early December.

November began warm and largely rain free across Kenedy County.  A cool front, with a wave of energy along it, would bring locally heavy rainfall to central and northern Kenedy County on the 19th and 20th, holding the Severe (D2) drought conditions  across the north half of Kenedy County, and a sliver of Extreme (D3) conditions from Sarita to Riviera through the end of the month.  Moderate, soaking rains on November 30th and December 1st would begin to end the agricultural (short term) drought in early December.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions returned across the northern half of Zapata County and Severe (D2) drought conditions returned across the central third of Zapata County at the end of November, areas where little rain fell even during the 19th and 20th, when welcome rains fell toward the coast.  Pockets of heavier rain on the 19th near the Starr County line by the Rio Grande kept drought from returning.  Moderate rainfall at the turn of November into December, followed by more rain and cooler temperatures, would end the agricultural drought in December.

Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions returned across all of Jim Hogg County to end November, a result of much less rainfall in the county than at locations farther east (Brooks and Kenedy), where rainfall estimates suggested between 3 and 5 inches fell in the northern halfs of these counties.  Severe conditions covered the southern two thirds of the county where Extreme conditions developed across the northern third.  Welcome rains would return to end November and begin December, hastening the end of the agricultural drought for Jim Hogg County in December.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX OUT 20 NM
events.event_narrative: The Texas coastal ocean observation network site at Baffin Bay reported wind gusts to 74.7 miles per hour the gusts occurred from 3:00 AM until at least 3:06 AM CST. Gust are estimated to be similar at the northern edge of the marine zone just south of Baffin Bay, about 3 miles away, based on nearly identical radar presentation of the storm.

Severe Drought (D2) Conditions continued across the northeast quarter of Zapata County through the month of October. A small sliver of Extreme (D3) conditions stretched just across the northeast border starting around the 20th.

A line of strong to severe thunderstorms marched through central and eastern Cameron County during the mid afternoon of October 26th.  Long duration wind gusts associated with the microburst produced peak winds of 56 mph at the Cameron County Airport, and 57 mph at the Realitos Peninsula Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network site less than 10 miles to the northeast.||NWS employees from Rancho Viejo (west of this track) and just north of Los Fresnos reported several small limbs down; an 8 to 12 inch diameter limb blown down in Rancho Viejo was rotting.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: A Texas Coastal Ocean Observing System Buoy located in Baffin Bay reported a wind gust ot 65.3 mph.  Wind gusts greater than 60 mph continued for at least 12 minutes.  Note:  Estimation of wind over the Laguna Madre just east of Kenedy County, or only 2 miles south of the buoy location, is given by proxy.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: A thunderstorm wind gust to 65.5 mph was recorded at the Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network buoy near Rincon del San Jose, beginning at 1:06 PM CST and continuing until at least 1:15 PM CST until the sensor briefly went offline.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: The Port Mansfield Harbormaster estimated a wind gust of 60 mph as a line of strong to severe thunderstorms swept across the Lower Texas coast.  Location of marine report is approximate and is a practical eastward extension of the land report, which is less than a mile from the Laguna Madre waters.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms preceded a cold front into the Lower Texas Gulf waters, producing at least 15 minutes of gale force sustained winds with gusts to storm force.  The peak gust of 53 knots (61 mph) occurred at 214 PM CST, with sustained winds of 43 knots (49 mph) lasting for at least 10 minutes beginning at 210 PM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms produced a long duration microburst as it swept across the Laguna Madre and into the Lower Texas Gulf coast.  At 154 PM CST, a 57 mph wind gust was recorded at the Realitos Peninsula Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network.  Gusts of 50 mph or greater occurred until 324 PM before the sensor temporarily became non operational.  Times are accurate within 6 minutes.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: A line of strong thunderstorms, enhanced by the strong cold front catching up to it, produced wind gusts nearing 70 mph as recorded by a Texas A&M University Automated Buoy System observation east of South Padre Island, beginning at 330 PM CST.  The microburst following the front maintained storm force gusts through at least 4 PM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: Wind gusts associated with a line of strong thunderstorms preceding a cold front increased to just over 37 knots at the Port Isabel C-MAN station, located a mile from the southmost portion of the Laguna Madre.  Gusts at or above gale force (34 knots) continued for 18 minutes, and returned an hour later as the frontal gradient moved across the area.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network location at the Realitos Peninsula recorded a wind gust just above 34 knots from a pulse thunderstorm.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A quick moving pulse thunderstorm that raced northward across the Laguna Madre produced a quick moving microburst that produced gale force gusts earlier between Port Isabel and South Padre Island also produced a brief gale force gust along the Realitos Peninsula, as recorded by the Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A developing small cluster of pulse thunderstorms moved through the south end of the Laguna Madre during the late afternoon October 25th, producing a brief downburst of gale force gusts as recorded by the Port Isabel C-MAN site.  Gusts lasted for at least six minutes.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020, approximately 40 nm east of uninhabited Padre Island east of Kenedy County, reported a wind gust near 39 knots as a morning thunderstorm briefly became intense in the Gulf of Mexico.

Light rains moved across portions of Zapata County on the 1st and again on the 4th of December. The rains, accumulating less than one inch, were too light to alleviate the drought conditions across most of the county. Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the northern one third of the County and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the central third of Zapata County the first week of December; Extreme conditions retreated to the northeast quarter of the county by the 8th.

Light to moderate rains affected Jim Hogg County on the 1st and the 4th of December, dropping measured and estimated rainfall between 1 1/2 and 2 1/2 inches.  The rains were not enough to improve the long term drought conditions across the county, but they gradually began to alleviate conditions. Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the northern third of the county and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across most of the remainder of the county through mid month.

Light to moderate rains moved across portions of Brooks County December 1st and 4th, dropping 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 inches of rainfall.  The initial rains were not enough to counter the long term drought conditions from the 2009 spring and summer, and Severe (D2) conditions would prevail across the northwestern half of the county through mid month.||A more significant rain event, dropping 1 1/2 to 3 inches across the county on the 15th and 16th, would finish the Severe drought conditions once and for all for the year by the 22nd.

Severe (D2) Drought would hang on across the northern two thirds of Zapata County during the third week of December, before light to moderate, steady rains and continued cool temperatures during that same week knocked conditions back to only moderate by the next Drought Assessment on the 22nd.

Severe (D2) Drought would continue across all but the southern tip of Jim Hogg County during the third week of December, before a period of moderate, steady rains dropped an other 1 to 2 1/2 inches from the 14th to 16th.  Combined with continued cool temperatures during that same week, drought conditions fell back to only moderate by the next Drought Assessment on the 22nd - effectively ending the 2009 drought.

November began warm and largely rain free across Zapata County.  A cool front, with a wave of energy along it, would bring pockets of moderate rainfall to southern Zapata County on the 19th, but the rains were not enough to allow any improvement across the northeast quarter of the county, where Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) conditions prevailed through the 23rd.

Daytime temperatures fell into the upper 30s to lower 40s during the afternoon of a chilly, cloudy December 4th, setting the stage for a widespread freeze overnight on the 4th into the morning of the 5th as skies cleared, winds calmed, and temperatures fell steadily from the 30s into the 20s in Brooks County.  By daybreak, lows fell to the mid or upper 20s, including 25 at the Falfurrias Cooperative station.   Estimated duration of freezing or below temperatures was 7 to 10 hours.

Daytime temperatures held in the lower to mid 40s even as skies cleared during the late afternoon of December 4th, setting the stage for a widespread freeze overnight on the 4th into the morning of the 5th as clear skies and calm winds allowed temperatures to fall steadily from the 30s into the 20s in Jim Hogg County.  By daybreak on the 5th, lows fell to the mid or upper 20s, including 26 at Jim Hogg County Airport northwest of Hebbronville and 24 at the Hebbronville Cooperative observing site.   Estimated and measured duration of 32 degree or lower temperatures was 7 to 10 hours.

Clearing skies and a chilly air mass (temperatures in the mid to upper 40s) during the afternoon on December 4th, set the stage for a widespread freeze overnight on the 4th into the morning of the 5th as winds calmed, allowing temperatures to fall steadily from the 30s into the 20s in Zapata County.  By daybreak on the 5th, lows fell to the mid or upper 20s, including 24 at Zapata County Airport in Medina, 27 at Falcon Dam in the southwest corner of the county, and 27 near Escobas.  Estimated and measured duration of 32 degree or lower temperatures was 7 to 10 hours.

Cloudy, drizzly, cold conditions (temperatures in the upper 30s to lower 40s) during the afternoon on December 4th set the stage for a widespread freeze overnight on the 4th into the morning of the 5th as skies cleared, winds calmed, and temperatures fell steadily from the 30s into the 20s in Kenedy County.  By daybreak on the 5th, lows fell to the mid or upper 20s, including 26 at the Sarita Cooperative site just east of Federal Highway 77, and 25 at Armstrong (southern half of the county).||Estimated duration of 32 degree or lower temperatures was 7 to 10 hours.

Clearing skies and a chilly air mass (temperatures in the upper 40s) during the afternoon on December 4th set the stage for a widespread freeze overnight on the 4th into the morning of the 5th as winds calmed, allowing temperatures to fall steadily from the 30s into the 20s in Starr County.  By daybreak on the 5th, lows fell to the mid or upper 20s, including 24 at Falcon Lake near the Zapata County line, and 26 at the Rio Grande City Cooperative Observer location.  Estimated and measured duration of 32 degree or lower temperatures was 7 to 10 hours.||The freeze was accompanied by several hours of frost, which combined with calm winds minimized notable damage to temperature sensitive crops.  Unprotected plants at individual residences may have received some damage, but costs were unknown.

After a cloudy, cold afternoon on December 4th (temperatures in the lower 40s), skies rapidly cleared during the early evening as winds calmed, setting the stage for a widespread freeze overnight on the 4th into the morning of the 5th.  Temperatures fell to or below freezing before midnight in rural locations north and west of the urban Federal Highway 83 corridor, as well as in rural pockets along the border.  By daybreak, low temperatures ranged from the mid and upper 20s north of Edinburg to 30 to 32 in urban areas, including Weslaco, McAllen, and Pharr.  Aforementioned rural pockets near the Rio Grande fell to the mid 20s, as well.||Duration of the freeze across northern Hidalgo County, as well as rural pockets near the river, was measured and estimated to range from 7 to 10 hours.||In urban areas, away from known heat islands, 32 degree or lower temperatures lasted from 1 to 3 hours, except 3 to 5 hours in the urban/rural interface in such areas as Edinburg and Alton. ||The freeze was accompanied by several hours of frost, which combined with calm winds minimized notable damage to temperature sensitive crops.  Unprotected plants at individual residences may have received some damage, but costs were unknown.

After a cloudy, cold afternoon on December 4th (temperatures in the upper 30s to lower 40s), skies rapidly cleared during the early evening as winds calmed, setting the stage for a widespread freeze overnight on the 4th into the morning of the 5th.  Temperatures were estimated to fall to or below freezing around or a little midnight in rural locations north west of Federal Highway 77 corridor, probably a bit later at night east of the highway toward the coast. By daybreak, low temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to around 30 degrees.  Measured low temperatures were 28 at Raymondville (Cooperative), and 26 degrees 4 miles southeast of Linn (in Hidalgo County just west of the Willacy County line).||Duration of the freeze west of Federal Highway 77 was estimated at 5 to 8 hours; duration east of Federal Highway 77 was estimated at 2 to 5 hours.||The freeze was accompanied by several hours of frost, which combined with calm winds minimized notable damage to temperature sensitive crops.  Unprotected plants at individual residences may have received some damage, but costs were unknown.

After a cloudy, cold afternoon on December 4th (temperatures in the upper 30s to lower 40s), skies rapidly cleared during the early evening as winds calmed, setting the stage for a freeze during the morning hours of the 5th.  Temperatures were estimated to fall to or below freezing around or a little after 4 AM on the 5th toward the immediate coast.  By daybreak, the measured low temperature in Port Mansfield was 30 degrees. Slightly lower temperatures may have occurred at locations surrounding Port Mansfield; temperatures likely remained above freezing on Laguna Madre and the uninhabited South Padre Island to the east.||The freeze was accompanied by frost, which combined with calm winds minimized notable damage to temperature sensitive crops.  Unprotected plants at individual residences may have received some damage, but costs were unknown.

After a cloudy, cold afternoon on December 4th (temperatures in the upper 30s to lower 40s), skies rapidly cleared during the evening as winds gradually calmed, setting the stage for a freeze during the morning hours of the 5th.  Temperatures were estimated likely fell to, or below, freezing around or a little after 530 AM on the 5th toward the immediate coast.  By daybreak, the measured low temperatures on the west side of the Laguna Madre ranged from 30 degrees in Port Isabel and Bayview to 32 degrees at the Laguna Atascosa/Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge near the Laguna Madre southeast of Arroyo City. Slightly lower temperatures may have occurred in normally colder locations away from the bay.  In the Town of South Padre Island, warming influence from the Bay and Gulf kept temperatures from dropping below the mid 30s.||The freeze was accompanied by frost, which combined with calm winds minimized notable damage to temperature sensitive crops.  Unprotected plants at individual residences may have received some damage, but costs were unknown.

A drizzly, chilly afternoon on December 4th featured temperatures falling into the upper 30s to around 40 before nightfall.  Clearing skies and calming winds right after dark set the stage for temperatures to steadily fall to or below freezing overnight.  By daybreak on the 5th, readings ranged from the upper 20s to around 30 area wide.  A daily record low was tied in Harlingen (31 degrees) and broken at the Valley International Airport (29 degrees).  ||Duration of freezing or lower temperatures varied by location.  Rural locations in southwestern and northwestern Cameron County likely had 8 hours or more of freezing temperatures; Valley International Airport, just east of populated Harlingen, had more than 6 hours of freezing temperatures.  Farther south and east, Brownsville International Airport had an hour of freezing temperatures; Los Fresnos had only two hours of freezing temperatures.||The freeze was accompanied by several hours of frost, and, with calm winds, there were no reports of notable crop damage in Cameron County.  Residential damage to temperature-sensitive plants likely occurred, but the extent was unknown.

Rain, heavy at times between the pre dawn hours and mid afternoon on the 16th, accumulated to more than 2 1/2 inches between midnight and noon at McAllen's Miller Airport and likely across nearby areas including Pharr and Edinburg.  The rainfall caused widespread, nuisance (minor) flooding of poor drainage roadways especially in Pharr and Edinburg during the daylight hours of the 16th, slowing traffic.  Event totals in Hidalgo County were among the highest in the Rio Grande Valley, including 4.22 inches at La Joya, 4.40 inches a little north of Pharr, and 3.66 inches at the McAllen/Miller Airport.

Rain, heavy at times during the daylight hours of the 16th, accumulated between 1 1/2 and 2 1/2 inches between 6 AM and 6 PM in a pocket of central Cameron County along and near Highway 77, between Brownsville and Harlingen. The rainfall caused areas of nuisance (minor) flooding of poor drainage roadways in the area during the daylight hours of the 16th, slowing traffic.  Event totals in Cameron County included 4.52 inches in Rancho Viejo, 3.82 inches near Brownsville, and 3.79 inches just west of Harlingen.

Rain, heavy at times during the daylight hours of the 16th, accumulated an estimated 1 1/2 to 2 inches between 6 AM and 6 PM in along the Highway 77 corridor of Willacy County.  High standing water occurred in these areas.  Event totals in Willacy County included 3.33 inches in Raymondville, and 2.92 inches in Port Mansfield.
Wind gusts, estimated between 45 and 50 mph based on a 323 AM peak gust observation at McAllen's Miller airport, helped to uproot a 40 foot tall live oak tree in Pharr.

Wind gusts, estimated between 44 and 48 mph based on observations at Harlingen/Valley International Airport earlier (353 AM, 48 mph) and Brownsville/South Padre Island Airport a bit later (431 to 438 AM, 44 mph), blew down a 50 foot section of aging fence along Alton Gloor Blvd. in the north side of the city at around 425 AM, and blew off shingles at an older apartment building near the intersection of Price Road and Old Port Isabel Highway several minutes later.

The second wave of gusty winds during the afternoon of Christmas Eve blew down a parking light pole onto several vehicles in McAllen, causing unknown damage to them, roughly around 3 PM CST.  Winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph in the area from noon until 4 PM, with the strongest recorded at McAllen's Miller Airport at 253 PM CST.

Despite abundant mid level cloudiness, shallow modified arctic air was able to reach into northern Zapata County before daybreak on the 8th, and continue through just before noon before temperatures rose a little above 32 degrees.

Despite abundant mid level cloudiness, shallow modified arctic air was able to reach into northern Jim Hogg County before daybreak on the 8th, and continue through just before noon before temperatures rose a little above 32 degrees. Low temperatures at Hebbronville reached 30 degrees between 8 and 930 AM.

Temperatures fell below freezing during the mid evening of the 8th, and ultimately fell into the lower 20s across much of Jim Hogg County for more than 5 hours between 2 and 8 AM on the 9th.  Freezing conditions lasted for 13 and a half hours; a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, lasted up to 9 hours.  Low temperatures reached 24 at Hebbronville Airport, but 19 at the cooperative location in town, where the sensor is at eye level and less affected by mixing winds.||Damage to grazing land was unknown as of this writing.

Temperatures fell below freezing during the mid evening of the 8th, and ultimately fell into the lower 20s across much of Zapata County for more than 6 hours between 2 and 9 AM on the 9th.  Low lying areas in central and southern Zapata County dropped into the upper teens, with the Zapata airport in Medina hitting 19 degrees.  Freezing conditions lasted for 13 and a half hours; a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, lasted up to 9 hours.  ||Damage to grazing land, as well as any local tender vegetation near the river, was unknown as of this writing.

Temperatures fell below freezing shortly before midnight on the 8th, and ultimately fell into the lower and mid 20s by daybreak on the 9th across much of Brooks County.  Freezing temperatures lasted up to 10 hours near Falfurrias and in locally colder pockets elsewhere, with a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, lasting between 4 and 8 hours, with the longest duration in aforementioned colder pockets.  The cooperative station at the Hollywood Hunting Camp near Falfurrias dipped to 20 degrees; Brooks County Airport dropped to 24.  ||Early planting of rangeland known as coastal grasses was severely damaged from the Freezes on the 9th and 10th.  Damage to these grasses, as well as any local tender vegetation, was unknown as of this writing.

Temperatures fell below freezing during the mid to late evening on the 8th, and ultimately fell into the lower 20s by daybreak on the 9th across much of the King Ranch.  Low lying pockets dropped into the upper teens, including Armstrong. Freezing temperatures lasted up to 11 hours, with a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, estimated to last 4 to 7 hours, longest in sheltered, wind protected areas.  ||Early planting of rangeland known as coastal grasses was severely damaged from the Freezes on the 9th and 10th in Brooks County, and similar damage may have been observed in Kenedy County.  Damage to these grasses, as well as any local tender vegetation, was unknown as of this writing.

Temperatures fell below freezing during the mid to late evening on the 8th, and ultimately fell to between 20 and 25 by daybreak on the 9th across inland Willacy County.  Raymondville fell to 21 shortly after daybreak.  Freezing temperatures likely lasted up to 10 hours, with a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, estimated to last 3 to 6 hours, longest in sheltered, wind protected areas.  ||Crop damage was unknown as of this writing, but information from surrounding areas with similar planting suggest minor damage to dry land crops and more significant damage to tropical, temperature-sensitive plants.

Temperatures fell below freezing around or shortly after midnight on the 9th, and ultimately fell into the mid or upper 20s by daybreak across coastal Willacy County.  Port Mansfield fell to 26 shortly after daybreak; similar or slightly cooler readings were likely immediately west, and closer to 32 degrees right at the coast line.  Freezing temperatures likely lasted up to 8 hours, with a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, estimated to last 2 to 4 hours, longest in sheltered, wind protected areas.  ||Crop damage was unknown as of this writing, but information from surrounding areas with similar planting suggest minor damage to dry land crops and more significant damage to tropical, temperature-sensitive plants.

Temperatures fell below freezing around or shortly after midnight on the 9th, and ultimately fell into the 20s by daybreak across inland Cameron County.  A record low was set at Harlingen/Valley International Airport when the low fell to 25 degrees.  Elsewhere, readings ranged from 26 at the Harlingen Cooperative station just west of the Airport, to 29 in Brownsville and 28 in Mercedes. Freezing temperatures likely lasted up to 9 hours, with a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, estimated to last 3 to 6 hours, longest in sheltered, wind protected areas.  ||Crop damage was unknown as of this writing.  Information from the Farm Services Agency of Cameron County suggested only minor damage to citrus plants, with most fruit and trees surviving the freeze.  Tropical tender vegetation did not fare as well, and there was substantial damage to sugar cane crops in the southwestern portion of the county.||Sugar damage estimates will be available later in the spring of 2010.

Temperatures fell below freezing by 1 AM on the 9th, bottoming out in the upper 20s to around 30 by daybreak across Coastal Cameron County.  Lows ranged from 28 at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge to 32 on South Padre Island. Freezing temperatures likely lasted up to 7 and one half hours.  A few pockets may have received an hour or two of a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees.||Crop damage was unknown as of this writing.  Information from the Farm Services Agency of Cameron County suggested only minor damage to citrus plants, with most fruit and trees surviving the freeze.  Tropical tender vegetation did not fare as well, but significant damage was not reported near the coast.

Temperatures fell below freezing during the late evening of the 8th, and ultimately fell to the lower 20s for most of Starr County by daybreak.  Coldest temperatures were found near ground level in low lying areas, including 18 at the Falcon Lake remote automated weather station location, and 21 at Rio Grande City. Freezing temperatures likely lasted up to 10 hours, with a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, estimated to have lasted 4 to 8 hours in rural, low lying areas, and 3 to 6 hours elsewhere, generally between 2 and 8 AM.||Crop damage was unknown as of this writing.  Information from the Farm Services Agency of Starr County suggested some crop and grassland damage, but no reports were available as of this writing.||Sugar cane damage estimates will be available later in the spring of 2010.

Temperatures fell below freezing by late evening on the 8th, and bottomed out between 20 and 25 across most of Hidalgo County.  Coldest locations, with sensors at eye level, recorded lows of 19 degrees.  These included both Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge locations near Linn/San Manuel (north portion of the county) and Santa Ana (along the Rio Grande just east of Pharr).  Other low temperatures include 22 at McCook, 25 at Edinburg, 26 at Weslaco, and 29 at McAllen's Miller Airport.||Freezing temperatures likely lasted up to 10 hours, with a hard freeze, defined as temperatures below 28 degrees, estimated between 4 to 8 hours in rural, low lying areas and 2 to 4 hours elsewhere, generally between 2 and 8 AM.||Crop damage was unknown as of this writing.  Information from the Farm Services Agency of Hidalgo County suggested minor damage to citrus plants and fruit, with most fruit and trees surviving the freeze.  Tropical tender vegetation did not fare as well, and there was substantial damage to sugar cane crops.||Sugar damage estimates will be available later in the spring of 2010.

Under clear skies and light winds, temperatures dropped sharply after sunset on the 9th, and reached 32 by mid evening.  Light winds continuing overnight allowed a more gradual fall across northern Jim Hogg County overnight, where Hebbronville airport fell to 27 degrees, and the cooperative site (observation at eye level) fell to 22 degrees.   Freezing temperatures lasted at least 10 hours, with hard freezes, or temperatures below 28 degrees, estimated to last from 4 to 8 hours, most prevalent in low lying, wind protected areas - between 1 and 7 AM.||Damage to grazing lands or tender vegetation was unknown as of this writing.

Clear, calm conditions allowed temperatures to plummet after sunset on the 9th across the Rio Grande Plains of Zapata County, reaching the freezing point by mid evening on its way down to near 20 degrees in rural pockets, and 20 to 25 degrees elsewhere, by daybreak on the 10th.  Temperatures touched 19 at Zapata County Airport in Medina and fell to 25 near Escobas; freezing temperatures lasted up to 10 and one half hours, with a hard freeze, or temperatures below 28 degrees, lasting between 4 and 8 hours in most areas.||Crop damage, particularly to grazing land, was not reported as of this writing.

Clear, calm conditions allowed temperatures to plummet after sunset on the 9th across the hunting grounds and King Ranch of Brooks County, reaching the freezing point by late evening on its way down to near 20 in rural pockets, and upper 20s elsewhere, by daybreak on the 10th.  Temperatures touched 20 at the Falfurrias cooperative site at the Hollywood Hunting Camp, but only fell to 28 at the Brooks County airport, exposed to more wind. Freezing temperatures lasted up to 9 and one half hours, with a hard freeze, or temperatures below 28 degrees, lasting between 3 and 6 hours in locations away from the city of Falfurrias.||Damage to newly planted coastal grasses was noted by the Farm Services Agency of Brooks and Jim Hogg County in eastern Brooks County from the freezing conditions between the 8th and 10th.  Dollar values were not available as of this writing.

Clear, calm conditions allowed temperatures to plummet after sunset on the 9th across the King Ranch, reaching the freezing point toward midnight, and bottoming out between 25 and 30 in most areas by daybreak on the 10th.  Temperatures touched 26 at Armstrong, and 30 degrees a bit east of Sarita.  While freezing temperatures lasted an estimated 8 hours or so, an overnight light wind from the Gulf kept a widespread hard freeze from developing.  Estimates from the cooperative sites suggest 2 to 4 hours of hard freeze, or temperatures below 28 degrees, during the pre dawn hours of the 10th.||Information on any grazing land damage was not known as of this writing.

Clear, generally calm conditions allowed temperatures to fall rapidly after sunset on the 9th, with readings reaching the freezing point shortly after midnight on the 10th and continuing for an hour after daybreak on the 10th.  Low temperatures early on the 10th range from the lower and mid 20s well west of Highway 77 toward Hidalgo County, to around 30 just east of Highway 77.  Raymondville fell to 29 degrees; freezing temperatures lasted generally from 4 to 8 hours, with a local hard freeze, or temperatures below 28, estimated to last from 2 to 4 hours across the western portion of the county.||While additional minor damage to dryland crops and tender vegetation was likely, the overall impact of the freeze for Willacy County was that of a bullet dodged since temperatures between each cold night rebounded into the upper 40s and lower 50s during the afternoon of the 9th.

Clear, generally calm conditions allowed temperatures to fall rapidly after sunset on the 9th. Near the coast, a light breeze from the Gulf arrived overnight, increasing humidity and holding temperatures from dropping much lower than the freezing point.  Along the coast and Laguna Madre, temperatures did not reach 32; however, locations within 5 miles of the coast likely fell below 32 for 2 to 4 hours.||No additional significant damage was likely with this freeze as temperatures hovered near 32 degrees rather than falling well below.

Clear, generally calm conditions allowed temperatures to fall rapidly after sunset on the 9th. Near the coast, a light breeze from the Gulf arrived overnight, increasing humidity and holding temperatures from dropping much lower than the freezing point.  Along the coast, temperatures did not reach 32; however, locations within 5 miles of the coast likely fell below 32 for 2 to 4 hours.  This included Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge, which dropped to 31 after 2 AM and remained between 31 and 33 degrees until after sunrise.  The Cameron County Airport near Bayview dropped to 30 and also held near 32 or just above for much of the night.||No additional significant damage was likely with this freeze.

Clear, generally calm conditions allowed temperatures to fall rapidly after sunset on the 9th. By mid to late evening, rural pockets and sheltered locations had fallen below 32 degrees, and temperatures would continue to drop well into the 20s overnight.  Elsewhere, after an sharp evening drop, readings leveled off for the rest of the night as a light north to northeast wind combined with a modifying air mass kept readings in the upper 20s to around 30 for most areas.  Wind protected locations fell to between 20 and 25 once again.  Duration of freezing temperatures ranged up to 11 and one half hours in some cold pockets, with a number of areas having a hard freeze, or temperatures below 28 degrees, for between 3 and 7 hours but locally up to 10 hours. ||Eye level temperatures in sheltered locations included 23 degrees at the Lower RGV National Wildlife Refuge near Linn/San Manuel, and 20 degrees at the Lower RGV National Wildlife Refuge at Santa Ana, just east of Pharr.  Urban locations either touched freezing or stayed above, including Edinburg at 28 degrees, Weslaco at 32 degrees, and McAllen Miller Airport at 35 degrees. ||Additional damage was likely with this second night of freezing temperatures, particularly to sugar cane but also to some citrus leaves and fruit, and tropical tender vegetation.  Damage reports will be available later this spring.

Clear, generally calm conditions allowed temperatures to fall rapidly after sunset on the 9th. By late evening, rural pockets and sheltered locations had fallen to 32 degrees, but temperatures would level off the rest of the night as a light north wind combined with a modifying air mass kept reading in the upper 20s for most areas.  Exceptions included wind sheltered locations, which dropped to between 20 and 25 once again.  Duration of freezing temperatures ranged up to 10 hours, with some areas receiving a hard freeze, or several hours of temperatures below 28.  Harlingen/Valley International Airport fell to 27 degrees.||While most areas did not receive a hard freeze, sheltered pockets had generally between 3 and 6 hours, particularly in western and northern Cameron County.||Additional damage was likely with this second night of freezing temperatures, particularly to sugar cane.  Reports on sugar damage will be available later this spring.

Clear, generally calm conditions allowed temperatures to fall rapidly after sunset on the 9th. By mid to late evening, many locations, particularly away from Highway 83, had fallen below 32 degrees, and temperatures would continue to drop well into the 20s overnight.  Wind protected locations fell to between 20 and 25 once again.  Duration of freezing temperatures ranged up to 10 and one half hours in some cold pockets, with a number of areas having a hard freeze, or temperatures below 28 degrees, for between 3 and 7 hours but locally up to 10 hours. ||Eye level temperatures in sheltered locations included 24 degrees at the Falcon Lake remote automated observing system location near the Zapata County line and near Rio Grande City. Inferred low temperatures across the east side of Starr County were in the mid or upper 20s.| |Additional damage was likely with this second night of freezing temperatures, particularly to any sugar cane, but also to some citrus leaves and fruit, and tender tropical vegetation.  Damage reports will be available later this spring.

A wildfire, started at a ranch containing dense, dry brush, quickly exploded to more than 1,000 acres shortly after noon on March 22nd.  Surface winds from nearby locations were light and variable during the onset and rapid growth phase, but relative humidity was estimated to have fallen to 10 to 15 percent.  Light March rainfall combined with several drying cold fronts may have contributed to relatively quick drying of open grassland with the increasing sun angle.||Fire departments from San Isidro, San Manuel, Edinburg, Pharr, Palmview, Rio Grande City, and Texas Parks and Wildlife all assisted in fighting the fire, with the aid of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

The Chief of Police in the City of Zapata reported one and one half feet of water was flowing on Alamo St. and State Highway 16. The arroyo at Highway 16 and Carla Street overflowed its banks, with one and one half feet of water flowing over the road there as well. Heavy creek and arroyo flooding was also reported at the Manuel Medina Addition colonia, south of Zapata County Airport.

Pendleton Park and City Park in Harlingen was under water. One lane of North Farm to Market Loop 499 was closed. Local newspapers reported water surging through city streets between 6 and 7 PM. Power was knocked out at Valley International Airport from 7 until around 830 PM from unknown causes related to the storm.  A daily record of 2.77 inches of rain fell in a very short time at Valley International Airport; radar estimates suggested 3 to 4 inches fell in areas which flooded.

Rainfall of more than 4 inches in a little more than an hour produced flash flooding from Mission to McAllen between 730 and 830 PM. Local television news reported one home with water flooding the ground floor, and vehicles submerged, in Mission, from a combination of poor drainage and the blinding rains. Floodwaters covered a driveway, reaching the garage of a home on Highland Park Ave. in Mission. State Road 107 and Farm to Market 495 each were closed with up to 2 feet of water covering them. Flooding on the frontage road of Expressway 83 between 23rd Avenue and Ware Road produced water up to the windshields of dozens of cars in McAllen. Rainfall reached 2.46 inches in McAllen/Miller Airport, 3.40 inches at the nearby cooperative station, 3.74 inches in Mission, and 4.08 inches just northeast of Mission, all falling in a little more than an hour. The aftermath of the frontage road flooding was documented by video posted on YouTube.  View the video at http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6viYuz8VBW8 .

Quarter sized hail was reported in Mission in two locations along or near Griffin Road (FM 495): At the intersection of Griffin and Glasscock, and just north of Griffin on Bryan Road.  Events occurred between 755 PM and 803 PM CDT.
Wind Gust measured in the City of Mission.

Heavy rainfall left 1 to 1 1/2 feet of water along Paredes Line Road, between Paseo Plaza near the intersection of Ruben Torres Blvd. (FM 802) and just north of CSR Blvd. and the Emerald Valley subdivision.  Storm estimated rainfall, which was very localized, was 2.5 inches.  Boundaries from these storms would later feed into more significant activity in Hidalgo County during the evening.
The public reported ping pong size hail fell across FM 490 east of Hargill.

Broadcast media reported a roof was blown off a mobile home during a thunderstorm that produced high winds across the area.  Radar indicated a couplet of winds, as well as a reflectivity overhang, had moved across the area, suggesting a possible tornado.  There were no confirmed reports of a tornado, however.

The Hidalgo County Emergency Manager reported strong winds occurred during a thunderstorm which knocked down some power lines in Weslaco. A funnel cloud was reported by the emergency manager approximately two miles west of Weslaco as the thunderstorm moved through the area. Peak winds of 43 mph were reported at the Mid Valley Airport, 2 miles east of Weslaco, estimated at around 812 AM CST.

A 20 year old cottonwood tree, renowned and visited often for having a purported image of the Virgin Mary on its bark, was blown down by strong thunderstorm winds estimated to have occurred between 905 and 910 AM CST at the intersection of East Levee and 10th Streets in downtown Brownsville.  Numerous, varying sized limbs were blown down in Greater Brownsville, with peak gusts recorded at the Brownsville/South Padre Island Airport reaching 54 mph at 928 AM CST, 5 miles east of downtown.

Winds within and ahead of the squall line increased to severe levels as they swept across Cameron County.  Racing from from west northwest to east southeast across the County, the winds, both measured and estimated at 60 mph, knocked down hundreds of different sized tree limbs and caused power outages from Santa Rosa through Harlingen and San Benito.  The ASOS (KHRL) at the Valley International Airport recorded a 60 mph gusts, and the public estimated a 60 mph gust moments later in San Benito.

The thunderstorm complex continued to generate strong, damaging winds as it moved across southeast Cameron County, affecting Bayview, Port Isabel, and South Padre Island.  The strongest wind core appeared to rip through Port Isabel across the southern portion of the Town of South Padre Island.  At Port Isabel, numerous power outages were the result of power lines and poles blown down at several locations throughout the city. ||As the storm reached South Padre Island, the U.S. Coast Guard Station located in the Bayside recorded a 64 mph wind gust (at 936 AM CST, a six minute recorded observation).  At nearly the same time (937 AM CST), a 60 mph gust was recorded by a Citizen Weather Observer Program sensor on Sheepshead Street. In the same area, palm trees were blown down along Coral Street; large metal signs were blown from their mounts along the Queen Isabella Causeway Bridge, and more power lines and a transformer were blown down at the intersection of Constellation Dr. and Laguna Boulevard, all between 930 and 940 AM CST (end time estimated by radar).

The squall line that tore through the heart of populated Hidalgo County dropped very heavy rainfall in an hour or less, creating numerous reports of urban flooding with embedded, more dangerous flash flooding especially in poor drainage locations of Mission, McAllen, and Edinburg. Four inches fell at the McAllen Cooperative (water plant) location, 2.82 inches at McAllen/Miller Airport, and 2.95 inches just southeast of McAllen.  In Mission, the Fire Department reported several roads throughout were under two to three feet of water.  In McAllen,  the City transportation department reported 7 to 9 automobiles stalled in floodwaters halfway up the doors at 10th and Pecan.  A video submitted via Twitter showed the depth of the water, at least 2 feet in some places, on the sides of the road.  Attendees of the Texas Hurricane Conference in McAllen reported significant high water along the Expressway 83 Frontage Road during the same time.  ||In Edinburg, University Drive was blocked by high water just east of the courthouse due to high water, which threatened businesses but appeared to have remained outside of them.
The Hidalgo County Emergency Manager reported hail up to one and one half inches in diameter fell at the La Quinta Inn on south 10th Street during a thunderstorm which moved through the area.

Slow moving and redeveloping thunderstorms dumped torrential rainfall in and near Falfurrias during the afternoon of May 25th. Urban flooding began in poor drainage locations soon after the rain began, and a little after 1 PM a semi trailer careened off Highway 281, destroying a health care clinic which was later condemned.  The driver sustained a minor head injury.||As the rain continued, about a foot of standing water covered a 500 foot section of business Federal Highway 281 on the south side of town. Traffic slowed to a crawl, with several vehicles stalled in the middle of the road. There were several other areas of Business Federal Highway 281 that had at least 8 inches of water on the roadway for 300 to 400 foot stretches. Firemen rescued an elderly woman from her home on Noble street which had 4 inches of water inside the house; fire fighters on a nearby location on Noble Street reported nearly waist���deep water while trudging to the house. ||There were several other areas in Falfurrias that had up to two feet of water on the roadway or in the alleys. A media report indicated 3 to 5 feet of water flooding on other streets, including some water reaching the lower floors of a Motel 9 on S. St. Mary's Street in the south portion of town.||Impressive rainfall totals were reported along and near State Highway 285. The Falfurrias cooperative observation at the Hollywood Hunting Camp just west of town blew away the entire monthly average with nearly 6 inches of rain during the event (5.94). An unconfirmed report of at least 8 inches was received from another location near Falfurrias, which was within reason based on the nature of the storms.||Flooding along and near Federal Highway 281 was exacerbated by construction of an elevated highway; dirt berms and dirt dams trapped water that would otherwise have drained more efficiently.
An off duty Central Region National Weather Service Employee reported a waterspout that briefly moved onshore near Port Isabel.  No damage was reported.

A squall line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved through northern and central Brooks County during the late evening of June 2nd, producing gusty winds which knocked down some power lines in Falfurrias.  Law enforcement measured a gust of 54 mph at 922 PM CST as the line plowed through.
Law enforcement reported that several power poles were struck by lightning late Wednesday evening throughout Hebbronville and western Jim Hogg County.

The Hidalgo County Sheriff's office reported that a large fire developed near McCook when a fuel storage tank was struck by lightning as a band of thunderstorms developed and raced across the area around midnight on June 3rd.

Law enforcement reported that four utility poles were toppled by strong gusty winds which occurred during a squall line which moved through Hebbronville late Wednesday evening June 2nd.  There was a brief power loss affecting the entire city of Hebbronville as a result of the utility pole damages.  At 834 PM CST, the public reported estimated gusts of 50 mph on the leading edge of the line.  At Hebbronville Airport (about 4 miles northwest of town), a peak gust of 38 mph was recorded at 820 PM CST.
Hail up to one inch in diameter fell south of Old 83 Highway south of Donna during a thunderstorm that moved through the Donna area in the afternoon.

A prolonged intense updraft was nearly stationary in the Donna-Alamo-San Juan area for nearly an hour, and at least two known quarter sized hail reports were received by the NWS office in Brownsville.  The first occurred at 357 PM CST along Business Highway 83 in San Juan, reported by a trained spotter, and a second occurred in Alamo at around 410 PM CST, reported by the general public. Hail of equal of larger size may have continued beyond this time, but no further data were available as of this writing.
A local broadcast meteorologist reported a wind gust of 62 miles per hour during a strong pulse thunderstorm that affected Pharr.

Several roads were under 2 to 3 feet of water from Donna to Alamo during the late afternoon commute after torrential downpours from nearly stationary strong to severe thunderstorms dropped an estimated 4 to 6 inches of rain in 2 hours or less.  Photographs verified the high water, including some where water was encroaching on property in both areas.

A microburst tore through a colonia (migrant community) between Donna and Alamo, causing significant damage to mainly mobile homes and other unanchored structures. Two mobile homes were completely destroyed, and one under construction wood framed home collapsed.  One outbuilding overturned.  A third mobile home lost its roof.  Each of the destroyed mobile homes were older and had questionable structural integrity.  One of the homes rolled and was not secured properly. The other had a residential addition, which was destroyed.||In the tipped over home, a mother, three children, and an infant were inside but fortunately were left uninjured.  Photographs showed most small trees remained standing, as were nearby single family homes.  Estimates from damage photos, media coverage, and emergency management quick response surveys suggested a pulse gust between 65 and 70 mph caused the damage.||Slightly lower winds knocked down several trees in nearby Alamo.

A structure fire was reported in Weslaco near the intersection of Salinas and Mile 12 North Road. The fire began after a thunderstorm moved through the area during the afternoon producing numerous lightning strikes in which a lightning bolt started the blaze.

A tornado was reported in the Hebbronville area by the border patrol and public.|A tornado touched down in the Hebbronville area just after 5 pm, flipping a tractor trailer, uprooting trees, snapping large limbs, and causing a gas leak.  The tornado knocked out power to at least 1762 AEP Power customers, more than half of the town. The tornado formed along a remnant shear axis left behind after Hurricane Alex dissipated in Mexico.  The elevated humidity levels combined with daytime heating and low to mid level turbulence likely contributed to the development of the tornado producing thunderstorm.||A preliminary assessment of damages in Hebbronville indicated areas of EF-1 (85 to 105 mph) winds. The EF-1 damages occurred in the central and southeast areas of Hebbronville into the center of town, EF-0 damages occurred from the center of town to areas northwest of town which included areas around Hebbronville High School.  ||The tornado formed to the southeast of Hebbronville between 450 and 5 pm. The tornado crossed State Highway 285 about 1/2 mile east of the intersection with State Highway 16, and entered a Texas Department of Transportation maintenance yard, tearing a section off a roof and collapsing a section of a metal parking area. It continued to the north northwest into a residential area, taking the roof off one modular home, snapping several power poles, rolling a mobile home onto its roof, and damaging numerous mesquite trees. The tornado continued moving northwest toward downtown and knocked down numerous power lines, then struck a grocery store and blew a billboard onto a few parked cars. A loaded tractor trailer was rolled onto its roof and against the grocery store. The tornado then moved north northwest, causing lesser tree damage along Maria and Frans Avenues. The weakening tornado crossed over a school, with no notable damage. It then moved by Hebbronville High School���s Gruy stadium, bending a goalpost and knocking over some fencing around tennis courts just west of the school campus. The tornado then lifted, with no damage noted beyond this location.||Considerable damage was rated EF-1 from the southeast side of Hebbronville until reaching downtown, with wind speeds of 90 to 100 mph. EF-0 damage (below 85 mph) was seen from northwest of downtown to the area around the high school.
Nickel sized hail was reported in San Carlos, 4 miles east of Edinburg.

Trees and large limbs were blown down on various streets in Raymondville.  Time and duration are estimated by radar, based on core of estimated winds between 50 and 52 knots a few thousand feet above the surface.

Persistent heavy thunderstorms dropped several inches of rainfall from Hebbronville to the northeast Jim Hogg/Brooks County line for a couple hours around sunset.  Emergency management reported extensive street flooding in downtown Hebbronville, but water heights and structural damage information was unavailable as of this writing.  Radar estimated heavier rains along and north of Highway 285 east of town.  Removing possible hail contamination, perhaps 6 inches fell in the northeast quarter of the county, similar to observed values just north in Duval County.  The cooperative observation at Hebbronville (north side of town) recorded 2.32 inches.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: A developing line of thunderstorms accelerated into the Lower Texas Gulf waters east of Kenedy County, producing a 35 knot wind gust during the mid morning hours of May 15th.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network location at the Realitos Peninsula recorded nearly a half hour of gale force wind gusts associated with an intensifying and slow moving thunderstorm. Peak winds of nearly 39 knots occurred at 624 AM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network site at Baffin Bay, just a few miles north of the Kenedy/Kleberg County line, recorded more than a half hour of nearly uninterrupted gale force wind gusts just after midday.  The wind surge was from the southeast, a result of outflows behind an intense squall line which had moved off the coast more than an hour earlier.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network site at Realitos Peninsula reported nearly 12 minutes of unbroken wind gusts in excess of 45 knots. Peak winds were 48.2 knots, or 56 mph, at 706 AM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The U.S. Coast Guard station along the bayside of South Padre Island recorded a peak gust of 55.6 knots as the squall line and associated microburst raced across the Lower Texas coast.  Duration of gale force or greater gusts was nearly a half hour; in fact, the sensor recorded storm force (48 knots) gusts through the entire period.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: The U.S. Coast Guard station along the bayside of South Padre Island recorded a peak gust of 55.6 knots as the squall line and associated microburst raced across the Lower Texas coast.  Duration of gale force or greater gusts was nearly a half hour; in fact, the sensor recorded storm force (48 knots) gusts through the entire period.  The combined data from land and marine sites, as well as rapid propagation across a one-half mile wide barrier island, strongly suggests that similar winds continued at least several nautical miles into the Lower Texas Gulf waters east of South Padre Island.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The NOAA C-MAN station just southeast of Port Isabel recorded a peak gust of 39.1 knots as the squall line and associated microburst raced across the Lower Texas coast.  Duration of gale force or greater gusts was a little more than 15 minutes; protection from nearby land and buildings may have reduced the speeds when compared with those recorded at the fully exposed U.S. Coast Guard site at South Padre Island (55.6 knots).

The cooperative observer in Hebbronville recorded 4.47 inches of rain in several hours as a cluster of slow moving storms moved across the Brush Country of Deep South Texas into the King Ranch region of Brooks and Kenedy County.  This one day rainfall was well above the monthly average and shattered the single day record for May 25th.  Urban type nuisance flooding occurred in town, with no threat to property.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020 recorded a 10 minute period of wind gusts of 43 to 44 mph (38 knots) as squall line of thunderstorms progressed into the Lower Texas Gulf waters before 11:59 PM on June 2nd.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network Station at Baffin Bay, just 3 miles north of the Kenedy/Kleberg County line adjacent to Laguna Madre, recorded near storm force wind gusts at 2318 CST June 2nd, during a peak period of Gale Force of higher gusts that lasted for a half hour.  These winds were likely associated with a mesoscale pressure gradient between a post-squall line meso-high and a wake low, arriving more than a half hour after similar peak gusts associated with the line itself.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network station at Baffin Bay, just 3 miles north of the Kenedy/Kleberg County line, recorded a peak gust of 44 knots as the squall line raced across the Lower Texas Gulf coastal waters during the late evening of June 2nd.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: The cooperative observer (Harbormaster) at Port Mansfield recorded a 42 knot (48 mph) wind gust as a squall line raced into the Lower Texas Gulf Waters during the late evening of June 2nd.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network measuring station at Realitos Peninsula recorded a peak gusts of 36.7 knots (42 mph) during the late evening (CST) on June 2nd as a squall line raced into the Lower Texas Gulf coastal waters.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Automated Surface Observing Sensor at Cameron County Airport, approximately 4 miles west of Laguna Madre (in Bayview), recorded peak winds to gale force or higher (39 to 44 mph) from 1139 PM CST until 1153 PM CST.  The South Padre Island Coast Guard station also reported peak gusts at or above gale force, at around 1149 PM CST until approximately 1156 PM CST (interpolated).  These gusts occurred as a vigorous squall line rolled into the Lower Texas Gulf waters.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: The South Padre Island Coast Guard station also reported peak gusts at or above gale force, at around 1149 PM CST until approximately 1156 PM CST (interpolated).  These gusts occurred as a vigorous squall line rolled into the Lower Texas Gulf waters.  Note:  Distance from the Coast Guard Station to the Gulf shoreline is less than 1 mile; given the rapid movement of the squall, proxy data were used to determine gale force gusts over the open Gulf adjacent to the Town of South Padre Island.
Penny sized hail was reported in McAllen on Cynthia Street near the Wellness Center in the northeast portion of the city.
NWS Student Volunteer (Oklahoma University) reported penny size hail near Edinburg.

A persistent funnel cloud was viewed by two local residents in the Weslaco/Donna area during the early evening of June 7th.  A resident in Donna reported a funnel on the south side of town reaching halfway to the ground at 420 PM CST.  Another resident on the southwest side of Weslaco viewed another funnel, possibly from the same parent storm, 12 minutes later southwest of the intersection of Hopper Road and 34th Street on the southwest side of town.  The second funnel lasted only a minute. Touchdowns were not witnessed in either case.

Feeder bands from Hurricane Alex began producing tropical storm force wind gusts during the late morning and early afternoon of June 30th in Cameron County.  As the center of Alex neared landfall about 100 to 110 miles south of the Cameron County/Mexico border, sustained winds peaked between 38 and 40 mph, with gusts peaking between 45 and 50 mph, during the late afternoon and evening (4 to 8 PM CST).  ||The strong and sometimes persistent winds briefly knocked out power to at least 8,000 City of Brownsville (and nearby communities) customers, and hundreds of tree limbs were blown down, many of them small to medium sized.  Minimal property damage was noted from the winds as of this writing, but did include a fireworks stand turned over, a fence blown down, and a car moved across the road by a pulse gust associated with a feeder band at 1130 AM CST along Wilson Road in Harlingen.  There was no confirmation of a tornado with this report, but several funnel clouds were reported by the public at various times during the afternoon, including near La Feria (1225 PM CST), the Harlingen/Valley Airport (158 PM CST), 346 PM CST near Santa Rosa, and 6 PM CST in Brownsville.

Feeder bands from Hurricane Alex began producing tropical storm force wind gusts during the very early morning of June 30th, continuing through mid evening in Coastal Cameron County.  As the center of Alex neared landfall about 100 to 110 miles south of the Cameron County/Mexico border, sustained winds peaked between 39 and 51 mph, with gusts peaking between 56 and 66 mph, during the late afternoon and evening (4 to 8 PM CST).  The peak sustained wind, 51 mph, was recorded at the National Ocean Service (NOS) station at the southeast tip of Port Isabel; a peak gust of 66 mph was recorded along the higher span of the Queen Isabella Bridge, with 62 mph recorded also at the NOS location and 56 mph on South Padre Island.  The Automated Service Observing System station at Cameron County Airport in Bayview recorded peak sustained winds of 39 mph, with a peak gust of 53 mph at 711 PM CST.  A single peak pulse gust to 51 mph was recorded at this location at 216 AM CST, from a fringe band.  ||No power outage estimates were available, except a quote of 1,441 in the American Electric Power (AEP) service area which includes Port Isabel. Structural damage was not significant from the tropical storm force winds alone.

Feeder bands from Hurricane Alex began producing tropical storm force wind gusts during the late morning and early afternoon of June 30th in Coastal Willacy County.  Outer feeder bands well ahead of the center of Alex produced sustained winds of 45 mph near Arroyo City (Cameron County, just south of the Willacy line) at 142 PM CST; a peak gust of 64 mph occurred in a outer band thunderstorm cell at 912 AM CST.  Gusts reached 47 mph at 5 PM CST at Rincon del San Jose (in the Laguna Madre of Kenedy County); interpolating between the two locations supports occasional sustained winds near Port Mansfield and other locations toward the coast of Willacy County.||No power outage estimates were available for the area, and there were no known reports of structural damage in Port Mansfield.

Feeder bands from Hurricane Alex began producing tropical storm force wind gusts during the late morning and early afternoon of June 30th in Coastal Kenedy County.  Outer feeder bands well ahead of the center of Alex produced sustained winds of 36 mph at Rincon del San Jose Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) platform shortly after noon, with a peak gust of 47 mph at 5 PM CST (along the Laguna Madre).  Stronger winds reached the Baffin Bay TCOON platform (3 to 4 miles north of the Kenedy County shoreline) by late afternoon, with sustained winds reaching 41 mph with a gust to 64 mph a little after 4 PM.  ||Sustained winds were below tropical storm strength over inland Kenedy County, interpolated from the nearby Kingsville Naval Air Station in Kleberg County, just 20 miles north.

The tornado appeared to begin near a home between Old Military Highway and Mary Lee Court, lifting a few old shingles before knocking down several large limbs in the front yard. The track continued across Old Military Highway, tipping over a water kiosk and tearing off numerous mesquite limbs before moving across Military Highway (Federal 281), where it blew down smaller mesquite trees before crossing a field and tipping over a trailer at a 45�� angle onto a recreational vehicle. Damage continued into a tree stand before ending. Well built homes in the neighborhood sustained no damage; power lines remained up and power never went out as the storm raced by.||Estimated winds were 60 to 65 mph.

A fence was reported blown in the middle of the street, and tree limbs were knocked down, behind a convenience store at the intersection of State Highway 100 and Musina Street in Port Isabel.  Damage occurred within a wind speed couplet embedded within a rain band, which had a trajectory that later produced a stronger tornado in San Pedro (southwest Cameron County) about 25 minutes later.  Estimated wind speed was between 50 and 55 mph.
Texas Military Forces reported a small, brief touch down near Highway 77 north of Raymondville.  No damage was reported as of this writing.

Widespread urban flooding affected an area from west of Brownsville through Brownsville, Olmito, Los Fresnos, and near Bayview during the afternoon and into the overnight hours of June 30th and into July 1st (see July report for continuation of event).  Much of the flash flooding, where water reached 3 feet or higher or threatened structures, occurred in typically poor drainage locations in all areas.  ||Total rainfall for the entire event ranged from 8 to near 10 inches in the areas that tended to flood, with an estimated 5 to 7 inches occurring during and just prior to the significant flood impacts.  Damage from freshwater flooding directly due to Alex was unknown as of this writing; a best estimate is provided.

Widespread urban and poor drainage flooding affected an area from Mercedes and Weslaco northwest to Edinburg, likely including known flood problem areas in Elsa, Edcouch, La Villa, and other places where drainage remained an issue nearly two years after Dolly. The flooding began toward sunset after more persistent heavy rains arrived in the area, and continued beyond the end of June and into July (see July report for additional times).  Much of the flash flooding, where water reached 3 feet or higher or threatened structures, occurred in these typically poor drainage locations in all areas.  ||Total rainfall for the entire event ranged from 8 to near 10 inches in the areas that tended to flood, with an estimated 4 to 7 inches occurring during and just prior to the significant flood impacts.  Damage from freshwater flooding directly due to Alex was unknown as of this writing; a best estimate is provided.||Crop damage, specifically sorghum (irrigated/dryland) losses, due to the widespread heavy rains affecting the crop at a key growing period at more than 1800 locations, approached $10 million.

More than 6 inches of nearly steady rain in less than 12 hours created poor drainage and flash flood conditions in the Town of South Padre Island, where main and secondary roads became impassible for a period of time during the afternoon of June 30th.  While water lapped at structures along Padre Boulevard (Highway 100), no significant damage was reported from the freshwater rainfall as of this writing.

Cooperative observers and adjusted radar rainfall estimates suggested between 6 and 8 inches of rain fell across northeast and central Willacy County associated with feeder bands from Hurricane Alex, mostly on June 30th.  As of this writing, no significant flash flooding was reported, but heavy rains caused local minor urban-type and field flooding which continued into July 1st.

Increasing and persistent east to northeast flow built seas above 22 feet east of the Lower Texas coast on June 30th with a swell period of more than 12 seconds brought a minor to moderate storm surge to South Padre Island and neighboring communities along Laguna Madre Bay, including Port Isabel, Laguna Heights, and Laguna Vista.  Peak surge reached 3.52 feet (4.19 total tide MLLW) at the Port Isabel tide station at 630 CST; a 3.44 foot surge (3.95 total tide MLLW) was recorded on the other side of the bay at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station.||On South Padre Island, the building waves pushed water through public beach access points 4 through 6 north of the resort area, temporarily closing State Highway 100 in these areas. Water reached into the dunes but did not breach them completely; beach surf was reported at 7 to 9 feet with very rough and confused waves.  The event and impact on the beach was similar to that from Gustav on Labor Day (September 1) 2008; erosion was minor to moderate and the beach recovered quickly.||In Port Isabel, reports and visual evidence showed flooded streets and water around raised homes in prone-areas, particularly along and near Island Avenue.  Only minor damage was reported in these areas.

Widespread urban and poor drainage flooding affected an area from Mercedes and Weslaco northwest to Edinburg, likely including known flood problem areas in Elsa, Edcouch, La Villa, and other places where drainage remained an issue nearly two years after Dolly. The flooding began toward sunset after more persistent heavy rains arrived in the area, and continued into the very early morning hours of July 1st (see June report for start times).  Much of the flash flooding, where water reached 3 feet or higher or threatened structures, occurred in these typically poor drainage locations in all areas.  ||Total rainfall for the entire event ranged from 8 to near 10 inches in the areas that tended to flood, with an estimated 4 to 7 inches occurring during and just prior to the significant flood impacts.  Damage from freshwater flooding directly due to Alex was unknown as of this writing. The primary estimate is shown in the June report.

Widespread urban flooding affected an area from west of Brownsville through Brownsville, Olmito, Los Fresnos, and near Bayview during the afternoon and into the very early morning hours of July 1st (see June report for starting time of event).  Much of the flash flooding, where water reached 3 feet or higher or threatened structures, occurred in typically poor drainage locations in all areas.  ||Total rainfall for the entire event ranged from 8 to near 10 inches in the areas that tended to flood, with an estimated 5 to 7 inches occurring during and just prior to the significant flood impacts.  Damage from freshwater flooding directly due to Alex was unknown as of this writing. For the July data, only a very small value is included, as the primary flood impacting rains fell on June 30th.

Repeating thunderstorm cells dropped locally heavy rainfall, causing nuisance urban type flooding near Rio Grande City during the late afternoon of July 6th.  The cooperative station at Rio Grande City recorded 1.1 inches of rain but radar estimated heavier rains of 3 inches or more from just north of La Grulla to a few miles north of Escobares.

Heavy rains of 1 to locally 3 or more inches fell roughly between Brownsville and the southwest corner of Cameron County during the mid morning of July 8th as weak Tropical Depression #2 made landfall along the Lower Texas coast.  Rainfall of more than 3 inches was recorded at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport over the course of two days, with 1.71 inches falling on the 8th.  Minor, nuisance urban-type flooding was reported in southern Cameron County as the rains moved through.

Heavy rains, estimated by radar between 2 and 4 inches and measured by both cooperative and CoCoRaHS rain gages (between 1.84 and 2.97 inches), including 2.41 inches in Mercedes, 2.24 inches in Edinburg, and 2.47 inches in Weslaco.  The core of the heavy rain fell between 1 PM and 330 PM CST and included Progresso, Weslaco, Donna, and Alamo.  Nuisance urban-type poor drainage flooding likely occurred in areas of heavy rain; there was no indication of any enhanced flooding along the main and north floodway between Progresso and Mercedes.

Incredible rainfall estimated to be more than 50 inches in around 10 days' time between June 30th and July 9th across the front range and peaks of the Sierra Madre Oriental in Coahuila Province, Mexico, ultimately flowed through the entire Lower Rio Grande basin for much of the summer of 2010. The rare and extreme event rapidly produced major flooding along the river in Starr County, the result of planned dam releases from Falcon International Reservoir, which lasted for nearly a month, beginning on July 9th and continuing through August 3rd.  ||Releases of water from reservoirs behind dams on both sides of the border began soon after the heaviest rains from Alex ended. On July 4th, releases began at the Marte R. Gomez Reservoir, flowing into Mexican Floodways but also toward the Rio Grande bordering Starr and western Hidalgo County. On July 5th, water levels had increased sufficiently at Amistad Dam, located much farther upstream near Del Rio, Texas, to begin releases down the river. By the 7th, with waters from Amistad having created major flooding in and near Laredo, Falcon Reservoir, located along the Rio Grande including Starr and Zapata County, began releasing water. ||The initial rate of 15,000 cubic feet per second (cfs) was initially within capacity of the United States side of the flood control system, and the expectation for a potentially critical flood area between Falcon and Anzalduas Reservoir just upstream from Mission (Hidalgo County) was high water, but little if any flooding. That would quickly change on July 8th, when releases from Falcon Dam were more than doubled to 39,700 cfs (1125 cubic meters per second, cms). Soon after these releases were increased,the river quickly rose from just above flood stage (50 feet) at Rio Grande City to above major flood stage (53 feet) on July 9th.  The time it took to rise from flood stage (1320 CST July 8th) to above major flood (630 AM July 9th) was a little more than 17 hours.    ||By July 14th, outflow from Falcon Dam was raised to 60,000 cfs (1700 cms) in order to relieve pressure on the dam from the reservoir pool, which had risen steadily above conservation stage of 301.2 feet at 822 AM CST July 12th.  This release rate would both raise and swell the Rio Grande downstream; reports from local emergency management noted the river up to 2 miles wide in some spots. Prior to the peak outflow, the river crested at 57.63 feet at 6 AM July 11th, the second highest level ever recorded.  A secondary peak occurred five days later - 57.31 feet at 4 PM CST July 16th.  ||All this water would continue to remain high and spread, and hundreds, of structures were impacted during the event.  The city of La Grulla was under mandatory evacuation by July 15th as increasing water levels and currents threatened more of the community than earlier in the week; these orders would continue until July 22nd when the waters began to recede slowly. As a precautionary measure in the city of Roma, three small subdivisions located in the low lying areas and along the bank just south of the Port of Entry were placed under mandatory evacuation. These included De La Cruz sub-division about (20 to 25 homes), Campo Verde (4 homes), and Garza sub-division (1 home).  By July 22nd, the flooding in Starr County had impacted 178 homes/businesses, including 65 in La Grulla and 39 in Roma.  166 families required temporary housing.  Preliminary damages to highways and bridges in Starr County was at $19 million; preliminary public and private property estimates were listed at an additional $18 million.  Agricultural damage was also notable in flooded areas.  Full accounting of both crop and property damage will be available during autumn, 2010.

Incredible rainfall estimated to be more than 50 inches in around 10 days' time between June 30th and July 9th across the front range and peaks of the Sierra Madre Oriental in Coahuila Province, Mexico, ultimately flowed through the entire Lower Rio Grande basin for much of the summer of 2010. ||The rare and extreme event rapidly produced major flooding along the river in southwest Hidalgo County, the result of planned dam releases from Falcon International Reservoir.  River flooding likely began along the banks of the Rio Grande in Hidalgo County less than 18 hours after flooding began at river side locations in Starr County.  Affected communities included Cuevitas, Havana, and the south portions of La Joya and Penitas - locations not protected by the Lower Rio Grande Valley Flood Control Project levee system. The city of Los Ebanos, surrounded on three sides by the river, was most impacted by the flood, which was well over a mile wide for several weeks.  Significant flooding continued into the first days of August.||Mandatory evacuations were initiated on July 12th for Los Ebanos, in the southwest corner of the County; the evacuation level was reduced to voluntary on July 20th. The early evacuations proved fateful, as pressure on a retention pond dike caused it to rupture, spilling water into some neighborhoods and forcing most residents to leave the area.
