Two young men drowned when a combination of along shore current with a possible embedded rip current moved them into deeper water east of Public Beach Access Point #2 on South Padre Island during the afternoon of July 4th.  While wave height and swell period had decreased markedly in the days following Hurricane Alex (June 30/July 1), enough residual wave and current action remained to create potential deadly conditions on what is normally one of the busier weekends of the summer season.||One of the men drowned between 2:36 and 2:50 PM CDT; the other perished four days later after falling unconscious and ultimately having life support turned off due to brain death.  Water conditions suggested a moderate rip current risk with a moderate along shore current, based on sea height of more than 5 feet, a swell period near 7 seconds, and an average period between 4 and 5 seconds, at a representative buoy about 66 miles northeast of the Town of South Padre Island.

A local surfing instructor and trained spotter found a man unconscious in the water after hearing shouts from concerned family members. Though the victim was estimated to be a weak swimmer, moderate to strong rip currents likely caused the fatality, based on surf heights still 4 to 6 feet in the area, offshore sea heights 5 to 6 feet at the estimated time of death, and swell period of 6 to 7 seconds, all from a primary east-southeast swell.

A young man was found unconscious in the surf immediately offshore of Isla Blanca Park on South Padre Island during the mid to late afternoon of July 14th.  The man was likely a poor swimmer, and succumbed to either a rip current enhanced by water movement near the jetties.  While seas and surf had fallen to moderate levels - offshore seas had dropped below 5 feet and peak swell period was around 6 seconds - enough residual dangerous surf and current may have contributed to the death.

Incredible rainfall estimated to be more than 50 inches in around 10 days' time between June 30th and July 9th across the front range and peaks of the Sierra Madre Oriental in Coahuila Province, Mexico, ultimately flowed through the entire Lower Rio Grande basin for much of the summer of 2010. The rare and extreme event ultimately led to increasing water levels at both Amistad International Reservoir (northwest of Del Rio, TX) and Falcon International Reservoir (adjacent to Zapata County), the result of inflow from Mexican tributaries and upstream reservoirs along the Rio Salado and Rio Conchos in Nuevo Leon and Coahuila State, Mexico.  ||At Falcon International Reservoir, where inflow from both the upstream Mexican tributaries and Amistad International Reservoir, which had begun releases of 35,000 cubic feet per second (cfs) on July 5th, the pool level rose above conservation stage (301.2 feet) during the morning of July 12th, and would continue a steady rise, reaching moderate flood stage (306.7 feet, the point where impacts begin along the shoreline) during the pre-dawn hours of July 14th. Despite an increase in releases from 39,700 cfs to 60,000 cfs from the Reservoir, the pool level continued to rise,  peaking at a new record stage of 309.31 feet during the evening of July 17th. The continued high pool level required maintaining releases of 60,000 cubic feet per second for nearly 14 consecutive days, in order to maintain a manageable water level at the dam. At Falcon, the previous record of 308.1 feet (set in October, 1958) was not only broken, but the pool level remained above the prior record for nearly 7 full days, from around 130 AM CDT on July 15th through 930 PM on July 22nd.  The pool level was above conservation level (301.2 feet) from the morning of July 12th through 4 PM on August 13th, more than a month. ||Releases were gradually lowered toward the end of the month as the pool level began to fall more steadily heading into early August.||During the period of time when the reservoir was in moderate flood, or above 306.7 feet, structures and infrastructure was impacted along the shoreline.  At least 33 homes had some level of water incursion; damages were still being assessed as of this writing.  Lakefront roads were under some water for weeks as well.  Individual damage reports included an estimated $35.5 thousand to water pumps and related equipment.  Business losses also mounted at the Reservoir, where bass fishing is popular.  At least $15.3 thousand in losses was reported at Falcon State Park. ||As of late September, a best estimate for property and infrastructure damage in Zapata County was at least $1 million; more is likely when the assessments are completed in autumn 2010.

Hermine arrived in fits and starts, with frequent gusty feeder band showers followed by relatively calm conditions through the day and early evening of September 6th. Between 830 and 9 PM CST, the action got underway as the central core of Hermine brought a rapid increase in sustained winds and gusts, along with increasingly heavy rainfall. Between 10 PM and 11 PM CST, the northern doughnut crossed the Rio Grande over lower populated southwest Cameron County. Meanwhile, intense feeder bands east of the center, where some of the strongest winds were sampled, pounded Brownsville with sustained winds of 40 to 55 mph and gusts as high as 69 mph at the Brownsville/SPI International Airport. Between midnight and 1230 AM, a very intense band would reform around the center, curling from just south of Harlingen to north of Brownsville. This band would cross Harlingen just prior to 1 AM, and produced near hurricane force gusts (72.5 mph) along with brief sustained winds of 59 mph (at 1158 and 1159 PM CST, respectively), which damaged a number of roofs, knocked down limbs and uprooted trees, and wiped out power to more than 14,000 residents, many in the Harlingen/San Benito area.  In all, between 46,000 and 50,000 customers in Cameron County were without power during the peak of the storm, including those in the AEP Texas, Brownsville PUB, and Magic Valley Electric Co-op service areas.||After the inner core of Hermine sliced through, winds quickly diminished below tropical storm force from south to north across the county, between 1230 AM CST near the river and 130 CST near the Willacy County line.||Significant damage included roof collapses to at least one apartment complex in Brownsville, and the La Casita apartments in Harlingen, displacing at least two families. A large part of an industrial building roof collapsed in north Harlingen, and other poorly constructed lightweight roofs were blown off in Brownsville and the Port of Brownsville. Hundreds of medium to large tree limbs fell along the Highway 77 corridor from Brownsville through San Benito and the central and east side of Harlingen.  ||Boaters, particularly Mexican shrimping vessels, did their best to seek refuge in the Port of Brownsville prior to the arrival of the storm.  The sharp increase in east winds ahead of the center's arrival drove breaking waves down the 17 mile Brownsville ship channel; some waves broke as high as the windows of the Harbormaster office. Sixty���four vessels reached the Port, but 5 others became stranded at the coast, including three running aground in Texas and two in Mexico when buoys floated toward the beach and guided the boats toward the rocks.  Each boat was able to beach safely, with no human casualties.

After ripping Harlingen's Valley International Airport with 72.5 mph wind gusts just prior to midnight CST (6 miles south of the Cameron/Willacy county line, the inner core of Hermine waned for a few moments before reintensifying in southern Willacy County, ultimately slamming through Raymondville at around 1 AM with wind gusts estimated just below hurricane force (70 mph). Widespread damage included hundreds of snapped limbs, dozens of uprooted trees, power outages to 75 to 80 per cent of the county, and destruction of several poorly constructed roofs and lean���tos. Feeder bands scraping along the Lower Texas Coast, first producing sustained winds generally around 50 mph gusting to more than 60 mph along and near the Cameron County coastline, scooted through Coastal Willacy County around and a bit after midnight on September 7th.  Peak sustained winds of 52 mph gusting to 64 mph at Realitos Peninsula (about 5 to 8 miles south of the county line) likely continued toward the Port Mansfield area (based on winds of 48 gusting to 58 mph at Rincon del San Jose, along the Kenedy County Laguna shoreline 15 miles north of the Willacy/Kenedy County line).  ||AEP Texas reported 4400 customers without power during the peak of the storm; most were likely in the Raymondville area where structural damage was most severe but there were reports of power outages in Port Mansfield as well.

The core of still-intense Hermine moved along and just west of Federal Highway 77 through the west section of the King Ranch in Kenedy County, likely bringing continued sustained tropical storm force winds between 40 and 50 mph with gusts to 60 mph or higher over the very rural county during the pre dawn hours of September 7th.  Farther east, feeder bands continued to produce sustained tropical storm force winds between 40 and 50 mph with gusts near 60 mph, as evidenced by reports at Rincon del San Jose (midway up the Laguna Madre in the county; 48 mph gust 58 mph at 100 CST) and at Baffin Bay Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (44 mph gust 56 mph at 324 CST). The core of still-intense Hermine moved along and just west of Federal Highway 77 through the west section of the King Ranch in Kenedy County, likely bringing continued sustained tropical storm force winds around 40  mph with gusts to 50 mph or higher over rural northeastern Brooks County during the pre dawn hours of September 7th.  There was a sharp drop off in winds to the west of the small core; the Brooks County Airport just east of Falfurrias reported a peak gust just at tropical storm force (39 mph) at 245 AM CST.  However, in Jim Wells County, Alice International Airport recorded peak winds of 39 mph with gusts to 54 mph between 440 and 553 AM CST.  ||Damage has not been estimated in Brooks County as of this writing.

Torrential and quick hitting rainfall associated with persistent feeder bands around the middle core of Tropical Storm Hermine left widespread farm/field flooding across extreme northeast Cameron County from late night into the pre dawn hours of September 7th.  Bias corrected radar estimates, combined with an observed report of 7.73 inches 9.4 miles northeast of Rio Hondo, indicated 6 to 8 inches fell in the area.  With most of the fields plowed over, damage from the flooding may have been minimal.  However, high standing water was discovered at the edge of FM 507 just across the Willacy County line 12 to 15 hours after the worst of the rains had fallen, indicating a brief period of true flash flooding was likely.

Torrential and quick hitting rainfall associated with persistent feeder bands around the middle core of Tropical Storm Hermine left widespread farm/field flooding across extreme northeast Cameron County from late night into the pre dawn hours of September 7th.  Bias corrected radar estimates, combined with an observed report of 7.73 inches 9.4 miles northeast of Rio Hondo, indicated 6 to 8 inches fell in the area on both sides of the northeast Cameron/southeast Willacy County line.  With most of the fields plowed over, damage from the flooding may have been minimal.  However, high standing water was discovered at the edge of FM 507 just in Willacy County line 12 to 15 hours after the worst of the rains had fallen, indicating a brief period of true flash flooding was likely covering some of the Farm to Market Roads, and a number of unimproved County Roads.

As Hermine quickly scooted along and just west of Federal Highway 77 in Kenedy County, surface winds shifted sharply from east to south, channeling higher tides brought into the Laguna Madre during the evening of September 6th and pushed water levels sharply higher in the thinner portion of the waterway, perhaps starting in Willacy County but definitely observed at both Rincon del San Jose and Baffin Bay (Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network locations).  At Rincon del San Jose, the water level rose over 6 feet and reached nearly 7 feet at around 300 CST - between 3 and 4 feet above predicted levels.  ||While no flooding was observed - the area is completely undeveloped along the Padre Island Seashore - the surge was notable.

Upper level energy, low level convergence, and a possible overnight low level jet stream of extremely moisture laden air from the Gulf of Mexico produced prolonged torrential rains across south central Cameron County between 2 and 7 AM CST September 19th.  The area shifted to the east and northeast between 7 and 8 AM CST, but not before dumping 5 to 7 inches of rain from Brownsville to San Benito and creating extensive flooding, impacting perhaps 100 or more structures, particularly in poorly draining areas.  ||Impacts included: Up to 60 homes with water incursion in Colonia Galaxia in West Brownsville along Military Highway; several homes with water in them in the nearby subdivision of Quail Hollow; 37 residents evacuated from 9 flooded homes in Laureles (2.5 miles northwest of Los Fresnos); several homes flooded in the Green Valley Farms area along FM 510 near San Benito, including one location where 17 small mixed-breed dogs were rescued.  Dozens of roads were closed temporarily or, in some cases, through the day.  Notable closures included Paredes Line Road just north of Ruben Torres in Brownsville, Pablo Kisel near the Morrison Blvd. intersection in Brownsville, FM 1575 near/at State Highway 100 in Los Fresnos, and portions of State Highway 345 between San Benito and Rio Hondo.  The Frontage Road near Price Road, along Federal Highway 77 in Brownsville had 2 to 3 feet of water well after the rains ended; notable poor draining roads in downtown Brownsville had similar high water.||Though the rains ended between 8 and 9 AM CST, significant poor drainage flooding continued through 11 AM CST and pockets of flooding remained into the morning of September 20th.  Dozen of pumps equipment were borrowed from Hidalgo County to assist with clearing water in poor drainage locations for the next few days.||Damage estimates will be into the $millions [final numbers available later this autumn].  Fortunately, no fatalities or injuries were reported as a direct consequence of the rains.

Heavy rainfall associated with a slow moving convergence zone slid east from what had been a train of 5 to 7 inches in 5 hours a bit farther west in Cameron County (Brownsville to San Benito).  Between South Padre Island and Laguna Atascosa/Arroyo City, measured and estimated 3 to 5 inches of rain produced more nuisance flooding with up to 2 feet of water covering Padre Boulevard (Town of South Padre Island), a known poorly draining road which frequently experiences minor flooding.  As of this writing, no significant damage was reported from the heavy rains in these areas.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020 recorded peak wind gusts of 38 and 39 knots as a thunderstorm cluster crossed overhead for 13 minutes.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network site at Realitos Peninsula recorded a peak wind gust of 37 knots at 1242 PM CST, with gusts above 35 knots continuing until an estimated 1251 PM CST before diminishing as a band of intense showers moved along the Laguna Madre.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A local charter boat captain witnessed at least four weak waterspouts approximately 15 miles northeast of Port Isabel during the early afternoon of October 2, 2010.  The spouts were small and not associated with thunderstorms, but did appear from dark bases along a line of moderate cumulus.  The spouts lasted for an estimated 35 minutes before lifting or dissipating.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network site at Baffin Bay, approximately 3 miles north of the Kenedy/Kleberg County line in the Laguna Madre waters, had a 6 or more minute period of gale force or higher gusts as the leading edge of a thunderstorm cluster raced through.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network site at Rincon del San Jose, in Laguna Madre halfway up Kenedy County, had a 12 or more minute period of gale force or higher gusts as the leading edge of a thunderstorm cluster raced through.  This was part of the same cluster which produced Gale Force Gusts about an hour earlier across Laguna Madre at the Kenedy/Kleberg County line.

A poorly designed roof was ripped off a mobile residential trailer just north of Weslaco during the late morning of Thanksgiving Day.  At the time of the incident, sustained winds of 31 mph gusting to 41 mph were occurring at Weslaco/Mid Valley Airport, less than a mile to the west.  The Automated Weather Observing System wind gust corroborated the estimate provided to local news media, 45 mph.

Near calm winds, clear skies, and a dry cool air mass allowed temperatures to fall steadily during the evening and overnight of November 26th and 27th.  Low temperatures at Brooks County Airport just southeast of Falfurrias hovered just above 32 degrees, while the cooperative site at the Hollywood Hunting Camp about 2 miles west of town recorded a low of 31 degrees. Proxy locations among many radiational cooling locations on the King Ranch in Kenedy County (Armstrong and east of Sarita) and in northern Hidalgo County (Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge) had minimum temperatures in the upper 20s, suggesting at least 3 hours of freezing or lower values in much of Brooks County.

Near calm winds, clear skies, and a dry cool air mass allowed temperatures to fall steadily during the evening and overnight of November 26th and 27th.  While low temperatures at Hebbronville hovered just above 32 degrees,  proxy values among known radiational cooling locations in Brooks (Hollywood Hunting Camp Cooperative), Zapata (Airport), and Starr (Falcon Lake) Counties showed temperatures falling into the upper 20s to around 30, suggesting at least 3 hours of freezing or below values across the southern two thirds of Jim Hogg County.

Near calm winds, clear skies, and a dry cool air mass allowed temperatures to fall steadily during the evening and overnight of November 26th and 27th.  By 130 AM, the typically colder Zapata Airport, located northeast of the Medina Addition, had fallen below freezing; the temperature would flirt with freezing with numerous observations at or below 32 through 730 AM, and a minimum temperature of 29 degrees.  The Remote Automated Weather Station at Falcon Lake, at the border of Starr and Zapata County, also fell to 29, with around 3 consecutive hours below 32 from 430 until 730 AM.

Near calm winds, clear skies, and a dry cool air mass allowed temperatures to fall steadily during the evening and overnight of November 26th and 27th.  By 430 AM, the Remote Automated Weather Station at Falcon Lake, at the border of Starr and Zapata County, also fell below 32 degrees and would bottom out at 29, with around 3 consecutive hours below 32 from 430 until 730 AM.  Proxy observations in northern Hidalgo and Zapata County, along with a number of known radiational cool spots in central and northern Starr County, argue for a slightly longer duration of time at or below 32 degrees, estimated to start around 3 AM CST.

Near calm winds, clear skies, and a dry cool air mass allowed temperatures to fall steadily during the evening and overnight of November 26th and 27th.  The typically well radiating soil of the King Ranch allowed the coldest temperatures of the region to be recorded, with 26 degrees at the Lebh Shomea House of Prayer east of Sarita, and 29 degrees in Armstrong (south central portion).  The Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge in northeastern Hidalgo County recorded 28 degrees, less than 10 miles from the Kenedy County border, starting just before 3 AM.

Temperatures dipped to 32 just before midnight on December 1st at Zapata County Airport near Medina, and would fall farther, reaching 24 degrees before daybreak.  At Falcon Lake Remote Automated Weather Station in Starr County, just across the County Line, recorded 24 as well, with 7 hours of freezing or below temperatures.  The Falcon Dam cooperative site also fell below freezing, reaching 31 degrees for a few hours.

Temperatures dipped to 32 just after midnight on December 1st at the Falcon Lake Remote Automated Weather Station in western Starr County, just across the Zapata County line, bottoming out at 24 with 7 hours of freezing or below temperatures.  The nearby Falcon Dam cooperative site also fell below freezing, reaching 31 degrees for a few hours, and Rio Grande City reached at least 30 degrees at around daybreak.  Similar temperatures are assumed to have occurred across the bulk of the county north and northeast of these locations, based on these and other proxy observations.

Temperatures dipped to 32 for just under 3 hours at the Jim Hogg County Airport northwest of Hebbronville. [The cooperative site was unavailable as of this writing].  Based on proxy observations in Brooks, northern Hidalgo, Starr, and Zapata County, interpolation among them suggest low temperatures across much of the County may have reached the upper 20s, with freezing temperatures lasting up to 5 hours.

Temperatures dipped to 32 by 3 AM at the Brooks County Airport just east of Falfurrias before the sensor went out of service.  The low temperature at the cooperative site at Hollywood Hunting Camp was 31 degrees; proxy observations from Kenedy County (Sarita; 28 degrees and Armstrong; 26 degrees) as well as Linn/San Manuel (10 miles south of the County line) which also dropped to 26 degrees with 8 hours of freezing or below, can be interpolated to assume widespread, long duration freezing temperatures elsewhere in Brooks County.

The cooperative observer at Armstrong (southern portion of the county) and east of Sarita, at the Lebh Shomea House of Prayer, recorded low temperatures of 26 and 28 degrees, respectively, around daybreak on December 1st.  Based on Automated Weather Observing System and Remote Automated Weather Stations in Brooks and Hidalgo County, as well as the Automated Surface Observing System at Kingsville (dropping to 29 degrees for two hours), interpolated information suggest up to 6 hours of freezing temperatures on the King Ranch.

Rural areas of Hidalgo County, accounting for more than half of the surface area, fell to or below freezing for several hours after midnight and just beyond daybreak.  The Remote Automated Weather Station at San Manuel dipped to 26 degrees for nearly 8 hours; the location at Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge east of Pharr fell to 29, with 5 hours of 32 degrees or lower.  The cooperative observer at San Manuel recorded 30 degrees.  Populated centers in south Central Hidalgo County remained just above freezing.

The combination of extremely low humidity (10 percent), recently cured fuels from earlier dry weather on November 30th and a dry freeze earlier on the 1st, and a tractor driving through high grass and producing sparks set off a blaze which would spread rapidly and become a 2,000 acre conflagration on the Burns (Encinitos) Ranch, mainly in Southwestern Brooks County along FM 755.  The fire, thankfully, was contained and controlled before reaching any oil tankers on the grounds of the 38,000+ acre ranch.  ||Twenty-four fire departments, as well as fire fighters from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the Texas Forest Service, helped quell the fire during the early morning hours of December 2nd. Firefighters from Brooks, Hidalgo, Starr, Jim Hogg, and other locations were staged on 50 vehicles through the event.||Damage estimates were unavailable as of this writing.

Freezing temperatures likely covered the majority of eastern Brooks County on December 9th, based on interpolation of proxy observations from Falfurrias Cooperative (29), the Remote Automated Weather Station near San Manuel (northern Hidalgo, 27), and cooperative observations at Sarita (30) and Armstrong (28) on the King Ranch in Kenedy County.

Freezing covered the western two thirds of Kenedy County (King Ranch) early on December 9th.  Cooperative observations at Sarita (30) and Armstrong (28) were recorded on the King Ranch in Kenedy County; the  Remote Automated Weather Station near San Manuel, 10 miles southwest of the county line, reached 27 for a full 7 hours (1 AM to 8 AM CST).

The cooperative observer at Sarita recorded a low temperature of 30 degrees around or just before daybreak; similar or lower temperatures were likely at Armstrong, whose observation was missing as of this writing. Proxy locations at the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge (10 miles southwest of the Kenedy/Hidalgo line) and Falfurrias cooperative station at the Hollywood Hunting Camp just west of town (27) support four hours of freezing temperatures across most of the King Ranch.

The cooperative observer at the Hollywood Hunting Camp just west of Falfurrias recorded a low of 27 degrees.  Proxy locations in Kenedy County (Lebh Shomea House of Prayer, 30) and northern Hidalgo County (Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge near San Manuel, 29, for three hours) support several hours of freezing temperatures across the Brooks County brush country.  In addition, dew points in the upper teens to lower 20s supported wet bulb readings in the mid to upper 20s.  Prolonged low wet bulb temperatures are known to create a proxy freeze to unprotected tender vegetation.

Though air temperatures failed to reach 32 degrees at the Jim Hogg County Airport or the Hebbronville cooperative station in town, dew points in the mid teens, as well as nearby observations of freezing temperatures in Zapata, near Falfurrias (Brooks County), and in southern Starr County argue for several hours of freezing temperatures in central and southern portions of Jim Hogg County.  ||The impressively low overnight dew points supported wet bulb temperatures in the mid 20s for four to seven hours after midnight on the 13th; prolonged low wet bulb temperatures are known to create a proxy freeze to unprotected, cold weather sensitive tender vegetation.

Freezing temperatures reached the Zapata County Airport in Medina by 2 AM, and would continue until around 9 AM before rising above 32 degrees.  Low temperatures fell to 26 degrees. Temperatures failed to fall below freezing in exposed locations, such as the Bustamante Gas Plant near Escobas. Along the Rio Grande, the Remote Automated Weather Station near Falcon Lake, just south of the Zapata/Starr County line, recorded four hours of freezing temperatures with a low of 31.  ||The impressively low overnight dew points, dipping into the low to mid teens, supported wet bulb temperatures in the low to mid 20s for four to seven hours after midnight on the 13th; prolonged low wet bulb temperatures are known to create a proxy freeze to unprotected, cold weather sensitive tender vegetation.

Along the Rio Grande, the Remote Automated Weather Station near Falcon Lake, just south of the Zapata/Starr County line, recorded four hours of freezing temperatures with a low of 31, and the cooperative observation at Rio Grande City also fell to 31 degrees, with unknown duration.  The cooperative location at Falcon Dam (near border of Zapata County), however, remained several degrees above freezing, bottoming out at 35 degrees.  Proxy data and known drainage locations support most of Starr County falling to or just below freezing.||The impressively low overnight dew points, dipping into the mid teens, supported wet bulb temperatures in the mid 20s for four to seven hours after midnight on the 13th; prolonged low wet bulb temperatures are known to create a proxy freeze to unprotected, cold weather sensitive tender vegetation.

The Automated Weather Observing Station at the Brooks County Airport just southeast of Falfurrias recorded more than 4 hours of freezing temperatures, falling to 27 degrees just after daybreak on the 26th. Proxy observations near Sarita and Armstrong in Kenedy County/King Ranch fell to 27 and 25 degrees, respectively.  The Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge Remote Automated Weather Station near San Manuel also reached 25 degrees, with freezing temperatures for just under 5 hours.

The cooperative observer at the Lebh Shomea House of Prayer east of Sarita recorded a minimum temperature of 27 degrees on December 26th; the location near Armstrong fell farther, reaching 25 degrees.  The Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge Remote Automated Weather Station near San Manuel, just 10 miles southwest of the Kenedy/Hidalgo County line, also reached 25 degrees, with freezing temperatures for just under 5 hours.

The Automated Weather Observing System at the Jim Hogg County Airport dipped to 27 degrees just after daybreak on the 26th, with duration of freezing temperatures lasting from just before 2 AM until around 815 AM.  Based on proxy observations in Brooks and Zapata County, interpolation suggests all of Jim Hogg County had several hours of freezing temperatures on either side of daybreak.

The Automated Weather Observing System at the Zapata County Airport dipped to 29 degrees just after daybreak on the 26th, with duration of freezing temperatures lasting from just before 4 AM until around 815 AM.  The Remote Automated Weather Station at Falcon Lake, in Starr County just south of the Zapata County line, fell to 26 degrees with more than four hours of freezing temperatures. Even Laredo (approximately 25 miles north of the Zapata/Webb County line), which is normally moderated by nearby urban and water features, dipped to freezing, though only briefly.

The Remote Automated Weather Station at Falcon Lake, in Starr County just south of the Zapata County line, fell to 26 degrees with more than four hours of freezing temperatures. The cooperative observer in Rio Grande City recorded 31 degrees for the calendar day low temperature, while the cooperative observer at Falcon Dam (not too far from the Falcon Lake RAWS) fell just shy of freezing, reaching 33 degrees.  Proxy observations from Hidalgo, Jim Hogg, and Brooks County suggest most of Starr fell to or below 32 degrees for several hours either side of daybreak.

The Remote Automated Weather Station at the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge near San Manuel dropped to 25 degrees, with more than four hours of freezing temperatures on the 26th. For the first time this season, locations closer to the larger population centers of Edinburg, McAllen, Mission, and Weslaco also reached 32.  At the Edinburg International Airport just north of town, the low reached 30; the cooperative observer in town fell just shy, reaching 33 degrees.||More than one half of the surface area of Hidalgo County was considered freezing for more than 2 hours.

The cooperative observer at Raymondville reported a minimum temperature of 29 degrees early on December 26th.  The nearby Remote Automated Weather Station at the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge near San Manuel (less than 10 miles west of the County line) dropped to 25 degrees, with more than four hours of freezing temperatures on the 26th.  reaching 33 degrees.||The combination of Raymondville's low temperature, proxy observations from the King Ranch and San Manuel, and the likelihood that more than half of the area of inland Willacy County reached freezing temperatures for several hours argues for a freeze event.

The coldest recorded temperatures of the 2010/2011 winter so far occurred in western Cameron County on the 26th. While minimum temperatures fell just shy of the freezing point in Brownsville and Harlingen (36 at Brownsville and 33 degrees at Harlingen), proxy observations from western Willacy County and eastern Hidalgo County, each where temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees for several hours, argue that locations west of Federal Highway 77 in Cameron County, an area covering half of the inland zone, did likewise.||The combination of Raymondville's low temperature, proxy observations from the King Ranch and San Manuel, and the likelihood that more than half of the area of inland Willacy County reached freezing temperatures for several hours argues for a freeze event.

Proxy observations from the Remote Automated Weather Station at the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge near San Manuel (minimum:  27 degrees, freezing for 7 hours) and the cooperative observer at Armstrong (Kenedy County, 31 degrees) argue for several hours of freezing temperatures across much of Brooks County during the pre dawn hours of December 27th.  The cooperative location at Falfurrias only reached 33 degrees and Brooks County airport did likewise, but for more than six hours.

Proxy observations from the Remote Automated Weather Station at the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge near San Manuel (minimum:  27 degrees, freezing for 7 hours) and the cooperative observer at Armstrong (Kenedy County, 31 degrees) argue for several hours of freezing temperatures across much of the King Ranch, particularly along and west of Federal Highway 77, during the pre dawn hours of December 27th.  The cooperative location at the Lebh Shomea House of Prayer east of Sarita did not fall to freezing, influenced by return flow from the nearby Gulf of Mexico.

The Automated Weather Observing Station at the Jim Hogg County Airport fell to freezing or just below, on and off, for nearly five hours between 2 AM and 7 AM on the 27th.  Data from the Hebbronville cooperative site were unavailable as of this writing. Proxy observations in Brooks, Starr, and Zapata County suggest that sheltered locations in the county were at or below 32 degrees for at least 3 hours prior to daybreak.

The Automated Weather Observing Station at the Zapata County Airport fell to freezing or just below, starting near 5 AM and continuing until just before 8 AM on the 27th and bottoming out at 30 degrees.  While proxy observations to the south (Falcon Dam cooperative and Falcon Lake RAWS) remained just above freezing, the low of 31on and off, for nearly five hours between 2 AM and 7 AM on the 27th. ||It can be assumed by proxy that the northern two thirds of Zapata County likely experienced yet another minor freeze before the end of the 2010 calendar year.

The National Drought Monitor depicted a swath of D2, or severe, drought across western Brooks County beginning on December 28th. The Drought condition was largely Agricultural (exceedingly dry grass and brush), as water reserves remained plentiful, though were slowly dropping at the end of the calendar year, following the summer of 2010 excessive rainfall in northern Mexico flowed into the Rio Grande basin and stored at Falcon and Amistad International Reservoirs.||At the cooperative station near Falfurrias, with 103 years of record, the preliminary three month total rainfall of 0.12 inches fell far short of the prior 60 year old record (1950) dry mark, four times higher with 0.48 inches.

The National Drought Monitor depicted a swath of D2, or severe, drought across all of Jim Hogg County beginning on December 28th. The Drought condition was largely Agricultural (exceedingly dry grass and brush), as water reserves remained plentiful, though were slowly dropping at the end of the calendar year, following the summer of 2010 excessive rainfall in northern Mexico flowed into the Rio Grande basin and stored at Falcon and Amistad International Reservoirs.||At Hebbronville cooperative station (105 year of record), the prior October to December driest spell of 0.61 inches in 1950 was shattered with a paltry 0.20 inches for the same period in 2010.

The National Drought Monitor depicted a swath of D2, or severe, drought across eastern Zapata County beginning on December 28th. The Drought condition was largely Agricultural (exceedingly dry grass and brush), as water reserves remained plentiful, though were slowly dropping at the end of the calendar year, following the summer of 2010 excessive rainfall in northern Mexico flowed into the Rio Grande basin and stored at Falcon and Amistad International Reservoirs.

The National Drought Monitor depicted a swath of D2, or severe, drought across northern Starr County beginning on December 28th. The Drought condition was largely Agricultural (exceedingly dry grass and brush), as water reserves remained plentiful, though were slowly dropping at the end of the calendar year, following the summer of 2010 excessive rainfall in northern Mexico flowed into the Rio Grande basin and stored at Falcon and Amistad International Reservoirs.

The National Drought Monitor depicted a swath of D2, or severe, drought all of Hidalgo County, where the combination of warmest, driest (humidity), and rain free weather was focused from the start of October 2010 and manifesting in a severe drought declaration by December 28th. The Drought condition was largely Agricultural (exceedingly dry grass and brush), as water reserves remained plentiful, though were slowly dropping at the end of the calendar year, following the summer of 2010 excessive rainfall in northern Mexico flowed into the Rio Grande basin and stored at Falcon and Amistad International Reservoirs.||Record dry rainfall (or lack thereof) occurred for the months of October through December at both McAllen reporting stations.  At Miller Airport, the three month total of 0.11 inches fell far short of the nearly 50 year prior record of 1.03 inches, set back in 1961.

Dry conditions continued across all of Deep South Texas with no rainfall the first week of January. Severe drought conditions (D2) continued across the north and northeastern portions of Zapata County the first week of January, before ending with generally one half to a little more than an inch of rain on the 9th and improving to abnormally dry.

Dry conditions continued across all of Deep South Texas with no rainfall the first week of January. Severe drought conditions (D2) prevailed across all of Jim Hogg the first week of January, but would improve to abnormally dry after one half to an inch of rain fell (two inches north of Hebbronville) early on January 9th.

Dry conditions continued across all of Deep South Texas with no rainfall the first week of January. Severe drought conditions (D2) prevailed across the northeastern third of Starr County the first week of January, before rains of generally one quarter to one half inch early on the 9th improved conditions to moderate.

Dry conditions continued across all of Deep South Texas with no rainfall the first week of January. Severe drought conditions (D2) prevailed across the southwest one third of Brooks County the first week of January, before returning to abnormally dry after one half to more than an inch of rain fell early on the 9th.

Dry conditions continued across all of Deep South Texas with no rainfall the first week of January. Severe drought conditions (D2) prevailed across most of Hidalgo County the first week of January, before improving to moderate after one half inch of rain fell across the north third of the county early on the 9th.

The public reported sheet metal damage occurred to a carport and aluminum siding was blown off of a house near the Falfurrias airport in Brooks County. The damage occurred as a line of thunderstorms moved through the area, producing gusty winds.  The same line dumped more than 1.5 inches of rain in Hebbronville.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network site at Rincon del San Jose reported a gust to 35 knots during the early morning hours of January 9th when a thunderstorm passed through.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Bayview/Cameron County Airport ASOS reported a gust to 34 knots near sunrise on January 9th.  Proximity to the Laguna Madre, only 3 miles east, implies similar wind gusts spread into the Laguna Madre as the broken line of showers raced through.

Emergency Management called in from Willacy County were notified of a rapidly growing wildfire in south central Kenedy County just west of Highway 77 near Rudolph.  Before it was over, more than 7,000 acres of ranchland burned.  Efforts from Willacy County Fire and Emergency Management, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and others helped contain the fire nearly 12 hours after it began.  ||There was no property damage or known livestock injury or death; only wide swaths of grass, brush, and some mesquite burned.

Temperatures fell to a morning low of 29 degrees on January 22nd.  Based on surrounding observations, most areas in Brooks County were assumed to have five hours of freezing temperatures from 3 to 8 AM.

Temperatures fell to a morning low of 29 degrees on January 22nd in Falfurrias, 33 miles east but typically similar, if not warmer, than much of Jim Hogg County.  Based on surrounding observations, most areas in Jim Hogg County were assumed to have five hours of freezing temperatures from 3 to 8 AM.

Temperatures fell to a morning low of 29 degrees on January 22nd in Sarita and Armstrong in Kenedy County.  Based on similar observations from across Deep South Texas, most areas on the King Ranch were assumed to have five hours of freezing temperatures from 3 to 8 AM.

Temperatures fell to a morning low of 28 degrees on January 22nd near Falcon Heights, along the Starr/Zapata county line, and at the Zapata/Medina Airport.  At Falcon, the freeze lasted from 3 until 8 AM CST; at Zapata, from 4 until 9 AM CST.

A brush fire began in Brooks County during the early afternoon of February 1st, rapidly spreading to more than 800 acres. At approximately 1:30 pm, a fire was noted near the intersection of State Road 285, County Road 107, and Farm to Market Road 339 approximately 15 miles west-northwest of Falfurrias, just south of the Brooks/Duval County line.   Gusty north winds in excess of 25 mph combined with cured fuels and humidity falling near or below 30 percent aided the accelerated growth.  The cause of the fire was unknown cause of the fire.  ||One residential structure with 1000 gallon gasoline and 500 gallon diesel tanks was threatened, but saved.  The fire came within one half mile of the building. Texas Forest Service sent a Task Force to the scene and used bulldozers to clear the area around home and tanks.  No injuries were noted.  As of 7 PM, the fire was 50% controlled at this time. Responding agencies included:  Brooks County Volunteer Fire Department, Jim Hogg County Volunteer Fire Department, Ben Bolt Volunteer Fire Department, Alice Fire Department, Premont Volunteer Fire Department, Falfurrias Volunteer Fire Department, and Highway Patrol Falfurrias.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees shortly after 2 AM on February 2nd in Falfurrias, then continued falling to 30 degrees for several hours after sunrise before slowly rising back above freezing by early afternoon.  Between 7 and 10 hours of freezing temperatures were reported/estimated in the county before readings rose a few degrees above freezing for the afternoon and evening.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees at around 5 AM on February 2nd in Harlingen and Bayview, then continued falling to 30 or 31 degrees for several hours after sunrise before slowly rising back above freezing at around noon.  Duration of freeze varied across the county; temperatures only touched 32 at the Brownsville/South Padre International Airport by mid morning, but remained at or below 32 at the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge for nearly 8 hours (530 AM until 130 PM), bottoming out at 30 degrees a little after 9 AM CST.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees at around 5 AM on February 2nd in Harlingen and Bayview, then continued falling to 30 or 31 degrees for several hours after sunrise before slowly rising back above freezing at around noon.  Duration of freeze varied across the county; temperatures only touched 32 at the Brownsville/South Padre International Airport by mid morning, but remained at or below 32 at the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge for nearly 8 hours (530 AM until 130 PM), bottoming out at 30 degrees a little after 9 AM CST.||Temperatures on South Padre Island flirted with 32 degrees thorugh much of the afternoon on the 2nd, but largely remained a hair above freezing.

Temperatures were estimated to have fallen to 32 degrees at around 4 AM on February 2nd in and near Port Mansfield, then continued falling to 30 degrees for several hours after sunrise before slowly rising back above freezing at noon or shortly thereafter.

Temperatures were estimated to have fallen to 32 degrees at around 4 AM on February 2nd in and near Raymondville, then continued falling to 30 degrees for several hours after sunrise before slowly rising back above freezing at noon or shortly thereafter.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees between 5 and 7 AM on February 2nd across Hidalgo County, with readings hovering near the freezing point until mid morning to around noon in different locations in the county under a steely gray overcast.  How long the freezing temperatures lasted varied from station to station.  McAllen/Miller airport fell to 32 for less than an hour; Edinburg International Airport for one and one half hours.  Meanwhile, the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge (NWR) at San Manuel had 8 hours of freezing temperatures, and the NWR at Santa Ana along the Rio Grande had 5 hours of freezing.  Lows ranged from 30 to 32 degrees countywide.

Across the northern third of Jim Hogg County, temperatures fell to 32 degrees just before midnight on February 2nd, and would not rise above 32 until 11 AM on the 4th - a total of 60 hours straight with temperatures below freezing!  Readings remained around or just below 32 through the 2nd under a steely gray sky.  Values would dip into the mid and upper 20s each morning (2nd and 3rd) but only rise to 31 degrees on the 3rd as a misty freezing rain spread westward across the area.  Temperatures would fall back into the upper 20s during the evening of the 3rd, then drop quickly to the lower 20s as the precipitation quickly moved east and skies cleared early on the 4th.  Ample sunshine on the 4th would finally push temperatures above 32 just before noon on the 4th.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees shortly after 2 AM on February 2nd in Falfurrias (Brooks County), with similar conditions likely occurring due east across the King Ranch. Temperatures continue to drop, reaching the upper 20s to around 30 from north to south during the mid morning hours, before slowly rising back above freezing by early afternoon.  Between 7 and 10 hours of freezing temperatures were estimated in the county before readings rose a few degrees above freezing for the afternoon and evening.  Low temperature at the Lebh Shomeah retreat east of Sarita was 26 degrees, mid morning of the 2nd.

The Automated Weather Observing System at Zapata/Medina Airport dipped to 32 degrees a little after 3 AM on the 2nd, bottoming out at 30 degrees during the mid morning hours before rising above freezing for a few hours during the afternoon.  Eight hours of freezing temperatures were recorded at the Falcon Lake Remote Automated Observing System near the Starr/Zapata line, with a low of 31 degrees there and at Falcon Dam, also near the Starr/Zapata line.

Eight hours of freezing temperatures were recorded at the Falcon Lake Remote Automated Observing System near the Starr/Zapata line, with a low of 31 degrees there and at Falcon Dam, also near the Starr/Zapata line.  ||The cooperative observer at Rio Grande City dropped to 32 degrees for an unknown period of time during the morning of the 2nd.  Time duration of the freeze was interpolated between Zapata (west) and Jim Hogg (north) Counties, and the fact that Starr County has a lower population than Hidalgo County to the east.

Air temperatures fell back to 32 degrees just after midnight on February 3rd, and would not recover above 32 until just before noon on February 4th - a total of 33 hours at or below 32 degrees.  The Remote Automated Observing site at San Manuel, about 10 miles south of the county line, recorded nearly 35 hours.  Low temperatures at Falfurrias were in the upper 20s on the 3rd and again on the 4th.  A hard freeze - temperatures below 28 degrees for 2 hours or more - was recorded during the early morning hours on the 4th.

Air temperatures fell back to 32 degrees prior to midnight on February 2nd at the Zapata County (Medina) Airport, and would not recover above 32 until just before noon on February 4th - a total of 39 hours at or below 32 degrees.  The Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) site at Falcon Lake, in Starr County along the Zapata/Starr County line, recorded a similar long duration freeze (35.5 hours).  Low temperatures at Zapata County Airport dipped to 26 degrees on the 3rd, and to 22 degrees on the 4th after skies cleared.  Temperatures were below 28 degrees for more than 14 hours at this location and the Falcon Lake RAWS also had 14 hours below 28 degrees on the 4th.  Temperatures were in the mid 20s (26 each morning) at Falcon Lake.

Air temperatures fell back to 32 degrees just before midnight on February 3rd, and would not recover above 32 until just before noon on February 4th - a total of 33 hours at or below 32 degrees.  The Cooperative observer at the Lebh Shomeah House of Prayer, 7 miles east of Sarita, recorded a low of 26 on the 3rd, with daytime temperatures not exceeding 30 degrees.  The low would dip to 26 again overnight on the 3rd.  Based on proximity to Kingsville, there were several long periods with temperature at or below 27 degrees - a hard freeze. Based on surrounding observations, between 32 and 39 consecutive hours of freezing temperatures occurred.

The Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) site at Falcon Lake, in Starr County along the Zapata/Starr County line, recorded a long duration freeze (35.5 hours).  Low temperatures dipped to 26 degrees  with a 14 hour duration of hard freeze on the 4th, when skies cleared for several hours around daybreak.   Temperatures were below 28 degrees for more than 14 hours at this location and the Falcon Lake RAWS also had 14 hours below 28 degrees on the 3rd and 4th, falling below 28 degrees as early as 7 PM on the 3rd.  ||At Rio Grande City, the cooperative observer dipped to 29 degrees early on the 3rd, only rising to 32 during the daylight hours before falling back to 26 degrees for several hours early on the 4th as skies cleared just prior to daybreak.

Between 30 and 35 hours of freezing temperatures covered Hidalgo County, beginning a little after midnight on February 3rd and continuing through late morning on February 4th after skies clears and sunshine warmed temperatures back into the 40s. North of Edinburg, and in sheltered pockets near the river, between 1 and 2 hours of hard freeze conditions - temperatures below 28 degrees - occurred around daybreak on the 4th. Through the period, temperatures held generally within a 3 degree range at any one location, between 28 and 32 degrees.||Fortunately, the long duration freeze was accompanied by a thickening coat of glaze ice.  This reduced the damage to citrus trees and fruit; agricultural extension agents noted minor damage to leaf, but tree damage was minimal. Unfortunately, the same stress caused more significant damage to tropical plants such as Emperor/Royal Palms and the sugar cane crop.  The Texas Agrilife Research Center in Weslaco reported some damage to cabbage, watermelon, peppers, leafy greens, and tomatoes. More significant damage was reported to the sugar cane crop, and goats (livestock) were lost at some ranches.  Damage estimates were preliminary of this writing.

Dry conditions across Zapata County continued in March. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Zapata County during the first week of March.

Dry conditions continued across Starr County in March. The severe (D2) drought conditions increased to include all of Starr County during the first week of March, would slip back to the eastern two thirds by the 15th after rains on the 5th, but recover to all of the county by the 22nd and intensify by the 31st as heat and wind continued to increase.

The dry conditions continued across Hidalgo County in March. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across the southwestern one half of Hidalgo County the first week of March, then spread across all of Hidalgo County by the 22nd and begin intensifying at the end of the month.

A lack of rainfall across all of Deep South Texas increased the severity of the drought conditions across the western and central portions of the Rio Grande Valley during the latter half of March. Severe D2 drought conditions developed again across all of Zapata County by the 22nd, and would continue and intensify by the end of the month as heat and low humidity dominated.

A lack of rainfall across Deep South Texas resulted in the Severe D2 drought conditions spreading across the Brush Country region during the latter half of March. Severe D2 drought conditions developed across all of Jim Hogg County beginning on the 22nd, and would continue/intensify through the end of the month.

A lack of rainfall across Deep South Texas resulted in an increase in the areal coverage of the severe D2 drought conditions across the entire Brush Country region  by the latter portion of March. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across the western one tenth of Brooks County by the 22nd, and would spread through the western one-half of the county by month's end.
Severe D2 drought conditions developed across the southern one third of Starr County the last week of February due to the continued lack of rainfall across portions of the Rio Grande Valley.

A wildfire, which may have begun as a prescribed burn, quickly surged out of control on the King Ranch in eastern Brooks County near the Kenedy County line during the early afternoon, February 7th.  The fire eventually covered 3,000 acres before being contained, then controlled, 12 hours later during the night. Conditions became hostile to any open burning, with freeze-dried 1 hour (grasses) and 10 hour (brush) fuels, humidity falling below 25 percent, and pulse gust north winds between 20 and 25 mph.||No structural damage was reported, though fire crews from Brooks County, Kleberg County, and Willacy County, the Texas Forest Service, and others worked together to quell the flames.

A power line was blown down in Port Isabel at around 1 PM CST February 9th, courtesy of gusty northwest winds in excess of 40 mph behind a strong cold front. At the Bayview/Cameron County Airport, a peak gust of 48 mph was recorded at around the same time.  Several residents lost electricity for a short while due to the power outage.

Temperatures fell to 32F around or just after midnight on the 11th, then continued to steadily drop, reaching down to the upper 20s in most areas of the county. For most suburban and rural areas, 7 hours of freezing temperatures were recorded, though up to 11 hours were recorded in colder pockets.  In urban areas, 2 to 4 hours of freezing temperatures were recorded.  ||The following minimum temperatures were recorded:  McAllen/Miller Airport (29 degrees, 3 hours freezing); Edinburg Int'l Airport (28 degrees, 7 hours freezing); Weslaco/Mid Valley Airport (30 degrees, 3 hours); Linn/San Manuel Remote Automated Weather Station (23 degrees, 10.5 hours freezing, 10 hours hard freeze below 28 degrees), and Santa Ana/Lower RGV National Wildlife Refuge (25 degrees, 9 hours freezing, 6 hours hard freeze).

Temperatures were estimated to have fallen to 32F or slightly lower by midnight on the 11th, then continued to steadily drop, reaching the lower and mid 20s across teh King Ranch by daybreak.  At least eight hours of freezing temperatures were recorded, though up to 10 hours may have occurred in colder pockets.  The minimum temperatures at both Lebh Shomea House of Prayer, 7 miles east of Sarita, and Armstrong, reached 24 degrees just after sunrise.  Hard freeze conditions (less than 28 degrees) likely lasted for 5 to 7 hours, perhaps longer in other sheltered locations along the Brooks/Kenedy County line.

Temperatures dropped to 32F shortly after midnight on the 11th, and fell a few degrees further by sunrise, bottoming out at 28F at Harlingen/Valley International Airport before rising above freezing just before 8 AM.  The long duration freezing temperatures were likely confined to rural and typically colder areas covering the north and west half of the county; Brownsville/South Padre Island Int'l Airport only fell to 36F, a likely combination of low level mixing of northerly winds with veering winds off the surface from the warmer Gulf of Mexico.

Temperatures dropped to 32F shortly after midnight on the 11th, and fell a few degrees further by sunrise, bottoming out at 27F at Raymondville shortly after sunrise.  Typically colder locations west of Lyford and Raymondville may have had several hours of a hard freeze - temperatures below 28 degrees, along with up to 10 hours of freezing temperatures overall.  The Remote Automated Weather Station at Linn/San Manuel, 8 miles west of the Willacy/Hidalgo County line, recorded a minimum temperature of 23 degrees with 10 hours of a hard freeze - or temperatures below 28 degrees.

A vehicle fire near the Turcotte West Gate on the King Ranch quickly spread out of control, fed by extremely cured fine fuels, fairly low humidity (estimated near 30 percent based on nearby observations at the Brooks County Airport), and estimated 20 foot southeast winds 10 to 15 mph with gusts to 20 mph at times. ||The fire traveled north while increasing to at least 600 acres in coverage.   Fire departments from Willacy and Kleberg County joined the fight, including from Rivera, Ricardo, and Kingsville (Kleberg) and Willacy/Raymondville.  The fire was contained by 6 PM as well positioned fire breaks combined with lowering winds and increasing humidity at sunset.
Severe (D2) Drought would briefly develop across western Jim Hogg for the first week of March, before a band of locally heavy showers on the 5th temporarily knocked it back to moderate by the 8th.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions stretched into most of Cameron County by the end of March, courtesy of above to much above normal temperatures in the 80s to near 90, persistent strong winds, and no rainfall.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions stretched into most of Willacy County by the end of March, courtesy of above to much above normal temperatures in the upper 80s to lower 90s, persistent strong winds, and no rainfall.

The Texas Forest Service and local fire departments reported the closure of the eastbound lanes of Federal Highway 83 between the Cities of La Joya and Sullivan City due to a moderate sized wildfire. The 80 acre fire was eventually controlled and extinguished, and the highway was reopened. One structure was destroyed. Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) Aircraft and local fire departments - most likely from Sullivan City and La Joya - responded. (Hidalgo County Fire Marshal, DPS McAllen).  Reported by Texas DEM Region 3A.

According to the local Fire Chief, the 600-acre Ramirez Ranch Fire, located two miles south of Falcon near the intersection of US 83 and Pedernal Road, began when lighted cigarette(s) were tossed out a vehicle window. Two oil wells were threatened and saved. No injuries were reported. Zapata County FD and Zapata County SO Deputies responded. The fire was contained. (RLO 6).  At Zapata County Airport in Medina, humidity fell below 30 percent, southeast winds gusted to 22 mph, and the high temperature reached 99 degrees - all ingredients which combined with already severe drought conditions to create an ideal situation for rapid wildfire growth.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network site at Rincon del San Jose, along Laguna Madre in Kenedy County, recorded a nearly two hour period of peak gusts of 34 knots or higher from just before 11 AM CST to a little after 1230 PM CST on March 5th.  The initial surge, which reached 40 knots at 1100 AM, arrived with a band of showers and storms along a moderate cold front.  Gusts continued at or above gale force due to gradient winds behind the front until 1236 PM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network site at Realitos Peninsula, just south of the Arroyo Colorado, recorded a peak gust of 36 knots at around 11 AM March 5th as a developing line of showers and storms moved into the region immediately behind a cold front.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network site at Realitos Peninsula, just south of the Arroyo Colorado, recorded a second set of peak wind gusts just after noon on March 5th, as a line of showers and storms immediately behind the cold front intensified and passed through the Lower Texas gulf of Mexico waters.  Gusts peaked at 38 knots at 1224 PM, but were persistently at or above 34 knots starting at 1218 PM.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: Several stations between Port Isabel and South Padre Island recorded wind gusts of 35 knots as a quick developing line of showers and thunderstorms plowed into the Lower Texas Gulf waters, immediately behind a cold front.  Peak winds reached 35 knots at the Port Isabel C-MAN observing station on the south end of town; the South Padre Island Coast Guard station recorded 34 knots, each around 12 PM CST; and the South Padre Island Heliport, about a mile from the Coast Guard station, recorded 35 knots as the line passed between 1215 and 1245 PM.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: Peak winds reached 35 knots at the South Padre Island Heliport, about a mile from the Coast Guard station and one half mile from the Gulf shoreline, recorded 35 knots as the line passed between 1215 and 1245 PM. Radar data and proximity to the coast suggest the showers and storms continued at similar intensity across American waters for about 30 minutes after the first gust; later gusts were behind the front, associated with building Canadian high pressure.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: The NOAA Buoy 42020, approximately 35 NM northeast of Port Mansfield, recorded a peak wind of 39 knots as a broken line of showers and a few storms moved across the Lower Texas Gulf waters immediately behind a moderate cold front on March 5th. Gusts continued frequently between 36 and 39 knots (estimated persistence) as the precipitation moved through, and near gale force gusts prevailed for several hours under cloudy skies as Canadian high pressure built across the waters.

The drought conditions intensified across Zapata County in early April. Severe D2 drought conditions had occurred across Zapata County in March.  However extreme D3 drought conditions developed across all of Zapata County by April 5th due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.||Dryland crop damage began developing by month's end, and livestock feed was affected.  Details on degree of crop damage will be available in the May Storm Data report.

The drought conditions intensified across Jim Hogg County in early April. The severe D2 drought conditions which had occurred across Jim Hogg County in March intensified to extreme D3 drought conditions in early April due to the continued lack of significant rainfall combined with record heat.||Dryland crop damage began developing by month's end, and livestock feed was also affected.  Details on degree of crop damage will be available in the May Storm Data report.

The drought conditions intensified across Starr County in early April. The severe D2 drought conditions which had occurred across Starr County in March intensified to extreme D3 drought conditions in early April due to the continued lack of significant rainfall and record heat.  Some areas in southern portions of the county received less than an inch of rain since October 1st, 2010.||Dryland crop damage began developing by month's end, and livestock feed was affected.  Details on degree of crop damage will be available in the May Storm Data report.

The drought conditions intensified across Hidalgo County in early April. The severe D2 drought conditions which had occurred across Hidalgo County in March intensified to extreme D3 drought conditions in early April due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.  Some areas in southwest Hidalgo County had received less than an inch of rain since October 1st, 2010.  Intense, record heat (for April) and gusty winds exacerbated the drought as well.||Dryland crop damage began developing by month's end, and livestock feed was also affected.  Details on degree of crop damage will be available in the May Storm Data report.

The drought conditions intensified across Brooks County in early April. Extreme D3 drought conditions developed across the western half of Brooks County in early April due to the continued lack of significant rainfall, combined with record heat and wind.

Extreme D3 drought conditions developed across the western half of Cameron County and Severe D2 drought conditions developed across the eastern half of Cameron County in early April. A lack of significant rainfall across Deep South Texas the end of March resulted in the worsening of the drought conditions across the county; record to near record heat and drying winds contributed as well.

Extreme D3 drought conditions developed across the western half of Willacy County and Severe D2 drought conditions developed across the eastern half of Willacy County in early April. A lack of significant rainfall across Deep South Texas the end of March resulted in the worsening of the drought conditions across the county; record to near record heat and persistent drying winds contributed as well.

Severe Drought (D2) conditions developed across the southwestern one tenth of Kenedy County to begin April, and would spread into the entire southern half of the county by April 19th, continuing through the end of the month. A lack of significant rainfall across Kenedy County at the end of March resulted in the worsening of the drought conditions across the county; record to near record heat, persistent wind, and no rain in April exacerbated conditions heading into May.

The drought conditions intensified across Brooks County the last two weeks of April.  Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across the western half of Brooks County, D2 drought conditions developed across the north, central, eastern and southern one half of Brooks County with the exception of the extreme northeastern corner of the County due to the continued lack of significant rainfall; record to near record heat and persistent winds exacerbated drought conditions.||Dryland crop damage began developing by month's end, and livestock feed was affected.  Details on degree of crop damage will be available in the May Storm Data report.
A lack of rainfall continued across Deep South Texas the first of April. D2 Severe drought conditions occurred across all of Zapata County.
A lack of rainfall continued across Deep South Texas the first of April. D2 Severe drought conditions occurred across all of Jim Hogg County.
A lack of rainfall continued across Deep South Texas the first of April. D2 Severe drought conditions occurred across all of Starr County.

A lack of rainfall continued across Deep South Texas the first of April. D2 Severe drought conditions occurred across the southern one tenth of kenedy County.

Three young men from northern Mexico were swept to their deaths in dangerous rip currents near the Isla Blanca jetties on South Padre Island. The men took advantage of the warming surf temperatures to venture into the water, only to drown due to the strength of the current and a combination of lack of swimming ability in dangerous surf, and potential panic.  ||Conditions were ripe for rip currents.  A front had shifted winds to the north and northeast, and swell period increased to 8 and 9 seconds, with average period rising to 6.9 seconds at the NOAA Buoy about 35 NM east northeast of Port Mansfield. Surf heights were likely 4 to 6 feet, and the swell direction was from a favorable east-southeast direction.||The swimmers ventured out at around 6 PM.  A 22 year old was pulled out of the water during the mid evening and taken to Valley Baptist Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.  An 18 year old was last seen in distress and unable to be rescued Wednesday evening; the Coast Guard found him early on the 29th at Boca Chica Beach, several miles south of the location where he entered the water.  A third victim, 12, was never found after several days of Coast Guard searches, which ended on May 1st.

A wildfire quickly spread to 35 acres in the Baullion area of Hidalgo County during the afternoon of the 7th, threatening four homes which were saved by local fire fighters.  One firefighter was injured.

A 10 acre wildfire, known as the Alton-Moorefield Fire on Moorefield Road between Farm to Market (FM) 107 and FM 1925 in Alton, Hidalgo County, spread rapidly from grass and brush into a five-acre tire dump.  At least 190,000 tires burned, with northerly winds of 20 to 30 mph, rapidly falling humidity below 15 percent, extremely dry grass and brush, and temperatures rising into the upper 90s during the event, pushing thick, acrid black smoke and dangerous fumes into nearby neighborhoods.||Three subdivisions (180 homes) were evacuated; all the homes were threatened by the fire.  Two structures were destroyed, including one home after the fire spread from palm trees into the residence.  Another unknown structure was destroyed. Moorefield Road was temporarily closed between FM 107 and FM 1925. Two firefighters sustained minor injuries. The fire was 85% contained by late afternoon. Dozens of local and regional agencies were called in to fight the fire, including: Alton, Mission, Palmview, Edinburg, McAllen, Alamo, Weslaco, Pharr, Los Fresnos, and Linn-San  Manuel Volunteer Fire Department. The Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office, Fire|Marshal's Office, Emergency Management Coordinator, Public Works and the Regional Liaison Officer for Region 3A (Lower Rio Grande Valley) responded to the event.
A lack of rainfall continued across Deep South Texas the first of April. D2 Severe drought conditions spread into coastal agricultural areas of Willacy County to begin the month.
A lack of rainfall continued across Deep South Texas the first of April. D2 Severe drought conditions spread into coastal agricultural areas of Cameron County to begin the month.

The drought conditions across Zapata County the first 9 days of May remained the same as the last week of April. Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across all of Zapata County the first 9 days of May due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.||Dryland crop damage slowly increased and the livestock feed has been impacted.

The drought conditions across Starr County the first 9 days of May remained the same as the last week of April. Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across all of Starr County the first 9 days of May due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.||Dryland crop damage slowly increased and the livestock feed has been impacted.

The drought conditions across Hidalgo County the first 9 days of May remained the same as the last week of April. Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across all except the extreme northeast tip of the county which had severe D2 drought conditions the first 9 days of May due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.

Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across the western half of Cameron County and Severe D2 drought conditions continued across the eastern half of Cameron County the first 9 days of May due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.

Extreme D3 drought conditions prevailed across the western half of Willacy County and Severe D2 drought conditions prevailed across the eastern half of Willacy County the first 9 days of May due to the continued lack of significant rainfall across Deep South.
Severe Drought (D2) conditions continued across the entire southern half of Kenedy County the first 9 days of May due to the lack of significant rainfall.

The drought conditions across Jim Hogg County the first 9 days of May remained the same as the last week of April. Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across all of Jim Hogg County the first 9 days of May due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.

The drought conditions continued across Brooks County the first 9 days of May.  Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across the western half of Brooks County, D2 drought conditions continued across the north, central, eastern and southern one half of Brooks County with the exception of the extreme northeastern corner of the County due to the continued lack of significant rainfall.

The continued lack of rainfall across the Rio Grande Plains resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions across Zapata County. Exceptional D4 drought conditions had developed across all of Zapata County by the 10th of May and continued through month's end, as locally welcome rainfall on May 12th, 15th, and 20th largely bypassed the county with the exception of San Ygnacio toward Escobas and points north.  Rains in these areas were not enough to reduce the long term dry conditions, particularly the combination of heat, low humidity, and frequent winds.||Livestock began feeling the effects by month's end, as withering feed supplies (hay, etc.) began taking a toll on ranchers' ability to maintain well fed herds.

The continued lack of rainfall across Deep South Texas resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions across the western Brush Country region of Jim Hogg County. Exceptional D4 drought conditions had developed across all of the county by the 10th of May and would continue for a few days before welcome rains associated with a cool front on May 12th, then the northward return of the front on the 15th, brought some relief to the eastern third of the county.

The continued lack of rainfall across Deep South Texas resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions across the mid and upper Rio Grande Valley. Exceptional D4 drought conditions had developed across nearly all of Starr County by the 10th of May and would continue into June.  Dryland crop damage, particularly to sorghum, began by late month with several fields being plowed under as May turned to June.  ||Final damage estimates for the 2011 Drought (through June) will be provided in the June Storm Data report under Crop Damage.

The continued lack of rainfall across the Rio Grande Valley resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions across Hidalgo County. Exceptional D4 drought conditions had developed across all of Hidalgo County except for the northeastern one tenth to one third of the county from May 10th through the end of the month; locally heavy rains on May 15th and May 20th briefly improved conditions to Severe (D3) north of Edinburg before month's end.  ||The long duration of Exceptional drought across the more fertile lands of southern Hidalgo County took a toll on dryland crops; much of the un-irrigated sorghum had to be plowed under by month's end. A final damage total for Hidalgo County will be provided in the June Storm Data report under Crop Damage.

The continued lack of rainfall across the Brush County and King Ranch of Deep South Texas resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions into mid May. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions had developed across the southwestern one tenth of Brooks County by the 10th of May while the rest of the county was in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.  The northeastern one tenth of the county remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions by the 10th of May.

The continued lack of rainfall across the Lower Rio Grande Valley resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions in Cameron County. Drought conditions intensified across Cameron County to Extreme (D3) levels by the 10th of May.  These conditions would further intensify later in the month.

The continued lack of rainfall across the Lower Rio Grande Valley resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions. Drought conditions intensified across Willacy County to Extreme (D3), and these conditions prevailed across the county through the end of the month.  Dryland crops began to fail in some areas, and livestock began feeling the effects of lowered yields by month's end.  The drought would worsen into late June; dollar damages will be provided in the June report under Crop Damage.

Across the King Ranch of Kenedy County, drought intensified to extreme (D3) across the south portion, and severe (D2) across the north portion, starting on May 10th and continuing largely through month's end.  Thunderstorms on May 12th and May 20th kept conditions from worsening; in fact, the rains temporarily reduced extreme conditions to severe across the southern half of the county with the exception of the immediate coast. ||Livestock across Deep South Texas began feeling the effects of the heat and drought by month's end; while damage was not reported from the King Ranch, some livestock were readied for early sale due to dwindling supplies of feed corn and hay.  Any damage information received from Kenedy County will be reported in June Storm Data under Crop Damage.

The continued lack of rainfall across the Lower Rio Grande Valley resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions, including the coast. Drought conditions intensified across coastal Willacy County to Extreme (D3) levels by May 10th; these conditions would continue through the end of the month.

The continued lack of rainfall across the Lower Rio Grande Valley resulted in an intensification of the drought conditions, extending to the coast. Drought conditions intensified across Coastal Cameron County to Extreme (D3) by May 10th and would continue at this level through the 16th.

Drought conditions improved slightly across eastern Jim Hogg County as a few showers and isolated thunderstorms moved across the county the middle of May. |Exceptional D4 drought conditions remained across the western and south central half of the county but conditions improved to extreme D3 drought conditions across the eastern and north central half of Jim Hogg County.||Livestock began to feel the effects of the drought by month's end, as feed supplies, particularly hay, corn, and sorghum, withered in the dry heat.  Details on livestock and grain impacts will be provided in the June Storm Data report under Crop Damage.
