Drought conditions intensified across Cameron County the middle of May as locally heavy rainfall that accompanied a cooling front on May 12th, and the returning warm front on May 15th, left only sprinkles and a few light showers. Exceptional D4 drought conditions spread across the western and southern two thirds of Cameron County by the 17th. Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across the northern and northeastern one third of Cameron County. Both conditions continued across Cameron County through the end of the month.||Dryland crops began to wither under the lack of rainfall as May turned to June.  Related damage to crops and livestock will be provided in the June Storm Data report under Crop Damage.

Drought conditions would fluctuate in Brooks County after May 17th, courtesy of several rainfall events.  Widespread, locally heavy rains fell on the 12th ahead of a cool front.  Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed on the 15th as a the front retreated northward and a weak disturbance moved along it.  Finally, intense heating and increased humidity combined with an enhanced sea breeze on the 20th to produce locally torrential rains and hail which stretched from the southwest ranchlands northeast into Falfurrias.  ||The rains knocked conditions back to Extreme (D3) with a pocket of Severe (D2) around Falfurrias from the 17th to 30th; Extreme conditions would retreat to the western quarter of the county on the 31st with Severe conditions covering the remainder of the county.||The rains temporarily slowed crop and livestock stress, which had increased rapidly through April and mid May.  Unfortunately, dry and very hot conditions returned for much of June, increasing stress on agriculture.  Any damage information will be provided in the June Storm Data report under Crop Damage.

Drought conditions intensified across Coastal Cameron County by the middle of May, and would continue through month's end. Locally heavy rains which impacted the Brush Country and King Ranch dwindled to only a sprinkle for the Lower Texas coast.  Exceptional D4 drought conditions spread across the southern half of Coastal Cameron County the middle of May. Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across the northern half of Coastal Cameron County. These conditions continued through the end of the month.
A lack of rainfall continued across the Lower Rio Grande Valley to begin May, reaching toward the coast.  Severe D2 drought conditions spread across the Coastal Willacy County the first week of May.

A lack of rainfall continued across the Lower Rio Grande Valley into early May, reaching toward the coast.  Severe D2 drought conditions spread across the Coastal Cameron County the first week of May.

The public reported a wind gusts estimated to be 45 miles per hour occurred during a thunderstorm that moved through Falfurrias during the early afternoon on May 12 2011. Small branches were broken in some trees.

The Zapata County Sheriff department reported hail up to one inch but predominately dime to nickel size fell during a thunderstorm which moved across the City of Zapata  between 10:44 and 10:51 AM CDT.  The Fire Department (EOC) reported penny size hail during the same period, as did a trained storm spotter.
Penny size hail was reported by Law enforcement west of Encino (Brooks County) during the early evening of May 20th.
Law enforcement in Falfurrias reported hail up to one inch fell across some areas as a thunderstorm moved through the area.
A spotter reported penny size hail fell for approximately 3 or 4 minutes east of San Perlita near the intersection of FM 3142 and Highway 186.

Lack of rainfall across the Rio Grande Plains maintained exceptional (D4) drought conditions across all of Zapata County in June.  While much needed rainfall soaked into soils farther east during the last full week of the month, less than an inch fell on areas which had only received an inch for the water year (October 2010 to the present) thus far.  ||Heavy irrigation and high evaporation rates allowed both Falcon International Reservoir and La Amistad International Reservoir to continue falling.  Falcon fell to 59 percent of capacity, only months after the pool level had been maintained slightly above 100 percent of capacity through the late winter months.  Amistad, which has higher  capacity and retained more water, dropped to 92 percent of capacity.||Livestock feed quality suffered, and many ranchers began selling off heads of cattle as the drought worsened.  Estimated damage from the spring drought in Zapata County was [fill in here].

Lack of rainfall across the Upper Rio Grande Valley maintained Exceptional (D4) drought conditions across all of Starr County, except the extreme northeastern tip, which had Extreme (D3) drought conditions the first week of June before they, too, reached Exceptional conditions.  While locations in the Lower and Mid Valley received some quenching rainfall the final week of June, totals were lower in Starr County, until the final day when between one and two inches fell in some areas.  ||Even after these rains, more than 10 inches were needed at Rio Grande City to make up a shortfall from what the average rainfall should be through June 30th.  The hot, dry, windy weather took its toll on crops and livestock.  Insured damage to dryland crops of cotton and sorghum in Starr County added up to nearly $2.2 million, about a quarter of all crop damage in the Rio Grande Valley (data from the Texas AgriLife Extension Service in Weslaco).  Livestock loss data was not available as of this writing.

Residual moisture in the soil from rainfall between May 12th and 20th slowed the progress of drought intensification in Brooks County into early June.  Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the western two-fifths of the County, with Severe (D2) drought conditions continuing across the eastern three-fifths of Brooks County through the first week in June.

Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across all but a sliver of eastern and southern Jim Hogg County through June (Extreme - D3 - drought conditions prevailed in these locations).  Rainfall which reached the Lower Rio Grande Valley on the 22nd and 23rd failed to stretch toward the Rio Grande Plains/Brush Country.  At month's end (June 30th), rainfall from outer bands of Tropical Storm Arlene dumped more than two inches across the south and east, providing some relief for July.  Hebbronville, with less than an inch of rain in June, remained more than 10 inches below the average for the current water year (beginning October 1, 2010). ||Dryland crop damage and livestock/ranchland impacts were heavy across the Brush Country.  Many head of cattle were being sold early due to low/low quality feed supply.  [Details on damage/livestock loss will be provided here].

Hidalgo County maintained a combination of Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought conditions through June.  The withering heat, wind, and low to moderate humidity finished off a number of dryland crops, and began impacting livestock/cattle herds on ranches across the north and west portions of the county as the month wore on.  Exceptional drought dominated the south and west portions of the county through June 28th, with Extreme conditions elsewhere.  ||Torrential rains of 4 to 6 inches across the eastern half of the county on June 22 and 23 dropped conditions from Exceptional to Extreme including Weslaco, Donna, and Mercedes. The drought would be truly dented - finally - with the passage of outer bands of Tropical Storm Arlene (June 30th), seen by early July.  Monthly rain totals ranged from more than 8 inches in the southeast corner of the county, to less than three inches across the far west and north.  While departure from water year (beginning October 1st 2010) averages recovered to a few inches shy in Weslaco, values remained more than 10 inches below the water year average in McCook and La Joya/Mission.  ||Dryland crops and un-irrigated fields suffered total losses, shown best by many fields of burned/stunted corn.  Irrigable crops largely grew normally, though frequent winds may have increased evaporation rates through the 21st. Hundreds of head of cattle were sold early due to dwindling/low quality feed supply.  As of the end of June, total insured crop damage/loss was just under $4.4 million (cotton, corn, sorghum), roughly half of the total for the Rio Grande Valley (reported by the Texas AgriLife Extension Service in Weslaco).

Hot, rain free, and frequently windy conditions would return nearly all of the King Ranch (Kenedy County) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions after the month began with the northern two thirds of the county in Severe (D2) conditions.  Conditions would briefly worsen for the third week of the month before some welcome rains (2 to 4 inches) arrived on the 22nd and 23rd.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions covered all but the northern quarter of Cameron County through June 20th; Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across these areas (Combes to Arroyo City) through June 20th before moving to Exceptional to close out the month.  Across the County, the withering drought torched most dryland crops, particularly un-irrigated corn.  Grasslands turned brittle and brown and failed to grow (short).  In all, more than $1.8 million of insured losses to cotton, corn, and sorghum was reported by the Texas AgriLife Extension Service in Weslaco.  Ranchers may have been sold livestock, unable to provide sufficient feed.  Livestock loss data was unavailable as of this writing.  ||Locally heavy rainfall on June 22nd and 23rd began a slow process of dialing back the drought, as 4 to nearly 6 inches fell from Brownsville to Harlingen and points west.  Torrential, tropical rains from outer rain bands of Tropical Storm Arlene would put a true dent into the drought to begin July, as another 3 to 5 inches fell countywide on June 30th and July 1st.  ||[Damage details to dryland crops and livestock herds will be provided here].

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across all of inland Willacy County through mid June, and would temporarily worsen toward month's end before drenching rains provided some relief, beginning on the 22nd and 23rd.  Damage information for the 2011 Drought is provided in the entry for Exceptional (D4) Drought later in this report.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions covered all but the northern tip of Coastal Cameron County through June 20th; Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across these areas (east of Arroyo City) through June 20th before moving to Exceptional to close out the month.  The withering drought impacted wildlife at the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge as water supplies became limited to nil while near record heat was provided by sunny, breezy days and breezy, sultry nights with no dew. ||Locally heavy rainfall on June 22nd and 23rd began a slow process of dialing back the drought, as 2 to 3 inches fell from South Padre Island to Laguna Atascosa.  Torrential, tropical rains from outer rain bands of Tropical Storm Arlene would put a true dent into the drought to begin July, as 3 to 5 inches fell toward the coast from June 29th through July 1st.  ||[Damage/impacts to wildlife will be reported here].

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across all of coastal Willacy County through mid June, and would temporarily worsen toward month's end before drenching rains provided some relief, beginning on the 22nd and 23rd.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions deteriorated to Extreme (D3) in all of Brooks County on June 7th, and would continue through the end of the month.  Rainfall of more than 2 inches across the southern half of the county would provide a bit of relief at month's end.  Livestock, particularly cattle head, were affected most as very short moisture levels dwindled available feed and required [a large sale] of cattle much earlier in the year than usual.  [Hay supplies were limited/damaged by the extreme drought - details here].

Extreme (D3) Drought covered the northern four-fifths of Kenedy County during the third week of June, with Exceptional (D4) conditions reaching into the county from the south, northward to Norias/Rudolph. Some relief, in the form of 2 to 4 inches of rain from scattered to numerous thunderstorms, would dial the drought back to close the month.  ||Ranch moisture remained very short through the peak of the drought, and impact on low quality/dwindling feed supplies forced owners to sell off [# of] head of cattle much earlier in the year than normal.  Dryland crops [if known] withered under the hot sunshine and breezy to windy days, with little if any dew recovery overnight.||[Damage details will be provided here].

Exceptional (D4) conditions spread across all of inland Willacy County by the 21st. Immediately after the designation, some relief, in the form of 2 to 6 inches of rain from numerous thunderstorms, would dial the drought back to close out the month. Ranch moisture remained very short through the peak of the drought, and impact on low quality/dwindling feed supplies forced owners to sell off an unknown number of head of cattle much earlier in the year than normal. ||The Texas AgriLife Extension Service reported insured crop losses to cotton, corn, and sorghum added up to $430,811, which was a small portion of much greater loss across the remainder of the Rio Grande Valley, by the peak of the drought in late June.

Exceptional D4 drought conditions spread northward across Coastal Willacy County by the third week in June. These conditions would continue the end of the month, as welcome rainfall of 2 to 6 inches farther inland did not reach the coast, where less than 2 inches would fall from isolated to scattered thunderstorms on the 22nd and 23rd.

Rainfall of 2 to 4 inches across most of Kenedy County on June 22nd and 23rd would return the southern fifth, including Norias and Rudolph, to Extreme (D3) Drought from Exceptional (D4) Drought beginning on June 28th.  Further improvements would arrive in July after more locally heavy rains moved through the area on June 30th and July 1st.||Crop damage and potential livestock impacts are provided in the June 21st through 27th episode report.

Rainfall of generally 3 to more than 6 inches on June 22nd and 23rd across the heart of Willacy County provided the start of drought relief.  Inland Willacy, which received the balance of the heavy rain, dialed back from Exceptional (D4) to Extreme (D3) conditions beginning on June 28th.  Further improvement would occur into early July, courtesy of another couple of inches on June 30th/July 1st in the heart of the agricultural region include San Perlita and Porfirio (east of Raymondville).   ||Damage information to dryland crops and any livestock impacts are discussed in the June 21st through 27th Exceptional drought entry.

Slow moving thunderstorms, containing more than an hour of torrential rains, dumped between 3 and 6 inches in central Willacy County during the early and mid afternoon of June 22nd.  In Raymondville, up to a foot of standing water was observed by storm spotters and the county Emergency Manager; several roads were temporarily closed due to the urban/poor drainage flooding.  No water reached structures.  Observed rainfall ranged from just under 3 inches on the west side of Raymondville to 6.10 inches 6 miles east of Raymondville (San Perlita). Other minor flooding was reported in Sebastian (just north of the Cameron/Willacy County line), with backyards turning to low water lakes and streets with more than a foot of water in them.||The flooding in Sebastian intensified on the 23rd, reaching into properties as poor drainage structure in town (pipe structure) could not handle the heavy rains and flooding reached into the ground floor of a number of structures in town.

Deep tropical moisture worked on boundaries left over from showers and storms on June 22nd and into the early morning of June 23rd to produce locally heavy squally rains in the City of Brownsville during the early afternoon of June 23rd, adding another 2 to 3+ inches of rain to the somewhat lesser, but notable, totals from June 22nd.  Brownsville/SPI International Airport reported 3.52 inches of rain, and nearby CoCoRaHS observers recorded between 2.18 and 3.15 inches.  ||Urban flooding, particularly in the lower lying areas along Boca Chica Boulevard stretching downtown, developed through the afternoon before waters receded after 4 PM or so.  Significant damage was not reported despite the more than one foot of standing water in city streets.

The ASOS platform at the Harlingen Valley International Airport recorded a wind gust of 66 miles per hour as a downburst moved through during a thunderstorm during the early afternoon. No damage was reported to the tower or on the field.

This short-lived tornado touched down in a subdivision approximately 4 miles east-northeast of the city of Hidalgo in southern Hidalgo County.  Most of the damage in this area was limited to the overturning of trampolines, the knocking down of wooden privacy fences, an outdoor storage building, and minor shingle damage to the roof of two homes.  A (relatively empty) moving truck was also blown on its side in the subdivision.  The tornado strengthened as it approached an import/export business on the west side of US-281.  Here, an office building lost between 25% and 33% of the roof as the tornado continued moving westward.  Much of the roofing material landed on a car parked behind the office building, resulting in the injury of the driver.  In this area, a single-wide mobile home was heavily damaged, as well as a couple of semi trucks.  Before lifting, tornadic winds knocked down several hundred feet of concrete block fencing.  No damage was seen beyond this point by the National Weather Service survey crew or officials from the city of Pharr.
The continued lack of rainfall across Zapata County resulted in the exceptional D4 drought conditions persisting across all of Zapata County the beginning of July.

Exceptional D4 drought conditions continued across all of Starr County at the beginning of July.  Rainfall between June 22nd and June 30th helped alleviate some of the worst conditions; damage information for the prime growing season in 2011 (April - June) is provided in the report for June.

Exceptional D4 drought conditions continued across the western and south central half of Jim Hogg County and extreme D3 drought conditions continued across the eastern and north central half of Jim Hogg County the beginning of July as dry conditions persisted across the County Warning Area.

Rainfall across Hidalgo County the last week of June began easing drought conditions across the eastern one half of the County to start July. Exceptional D4 drought conditions continued across the western one half of Hidalgo County and Extreme D3 drought conditions prevailed across the eastern one half of  Hidalgo County the beginning of July.  Note:  Crop damage information for the 2011 spring/early summer drough is provided in the June report.

Rainfall across Kenedy County on the 22nd and a little on the 23rd of June began slowly improving drought conditions across the County.  The rainfall was sufficient to ease the drought across the southern one fourth of the County from the exceptional D4 drought conditions to extreme D3 drought conditions. Extreme D3 drought conditions prevailed across all of Kenedy County through July 11th, with the southern tip of the county improving to Severe (D2) conditions after the 4th.

Despite locally heavy rainfall on June 22nd, and a little on June 23rd, Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across the southern and eastern one tenth of Willacy County with extreme D3 drought conditions prevailed across the remainder north, central and western nine tenths of Willacy County the beginning of July. Note:  Crop damage information is provided in the June report, during the peak of the hottest and driest conditions.

Despite welcome rains on June 22nd and June 23rd, the long term drought continued to begin July in Cameron County. Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions across most of the county the beginning of July, except for the northwest tip.  Note: Crop damage information is provided in the June report, based on the peak of the hottest and driest conditions impacting spring growth.
Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across Coastal Willacy County to start July, despite the arrival of some much needed rainfall on June 22nd.
Despite some much welcome rainfall on June 22nd and a little more on June 23rd, Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions continued across Coastal Cameron County to start July.

Despite locally heavy rainfall on June 22nd, Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued through the first eleven days of July across the countyDry conditions persisted across Brooks County the beginning of July. Extreme D3 drought conditions prevailed across all of Brooks County, except the extreme southwestern tip where exceptional D4 drought conditions prevailed through July 4th.

The beneficial rains which moved across the Rio Grande Plains between June 30th and July 2nd, combined with other rains from June 22nd, finally  improved the drought conditions a little bit across Zapata County the first full week in July. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across all of Zapata County with the exception of the extreme northwestern tip of the county which still had Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions.

The beneficial rains which moved across the mid and upper Rio Grande Valley July 1st and 2nd, combined with rain on June 22nd, finally began miproving drought conditions in Starr County the first full week in July. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions replaced Exceptional (D4) conditions during the first full week of July.

The beneficial rains which moved across the Deep South Texas Brush Country June 22nd, and again on July 1st and 2nd, finally helped improve drought conditions a little bit in Jim Hogg County.  Extreme (D3) Drought conditions replaced Exceptional (D4) conditions which had plagued the County for most of June.

The beneficial rains which moved across the Lower Rio Grande Valley on June 22nd/23d, and again from the outer bands of Arlene on June 30th and residual showers and storms on July 1st put a dent into the 2011 drought in Hidalgo County.  Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across the western and central two thirds of Hidalgo County and Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the eastern one third of Hidalgo County the first full week in July, replacing Extreme to Exceptional (D4) Drought just a couple of weeks earlier.

The beneficial, locally torrential rains which covered Inland Willacy County on June 22nd, with additional rains on the 23rd were followed by another round of steady rain on June 30th (outer bands of Arlene).  These rains combined to make a notable dent in the 2011 Drought.  By July 5th, conditions had improved to Severe (D2) from Extreme (D3) across all of the County.

Beneficial rains which dumped heavy rains in excess of 8 inches in portions of Inland Cameron County on June 22nd, 23rd, and 30th made a notable dent into the 2011 drought after July 4th.  All of Cameron County shifted from Exceptional (D4) Drought down to Extreme (D2) Drought conditions between the end of June and the first full week of July.

The beneficial rains which moved across the Lower Rio Grande Valley on June 22nd, and again with the outer bands of Tropical Storm Arlene (June 30th) brought drought conditions from Extreme/Exceptional (D3/D4) along the Willacy County coast down to Severe (D2) by July 5th.

The beneficial rains which dropped more than 5 inches of rain between June 22nd and 30th had improved the drought conditions across all of Coastal Cameron County by the first full week in July. Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions in late June were shifted down to Severe (D2) conditions by July 5th; these conditions would continue through month's end.

A developing line of thunderstorms, containing torrential rains, moved through northern Brooks County during the early afternoon producing pockets of poor drainage and nuisance urban-type flooding along Highway 281 in Falfurrias. The Brooks county Sheriff department reported twelve inches of water was on Highway 281 and South FM 1418 by 315 PM CDT; less than an hour later, one and one half feet of water was also reported in several other locations along Highway 281.  Most of these locations have become flood prone due to overpass/bypass construction, which has caused clogging of normally well draining areas along the highway.
Power lines were knocked down by estimated winds near 60 mph from a severe thunderstorm in southwest Brooks County, along Farm to Market 755.

A re-forming strong to severe storm dropped several inches of rain in less than two hours in rural southern Brooks County, west of Federal Highway 281 and north of Farm to Market 755, west of Encino.  Excluding hail contamination, Doppler Radar estimated 2 to 4 inches of rain likely fell in this area, which includes a portion of the Encinitos Ranch.

The Texas Forest Service reported a 2,800 acre wildfire in Brooks County, most likely in the central and southern sections, which threatened several gas and oil wells but was contained fairly quickly before significant damage was realized.  Times are estimated.  Weather conditions featured a continuation of very hot temperatures (near 100 degrees) with humidity falling to or below 35 percent.  Winds were relatively low across the county, ranging from 10 to 15 mph with a few higher gusts.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose (along Laguna Madre in eastern Kenedy County) recorded a wind gust to 42 knots (48 mph) with sustained winds of 35 knots (40 mph) as a line of thunderstorms raced across the area during the mid afternoon of May 12th.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: The NOAA Buoy 42020, about 35 nm northeast of Port Mansfield, recorded prolonged wind gusts in excess of 40 knots as the line of strong storms and associated wake low pressure passed through the Lower Texas Gulf waters east of Kenedy County.  Peak gusts were 40 knots or higher for a little more than an hour; peak sustained wind reached 34 knots at 520 PM CDT but otherwise remained in the 30 to 33 knots range through most of the gale force gusts.  The peak gust of 43 knots (49 mph) occurred at 508 PM CDT.

A friend of an NWS employee reported Golfball size hail in Raymondville, some which caused dents and dings to several vehicles parked outside, as the first of two hailstorms scooted through Willacy County during the mid afternoon of May 15th, 2011.

A wildfire grew rapidly to 400 acres on the Henry Garza Ranch, 13 miles east of the City of Zapata, during the late afternoon of June 9th before being rapidly contained shortly after sunset.  One house and three oil facilities were threatened and saved by Zapata County and City fire crews. Otherwise, the fire affected only grassland.

A wildfire rapidly spread to 1,200 acres of range land, which burned from 4 PM until midnight at the Barberio Ranch and Loma Blanca Vela Ranch, 11 to 13 miles south of Zapata.  Grasses and mesquite were blackened by the blaze, but no structures were threatened.  Livestock damage information was unavailable at the time of this writing. Fire departments from Salineno and La Rosita (southern portion of county) responded, as did the Regional Liaison Officer for region 6 (San Antonio/Bexar County).

Sparks from a hot catalytic converter on a ranch vehicle most likely set rangeland ablaze in Northwest Brooks County (about 13 miles west-southwest of Falfurrias), beginning at around 10 AM on June 18th. In rapid succession, the fire, driven by near record hot temperatures, humidity near 25 percent, highly cured fine and coarse fuels, and frequent wind gusts near or above 30 mph day and night, spread to 3300 acres by late afternoon on the 18th, 8000 acres by mid evening, and more than 10,000 acres before midnight on the 19th. The fire exceeded 12,000 acres early on the 19th, and continued to grow despite some successful containment efforts. By June 20th, the acreage had reached 22,500, placing it only behind the Encinitos/Burns Ranch event of March 18, 2008, in recent years. Unofficial reports early on June 21st indicated an estimated 30,000 acres had burned in Brooks County, with the fire having neared State Highway 285, the main thoroughfare between the King Ranch and the Rio Grande Plains in Deep South Texas.  At times during the event, heavy smoke forced the closure of the highway.||By mid morning June 22nd, the fire had peaked at 32,000 acres, and was 100 percent contained after light to moderate rains and lighter winds arrived. Texas Forest Service personnel noted that the steady increase in acreage through the 21st was due to continued dry and breezy daytime conditions, but also to the firestorm environment, which kept humidity low through the night due to the localized heating and additional wind generated by the blaze. ||By June 21st, the blaze had burned down several unoccupied deer hunting camp buildings, including houses, lean-tos, and outbuildings, on or near Rancho de los Jefes, and had moved into extreme southeastern Duval County and was within a couple of miles of the Jim Hogg County line. The largest ranch affected was the SMAC Ranch; the Palo Blanco Ranch also burned. Rapid response by up to 30 fire departments from the Lower Rio Grande Valley to the Coastal Bend, along with assistance from the Texas Forest Service and state level emergency management personnel, helped save at least 20 threatened homes on the 18th and 19th. Texas Department of Public Safety Aircraft located and evacuated a family of four trapped inside a threatened home.  At least 300 first responders, from the Rio Grande Valley to the Coastal Bend, were able to contain and control the massive blaze on the 22nd and 23rd, as cloud cover, lighter winds, higher humidity, and light to moderate rains arrived.||Three partially burned bodies were discovered by the firefighting force during containment efforts.  The bodies were in various states of decomposition when they were found, suggesting that the persons had died well before the wildfires arrived. Causes for the deaths were unknown and likely were from a combination of lack of food/water and heat.

Slow moving thunderstorms, containing more than an hour of torrential rains, dumped between 3 and 5 inches in western Cameron County during the early and mid afternoon of June 22nd.  Numerous instances of nuisance urban flooding were reported, much in the typical poor drainage locations that see flooding with any locally heavy rainfall.||Across the Lower Valley, nuisance flooding of roads, ditches, and even some properties occurred each afternoon. On the 22nd, locally high water was reported in La Feria, Palm Valley/Harlingen, and San Benito. An estimated 5 inches of rain flooded the Mariposa subdivision near La Feria ��� an area which often has poor drainage issues and suffered greatly after Hurricane Dolly. The water rose to around 2 feet in neighborhood roads, closing them but not reaching into structures. On the west side of Harlingen, CoCoRaHS observers reported between 4 and 5.27 inches of rain.

Slow moving thunderstorms, containing up to an hour and a half of torrential rains, dumped between 3 and 4 inches across the heart of populated Hidalgo County, from Mission to Weslaco, during the early and mid afternoon of June 22nd.  Numerous instances of nuisance urban flooding were reported, much in the typical poor drainage locations that see flooding with any locally heavy rainfall.||Nuisance flooding of roads and ditches were reported in the typical poor drainage locations of McAllen/Pharr and Weslaco.  At McAllen/Miller airport, 3.13 inches of rain fell in less than two hours before the power was knocked out due to lightning in the area. CoCoRaHS observers reported 3.08 inches and 3.18 inches in Mission and Edinburg, respectively, and nearly 3 inches (2.84) fell at the Mid Valley Airport in Weslaco.

The Weslaco/Donna Emergency Manager reported extensive flooding along both sides of Highway 83 (frontage roads along the expressway), as well as significant street flooding along Business 83 and Texas Boulevard (Farm to Market 88).  Local media reports indicated more than 2 feet of water in roads, some which impacted properties in town.  The flooding was caused by another round of torrential, tropical rains between 130 and 330 PM, which dropped more than 3 inches on top of the 2.84 inches which had fallen on the 22nd. More than 6 inches fell in Weslaco during the two day period.

Frequent cloud to ground lightning, particularly on the 22nd, caught a 400 barrel oil container on fire in Willacy County, and effects of another strike injured a woman attempting to enter her vehicle, all occurring around 3 PM CDT. The container fire was put out by the torrential rains; the woman was admitted to Valley Baptist Medical Center for observation.

Feeder bands associated with the fringe of Tropical  Storm Arlene, which made landfall 300 miles south of Brownsville, dropped a total of 3 inches at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport between 7 AM and 2 PM CDT, with the heaviest rains falling from mid morning through early afternoon.  Media accounts (videos and still photos) showed the typical urban flooding in low lying areas of the city, particularly from along and near Boca Chica Boulevard through Downtown.  CoCoRaHS observers in and near the city recorded generally 2 1/2 to a little more than 3 inches during the same period.

Report of a 300-acre brush fire located east of Federal Highway 281 near Encino in Brooks County. The fire was 100 percent contained. One home was threatened and saved. One firefighter was injured and transported to a local hospital. Responding agencies included: Southern Brooks County Fire Department (FD), Falfurrias FD, McAllen FD, Palm View FD, Edinburg FD, Pharr FD, San Miguel FD, McAllen FD, McAllen Public Works Department, Starr Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Texas Department of Public Safety (TXDPS) McAllen Aircraft.

Report of the 3,200-acre brush fire located on Farm to Market (FM) 755, 25 miles west of Federal Highway 281, at the Brooks/Hidalgo County line in Brooks and Hidalgo Counties. The fire was 100 percent contained. Four structures were threatened and saved. Responding agencies were: Southern Brooks County Fire Department (FD), Falfurrias FD, Linn San Miguel FD, Edinburg FD, Pharr FD, Mission FD, McAllen FD, Jim Hogg FD, Jim Wells FD, Hidalgo Precinct 4 Dozer Team, McAllen Public Works, Starr and Gemini Ambulance Services, Hidalgo Health Department Command Trailer. Weslaco Rehab Team, Texas Department of Public Safety (TXDPS) McAllen Aircraft, Texas Forest Service (TFS) Air Attack and Dozer Task Force and Regional Liaison Officer (RLO) 3C.

Scattered showers which ended in Zapata County by July 2nd manifest themselves in slightly improved drought conditions across portions of the county for the middle and latter part of the month. Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across two thirds of Zapata County while Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across a northwest to southeast slot encompassing the central and southeastern one third of the county.  The lack of rain to close the month would increase drought levels to D3 everywhere by the 26th.

Scattered showers with local downpours through July 2nd manifest themselves in slight improvement in drought moved across portions of Starr County the second full week in July. Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across two thirds of Starr County, with  Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed across the remainder of Starr County encompassing the northwestern one third and extreme northeastern tip of the county. D3 conditions would spread a bit farther north by the 26th.

Scattered showers continuing through July 2nd manifest into improved drought conditions across portions of Jim Hogg County the second full week in July, improving the drought conditions across the central and southern portions of the county. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across the north and northwestern one half of Jim Hogg County. Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the central and eastern one half of Jim Hogg County the second full week in July; these conditions would continue through month's end.

A few showers affecting mainly southern Brooks County through July 2nd manifest into improved drought conditions across the southern and central portions of the county by the 2nd week of July. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across the northern one half of Brooks County and Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the southern one half of the county the second full week in July, and would continue through month's end.

Scattered to numerous showers moved across Hidalgo County on July 1st and 2nd, dropping up to 2 inches of rain (radar estimated) which manifested into improved drought conditions, when combined with late June torrential rains, across the county for the second week of July through month's end. Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across a small sliver of western Hidalgo County; otherwise, Severe (D2) conditions covered all but the southeastern quarter of the county, where Moderate (D1) conditions prevailed.  These conditions held through month's end.

Scattered showers on July 1st, and isolated showers on the 9th and 10th, manifest improved drought conditions across Kenedy County by the second full week in July, which continued through month's end.  Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across the northern one fifth of the County; Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the remainder of the County throgh the 26th, with a small area of Moderate (D1) conditions noted across the southern fifth of the County starting on the 26th.

Heavy rainfall in late June, combined with a few more showers through July 2nd, and isolated activity on the 9th and 10th, combined to eliminate, temporarily, Severe or greater drought conditions in Willacy County. Severe D2 drought conditions continued across the northern and eastern one fifth of Willacy County from the second full week in July through July 25th, with Moderate (D1) elsewhere.  Moderate conditions covered all of the county starting on the 26th.

The combination of torrential rain in late June, leftover activity on July 2nd and 3rd, and isolated activity on the 9th and 10th manifest into improvement in drought conditions across all but the eastern third of inland Cameron County, beginning July 12th and continuing through month's end. Elsewhere in the County, Moderate (D1) conditions were noted.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions continued across all of Coastal Willacy County the second full week in July; isolated showers on July 10th allowed Drought conditions to subside to Moderate (D1) beginning on the 26th.

A 66 year old man from Monterrey (state of Nuevo Leon) Mexico became in distress after being reportedly swept away from the Isla Blanca Park jetties on South Padre Island shortly after noon of June 17th.  The man was found about one half mile north of the jetties and brought to shore, but by the time paramedics arrived, was unresponsive.  After no revival after CPR was administered, the man was pronounced dead.||While the weather was sunny and hot, the water was disturbed.  Winds at offshore buoys ranged from 14 to 21 knots, with frequent gusts from 15 to as high as 27 knots through the day.  Seas at a NOAA Buoy about 50 nautical miles east northeast of Port Mansfield rising to 7.2 feet, with a 7 to 8 second swell period, from late morning through early afternoon.  Photos taken by a local surfing instructor showed estimated 2 to 3+ foot waves with choppy waters.

A grass fire rapidly spread to near 1,000 acres during the afternoon of August 3rd near Puerto Rico in northwest Hidalgo County. The fire started when a vehicle servicing local telephone poles sparked; the vehicle caught on fire and was heavily damaged.  One barn and one home were saved by fire crews, which numbered up to 15 departments from at least Hidalgo and Starr Counties. The fire was reported to be contained by evening.

A 44 year old man visiting from Monterrey, Nuevo Leon, Mexico was found face down in the surf just north of the Los Corales Condominiums north of Andy Bowie Park (8500 block of Padre Boulevard), near Public Beach Access Point 5. After attempts to revive the man were unsuccessful, he was pronounced dead either en route or after arrival at Valley Baptist Hospital in Harlingen.

A truck, driving erratically through dry brush, eventually got stuck and sparks likely from a hot catalytic converter set off a blaze, which quickly grew to 50 acres by noon and would grow rapidly through the afternoon, as east winds increased to 20 mph with gusts which may have reached 25 mph.  The fire was contained by late afternoon and controlled during the evening after several flare-ups.||The final report indicated 500 acres burned on the Robert East Ranch,|one mile northwest of Port Mansfield, in Willacy County. During containment and control, eight firefighters were treated for heat exhaustion/dehydration, and one firefighter was treated for a sprained knee.||Responding agencies included: Port Mansfield, Raymondville, San Perlita, Lyford, Santa Monica, La Feria, Rio Hondo, Linn-San Manuel and Edinburg Volunteer Fire Departments (VFDs), McAllen and Harlingen Fire Departments (FDs), McAllen Public Works, Willacy County Sheriff���s Office (SO), Emergency Medical Service (EMS), Hidalgo County Emergency Management Coordinator (EMC) and Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD).
The lack of rain at the end of July increased the drought levels to Extreme D3 everywhere in Zapata County the end of July through the middle of August.
Extreme (D3) Drought conditions covered all but a sliver of northern Starr County (Severe, D2) for the last week of July through August first.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions generally prevailed across the south half of Jim Hogg County, with Extreme (D3) conditions across the north half, during the first week of August.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across the northern one half of Brooks County and Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the southern one half of the county from August 1st through the 15th, with some increase in coverage of Extreme Drought sliding to the southeast after the 9th.

Drought conditions in Hidalgo County maintained their levels seen in July through the first two weeks of August. From east to west, conditions ranged from none/Abnormally Dry (D0) in the extreme southeast corner - courtesy of the heavy rainfall to end June and start July along with seasonable temperatures thereafter - to D2 across the western and northern portion of the county, where rain was much more scarce in early July.  The remains of Tropical Storm Don reached southeast Hidalgo, but dropped a paltry less than a quarter of an inch and even less to the north and west.  By August 9th, a sliver of Extreme (D3) Drought would return to the southwest corner of the county.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across the northern one fifth of Kenedy   County; Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the remainder of the County, with a small area of Moderate (D1) conditions noted across the southern fifth of the county on August first.

Severe D2 drought conditions prevailed across the eastern third of inland Cameron County the first day of August.  Elsewhere in the County, Moderate (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0) Drought conditions were noted.  The conditions would improve at the next release of the state Drought Monitor on August 2nd, as gentle rainfall of one half to three quarters of an inch associated with a fizzling Tropical Storm Don covered the eastern two thirds of the county on July 29th.

Drought conditions improved from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) across Starr County on August 2nd, a result of scattered showers and storms from the remains of Tropical Storm Don on July 29th and 30th.  The slightly improved conditions would only last a week, as dry hot weather would deteriorate conditions by the 9th.
The drought conditions intensified across Jim Hogg County the second week of August. Extreme D3 drought conditions engulfed the entire county due to the continued lack of rainfall.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions spread across most of Starr County the second full week in August. Extreme D3 drought conditions engulfed the all of the county except for the southwestern quarter and the northeastern tip of Starr County from the 9th to the 15th.

D4 Exceptional drought conditions developed across the extreme northern portions of Zapata County as the month of August progressed due to the lack of rainfall across the county.  Extreme D3 drought conditions prevailed across the rest of Zapata County the second week of August.

The drought conditions intensified across Jim Hogg County as the month of August progressed. Exceptional D4 drought conditions prevailed across the northern one third of the county and Extreme D3 drought conditions continued across the southern and central two thirds of the county.

The drought conditions intensified across Starr County as the month of August progressed. Extreme D3 drought conditions engulfed the entire county due to the continued lack of rainfall.  By month's end, the annual total crop loss and damage to cotton, corn, and sorghum totaled $1,277,473.37.

Exceptional D4 drought conditions developed across the northern one third of Brooks County as the month of August progressed. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the south and central two thirds of Brooks County.

Lack of rainfall across the north and west portions of Hidalgo County would deteriorate drought conditions by mid month, with these areas reaching Extreme (D3) by the 16th.  Severe (D2) Drought expanded east across Highway 281, but Abnormally Dry (D0) to Moderate (D1) conditions would prevail across the Lower Valley portion (Pharr to the Cameron County line, generally south of Highway 83) through the remainder of the month, aided by additional pockets of rain, particularly on the 26th and the 31st. ||A bit to the north, Extreme (D3) conditions would expand to all areas west of Highway 281 from Edinburg South, and to all of northern Hidalgo County, by the 23rd; Severe Conditions would cover all but the southeast corner from the 23rd through the 31st.  This increase occurred despite some of the aforementioned rain, which was not enough to counter the climatological rise in rain frequency that occurs from late August into September.||By month's end, preliminary crop damage and production loss to corn, cotton, and sorghum totaled $4,690,154.80.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions developed across the northern one quarter of Kenedy County as the month of August progressed due to the lack of rainfall. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the north central and western one half of the county; while Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the central and west central one quarter of the County.||Extreme conditions would spread to all but the southern quarter of the county, with Severe conditions covering the southern quarter, from the 23rd through the end of the month.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the northwestern quarter and eastern third of Willacy County near the end of August, as dry, hot, and breezy conditions continued across the county.  Though some rain fell on August 25th and 31st, it was not enough to quench the increasingly dry conditions, in part based on climatological average values of rain which peak from the end of August into September.||Preliminary insured crop damage to corn, cotton, and sorghum was highest in Willacy County for all preliminary data for the Rio Grande Valley during the 2010/2011 season.  In all, $7,249,055.17 was damaged or lost, with the vast majority from failed dryland cotton.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the northern and eastern two thirds of Cameron County near the end of the month of August as dry conditions and a lack of rainfall continued across the county.  While some rainfall returned to these areas, particularly on the 25th/26th and 31st, it was not enough to recover rainfall back toward the climatological averages, which typically increase by month's end.||Preliminary insured damage and production loss to cotton, corn, and sorghum totaled more than $4.5 million for the second reporting period (late July through the end of August).

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions developed across the extreme northern portions of Zapata County the end of the month of August and continued the first of September due to the lack of rainfall across the county.  Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the rest of Zapata County the first of September.

The drought intensified across Jim Hogg County the end of the month of August. Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions prevailed across the northern one third of the county and Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued across the southern and central two thirds of the county the first of September.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions developed across the northern one third of Brooks County the end of the month of August and continued through the first of September. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the south and central two thirds of Brooks County the first of September.
The drought intensified across Starr County the end of the month of August.  Extreme (D3) Drought conditions engulfed the entire county due to the continued lack of rainfall the first of September.

The drought intensified across the central portions of Hidalgo County near the end of the month of August. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the northern and western two thirds of Hidalgo County and Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the south central one quarter of the county the first of September.   The rest of the county  (Mercedes and Weslaco) experienced Moderate (D1) or less drought conditions.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions prevailed across the northern one quarter of Kenedy County the end of the month of August and continued into the first of September. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the central and western two thirds of the county; while Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the southern one fifth of the County.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the western quarter and eastern quarter of Willacy County the end of the month of August and continued into the first of September as dry conditions and a lack of rainfall continued across the county.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the northern and eastern two thirds of Cameron County the end of the month of August and into the first of September as dry conditions and a lack of rainfall continued across the county.

Severe D2 drought conditions prevailed across coastal Cameron County the first day of August. The conditions would improve at the next release of the state Drought Monitor on August 2nd, as gentle rainfall of one half to one inch associated with a fizzling Tropical Storm Don covered the area from the beaches to Port Isabel/Bayview on July 29th.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across coastal Cameron County near the end of the month of August as dry conditions and a lack of rainfall continued across the county.  While some rainfall returned to these areas, particularly on the 31st, it was not enough to recover rainfall back toward the climatological averages, which typically increase by month's end.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across coastal Willacy County near the end of August, as dry, hot, and breezy conditions continued across the region.  Though some rain fell on August 25th and 31st, it was not enough to quench the increasingly dry conditions, in part based on climatological average values of rain which peak from the end of August into September.

The US Fish and Wildlife Service reported the development of several wildfires during the afternoon of September 12th on tracts of the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge in northwest Willacy County.  The fires, which covered 300, 81, and 105 acres, respectively, morphed into a complex that covered 465 acres in an area bounded by State Highway 186, the Hidalgo County line, and East Lake.  ||Weather conditions across the area for much of the month prior to the fires' development features afternoon humidity between 15 and 20 percent, temperatures between 100 and 107 degrees, and pulse gust 20 foot winds between 15 and 20 mph.  ||On the day of the rapid fire growth, afternoon temperatures reached 103, humidity fell below 25 percent, and winds gusted between 14 and 20 mph.  The fires were gradually contained through the 13th and 14th, with 75% containment by 5 PM CST on the 14th and 90 percent containment by 8 PM CST on the 14th.

A small but severe thunderstorm, featuring a bow-shape on its front edge and containing small cores of microbursts, raced through southwest Starr County around 1030 PM CDT September 17th. One of those microbursts reached ground.||KRGV-TV-5 reported structural damage in the small community of Fronton (along the Rio Grande). Damage included at least two roofs torn off/peeled back, several fences blown down, power lines blown down, and numerous large mesquite and live oak limbs broken off trees.

Slow moving thunderstorms moved into extreme southeast Zapata and southwest Starr County between 930 and 1030 PM, September 17th, initially producing a microburst in Fronton but ultimately dumping nearly 3 inches of rain in some locations before sliding south of the Rio Grande just before midnight.  At the Falcon Dam cooperative observing location, 2.80 inches of rain fell, most likely in less than two hours.  No significant flooding was reported in the Roma to Falcon Heights area as of this writing.
Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions spread across all of Zapata County the middle of the month of September with no rainfall occurring across the county.
Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions spread across all of Jim Hogg County the middle of the month of September with no rainfall occurring across the county.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions spread across all of Starr County the middle of the month of September with no rainfall occurring across the county.  Pockets of thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall, perhaps more than 4 inches in spots on September 17th in northwest Starr dipped the drought intensity in this sliver of the county to D3 (Extreme) from the 20th through the 30th.
Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions spread across all of Brooks County the middle of the month of September with no rainfall occurring across the county.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions spread across the western, central and northern sections of Hidalgo County the middle of the month of September with no rainfall occurring across these areas of Hidalgo County. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the central two tenths of the county oriented in a southwest to northeast line. Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the east central one tenth of the county also oriented in a southwest to northeast line through the final week of the month, with moderate conditions in the southeast corner (Weslaco-Mercedes).||During the final week of the month, Severe (D2) conditions would stretch into the Mercedes/Weslaco area as rainfall was significantly lower than average - which peaks at this time of year.  No changes to the Extreme to Exceptional drought were noted to close the month elsewhere.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions spread southward across Kenedy County encompassing the north and central three quarters of the county the middle of September.  Extreme (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across the south central one quarter of Kenedy County the middle of the month of September, but would be swallowed into Exceptional (D4) by the last week of the month due to paltry rainfall in a time when average precipitation peaks for the month, and the year.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across the northern, southwestern and eastern one half of Willacy County the middle of September. Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across south central one half of Willacy County the middle of the month of September as rainfall continued scarce across the county.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across the eastern one quarter of Cameron County the middle of the month of September. Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the central one half of Cameron County the middle of the month of September as rainfall continued scarce across the Cameron County.
Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across all of Coastal Cameron County the middle of the month of September.
Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across all of Coastal Willacy County the middle of the month of September.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions continued across the north and northwestern one third of Zapata County the third week of September. However, heavy thunderstorms moved across the south and central portions of the county, dropping more than 3 inches of rain (2.80 inches just south of the line at Falcon Dam) and improving drought conditions to Extreme (D3) conditions across the central and southern two thirds of Zapata County.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions continued across the southeastern one quarter of Jim Hogg County the third week of September. However, a cluster of heavy thunderstorms during the evening of the 17th dumped an estimated 3 to 4 inches, locally 5 inches, of rainfall across southern and western Jim Hogg County. These rains, as well as a little more rain on the 18th, improved drought conditions to Extreme (D3) across the western, northern and central three quarters of Jim Hogg County.

Exceptional D4 drought conditions developed across the north and eastern one half of Willacy County the last week of September.  Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across the south central and south west one half of Willacy County; each continued through month's end.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions developed across the eastern one quarter of Cameron County the last week of September. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across the central one half of Cameron County and Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the western one quarter of Cameron County. Each would continue through month's end.
Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions developed across all of Coastal Willacy County the last week of the month of September and continue through month's end.
Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions developed across all of Coastal Cameron County the last week of the month of September, and would continue through month's end.

Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across the north and northwestern one third of Zapata County into the first week of October, with Extreme (D3) conditions dominating the remainder of the county.

Severe (D3) Drought conditions prevailed across all but the extreme southeast and extreme north sections of Jim Hogg County, where Exceptional (D4) conditions prevailed, through October.  Locally heavy rainfall across the south central and southwest portion of the county on the 1st assured that worsening conditions would hold off through the month.

Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions dominated the county through October.  The month began with all but the northwest sliver of the county in Exceptional Drought; locally heavy rains up to 2 inches or more fell generally along a Roma to Rio Grande City line, extending northward into southern Jim Hogg County during the late afternoon of October 1st.  These rains would slightly improve conditions to Extreme across the western half of the county, which would continue through month's end.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions dominated all but a small sliver of northwestern Brooks County through October, which improved slightly to Extreme (D3) by October 4th after a few thunderstorms dropped slightly hopeful rains.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions dominated Hidalgo County with the sole exception of communities along the Rio Grande from Penitas to the Cameron County line, where Exceptional (D4) conditions improved slightly to Extreme (D3, Penitas to Pharr/McAllen) on the 11th.  Extreme conditions prevailed around Weslaco/Donna, with Severe (D2) holding on in Mercedes, where enough rain fell to temporarily keep conditions from worsening.||The extended drought in one of the Valley's agricultural heartlands may have impacted the coming autumn citrus harvest.  Details and damage estimates may be provided in the December report.

Exceptional (D4) drought conditions covered nearly all of Kenedy County through October.  A brief period of improvement to Extreme (D3) spread into the county from Armstrong to the Willacy border, after 2 to 3 inches of rain fell on October 9th.  The area of Extreme Drought would continue through the end of the month.

Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions prevailed across inland Willacy County through October.  Extreme conditions (slight improvement) appeared across the western half of the county by October 4th, after some welcome rainfall on the 1st; measured/estimated rainfall between 1 and 2 inches on the 9th maintained the slightly improved area through the remainder of the month.  Locations east of State Highway 77 and south of State Highway 186 saw less rain, and continued at Exceptional levels.

Severe (D2) to Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions prevailed across inland Cameron County through the month of October.  Rain events on October 1st and 9th helped to reshape the areas through the month.  In general, Exceptional conditions prevailed east of State Highway 77; Extreme (D3) prevailed in a thin band along and just west of the highway, including Brownsville and Harlingen, and western Cameron County (Santa Rosa-La Feria) remained in Severe conditions.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions persisted across coastal Willacy County through October.  A pocket of heavy rainfall a little more than an inch was far shy of the monthly average (around 4 inches), except near Port Mansfield, and did little to improve the long term dryness.

Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions persisted across all of Coastal Cameron County through October.  Estimated rainfall of 1 to 2 inches on October 9th from Arroyo City to Laguna Atascosa was not enough to reduce the long term drought; monthly totals were still less than one half of average.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across the areas near the coast of Willacy County by the end of the month of August and continued into the first of September as dry conditions and a lack of rainfall continued across the county.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed across locations near the coast of Cameron County the end of the month of August and into the first of September as dry conditions and a lack of rainfall continued across the county.

An off duty inspector for Zapata County reported, and photographed, wind damage to an under construction foam building in Zapata after a vigorous outflow boundary/gust front crossed the area during the late afternoon of September 29th.  Winds at nearby Zapata County Airport (Medina) were clocked at 44 mph 5 minutes earlier. Construction type and damage, combined with no nearby reports of more traditional damage (large limbs, roof material, etc.) suggested a pulse gust below 58 mph.

The Zapata County Sheriff's Office reported minor flooding to curb level along State Highway 16 and Federal Highway 83, stretching south toward 9th Avenue. The emergency manager reported 1.75 inches at the fire station; other estimates suggested around 2 inches in less than an hour with the heavy thunderstorm which crossed the city between 8 and 9 PM that evening.

Lightning struck a radio tower near the Brownsville Public Utilities Board (Brownsville PUB) facility just before noon on September 29th, starting a small blaze in a storage room which was quickly put out by firefighters.  Fiber stored in the room were deemed a total loss. Dollar damage was not available as of this writing but assumed to be in the thousands of dollars.

Rainfall on October 1st, and again on October 9th across Zapata County removed the area of Exceptional (D4) Drought in the northwest corner, leaving the entire county at Extreme (D3) levels on the 11th - conditions which prevailed into early November.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: The harbormaster at Port Mansfield reported a gust of 41 mph with a strong thunderstorm during the late afternoon of October 9th.  By proxy, it is assumed that similar winds occurred in the Port Mansfield channel and adjacent waters of the Laguna Madre, about a mile east of the report location.

The cooperative observer at Armstrong reported 3.64 inches of rain from mid afternoon thunderstorm clusters passing through central Kenedy County on October 9th.  Estimated rainfall of 2 to 3 inches also fell in northern Willacy County as the clusters moved and developed toward the Lower Rio Grande Valley.

A wildfire, with unknown causes (as of this writing), began on sandy ranchlands of southern Brooks County and spread rapidly into northern Hidalgo County on the strength of 15 to 25 mph northwest winds, humidity below 20 percent, and very dry grasses and brush. ||Nearly a dozen fire departments from across the Rio Grande Valley worked together to battle the blaze, which was reported to reach 2,000 acres in both counties (assumed 1,000 in Brooks). Homes along FM 755 about 14 miles west of Federal Highway 281 (Hidalgo County) were threatened and saved. Agencies responding to the blaze include Falfurrias, Pharr, Weslaco, McAllen, Alamo, Alton, Palmview, U.S. Fish and Wildlife, Edinburg, Linn-San Manuel, Mercedes and Brooks County.  A state Department of Public Safety helicopter was dispatched to drop retardant on the flames.||The fire had not been contained at 6 PM, but cooling temperatures and diminishing winds after sunset allowed crews to get on top of the situation, with only hotspots left by 9 PM CST.

A wildfire, with unknown causes (as of this writing), began on sandy ranchlands of southern Brooks County and spread rapidly into northern Hidalgo County on the strength of 15 to 25 mph northwest winds, humidity below 20 percent, and very dry grasses and brush. ||Nearly a dozen fire departments from across the Rio Grande Valley worked together to battle the blaze, which was reported to reach 2,000 acres in both counties (assumed 1,000 in Hidalgo). Homes along FM 755 about 14 miles west of Federal Highway 281 were threatened and saved. Agencies responding to the blaze include Falfurrias, Pharr, Weslaco, McAllen, Alamo, Alton, Palmview, U.S. Fish and Wildlife, Edinburg, Linn-San Manuel, Mercedes and Brooks County.  A state Department of Public Safety helicopter was dispatched to drop retardant on the flames.||The fire had not been contained at 6 PM, but cooling temperatures and diminishing winds after sunset allowed crews to get on top of the situation, with only hotspots left by 9 PM CST.

Exceptional (D4) Drought continued to cover all but the northwestern corner of Brooks County through November. Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated. Loss/damage estimated were not available as of this writing.

Extreme (D3) Drought covered the western two thirds of Cameron County through most of November, with the exception of a small pocket of Severe (D2) Drought from Santa Rosa to La Feria which held on for the first week of the month (November 1st to 7th).  Exceptional (D4) Drought continued east of Federal Highway 77.   A bout of light rain, adding up to 0.25 to 0.50 inches along Highway 77 on the 10th, was not enough to alleviate conditions, as dry air surged in behind the rain, which was non-tropical in origin.||Windy and extremely dry conditions to close out Thanksgiving weekend and continue through the 29th moved the needle to Exceptional (D4) for the entire County by month's end.  Impact on the citrus, sugar, onion, and other harvests were still to be determined. Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated.

Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across coastal Cameron County through November.  A bout of light rain, adding up to nearly half an inch on the 10th, was not enough to alleviate conditions, as dry air surged in behind the rain, which was non-tropical in origin.

Extreme (D3) Drought covered the western half of inland Willacy County, with Exceptional (D4) Drought continuing over the eastern half of inland Willacy County (not including Port Mansfield), through November.  ||A blue norther cold front swept the area on the 27th, leaving gusty winds and extremely dry conditions.  The extreme dry continued into the 29th.  Impact on harvests of citrus and vegetables was unknown as of this writing. Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated.
Exceptional (D4) Drought covered coastal Willacy County through November.

Exceptional (D4) Drought continued or intensified for nearly all of Hidalgo County for the majority of November.  Initially Severe (D2) Conditions over extreme southeast portions, including Mercedes, deteriorated to Extreme (D3) on the 8th. Extreme (D3) conditions from Weslaco to Hidalgo (city) to begin the month deteriorated to Exceptional (D4) on the 8th.  Grasses and harvests continued to wither dryland and citrus; additional damage/loss data was not available as of this writing.  Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated.||A blue norther cold front swept through on Thanksgiving weekend, exacerbating the drought with extremely dry conditions through the 29th, gusty winds on the 27th, and a dry freeze in many areas on the morning of the 28th.  By the 29th, the entire county was in Exceptional Drought.

Exceptional (D4) Drought continued over the eastern half of Starr County, with Extreme (D3) Drought continuing over the western half of the county through November.  The withering drought over the eastern half maintained a period, extending fourteen months, where less than five inches of rain fell in some spots!  ||Harvest production (vegetables and some citrus) continued through the month; damage/loss estimates were unknown as of this writing.  Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued over Zapata county through November.  ||Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated. Damage/loss information was not available as of this writing.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued over all but the southeast corner of Jim Hogg County through November, where Exceptional (D4) Drought prevailed.  ||Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated. Damage/loss information was not available as of this writing.

Exceptional (D4) Drought continued over all but the south central third of Kenedy County through November, where Extreme (D3) Drought prevailed due to residual soil moisture left behind from locally heavy rainfall on October 9th. ||A blue norther crashing through the ranch on the 26th/27th brought three days of extremely dry condtions, with afternoon humidity falling to or below 10 percent through the 29th.  Gusty winds to 40 mph further exacerbated conditions on the 27th, as did a dry freeze early on the 28th.  ||Impact on livestock remained extreme, with no grazing available and herds being liquidated. Damage/loss information was unavailable as of this writing.

Temperatures fell below freezing in wind protected areas, including Falfurrias, between 3 and 4 AM and continued until 8 AM on the 28th.  Minimum temperature at the Hollywood Hunting Camp, 3.5 miles west of Falfurrias, dipped to 26 degrees between 7 and 8 AM.  Temperatures in non wind protected areas only fell into the mid 30s, including Brooks County Airport (2 miles southeast of Falfurrias).

Temperatures fell below freezing in wind protected areas, including Hebbronville, between 3 and 4 AM and continued until 8 AM on the 28th.  Minimum temperature at the Hebbronville Executive Inn (cooperative site) on the north side of town, dipped to 29 degrees between 7 and 8 AM.  Temperatures in non wind protected areas only fell into the mid 30s or higher, including Jim Hogg County Airport (4.5 miles northwest).

Temperatures fell below freezing in wind protected areas, including the Zapata County Airport (near Medina, northeast of Zapata), shortly after 5 AM and continued until 8 AM on the 28th.  Minimum temperature at the airport was 27 degrees. A Remote Automated Weather Station at Falcon Lake, just south of the Zapata/Starr County line, dipped to 25 degrees; temperatures reached freezing as early as midnight.

Temperatures fell below freezing in wind protected areas of Starr County after midnight on the 28th, bottoming out in the mid to upper 20s.  Non protected or higher ground locations remained at or above freezing. At the Remote Automated Weather Station at Falcon Lake (just south of the Zapata/Starr County line), temperatures flirted with 32 degrees between midnight and 2 AM, and fell below 32 by 330 AM, reaching a minimum of 25 degrees just after 7 AM.  The cooperative station at Falcon Dam stayed just above freezing, while Rio Grande City reached 30 degrees between 7 and 8 AM.

Temperatures fell below freezing in wind protected areas of Hidalgo County after midnight on the 28th, bottoming out in the mid 20s in these areas, around freezing in rural locations with less wind protection, and in the mid to upper 30s in urbanized sections from Weslaco to Mission.  The primary time for continuous subfreezing temperatures was between 4 and 8 AM, though some pockets fell to freezing as early as 2 AM.  ||Low temperatures included 24 degrees at both the Lower Rio Grande Valley Wildlife Refuge sites of Santa Ana (along the Rio Grande southeast of Pharr) and Linn/San Manuel (along the Willacy County line near SR 186), 31 degrees at the Climate Reference Network site along SR 186 near San Manuel, and 32 degrees at Edinburg International Airport, the San Manuel cooperative site, and near La Joya.  ||Agricultural damage was unknown as of early December.  However, the dry freeze and associated low wet bulb temperatures, which ranged from the upper 20s to 31 degrees even in areas where air temperatures were a few degrees above freezing, likely caused minor problems to cold sensitive crops, particularly tender tropical vegetation.  The freeze reinforced the impacts from the intense drought (Exceptional for most of the county).

Temperatures fell below freezing in wind protected areas of western Willacy County after midnight on the 28th, bottoming out in the mid 20s in these areas, and around freezing in rural locations with less wind protection.  The primary time for continuous subfreezing temperatures was between 4 and 8 AM, though some pockets fell to freezing as early as 2 to 230 AM.  ||Low temperatures included 24 degrees at the Lower Rio Grande Valley Wildlife Refuge site Linn/San Manuel (along the Willacy County line near SR 186), 31 degrees at the Climate Reference Network site along SR 186 near San Manuel, and 32 degrees at the Raymondville cooperative site.  ||Agricultural damage was unknown as of early December.  However, the dry freeze and associated low wet bulb temperatures, which ranged from the upper 20s to 31 degrees even in areas where air temperatures were a few degrees above freezing, likely caused minor problems to cold sensitive crops, particularly tender tropical vegetation.  The freeze reinforced the impacts from the intense drought (Extreme to Exceptional for most of the county).

Temperatures fell below freezing in wind protected areas of Kenedy County after midnight on the 28th, bottoming out in the mid 20s around daybreak.  The cooperative sites at Sarita (Lebh Shomeah retreat, 7 miles east) and Armstrong (on the King Ranch) each dipped to 25 degrees between 7 and 8 AM.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The U.S. Coast Guard station at South Padre Island recorded a wind gust to 49 mph at 10 PM on the 26th, and gusts continued above 40 mph through 4 AM.  Two small moored boats reportedly capsized along the bayshore near the Sea Ranch Marina, virtuallyl adjacent to the Coast Guard Station, sometime during the night. No injuries or fatalities were reported, and damage was unknown as of this writing.

An off duty NWS Employee reported a collapsed awning over a car wash facility during the morning of November 27th, after a night of frequent wind gusts to or above 40 mph.  Peak gusts at the South Padre Island Heliport reached 41 mph (1135 PM/26th), but the nearby U.S. Coast Guard station had a peak gust to 49 mph (10 PM/26th).  Similar gusts continued until 3 to 4 AM on the 27th. ||Damage values to the facility are estimates.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees around 330 AM, and continued falling into the 20s across most of Brooks County before rising above 32 degrees toward 9 AM.  Minimum temperatures dropped to a new calendar day record of 23 degrees at the Cooperative observing station west of Falfurrias most likely between 7 and 8 AM.  At Brooks County Airport just southeast of town, temperatures were at or below freezing from 4 AM to 8 AM, bottoming out at 28 degrees.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees between 130 and 5 AM, and continued falling into the 20s to around 30 across Jim Hogg County before rising above 32 degrees after 8 AM.  Minimum temperatures dropped to 26 degrees at the Cooperative observing station in Hebbronville most likely around 7 AM.  At Jim Hogg County Airport just northwest of town, temperatures were at or below freezing from 130 AM to 815 AM, bottoming out at 29 degrees.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees around 3 AM and continued falling into the 20s across Zapata County before rising above 32 degrees after 815 AM.  Minimum temperature dropped to 26 degrees at the Zapata County Airport in Zapata, most likely around 730 AM.  At the natural gas processing plant in Escobas, temperatures were at or below freezing from 5 AM to 815 AM, bottoming out at 30 degrees.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees around 3 AM and continued falling into the 20s across Starr County before rising above 32 degrees after 815 AM.  Minimum temperature dropped to 26 degrees at the Cooperative Observer site at Falcon Lake. At the Cooperative Observer site in Rio Grande City, the minimum temperature was 31 degrees.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees around 330 AM and continued falling into the 20s across much of Kenedy County before rising above 32 degrees after 830 AM.  Minimum temperature dropped to 25 degrees at the Cooperative Observer site in Armstrong. At the Cooperative Observer site in Sarita, the minimum temperature was 28 degrees.
