Temperatures fell to 32 degrees around 345 AM and continued falling into the 20s and lower 30s across the northern third of Hidalgo County and a highly populated stretch of Hidalgo County east of the Highway 281 corridor, between McAllen and Weslaco.  Temperatures rose above 32 degrees around 745 AM. Minimum temperature dropped to 26 degrees at the Cooperative Observer site in San Manuel and at the Santa Ana RAWS site. A citizen weather site in La Joya also recorded a minimum of 32 degrees.

Temperatures fell to 32 degrees around 330 AM and continued falling into the lower 30s across the eastern two thirds of Willacy County. Temperatures rose above 32 degrees around 830 AM. Minimum temperature dropped to 30 degrees at the Cooperative Observer site in Raymondville. The Cooperative Observe site in Port Mansfield also recorded a minimum of 32 degrees.

Exceptional (D4) Drought persisted across all but the northwest corner of Brooks County through December.  Rainfall estimated between one and 1.5 inches during the last three weeks of the month was not enough to change the long term condition.  Cattle and other herds continued to be thinned considerably due to very short grassland.

Exceptional (D4) Drought persisted across all but the extreme southern portion of Kenedy County (King Ranch area) through December.  Rainfall averaging around one inch across the county during the last three weeks of the month was not enough to change the long term condition.  Cattle and other herds continued to be thinned considerably due to very short grassland.

Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought persisted across inland Willacy County through December.  Rainfall generally between one half and one inch across the county during the last three weeks of the month was not enough to change the long term condition.  Cattle and other herds continued to be thinned considerably due to very short grassland.  Additional data on crop damage may be added in early January.

Exceptional (D4) Drought persisted across coastal Willacy County through December.  Rainfall generally between one half and one inch across the coastal areas during the last three weeks of the month was not enough to change the long term condition.

Exceptional (D4) Drought persisted across coastal Cameron County through December.  Rainfall generally between one half and one inch across the coastal areas during the last three weeks of the month was not enough to change the long term condition.

Exceptional (D4) Drought persisted across inland Cameron County through December.  Rainfall averaging near one inch during the last three weeks of the month was not enough to change the long term condition.  Additional crop damage may have been realized during late harvests.

Extreme (D3) Drought persisted across Zapata County through December.  That said, significant rainfall near 2 inches fell during the last three weeks of the month, alleviating conditions and allowing modest green up of some rangeland.  Cattle herds continued to thin or be sold due to the lack of available feed and continued short grasses.

Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across the eastern half of Starr County through December 12th - an area which until then had received less than 5 inches of rainfall in fourteen months.  Extreme (D3) Drought prevailed across western Starr County. Rangeland continued to wither to dust, and ranchers sold off more of the cattle herd due to insufficient feed in most areas.  Relief would arrive on December 10th, when between 2 and 4 inches fell across much of the county.

Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across all of Hidalgo through December 12th.  Areas west of Mission continued to be pummeled the worst, with some locations still holding at less than 5 inches of rain since October 1, 2010!   Rangeland continued to wither to dust, and ranchers sold off more of the cattle herd due to insufficient feed in much   of western and northern Hidalgo County.  There may have been additional crop damage from any late harvests. Relief would arrive on December 10th, when between 1.5 and 2.5 inches of soaking rain fell.

Extreme (D3) Drought continued across all but the southeast corner of Jim Hogg County, where Exceptional (D4) Drought prevailed, through December 12th. Rangeland continued to wither to dust, particularly in the southeast corner of the county, and ranchers sold off more of the cattle herd due to insufficient feed in much of the county.  Relief would arrive on December 10th, when between 1 and 1.5 inches of soaking rain fell.

Rainfall generally between 1.5 and 2.5 inches, particularly west of Federal Highway 281, put a small dent into the 2011 Drought by nudging conditions down one level from Exceptional (D4) to Extreme (D3) across the southwestern two-thirds of Hidalgo County.  The rains were not enough to budge the remainder of the county, including Weslaco, Mercedes, and Linn/San Manuel, from the Exceptional level. ||Rainfall of more than 2 inches in two days (December 10-11) at La Joya (west of Mission) virtually /doubled/ the prior rainfall of 4.93 inches from the fourteen month period of October 2010 through early December 2011!  Despite the rainfall, more than ten inches was needed to bring values back to normal for the calendar year.

Rainfall generally between 2 and more than 3 inches, mainly along and south of Federal Highway 83 including most of the Starr County population as well as a number of nearby ranches, put a small dent into the 2011 Drought by nudging conditions down one level from Exceptional (D4) to Extreme (D3) across the eastern half of the  County.  After the initial heavy rain event, the entire county was in Extreme Drought, which continued through month's end.

Rainfall around 1.5 inches across southern Jim Hogg County December 10-11 put a small dent into the 2011 Drought by nudging conditions down one level from Exceptional (D4) to Extreme (D3) across the the southeastern corner County.  The initial heavy rain event, followed by repeated cool, damp, and drizzly weather on successive weekends, left the entire county in Extreme Drought, which continued through month's end.

A COOP site reported a low of 25 degrees in Falfurrias. Proxy observations from the Lower Rio Grande Valley NWR site at San Manuel (28) indicate up to five hours of freezing temperatures during the early morning hours.

Temperatures fell below degrees between 6:15 AM and 8:15 AM across Kenedy  before rising above freezing after 8:15 AM. Interpolation between the more sheltered observation at the Lower Rio Grande NWR east of San Manuel (Hidalgo County) suggests that temperatures in rural ranchlands fell as low as 30F or more through the night.

The cooperative observing locations at Sarita and Armstrong reported low temperatures of 29F a between 7 and 8 AM on December 8th.  Based on proxy observations from the Brooks County Airport (several hours beginning at 215 AM and ending just before 7 AM), the Lower Rio Grande Valley NWR site at San Manuel (around 5 miles southwest of the Kenedy/Willacy/Hidalgo border), and Kingsville NAS (4 hours below freezing, low temperature 27F), Kenedy County had at least five hours of freezing temperatures early on the 8th.

The Jim Hogg County Airport, 5 miles northwest of Hebbronville, recorded a little more than 2 hours of freezing temperatures, with a low of 30F just before 6 AM CST on the 8th.   Based on interpolated observations in Brooks and Zapata County, at least five hours of freezing temperatures likely occurred from Hebbronville through the open ranchlands of Jim Hogg County during the early morning hours.

Jim Hogg County continued to see improvement in drought conditions. Much of the county improved to D1 and D0 drought, with only the far NW corner in D2 drought.

Public reported 60 mph wind gusts at Stewart and 21st in Mission.  No damage was reported with the gusts.
Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office reported quarter to golfball size hail fell in the vicinity of McCook.
Golf ball to baseball size hail was reported over a swath of the heavily populated urban center of Mission and McAllen.
Reports of quarter to golf ball size hail were reported over a swath of heavily populated urban Mission and McAllen.
Willacy County emergency manager reported penny to golf ball size hail across Raymondville.
Public reported golf ball size hail on Highway 77 near Lyford.
Public reported nickel to quarter size hail across portions of Harlingen, from near Harlingen High School to the Treasure Hills area.
Public reported nickel size hail near Laureles.
Trained spotter reported nickel to quarter size hail falling across Los Fresnos.
Public reported nickel to quarter size hail at the intersection of Southmost and International Blvd in Brownsville.

Cameron County emergency manager reported a funnel and touchdown southwest of Highway 77 in Harlingen. Resident at the intersection of Rangerville Road and CR 800 reported split tree blown across road and debris in backyard.
Tornado reported near Wal-Mart in Raymondville. Tornado touched down briefly. No damage reported.

Public reported softball size hail at McAllen High School.  These hailstones, as well as golfball to baseball sized stones which fell for more than twenty minutes while traversing the McAllen/Mission/Pharr area, caused unknown damage to vehicles but little damage to other structures as of this writing.  Dollar damage estimates are available in the baseball size hail entry for this area between 17:20 and 17:50 (520 and 550 PM CDT).
Dime to nickel sized hail on Highway 77 was reported by the Border Patrol.
Hidalgo S.O. relayed report from the general republic of 1.5 inch hail west of San Isidro.
Runoff from storms in Hidalgo County was moving so swiftly that it caused the collapse of a weir in Willacy County. Estimates for repair of the structure are around $2 million.
Zapata County emergency manager reported thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 65 mph occurred in San Ygnacio. Three to four homes were reported to have roof damage and one mobile home was destroyed.
AWOS at Zapata reported a 62 mph thunderstorm wind gust.
Public reported quarter size hail at the intersection of Lincoln and 5th Street.
Public reported estimated wind gust of 60 to 65 mph at Lincoln and 5th Street.

Street flooding with briefly up to 3 feet of moving water near the intersection of Irene and US 83.  Photos also showed urban type flooding at a local park in the city of Zapata, with an estimated 1 foot of water depth.

A semi trailer was blown over on US 281, 6 miles north of TX HWY 186. Driver of semi was injured. Driver stated that he had pulled onto the shoulder due to blinding rain and pelting hail and soon after, the downburst moved the trailer onto the dirt shoulder and then turned over. The trailer was carrying 5 tons of cargo (vacuum cleaners) and at least 200 gallons of diesel, which had to be removed from the scene.||The Precinct Constable, who lives about a mile southwest of the trailer incident, reported numerous asphalt shingles pulled from the northwest facing roof, and one window was blown out. Numerous mesquite trees were snapped or had large healthy limbs broken and healthy ebony and oak trees were also damaged on the ranch. Heavy cable was torn out of a telephone tower (0.2 miles SE of the ranch house) at an estimated height of 200 feet above the ground.||A peak instantaneous wind gust of 102 mph was recorded at a 10 meter temporary wind platform as the microburst surged through.  The same platform recorded 35 minutes of wind gusts to 50 mph or higher; the platform was less than one half mile from the Constable's house.
Emergency manager reported winds from 50 to 60 mph in Raymondville.

The Meteorologist-in-Charge of the NWS office in Brownsville witnessed a downburst/microburst about one mile east of U.S. Highway 77 approximately 10 miles south of Sarita. The microburst produced a tremendous amount of dust; winds were estimated the winds to be near 60 mph.

Willacy County emergency manager relayed a report of a tornado on the Yturria Ranch, just east of Highway 77 in the northern portion of the county. There was a brief touch down and debris seen, but no damage reported.

Between 9 and 945 PM, winds increased, rain poured down, and hail developed as the storm formed and began moving east. At approximately 930 PM, a microburst and large hail struck a colonia in Doolittle, damaging nearly every home (most were of poor construction) and rolling two unanchored trailers. One resident���s ceiling caved in from the combination of hail, estimated to be quarter sized, torrential rains, and driving 60 to 65 mph winds. Another tin roof was completely blown from a mobile home. A man was inside one of the trailers when it rolled; fortunately, he was not injured. Nearby, several large limbs were broken from mesquite trees, and one tree was partially uprooted. Shed damage was also noted at the Diamond B Ranch, just north of the colonia, which occurred moments before the downburst wrecked the colonia.
Public reported penny size hail 10 mile NE of Edinburg near Elsa at the intersection of FM2812 and Val Verde Road.
Border patrol checkpoint 15 miles south of Sarita reported predominantly nickel size hail with embedded quarter size hail.

After an initial report of baseball to softball sized hail in Sebastian, visual evidence from an NWS storm survey indicated no discernible hail impact in Sebastian. Estimated size was penny sized based on conversations with affected residents. the hail lasted up to 10 minutes.
Willacy County emergency manager reported golfball size hail 2 miles south of Raymondville.

Penny to quarter sized hail was reported at two locations in the City of Zapata between 1115 and 1125 PM local daylight time as severe thunderstorms marched across the area.  The first report was an unknown location; the second was at the intersection of 5th Avenue and Lincoln Street.
Trained spotter estimated wind gusts of 65 to 70 mph in downtown Zapata at the intersection of 5th and Lincoln Street. Initial report time was 1122 PM CDT; final time range estimated by radar.
Jim Hogg County Sheriff's Office reported quarter size hail in Randado.
Jim Hogg County Sheriff's Office reported tornado briefly touched down at the intersection of Highway 16 and FM 649 in the vicinity of Randado.

A tornado was reported on the Kenedy Ranch, approximately 3 miles south of Rivera (Kleberg County).  This storm would later produce a damaging tornado near Kingsville.  The National Weather Service Office in Corpus Christi relayed the report to from the general public.
An off-duty NWS employee reported an estimated 3 to 4 inches of rain along FM 510 near Bayview, with several inches of water flooding nearby roads.
Public reported nickel size hail near Raymondville, about 2 miles east of Highway 77.

The Willacy County Emergency Manager reported quarter size hail near Yturria. The public reported quarter size hail on the north side of Raymondville.  Each report was from the same hail core, which moved quickly northeast of town and may have dropped larger hail over rural locations north of the City.

Nickel sized hail was reported at the intersection of 1st St. and Tampico Ave., also on the north side of town, at 434 PM CDT, by the public.  Report was relayed to the NWS by a local weather broadcaster.

Nickel sized hail was reported by the public on the west side of Harlingen along the Highway 77 and 83 interchange at 515 PM; penny sized hail was reported at the intersection of Harrison and U.S. Highway 77 at 520 PM, with another report of penny sized hail at the same time relayed by amateur radio from the general public in the same area.  Continuation of the hail for another five minutes was estimated by radar.
Public reported quarter size hail near La Feria.

Nickel to quarter size hail reported at Altas Palmas and Highway 83 and quarter size hail along Highway 83 on the west side of Harlingen. Report from spouse of NWS employee that car windshield was broken from the hail.
Cameron County Emergency Manager reported quarter size hail at the intersection of County Road 800 and Rangerville Road.

Hidalgo County saw no improvement in drought conditions. D2 (severe) drought remained only in a sliver on the far eastern boundary of the county, while the rest of the county was in D1 (moderate) and D0 (abnormally dry) drought conditions. Periodic rainfall between th 8th and 12th would improve drought conditions, removing the entire county from anything more than moderate (D1) by the 15th.

Jim Hogg County saw little change in drought conditions through May, despite periodic rainfall, especially between the 8th and 12th. Conditions in the county began with a wide range from south to north, with D0 (abnormally dry) across the southern tier and D2 to D3 (severe to extreme) conditions across the north/northwest sliver, with D1 (moderate) in the central portions.  These conditions would persist through the month, with D2 confined to the extreme northwest/north until near month's end when extreme (D3) conditions returned to near Hebbronville.

Brooks County remained in moderate (D1) to severe (D2) drought through the month of May.  Through May 14th, D2 (severe) held across the eastern third of the county; after May 14th, the D2 area shifted to the northern sliver of the county, including Falfurrias, with the remainder of the county at D1.

Kenedy County continued to be one of the driest counties across Deep South Texas into mid May; coastal regions continued at D3 (extreme) with inland locations at D2 (severe) through the 14th. Occasional thunderstorms the second week of the month would help reduce the drought a bit after the 14th.
Inland Willacy County continued to be one of the driest regions across the Rio Grande Valley into mid May.  D2 (severe) drought conditions prevailed through the 14th.
Inland Cameron County continued to be one of the driest areas across the Rio Grande Valley into mid May.  D2 (severe) drought conditions prevailed through the 14th.

Coastal Cameron County saw no change in drought conditions and remained among the worst levels in Deep South Texas/Rio Grande Valley region. D3 (extreme) drought conditions prevailed through May 14th. Relief would arrive during the second week of the month and manifest in lower drought levels beginning on the 15th.

Coastal Willacy County saw no change in drought conditions and remained among the worst levels in Deep South Texas/Rio Grande Valley region. D3 (extreme) drought conditions prevailed through May 14th. Relief would arrive during the second week of the month and manifest in lower drought levels beginning on the 15th.

Zapata County saw a slight increase in D3 (extreme) drought conditions across the northern third of the county. The remainder of the the county so no change in drought conditions with the southern tip of the county remaining in D1 (moderate) drought conditions and the middle of the county staying in D2 (severe) drought conditions. Periodic rains between the 8th and 12th would improve drought somewhat beginning on the 15th.
Drought conditions improved across Zapata County. The northern half of the county slipped into D2 drought conditions, while the southern half of the county saw D1 drought conditions.
Palm Valley resident reported 5 palm trees set on fire by a lightning strike.

The Hidalgo County Precinct #4 Constable recorded 4 to 4.5 inches of rainfall across his ranch to the northwest of U.S. Highway 281, approximately 6 miles north of Linn.  High standing water of unknown depth was reported on unpaved roads and in some of the fields.
Several residents of a colonia in Doolittle reported at least five minutes of hail, up to the size of quarters, with a severe thunderstorm that also produced a damaging microburst in the area.

The Zapata County Sheriff's Office reported 3 feet of flowing water along U.S. Highway 83 in the vicinity of El Clareno Ranch, about 7 miles south-southeast of the City of Zapata.  The highway was closed from 1140 PM on the 10th until 130 AM on the 11th.  No damage, injuries, or deaths were reported.
Heavy rainfall of unknown amount caused minor flooding in the Medina Addition section of the City of Zapata.

A mini-supercell thunderstorms dropped a very brief tornado, containing estimated 80 mph winds (high end EF0 on the Fujita Scale) on top of a single family home, causing considerable damage to property at the well built structure.  Damage included:  four sections of cyclone fence bent in different directions around the home; a boat and trailer flipped over, numerous snapped tree limbs in different directions, and other limbs that came from an undetermined tree, barrel-tile roof shingles lifted off, one broken window, and a damaged carport.  Unusual was the singular nature of the damage - striking only this property - with one of the shortest track lengths (a tenth of a mile) one would see on survey.

Frequent to excessive lightning struck McAllen and Pharr as an individual strong thunderstorm followed the initial line of activity.  The City of McAllen reported 4,200 customers without power during the peak of the storm. Lightning caused a structure fire just east in Pharr and knocked out power to some residents of the city.
Frequent to excessive lightning knocked out power to the south half of the City of Zapata during a severe thunderstorm during the late evening of May 10th.

A strong thunderstorm raced through central and eastern Cameron County, and briefly intensified. Winds estimated at 55 mph blue a poorly anchored roof from one mobile home at the Tropical Trail MHP along U.S. 77 (business) near Oscar Williams Road.  A few mesquite limbs were also torn from one or two trees near the home; other structures were unharmed.

Periodic rains between May 8th and 12th helped douse the drought somewhat across the King Ranch by May 15th.  Levels across the county dropped one notch, from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) along the coast, and from Severe (D2) to Moderate (D1) inland.

Periodic rainfall from strong to severe thunderstorms during the week of May 8th to 12th improved drought across inland Willacy County from Severe (D2) to mostly moderate (D1) with a sliver of Severe (D2) remaining east of U.S. Highway 77.

Periodic rainfall from strong to severe thunderstorms during the week of May 8th to 12th improved drought across inland Cameron County from Severe (D2) to mostly moderate (D1) with a sliver of Severe (D2) remaining east of U.S. Highway 77.

Periodic rainfall from strong to severe thunderstorms during the week of May 8th to 12th improved drought across coastal Cameron County from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) by mid month, which continued until the end of May.

Periodic rainfall from strong to severe thunderstorms during the week of May 8th to 12th improved drought across coastal Willacy County from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) by mid month, which continued until the end of May.

Heavy rain fell during the afternoon hours across Brownsville. Western and downtown portions of Brownsville were especially hard hit with rainfall totals over 5 inches reported by a spotter and CoCoRaHS reports. Flash floods closed several roads, overtopped resacas, and reached into properties near and in downtown.   A trained spotter reported water in the streets and resacas out of their banks and over walls; this spotter also reported five inches of rain. A NWS employee reported that Price Road was impassible with at least a foot of water over it in western Brownsville.  Emergency manager reported water in a few homes in downtown Brownsville and resacas getting high. Emergency manager also reported that Price Road was mostly closed, Boca Chica Blvd was closed in a few spots, and a few other streets were closed as well.
At Law enforcement reported water completely covering Highway 83 at Lopeno.
Law enforcement reported water over the road at Highway 83, near Falcon Heights.
Severe Drought (D2) conditions continued across the northern third of Zapata County, with Moderate (D1) elsewhere through June.

Little change in drought conditions was observed across Jim Hogg County from the end of May until the end of June. The county remained split into thirds, with the southern third of the county in abnormally dry (D0) conditions, the middle third in Moderate (D1) Drought, and the northern third of the county in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought, including the city of Hebbronville.

Welcome rainfall in April and May would gradually be erased in June across the Brooks County ranchland, as Severe (D2) Drought slowly spread from north to south into the middle portion of the county through the 25th.  Moderate (D1) conditions began the month for all but the northern sliver, but by the 25th were confined to the southern sliver.

Drought Conditions would fluctuate across inland Cameron County throughout June. Residual ground moisture from late May rainfall would edge Severe (D2) Drought to Coastal Cameron County by June 5th, but dry, hot weather would quickly return Severe Drought to most of the County by June 12th, which continued through month's end.  Torrential rains in a small area near the Rio Grande would reduce the level in that corner by early July.

Drought conditions varied across inland Willacy County through June, but Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) was the general rule.  After a brief respite between June 5th and 11th, when residual ground moisture from late May rains brought levels to Moderate everywhere, the start of a hot, dry summer quickly returned Severe levels to most of inland Willacy County through the 25th.  Spotty sea breeze rainfall across northern Willacy County in mid June slivered Severe conditions to the southern 1/4 of the County to close the month.
All of coastal Cameron County remained in Severe (D2) Drought, as any spotty sea breeze induced storms formed about 10 miles or so inland, until the final day of the month.

All of coastal Willacy County remained in Severe (D2) Drought through most of June, as needed rainfall tended to fall in spotty sea breeze thunderstorms along the Highway 77 corridor away from the coast. Some rains toward month's end would shrink the Severe area to the extreme southeast corner of the County by month's end.

Spotty, mainly seabreeze-induced rainfall shifted drought conditions around Kenedy County through June.  Overall, Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) prevailed.  In general, Moderate (D1) conditions shifted toward the coast with the sea breeze rain, while severe (D2) dominated areas of the King Ranch west of Highway 77.

After April and May rainfall temporarily brought drought relief to Hidalgo County, June brought a hot, rain-free start which soon turned typical early summer dry conditions back to pockets of Severe (D2) Drought.  From June 12th through 25th, Severe Drought was confined to the eastern sliver of the County, including Mercedes and Weslaco.  By month's end, a second area began developing north of Edinburg.

Zapata County law enforcement officials reported flash flooding was occurring in northwestern Zapata County, north of San Ygnacio.  Officials reported that water and mud was flowing across HIghway 83.
An area of bias-corrected rainfall of 4 to 6 inches fell in rural Jim Hogg County during the evening of July 13th.

Spotty rainfall maintained Moderate (D1) drought conditions east of Highway 77 and Severe (D2) drought conditions west of Highway 77 until mid month; Severe (D2) conditions would spread across nearly all of Kenedy County for the second half of July.
Spotty rainfall, from seabreeze convection, maintained Moderate (D1) drought conditions generally east of Highway 77 and Severe (D2) drought conditions west of Highway 77.

July would begin with all of coastal Cameron County in Severe (D2) Drought, but effects from rainfall on June 30th would kick in to the Drought Monitor by July 3rd, with several inches of rain in locations from Laguna Atascosa to South Padre Island resulting in drought conditions improving to Moderate (D1).  These conditions would continue through month's end but deteriorate once again as little additional rain fell after the 1st.

Despite showers and thunderstorms at the end of June and infrequently along the sea breeze, Severe (D2) Drought continued west of Highway 77 and Moderate (D1) drought conditions persisted east of Highway 77.  Across the far southern portion of the county, nearly 1.75 inches of rain fell, maintaining the Moderate (D1) drought conditions early in the month; little additional rain would expand the Severe Drought across the entire County by July 31st.

Despite spotty showers, little change occurred to drought conditions in Brooks County during July. during the first half of July across Brooks County. Severe (D2) Drought conditions persisted across all but the northern sliver of the County through the month; locations along State Highway 285 held in Extreme (D3) Drought.

Little change in drought conditions was observed across Jim Hogg County during July, despite significant rainfall of 4 to 6 inches across portions of rural western Jim Hogg County. The county remained split into thirds, with the southern third of the county in Moderate (D1) Drought, the middle third in Severe (D2) Drought, and the northern third of the county in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought, including the city of Hebbronville.

Severe Drought (D2) conditions continued across the northern third of Zapata County. Moderate (D1) conditions continued across much of the remainder of the county, with a small area of D0 conditions pushing into the southern tip of the county. These conditions would improve after mid month rains, and the entire county would be removed from Severe or greater drought conditions, dropping to Abnormally Dry (D0) to Moderate for the last week of the month.

Moderate Drought (D1) prevailed over all but a couple of slivers of eastern Hidalgo County (Weslaco-Mercedes) and extreme northern portions through July 16th.  Limited rainfall would see Severe (D2) Drought engulf the County by the middle of July. Despite spotty showers across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley, Hidalgo County did not see much, with the ASOS at McAllen Miller International Airport recording only 0.03 inches of rain during the first two weeks of the month.

Very little rainfall allowed Severe (D2) drought conditions to engulf the entire county, causing the Moderate (D1) drought conditions east of Highway 77 earlier in the month to intensify to Severe (D2) drought conditions by the middle of the month (July 17), spreading to all of the County by month's end.

Severe drought (D2) conditions covered Hidalgo County during the second half of the month (July 17th to the 31st). Spotty showers resulted in only 0.14 inches of rain recorded by the ASOS at McAllen Miller International Airport.

Locally heavy rainfall at the end of June and again near mid month (just under 2 inches at Bayview between the 13th and 15th) was no match for hot, breezy, and rain-free conditions to close out July.  The lack of precipitation in a normally wetter region deteriorated drought conditions to Severe (D2) along the Cameron County coast by July 31st.

Locally heavy rainfall at the end of June and again near mid month (just under 2 inches at Bayview, less than 15 miles south of the Cameron/Willacy border between the 13th and 15th) was no match for hot, breezy, and rain-free conditions to close out July.  At Port Mansfield, less than 0.05 inches fell after the 15th. The lack of precipitation in a normally wetter region deteriorated drought conditions to Severe (D2) along the Willacy County coast by July 31st.

Little to no rain fell across Willacy County the first half of the month (August 1st ��� 13th) allowing drought conditions to worsen across the western half of the County. Areas west of Highway 77 slide into Extreme (D3) drought conditions, while areas east of Highway 77 remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Little to no rain fell across Coastal Willacy County the first half of the month (August 1st ��� 13th) allowing Severe (D2) drought conditions to continue.  The CoCoRaHS site at Port Mansfield recorded no precipitation for August.

Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across the county during the first half of the month.  Close to 3.5 inches of rain fell at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport August 6th and 7th.  However, north of Brownsville, in Harlingen, significantly less rain fell during this period, less than 0.2 inches of precipitation was recoded at Valley International Airport. This beneficial rainfall was not enough to put a dent in the drought conditions across Cameron County, but it was enough to keep the county from slipping into the Extreme (D3) drought conditions that the surrounding counties were experiencing.

Hot and dry conditions continued through August across Coastal Cameron County. Little to no rain fell during the first half of the month continuing Severe (D2) drought conditions. Pockets of rain fell along the sea breeze just inland from the coast, maintaining severe levels.  Bayview received a total of 0.15 inches of rainfall for the month of August, 1.91 inches below normal, with all of the precipitation falling during the last two weeks of the month and Port Isabel reported 0.66 inches of rain for the month of August. The little rainfall received was not enough to prevent Coastal Cameron County for sliding into Extreme (D3) drought conditions by early September.

Severe (D2) drought conditions remained across nearly all of Kenedy County the first week of the month.  Continued little rainfall allowed drought conditions to worsen across Kenedy County, with all of Kenedy County sliding into Extreme (D3) drought conditions by the middle of the month.

Dry conditions combined with high temperatures resulted in drought conditions worsening across much of the county. Severe drought (D2) conditions across Hidalgo County continued through the first week of the month, with only trace amounts of rainfall recorded at McAllen Miller International Airport on the 6th.  August 13th was a day of more widespread rainfall across Hidalgo county with several CoCoRaHS sites reporting rainfall ranging from 0.19 inches in La Joya to 0.87 inches in Edinburg.  By the middle of the month, the eastern three-fourths of the county entered into Extreme (D3) drought conditions, leaving only the far western quarter of the county in Severe (D2) drought.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across all but the northern sliver of the county through the first week of August, with locations along State Highway 285 holding in Extreme (D3) drought. By the middle of the month, all of Brooks County slid into Extreme (D3) drought conditions, despite spotty rainfall during the first of the month, with a CoCoRaHS site reporting 0.72 inches of rain on the 4th of the month.

Little change occurred during the first week of the month across Jim Hogg County. The county remained split into thirds, with the southern third of the county in Moderate (D1) drought, the middle third in Severe (D2) drought, and the northern third of the county in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought, including the city of Hebbronville.

Inland Willacy County received around half an inch of rain on the 19th and 1.91 inches of rain on the 29th according to CoCoRaHS data.  However, this rain was not enough to overcome the dry conditions earlier in the month and the areas east of Highway 77 slipped into Extreme (D3) drought conditions by the last week of the month, bringing the entire county into Extreme (D3) drought.

No improvement was seen across Coastal Willacy County during the second half of August. Bayview, less than 15 miles south of the Cameron/Willacy border recorded 0.15 inches of rain during the last half of the month. Despite the rainfall, it was not enough to overcome dry conditions earlier in the month and Coastal Willacy County slipped into Extreme (D3) drought conditions the last week of the month.

Drought conditions would not improve during the latter half of the month, despite a few showers here and there. A coop observer site in Sarita reported 0.70 inches of precipitation for the month. By the last week of the month, Exceptional (D4) drought conditions started to emerge along the northern county border of Kenedy County, while the remainder of the county remained entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

During the latter half of the month, rain fell in patches across Hidalgo County. McAllen Miller International Airport recorded a total of 0.29 inches of rain for the month (all in the last half), resulting in 1.92 inches below normal for precipitation.  Despite the rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions spread west, claiming the entire county.

Spotty rainfall continued through the end of the month with a CoCoRaHS site in Falfurrias reporting rainfall about once a week: 0.43 inches on the 14th, 0.88 inches on the 20th, 0.27 inches on the 29th and 0.8 inches on the 30th, for a total of 3.39 inches for the month of August.  Hot conditions battled against this beneficial rainfall and ended up the victor, with Extreme (D3) drought conditions claiming the entire county by the 20th, and Exceptional (D4) drought conditions starting to emerge along the northern county boundary.

Very little rainfall during the first half of the month combined with hot temperatures to allow drought conditions to worsen across portions of Jim Hogg County. Extreme (D3) drought conditions engulfed the northeast half of the county, while the other half remained split between D2 and D1 drought conditions. By the end of the month, Exceptional (D4) drought conditions emerged along the northern county border.

More than three inches of rain fell in a two hour period across southern Cameron County. The ASOS at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport measured 3.08 inches and a CoCoRaHS site measured 3.35 inches of rain. Nuisance urban flooding of poor drainage locations in downtown and along Boca Chica Boulevard occurred during the time of the heaviest rainfall.

Lack of rainfall throughout most of Cameron County, especially west of highway 77 north of Brownsville, brought drought conditions from Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) in these areas by August 21st.  These conditions would continue through month's end.  Rainfall in the Extreme areas generally ran one to two inches below average; only 0.52 inches fell in Harlingen (Valley Airport, 1.39 inches below average) while 3.85 inches fell in Brownsville  (1.41 inches above average).

While decent July and periodic August rainfall drifted from Jim Hogg into west central Starr County at times, little to no rain fell in eastern Starr County through August, and temporary drought relief faded to Severe (D2) levels by the 7th, and deteriorated further to Extreme (D3) levels by month's end.

Isolated showers and thunderstorms dropped 1.76 inches of rain at Hebbronville through the 19th of the month. Despite this rainfall, Exceptional, D4, drought conditions continued to spread south across the county, encompassing the far eastern third of the county. By the third quarter of the month, Extreme, D3, drought conditions spread over the remainder of the county.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping around 0.75 inches of rain in pockets of the county, during early September, more intense drought conditions began to spread west across the eastern half of the county. The far eastern quarter of the county deteriorated from Severe D2 drought conditions to Extreme D3 drought conditions, while the center eastern quarter of the county entered D2 drought conditions from D1 drought conditions. The western half of the county remained in D1 and D0 drought conditions.

Despite isolated showers across the county, dropping .5 to over 3 inches through the 19th of the month, there was no improvement in drought conditions in Hidalgo County. The county remained completely entrenched in Extreme, D3, drought conditions.  By the third quarter of the month, drought conditions deteriorated further across the NE corner of the county, where Extreme, D3, drought conditions slipped into Exceptional, D4, drought conditions.
Despite isolated showers during the first three quarters of the month, coastal Cameron County remained firmly entrenched in Extreme, D3, drought conditions from September 4th through 30th.

Isolated pockets of rain fell across coastal Willacy County during the first three weeks of the month. Some areas received greater than 1.75 inches of rain, but the area remained firmly entrenched in Extreme, D3, drought conditions, from the 4th through the 30th.

Despite spotty rainfall of half an inch to over an inch across the county, drought conditions intensified and Extreme D3 drought conditions spread further east and south across the county, firmly entrenching the entire county into Extreme D3 drought conditions which continued through the end of the month.  Despite some welcome rainfall along the river near Brownsville during the final three days of the month (2.75 inches total), the monthly total (3.76 inches) ended more than 2 inches below long term averages (5.92 inches).
Despite spotty rainfall of less than half an inch across the county, drought conditions intensified and Extreme, D3, drought conditions engulfed the entire county from the 4th through the 30th.

Isolated showers and thunderstorms allowed Sarita to receive 2.33 inches of rain through the 19th of the month. Despite spotty rainfall across the county, Extreme D3 drought conditions dominated the month. A stripe of Exceptional (D4) Drought would begin the month across the northern third of Kenedy County.  By the third week of the month, isolated rainfall allowed for a slight improvement in drought conditions across the northern third of the county (down to D3), while lesser rains along the Brooks County line nudged D4 conditions to a sliver along the western county border.

Isolated showers and thunderstorms dropped over just over an inche of rain across northern Brooks County from the 31st of August through the 10th of September. However, continued hot days with low to moderate humidity did little to maintain good soil moisture. A stripe of Exceptional (D4) Drought across the northern quarter of the county, with Extreme (D3) Drought elsewhere, prevailed through the 10th.

The majority of Brooks County deteriorated to Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except for a small sliver along the south and southwest border, which remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions through the end of September.
At 612 pm CDT, local law enforcement reported trees down at 210 and Eucalyptus in Falfurrias due to thunderstorm winds.

The lack of significant rainfall, combined with hot, dry conditions which ranked among the top 5 (of 70+ years of data) in McAllen and La Joya (90+ years of data) deteriorated drought conditions from Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) across the northern half of the County by the 25th, continuing through the end of September.

Lack of rainfall in Zapata County continued the rapid deterioration of drought conditions, after some promise of decent rains in July and August.  By the 25th, all but the southern corner of the county had slipped into Extreme (D3) conditions, with Severe (D2) conditions holding at the south end of Falcon Lake.  ||Locally heavy rainfall, on the order of 3 to more than 5 inches across the ranchlands near San Ygnacio extending to the northeast corner of the County - moisture from the remnants of Pacific Tropical Storm Norman - would improve the drought conditions in early October, while the higher population area along Falcon Lake would see little of the needed rain for improvement.

Drought would worsen across the northern two thirds of Zapata County from Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) by September 18th.  Lack of rainfall during the wettest part of the calendar year (2nd to 3rd weeks of September) would slide drought into Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) across the county by the 25th.

A meteorologist from the U.S. National Weather Service in Brownsville surveyed the damage, which occurred in and around the San Perlita area. The damage was found to be the result of damaging straight line winds, with wind speeds estimated between 70 and 80 mph.||Damage appeared to initially occur to the roof of a mobile home in the northwestern part of San Perlita. At this location, roofing material was removed and blown toward the southeast. As the severe thunderstorm moved southward, additional small tree limbs and branches were blown down across the city. An additional damage area was noted near the San Perlita ISD complex, where interviews with ISD officials indicated a poorly attached door was removed to the district's bus barn. High winds also uprooted an oak tree on school property, which resulted in damage to a chain link fence. No further wind damage was noted south of this location.
Nickel to quarter sized hail fell in San Perlita. Event time based on radar.
Willacy County Sheriff's Department reported golf ball size hail fell on FM 490, 6 miles west of Willamar at 6 pm.

Public reported quarter to golf ball size hail at Monte Cristo and Filegonia Road in Elsa. Hail fell at approximately 630 PM, according to the report and radar reconciliation, and appears to have continued at quarter to golf-ball sized as the updraft redeveloped over and just south of Edcouch between 630 and 640 PM CDT.

A supercell thunderstorm dropped hail the size of golfballs across a several mile swath of rural eastern Hidalgo County. The initial reports from the  public indicated golf ball sized hail fell in Monte Alto at 615 pm CDT; radar reconcilation suggested the hail core drifted southward from Monte Alto for about 2.5 miles (north of Edcouch/Elsa) between 610 PM and 625 PM.
Public reported quarter size hail at the intersection of Mile 12 and FM 491.

Little to no rain fell across Zapata County during October. This combined with above normal temperatures allowed the vast majority of the the county to remain in Severe (D2) drought conditions.  The far NW corner of the county remained in moderate (D1) drought conditions.

Welcome rains at the end of September across the ranches of northeast Starr County helped nudge the area of Extreme (D3) drought into the southeast corner of the county.  Otherwise, with little or no rain across Starr County during October, the southeast corner of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions,  while the NE portion of the county dipped to Severe (D2) drought on the 2nd and remained there.  The western half of the county remained in less severe drought conditions, with the northwest corner of the county in Moderate (D1) drought conditions and the southwest corner, which remained in decent shape after some rain through the summer, in abnormally dry conditions.

Isolated showers on the 11th were a welcome relief after a generally dry start to the month. Rain fall was spotty and light across Jim Hogg county thereafter, with Hebbronville recording 0.24 inches of rain.  However, this rainfall did little to alleviate drought conditions across Jim Hogg County. The county remained split in half, the southwest half of the county in Severe (D2) drought conditions, while the northeast half of the county remained in Extreme ( D3) drought conditions.

Isolated showers on the 12th dropped 0.50 inches of rain in Falfurrias, and allowed for a temporary respite from the overall dry conditions of October. A majority of the county received little or no rainfall. The limited precipitation did little to alleviate the drought conditions across the County.   The great majority of the county remained entrenched in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, while the far SW corner of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Isolated showers and thunderstorms provided spotty rain fall across Hidalgo county during October, and was no match for the 2012 Drought.  Rain fall amounts ranged from nothing at all to a little more than half an inch in Mercedes on the 13th. Scattered thunderstorms on the 18th in eastern Hidalgo County provided virtually no relief, as dry and hot weather quickly evaporated any rainfall before the water could soak into parched soil. All of the county except for the NE corner remained deeply entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions remained ever present in the NE corner of the county.

Portions of Cameron County received rainfall during the first half of the month. Several days of seabreeze convection combined with the first cold front of the month resulted in precipitation totals of 0.15 inches in Harlingen at the Rio Grande Valley International Airport and 0.21 inches in Brownsville at the Brownsville/ South Padre Island International Airport. Heavier rainfall, in excess of two inches on the 7th and 12th across the eastern third of the county, allowed drought conditions to improve from Extreme (D3) drought conditions to Severe (D2) drought conditions across the eastern half of the county. The western two thirds of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Coastal Cameron County received significant rainfall during the first half of the month, thanks to seabreeze convection and a cold front.  Almost 2 inches of rain (1.94) fell at the Cameron County Airport in Bayview on October 7th. This was followed by more rain on the 12th and 13th totaling almost another inch (.91 inches).  This rain allowed Coastal Cameron County to experience overall improvement in drought conditions, as the area went from Extreme (D3) drought conditions to Severe (D2) drought conditions beginning on the 9th.

Isolated showers fell across Willacy County during the first third of the month, with Raymondville receiving 0.15 inches of rain. A band of heavy thunderstorms on the 7th largely missed Willacy County and slammed eastern Cameron; some drought relieving rains wouldn't arrive in the county until October 18th. Drought conditions did not improve for the area and remained at Extreme (D3) levels.

Isolated showers and thunderstorms dropped spotty rain across Coastal Willacy County during the first half of the month. Port Mansfield recorded 0.12 inches of rain during the first half of the month, while areas just south of the Cameron/Willacy County line toward the coast saw greater amounts, as was evidenced by the almost 2 inches of rain that fell in Bayview.  The spotty rainfall through the first 17 days of the month kept Coastal Willacy County mired in Extreme (D3) drought, with a slight improvement to D2 (Severe) just north of the Cameron/Willacy line along the Laguna Madre.

Isolated showers and thunderstorms did little to alleviate the drought conditions across Kenedy County;  a co-op site in Sarita recorded 0.07 inches of rain on the 13th. All of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, except for a sliver of Exceptional (D4) drought conditions along the far western county boundary. Conditions would worsen across more of the county just before month's end.

Significant rain fell across the eastern third of Cameron County on the 7th, with 1.94 inches at Bayview/Cameron County Airport and 2.41 inches at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge a few miles to the north. Some of these rains reached farther west, mainly between Laguna Madre and Highway 77, and improved drought conditions one category, from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2). Additional rainfall on the 12th/13th and 18th, ensured these areas remained in only Severe (D2) Drought through the remainder of October. Farther west, lesser rains fell; events on the 18th and 19th dropped 0.26 inches of rain at Harlingen's Valley International Airport and 0.59 inches at the Brownsville/ South Padre Island International Airport. While drought conditions did not improve due to this rainfall, drought conditions did not worsen further in the western two thirds of Cameron County and remained at Extreme (D3).

A band of heavy thunderstorms on the 7th dropped 1.94 inches at Bayview/Cameron County Airport and 2.41 inches at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge a few miles to the north, helped improve drought one category along and near the Cameron County coast by the 9th, from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2).  Additional rains on the 12th/13th and 18th ensured drought would not worsen again through the rest of October.
Public reported water over the curbs in Edinburg, near the intersection of Trenton and 281, on either side of 7 PM CDT. Estimated two inches of rain fell in a short period of time in the area.

Estimated thunderstorm wind gusts of 65 to 70 mph, lifted a metal roof from a cinderblock shed at the residence of the brother of the Hidalgo County Emergency Manager, 3 miles north of Elsa. Debris from roof and building also injured livestock.

An amateur radio operator in McAllen reported a carport had blown into adjacent building by thunderstorm winds. A nearby carport also damaged, all around the intersection of  at Houston Street and 6th Avenue.

Additional rainfall on October 12th, and especially on October 18th, when an estimated 1.5 to 2 inches fell across agricultural areas of east-central Willacy County.  These rains were enough to tip the drought scales from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) for a couple of weeks, before lack of rainfall and intense heat for late October deteriorated conditions for all but the southeast section of inland Willacy County.

Additional rainfall on October 12th, and especially on October 18th, when an estimated 1.5 to 2 inches fell across agricultural areas of east-central Willacy County.  These rains were enough to tip the drought scales from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) for a couple of weeks along Laguna Atascosa, before lack of rainfall and intense heat for late October deteriorated conditions for all but the southeast section of coastal Willacy County.

Rainfall was scarce across most of Kenedy County (King Ranch) Texas in October.  The climate station at Lebh Shomeah retreat, 7 miles east of Sarita, recorded only .07 inches unofficially - more than 3 inches below average.  The ranch at Armstrong didn't fare much better, with only 0.18 inches recorded for the month.  Drought ultimately deteriorated to D4 (Exceptional) from the lack of rainfall combined with near record warmth.

Prior to 1 to 2.5 inches of estimated rainfall filtering into the Drought Monitor on October 2nd, conditions in Jim Hogg County remained Extreme (D3) except Exceptional (D4) across the northeast corner of the County along State Highway 285.

Prior to 3 to more than 5 inches of estimated rainfall across northern Zapata County filtering into the Drought Monitor on October 2nd, conditions in Zapata County remained Extreme (D3) for all but the southern quarter of county, which had Severe (D2) conditions.

Internet report of a large-diameter tree blown down by thunderstorm winds near the intersection of North Victoria and Mile 10 Road, just north of Donna.  Radar reconciliation suggest the winds fell just below severe limits.

Spotty rain fell across Hidalgo County throughout the month of November.  McAllen Miller International Airport received 0.84 inches of rain during the month, 0.05 inches below normal. Of the 0.84 inches of rain, 0.78 of that fell during on the 23rd. While the rainfall was welcome, it did little to alleviate drought conditions across Hidalgo County.  Drought conditions remained steady, with the vast majority of the county firmly entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, while the far NE corner of the county held steady in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Spotty but welcome rain occurred throughout the month of November across Brooks County.  A total of 1.73 inches was recorded at a Co-Op observer site in Falfurrias and a total of 1.94 inches was recorded at the Brooks County Airport. This rainfall across the month of November allowed for a steady state of drought conditions across Brooks County; drought conditions saw no improvement and no deterioration. The vast majority of the county remained firmly entrenched in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except for the far SW corner of the county, which held steady in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Spotty and sparse rainfall continued through November across Kenedy County.  The rain that fell was welcome and was enough to maintain drought conditions across Kenedy County, but was not enough to improve drought conditions. The vast majority of the county remained firmly entrenched in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except for the far SE corner of the county, which held steady in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Spotty and sparse rain fell across coastal Willacy County throughout the month of November.  At Bayview, just south of Willacy County, only 0.25 inches of rain was recorded for the entire month. What little rain did fall across the region was welcome but was only enough to maintain drought conditions and not improve them.  All of coastal Willacy County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions for the entire month of November.

November was a month of sporadic rainfall across coastal Cameron County.  Rainfall amounts varied significantly across the region, with only 0.25 inches recorded in Bayview to 1.25 inches reported by a Co-Op site in Port Isabel.  The rain that fell was welcome and was enough to maintain drought conditions across coastal Cameron County, but was not enough to improve drought conditions.  All of coastal Cameron County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions for the entire month of November.

Much of November proved to be a rather dry month, across Zapata County, as little rain fell, until the last week of the month. A cold front moving across the region on the 23rd and 24th sparked showers and thunderstorms that dropped 0.80 inches at Zapata County Airport.   Drought conditions remained steady for all of November across the county, with no improvement in drought conditions noted, nor any intensification of drought conditions; the northwest corner of Zapata County remained in Moderate (D1) drought conditions, while the remainder of the county maintained Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Spotty rain fell across Cameron County throughout the month of November.  Brownsville International Airport received a total of 0.16 inches of rain for the month, for a deficit of 1.66 inches.  Valley International Airport, in Harlingen, fared a little better, receiving a total of 0.35 inches of rain for the month, ending the month only 1.15 inches below normal. Cameron County Airport in Bayview, recorded 0.25 inches of rain for November and ended the month 1.90 inches below normal. The spotty rainfall was not enough to alleviate drought conditions across Cameron County and in fact, drought conditions would worsen by month's end.

Spotty rainfall occurred across Willacy County during the month of November, provided much needed rainfall.  Raymondville recorded 0.93 inches of rainfall during the month, an amount that was 0.06 inches below normal.  Despite the precipitation, no improvement was seen in drought conditions across Willacy County. Instead, drought conditions intensified, with the last remaining vestiges of Severe (D2) drought conditions on the southern boundary of the county slipping into Extreme (D3) drought conditions, resulting in the entire county being blanketed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Residual moisture from spotty rainfall during the last week of October maintained only Moderate Drought (D1) across the western two-thirds of Starr County, with Severe (D2) and Extreme (D3) conditions holding across the eastern third through November 5th.  Conditions began deteriorating once again thereafter with no rainfall to begin the month.

Rainfall was spotty across wide portions of Jim Hogg County during the first half of the month. This lack of rain fall allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to spread from the northeast two thirds of the county and replace Severe (D2) Drought across all but a sliver of the western portion of the county by the 20th. Only a tiny sliver along the western border of the county was able to maintain Severe (D2) Drought conditions through the 26th.

The passage of a slow moving cold front on November 23rd produced beneficial rainfall across Starr County.  The Falcon Dam region received around an inch and a half of rainfall, while Rio Grande City received a little over an inch. Rainfall estimates were between 1.5 and 2 inches across the ranchlands of central and northeast Starr County, allowing drought conditions to improve across Starr County, with much of the county improving from Extreme (D3) drought conditions to Severe (D2) drought conditions, except for a tiny sliver along the eastern county border that continued to stubbornly cling onto Extreme (D3) drought conditions due to a local rainfall minimum.

Rainfall was spotty during the latter half of November across Jim Hogg County, but showers and thunderstorms associated with a cold front that moved across the county on the 23rd, dropped  0.75 inches of rain at the Jim Hogg County Airport. This rainfall was beneficial and allowed for drought conditions to improve across much of Jim Hogg County, with the western two thirds of the county improving to Severe (D2) drought conditions.  Extreme (D3) drought conditions remained confined to only the eastern third of the county.

No rainfall combined with dry weather deteriorated drought conditions in all but extreme southeast Starr County (which remained at D3, or Extreme) from Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) for the second and third week of November.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions across all but a sliver of western Starr County worsened to Extreme (D3) by November 20th, joining the small area of southeast Starr County, which had been among the worst impacted in the mid Rio Grande Valley.

Dissipating rainfall from a slow moving cold front on November 23rd dashed hopes for any drought improvement across Cameron and Willacy Counties.  Less than one tenth of an inch fell, and no additional rain fell through month's end.  This left county rainfall totals as low as 0.16 inch at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport, and 0.35 inches at Harlingen/Valley International Airport, and 0.52 at Harlingen/Cooperative. The low rainfall resulted in deteriorating drought conditions for inland Cameron County, dipping back to D3 (Extreme) to close out November.
Raymondville Police Department reported estimated 60 mph winds when the storm came through.
The public reported that a barn was destroyed 5 miles west of Raymondville. The barn also crushed a car.  Winds were estimated at 70 to 80 mph.

Raymondville Police Department reported that the Precinct 1 garage west of Raymondville on Highway 186 sustained heavy damage from straight line thunderstorm winds. The garage doors were blown down and a section of hurricane fencing near the garage was also blown down.
The public reported quarter to half dollar size hail fell in La Feria, near FM 506. The hail lasted for a few minutes.

No improvement was seen in drought conditions across Willacy County throughout the month of December, despite nearly half an inch of rain falling on December 5th. The entire county remained blanketed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

December started out with a little rain, as a line of thunderstorms moved across Cameron County on December 5th, dropping 0.30 inches at the Brownville/SPI International Airport and 1.06 inches at Valley International Airport in Harlingen. Despite this rainfall early in the month, little rain fell during the remainder of December and no improvement was seen in drought conditions. The entire county remained entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite very little rain falling across Zapata County, only 0.03 inches of rain was recorded at the Zapata County Airport, no improvement or deterioration of drought conditions was noted across Zapata County during the month of December. The northwest corner of the county remained in Moderate (D1) drought conditions, while the remainder of the county maintained Severe (D2) drought conditions.

The spotty and sparse rainfall that plagued Kenedy County in November continued through December, with only 0.04 inches of rain reported for the entire month, by a coop observer in Sarita.  The bulk of the county remained firmly entrenched in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except for the far SE corner of the county, which held steady in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

The first half of December started out with a little rain, as a line of thunderstorms moved across coastal Willacy County on December 5th, with 0.85 inches of rain fall reported by a co-op observer in Port Mansfield.  This rainfall was followed by 0.10 inches of rainfall on the 10th and 0.02 inches on the 15th, for a monthly total of just less than an inch.  While this rain was beneficial, it did not improve drought conditions across coastal Willacy County, but it did keep them from intensifying.  All of coastal Willacy County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions for the entire month of December.

The first half of December started out with spotty rain, as a line of thunderstorms moved across Cameron County on December 5th. CoCoRaHS observers reported 0.10 inches of rain in Laguna Vista and 0.29 inches of rain in South Padre Island. While this rain was beneficial, it did not improve drought conditions across coastal Cameron County, but it did keep them from intensifying.  All of coastal Cameron County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions for the entire month of December.

Little to no rain fell across Starr County during the first half of the month resulting in no change to drought conditions in the county. A co-op observer in Rio Grande City reported only 0.02 inches of rainfall on December 14th, as did a co-op observer at Falcon Dam. Much of the county remained Severe (D2) drought conditions, except for a tiny sliver along the eastern county border that continues to stubbornly cling onto Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

No improvement was seen in drought conditions across Jim Hogg County during the first half of December. Little rain fell during this period, a co-op observer reported 0.02 inches on December 14th and 0.01 inches was reported at the Hebbronville/Jim Hogg county airport the same day. This minute amount of rainfall provided little relief for Jim Hogg County, with the western two thirds of the county remaining in Severe (D2) drought conditions and Extreme (D3) drought conditions confined to only the eastern third of the county.

The first half of December started out with a little rain, as a line of thunderstorms moved across Hidalgo County on December 5th, with 0.35 inches reported by a co-op observer in Weslaco, 0.15 inches reported by a co-op observer in Mercedes, while only a trace was reported at McAllen Miller International Airport. Despite this rainfall early in the month, little rain fell after and no improvement was seen in drought conditions. The entire county remained entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Drought conditions continued in a steady state across Brooks County, the first half of the month. Rainfall was sparse, with the Brooks County Airport in Falfurrias reporting only 0.01 inches of rain on December 10th (the only rainfall reported for the entire month). The vast majority of the county remained firmly entrenched in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except for the far SW corner of the county, which held steady in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

A general lack of rainfall continued through the second half of the month across Starr County.  The only rainfall reported for the latter half of the month occurred on the 30th, with 0.07 inches reported by a co-op observer at Falcon Dam.  This lack of rainfall allowed for drought conditions to intensify and Exceptional (D4) drought conditions returned to the county and spread west to encompass the SE corner.  Meanwhile, the rest of the eastern half of Starr County slid into Extreme (D3) drought conditions, while the western half remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Rainfall was spotty and generally lacking through the latter half of December.  Extreme (D3) drought conditions spread further west across Jim Hogg County, with the vast majority of the county encompassed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.  A sliver in the far NE corner of the county, remained in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, while the far SW corner of the county and the far NW corner of the county (closest to Zapata County), held onto Severe (D2) drought conditions.

A general lack of rain summed up the second half of December across Hidalgo County. This lack of rainfall allowed Exceptional (D4) drought conditions to develop and spread west, encompassing the eastern half of Hidalgo County. The western half of the county remained in D3 drought conditions.

The lack of rainfall continued through the end of the month, resulting in deteriorating drought conditions across portions of Brooks County. The Exceptional (D4) drought conditions line moved west slightly, leaving only the SW corner of the county in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Over an inch of rain fell during the first half of the month across coastal Cameron County. A Cooperative site in Port Isabel recorded 1.86 inches of rain during the first 10 days of the month. This beneficial and welcome rain allowed for drought conditions to improve across all of coastal Cameron county.  ||The area began the month with Extreme (D3) drought conditions which would improve to Severe (D2) levels on the January 15th Drought Monitor.

Over an inch of rain fell during the first half of the month across portions of coastal Willacy County. A COOP site in Port Mansfield recorded 1.37 inches of rain during the first 10 days of the month. The month began where 2012 left off - Extreme (D3) Conditions.||Despite the rainfall in Port Mansfield, Drought conditions remained Extreme (D3) along the northern half of coastal Willacy County. Better rainfall closer to Cameron County improved conditions from Extreme to Severe (D2) by the 15th.

January 2013 began where December 2012 left off - with inland Cameron County remaining in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. First week cloud cover and light rain gave way to a period of heavier rain, spawned by a vigorous upper level disturbance, between the 8th and 10th.  A stripe of 2 to nearly 4 inches of rain fell from the Rio Grande near San Pedro (west of Brownsville) through Los Fresnos, including Harlingen and much of the City of Brownsville. Farther west, rainfall was closer to an inch - and drought relief was very brief.||Official observed values included 2.52 inches at Valley International Airport in Harlingen, and 1.44 inches of rain at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport. ||The general wet period through the 14th improved the Extreme (D3) levels to Severe (D2), with the exception of the western sliver of the county by the Hidalgo County line, on January 15th.

January 2013 began where December 2012 left off - with inland Willacy County remaining in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. First week cloud cover and light rain gave way to a period of heavier rain, spawned by a vigorous upper level disturbance, between the 8th and 10th. One to more than two inches of rain fell during the first half of the month across portions of Willacy County. 1.18 inches of rain was reported by a Cooperative observer in Raymondville for the first half of the month, and Community Collaborative Rain, Hail, and Snow (CoCoRaHS) network observers just across the border in northern Cameron recorded as much as 2.38 inches of rain. ||These rains, slightly cooler temperatures, and increased cloud cover improved drought across the southeast corner of the county, from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) Drought, by the 15th. The rest of the county remained in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, except for a sliver on the far western side of the county that remained in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions, with just over an inch of rainfall.

Despite a brief window of temporarily welcome rainfall, cloud cover, and cooler temperatures for the first half of January 2013, Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions were barely dented. Unlike the Lower Valley, the King Ranch missed out on the relatively heavy rainfall and saw less than an inch for the period.  The cooperative observer at Sarita recorded 0.98 inches of rain, while Armstrong, 25 miles to the south, recorded less than a third (0.31).  A small sliver along the western border of the county improved from Exceptional (D4) drought conditions to Extreme (D3) drought conditions, but little else changed.  Most of the county remained in Exceptional (D4) Drought, with the southeast corner of the county in Extreme (D3) Drought.

Between an inch and an inch and a half of rain fell during the first half of the month across portions of Brooks County. 1.25 inches of rain was reported by a CoCoRsHS observer in Falfurrias during the first half of the month. This rain was beneficial and welcome and allowed for improvement in drought conditions across Brooks County. Exceptional (D4) Drought dominated the County to begin the month, but the aforementioned rain would bring a one-category improvement by the 15th (to Extreme, or D3) with the exception of a small sliver of Exceptional (D4) Drought clinging to the far southeast corner of the county.  Along the western county boundary, a small sliver of Extreme (D3) Drought improved to Severe (D2) at the end of the period.

Helpful rainfall, cooler weather, and cloud cover during the first week of January would improve drought conditions across the Ranchlands of Jim Hogg County from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2), which would hold through mid-month and beyond. Between one half inch and an estimated more than 1 1/2 inches of rain fell during the first half of the month.  A stripe of Jim Hogg County received more rainfall during the first two weeks of the month, than is typically received during the entire month.|A Community Collaborative Rain, Hail, and Snow (CoCoRaHS) observer recorded 1.25 inches of rain in Hebbronville. Along the far SW corner of the county, a patch of Severe (D2) Drought improved to Moderate (D1) by the end of the period.

January 2013 began where December 2012 left off - with the eastern half of Starr County remaining in Extreme (D3) Drought and the western half in Severe (D2) Drought. First week cloud cover and light rain gave way to a period of heavier rain, spawned by a vigorous upper level disturbance, between the 8th and 10th. Portions of Starr and southern Jim Hogg County benefited from lift provided by the proximity of the upper level system, which would then bypass the southeast corner of Starr and Hidalgo County before re-emerging with enhanced Gulf moisture close to the coast. ||Between one half inch and a little more than 1 1/2 inches of rain fell during the first half of the month across a wide swatch of Starr County. A stripe of Starr County ranchlands received more rainfall during the first two weeks of the month than usually received during the entire month. In other areas, closer to half an inch of rain fell. The cooperative observer in Rio Grande City reported only 0.50 inches of rain. Farther west at Falcon Dam, 0.85 inches of rain was reported by the cooperative observer. ||This beneficial rain allowed for improvement in drought conditions across portions of Starr County during the first half of the month.  On the 8th, Extreme (D3) Drought improved to Severe (D2) Drought west of La Grulla; by the 15th, the last improvement arrived from Rio Grande City to Roma as conditions there temporarily improved to Moderate (D1). A very small sliver of Exceptional (D4) conditions held firm along the Hidalgo line just west of Sullivan City.

Bands of rain which improved drought conditions across the Upper Rio Grande Valley/Ranchlands (Starr/Jim Hogg) and the Lower Valley (Cameron into southern Willacy) largely bypassed Hidalgo County, which typically received 1 to 2 inches of rain through January.  Despite a period of generally cooler than average temperatures and some rainfall, Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought ruled the mid Rio Grande Valley.  Rainfall across Hidalgo County for the first half of the month ranged from one half inch across the northern ranchlands to 0.75-1 inch in the higher population and agriculturally rich region near the Rio Grande. McAllen/Miller International Airport received 0.96 inches of rain, a little further east, a CoCoRaHS observer in Weslaco recorded 0.75 inches of rain, and east of Weslaco in Mercedes, a CoCoRaHS observer reported 1.51 inches of rain. ||Exceptional (D4) Drought remained firmly entrenched across the middle of the county, with Extreme (D3) Drought on either side.

No improvement nor deterioration was noted in drought conditions across Zapata County during the first half of January.  Despite significant rain falling elsewhere across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley, Zapata County missed out on much of the action. Falcon Dam, situated just east of the Zapata County line received 0.85 inches of rain during the first half of the month, while Zapata received less than half an inch. Widespread Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across much of the county, with the NW corner of the county remaining in Moderate(D1) drought conditions.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of January, little to no significant rain fell during the latter half of the month.  During the final two weeks of the month, no improvement nor deterioration of drought conditions was noted.  All of coastal Cameron County remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of January, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month.  During the final two weeks of the month, no improvement nor deterioration of drought conditions was noted.  The southern half of coastal Willacy county remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions, while the northern half remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of January, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month.  During the final two weeks of the month, no improvement nor deterioration of drought conditions was noted.  The eastern half of Cameron County remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions, while the western half remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of January, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month across Willacy County.  During the final two weeks of the month, neither improvement nor deterioration of drought conditions was noted.  The southeast corner of the county remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions, while the rest of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, except for a sliver on the far western side of the county that remained in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of January, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month across Kenedy County.  During the final two weeks of the month, no improvement in drought conditions was noted. Drought conditions remained entrenched in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except for the SE corner of the county, which remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of January, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month across Hidalgo County.
