During the final two weeks of the month, neither improvement nor any deterioration in drought conditions was noted. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions remained firmly entrenched across the middle of the county, with Extreme (D3) drought conditions on either side.

No change was noted in drought conditions across Zapata County during the second half of January; dry conditions prevailed.  Widespread Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across much of the county, with the NW corner of the county remaining in Moderate(D1) drought conditions.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of the month, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month across Jim Hogg County.  During the final two weeks of the month, drought conditions held at Severe (D2) for all but the southwest corner, which remained at Moderate (D1) levels.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of the month, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month across Starr County and drought conditions remained stable to close the month. Exceptional (D4) Drought continued near the Hidalgo line by Sullivan City; Extreme (D3) continued mainly along and east of La Grulla; Severe (D2) conditions prevailed from east of Rio Grande City to La Grulla, and Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained west of Rio Grande City to Roma, Falcon Dam, and El Sauz.

Despite receiving significant rainfall during the first half of the month, little to no rain fell during the latter half of the month across Brooks County.  Extreme (D3) Drought would continue across all but a sliver of the western sections, which remained at Severe (D2) levels.

Strong and gusty winds associated with a cold front surging through the Rio Grande Valley resulted in sign damage at a gas station at the corner of Palm Boulevard and Boca Chica. A wind gust of 48 mph, was recorded by the nearby ASOS at the Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport, at 1217 PM; the damage time is estimated from this gust, which occurred five miles east of the reported damage.

A 44 year old man visiting from Missouri during the Winter Holidays drowned while swimming in dangerous longshore currents at Andie Bowie Park, which is maintained by Cameron County. This was the first and only rip or longshore current related drowning in 2012 on South Padre Island.
Trained Skywarn spotter reported golf ball size hail at the Zapata County Airport.
Zapata County sheriff's office reported quarter size hail fell in the community of Ramireno.

Local news KRGV Channel 5 reported a power outage in Edinburg due to a falling tree clipping a power line. Local utility, AEP, confirmed the power outage occurred at 1207 pm LST.  Indirectly, a small fire began in air conditioning unit from a spark at Edinburg North High School, at the school was forced to evacuate. AWOS at South Texas International Airport in Edinburg reported winds of 23 kts gusting to 31 kts at 1215 pm LST. Sustained winds during and prior to the event averaged around 23 knots and peaked at 38 knots (44 mph) at 335 PM CST.

Periodic but well below average rainfall during the month allowed Extreme to Exceptional Drought to hold steady during February across Kenedy county. A total of 0.55 inches of rain was reported by a COOP observer in Sarita. The great majority of the county remained in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions, while the southeast corner of the county remained in a little better shape, with Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.

Unseasonably warm temperatures and practically no rain fell during the month of February across all of Hidalgo County. Only 0.01 inches of rain was recorded during the month at McAllen Miller International Airport, 1.10 inches below normal. Elsewhere in the county, only trace amounts were reported by CoCoRaHS observers in Pharr and McAllen, and 0.02 inches was reported by a CoCoRaHS observer in Mission on February 7th. This overall lack of rainfall allowed for drought conditions to continue across Hidalgo County for the entire month. The southeastern half of the county remained in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, along with a sliver along the northwestern corner of the county, while a broad swath of Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions covered much of the northwestern half of the county.

Extreme (D3) Drought persisted into the first week of February for all but the southwest corner of Brooks County, which briefly remained in Severe (D2) Drought.  Dry, warm weather persisting since the end of January would worsen conditions in the northeast and southwest portions of the County on the 5th.

Little rainfall was the rule, rather than the exception, for much of February across Starr County. Only 0.01 inches of rain was reported during the month and that fell on the 6th. Remaining soil moisture from January and back in fall of 2012 disappeared, allowing a sliver of Moderate (D1) Drought from Rio Grande City to Roma to deteriorate to Severe (D2) Conditions by the 5th.  From the 5th through 18th, the eastern third of the county remained in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, while the western two thirds of the county held onto Severe (D2) Drought conditions.

No rainfall was reported for the first half of February for coastal Cameron County. This lack of rainfall combined with above normal temperatures allowed drought conditions to continue across coastal Cameron County. All of coastal Cameron County remained in Severe (D2) Drought conditions.

Very little rainfall was reported for the first half of February for coastal Willacy County. Only 0.01 inches of rain was reported, and this was by a COOP observer in Port Mansfield on the 6th. This general lack of rainfall combined with above normal temperatures allowed drought conditions to continue. The southern half remained in Severe (D2) Drought conditions, while the northern half remained in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.

No rain fell during the first half of February across Willacy County. The combination of no rain and above average temperatures allowed for drought conditions to continue across the county. No improvements nor worsening of drought conditions was noted. |The far western third of the county remained in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions,  the southeastern corner of the county continued in Severe (D2) Drought conditions, while the remainder of the county experienced Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.

Unseasonably warm temperatures were common across Cameron county during the first half of the month, where daily average temperatures ranged between 7.2 and 7.8 degrees above normal through the 14th before dropping back a bit after cooler air arrived by mid-month. A few instances of rain was reported across Cameron county during the first two weeks. 0.01 to 0.03 inches of rain was reported across the Brownsville area from the 10th of February through the 13th. A total of 0.20 inches of rain was reported at Valley International Airport in Harlingen. This rainfall was just enough to keep drought conditions from escalating. The western half of Cameron county remained in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, while the eastern half remained in Severe (D2) Drought conditions.

Rain did fall across portions of Jim Hogg county during the first half of February, but the rainfall was splotchy as observed by the differences between the reported rainfall amounts of the COOP and CoCoRaHS observers. The COOP observer in Hebbronville reported 0.11 inches of rain during the first two weeks of February, while the CoCoRaHS observer reported 0.62 inches of rain. The rainfall allowed drought conditions to remain steady across Jim Hogg county the first half of February.|The northeastern corner of the county remained in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, while the remainder of the county remained in Severe (D2) Drought conditions.

Showers and thunderstorms during the first two weeks of February across Zapata county prevented drought conditions from worsening, but they didn't provide enough moisture to allow for drought conditions to improve during the first half of the month. |Much of Zapata county remained in Severe D2 Drought conditions, with an area of Moderate (D1) Drought conditions in the northwest corner of the county.

The second half of February proved to be very dry across Zapata county and as a result drought conditions intensified across the county. By the 19th, the southern half of the county had entered into Extreme (D3) Drought conditions from Severe (D2) Drought conditions.  By the 26th of the month, drought conditions had intensified across northern Zapata county, where areas previously in Moderate (D1) Drought conditions became Severe (D2).

The second half of February proved to be drier than the first and as a result, drought conditions intensified in Willacy county. The southeastern corner of the county previously in Severe (D2) Drought conditions slid into Extreme (D3) Drought conditions by the 19th. The majority of the county reached Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, with a sliver of Exceptional (D4) Drought along the western border.

The second half of February continued in the same dry footsteps that the first half took. The lack of rainfall allowed drought conditions to deteriorate across the southern half of coastal Willacy county by the 19th of the month.  All of coastal Willacy County became entrenched in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.

The second half of February continued in the same dry footsteps that the first half took. The lack of rainfall allowed drought conditions to deteriorate across the southern half of coastal Cameron county by the 19th of the month.  All of coastal Cameron county slid into Extreme (D3) Drought.

The second half of February continued dry across Jim Hogg county, with only 0.02 inches of precipitation recorded on February 20th.  By the 19th, drought conditions intensified across Jim Hogg County as Extreme (D3) Drought conditions slid west across the county. Nearly all of the county was in Extreme (D3) Drought, except for a sliver along the southern border, which remained in severe (D2) drought conditions until the 26th. Extreme (D3) Drought covered the entire county by month's end.

Only a trace of rain was reported during the last half of the month, allowing drought conditions to intensify further across Cameron County. By February 19th, drought conditions intensified across far eastern Cameron county, with the easternmost third entering into Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, the middle third remaining in Severe (D2) Drought, and the far western third remaining in Extreme (D3) Drought by month's end.

The second half of February continued dry across Starr county.  By February 26th, Extreme (D3) Drought conditions continued to spread across Starr County, leaving only the western half of the county in Severe (D2) Drought which remained through the end of the month.

After a dry, warm end to January and a similar start to February, northeastern Brooks County would deteriorate from Extreme (D3) Drought to Exceptional (D4) Drought, and the southwest corner would deteriorate from Severe (D2) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought.  These conditions would continue through months end, and worsen further in March.

Despite, little to no rain falling across Coastal Cameron County during the month (Co-Op observers in Port Isabel and South Padre Island reported only 0.02 to 0.03 inches of rainfall for the entire month), drought conditions remained steady, with the entire area draped in extreme (D3) drought conditions.
Despite no rain falling across Coastal Willacy County during the month, drought conditions remained steady, with the entire area draped in extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Little to no rain fell across Hidalgo County and only a trace of rainfall was reported during the entire month of March at the McAllen Miller Airport and at by a CoCoRaHS observer in Pharr. This lack of rain allowed for drought conditions to deteriorate across the county, with  all of the county entrenched in exceptional (D4) drought conditions by the 12th of the month.

Despite a lack of rainfall during the month, drought conditions across Willacy County remained fairly steady. The majority of the county remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions, while a sliver of exceptional (D4) drought conditions along the western border, slowly crept eastward by the middle of the month.

March proved to be a rather dry month across Kenedy County. Pockets of light rain fell on March 8th, 0.03 inches was reported in Armstrong and 0.02 inches was reported in Sarita by Co-Op observers; however this was not enough to allow drought conditions to improve. Extreme (D4) drought conditions continued to push further southeast across the county, resulting in all of the county in extreme (D4) drought conditions by the 19th.

A general lack of rainfall during the first two weeks of the month allowed drought conditions to intensify, but a few showers and thunderstorms over the last half of the month allowed drought conditions to hold steady. Drought conditions intensified across much of Brooks County through the 12th of the month and then held steady.  At the beginning of the month, much of the county except for the very far southwest corner remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions. By the 12th all of the county was entrenched in exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

While pockets of Cameron County received light rain on a few occasions during the latter half of March (the ASOS at KBRO reported only 0.02 inches for the second half of month, while the ASOS at KHRL reported only 0.05 inches) it was not enough to keep drought conditions at bay or to allow for any improvements. Drought conditions intensified across the far western side of the county, where exceptional (D4) drought conditions had nosed in. The vast majority of the county remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions.

While areas of Zapata County received some rain during the last half of March, it was not enough to stave off the intensification of drought conditions across the county. By the 26th of the month, extreme (D3) drought conditions had spread across the northern two thirds of the county, while the southern third of the county remained entrenched in exceptional (D4) drought conditions.||For the month, relative humidity dropped below 15 percent on at least 13 (of 31) afternoons, resulting in late spring to earl summer-like evaporation rates.

Jim Hogg County was granted a slight reprieve in terms of precipitation on the 20th as rain fell over Hebbronville; a Co-Op observer reported 0.34 inches of rain that day. Unfortunately, while the rainfall was welcome, it would do little to alleviate the drought. By the 12th of March all of the county was in exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except the northwest corner of the county, which remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions.||At the Remote Automated Weather Station site in Hebbronville, 13 of the 31 March afternoons saw humidity fall to 15 percent or lower, which helped worsen the drought and accelerate evaporation rates at area ranches.

A lack of rain during the first half of March, allowed drought conditions to worsen across the county. By the end of the first full week of the month, the county had been split into thirds, with the northwest third of the county clinging onto Severe (D2) drought conditions, the middle third holding steady in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, and the southeast third sliding into Exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Little to no rain fell across Starr County through the first week of March. A continued lack of rain allowed drought conditions to deteriorate. The western half of the county previously in severe (D2) drought conditions slid into extreme (D3) drought conditions, while the far southeast corner of the county slid into exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

While pockets of Cameron County received showers on March 8th (the ASOS at KBRO reported only 0.26 inches, while the ASOS at KHRL reported only 0.01 inches), it was not enough to keep drought conditions at bay or to allow for any improvements.  The lack of rain allowed drought conditions to intensify across the middle of the county, where severe (D2) drought conditions became extreme (D3) drought conditions. This resulted in the entire county being in extreme (D3) drought conditions.
Golf ball size hail was reported in Falfurrias by local law enforcement and nearby by a trained spotter during the mid evening.
Half dollar size hail was reported near the Hollywood Hunting Camp about 3 miles west of Falfurrias by a Cooperative Observer.

Breezy to windy, mild, and extremely dry conditions during the first week of March worsened drought conditions by one category in the central portion of the county, from Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) between March 5th and 11th.

Breezy to windy, mild to warm, and extremely dry conditions quickly deteriorated drought across the entire county from Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) by March 12th. These conditions would remain through the end of the month; between 11 and 13 afternoons - one third to nearly one half of the days - saw afternoon humidity fall to 15 percent or lower.
Extreme (D3) Drought would continue across nearly all of Jim Hogg County to begin March, as very dry, breezy, and mild days set the stage for further deterioration by mid month.

Overall dry conditions and above normal temperatures allowed for drought conditions to persist across Starr County. A few isolated showers and thunderstorms allowed for some rainfall across the county, but it was not enough to improve drought conditions. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued to engulf the entire county.

Overall dry conditions and above normal temperatures allowed for drought conditions to persist across Cameron County. Very little rain fell across the county during much of the month. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions spread further east across the county, encompassing all of the county, except for the southeast corner by the 16th of the month.

Overall dry conditions and above normal temperatures allowed for drought conditions to persist across Brooks County. Very little rain fell across the county during much of the month. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued to engulf the entire county.

A general lack of rain and warm temperatures allowed for drought conditions to intensify across Kenedy County. By the 16th of the month, all of the county was entrenched in exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

A general lack of rain and warm temperatures allowed for drought conditions to intensify across coastal Willacy County. By the 16th of the month, all of coastal Willacy county was entrenched in exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

A general lack of rain and warm temperatures allowed for drought conditions to intensify across coastal Cameron County. By the 16th of the month, exceptional (D4) drought conditions had spread across the northern half of coastal Cameron county, while the southern half remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions.

A general lack of rain and warm temperatures allowed for drought conditions to intensify across Jim Hogg County. By the 16th of the month, exceptional (D4) drought conditions had spread across the entire county.

A general lack of rain and warm temperatures allowed for drought conditions to intensify across Willacy County. By the 16th of the month, exceptional (D4) drought conditions had spread across the entire county.

Overall dry conditions and above normal temperatures allowed for drought conditions to persist across Zapata County. A few isolated showers and thunderstorms allowed for some rainfall across the county, but it was not enough to improve drought conditions. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued to engulf the entire county by the 16th.

Overall dry conditions and above normal temperatures allowed for drought conditions to persist across Hidalgo County. Very little rain fell across the county during much of the month. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued to encompass the entirety of the county.

Significant rainfall of 1 to 4 inches fell across much of Cameron County during the last week of April.  This rainfall allowed for the exceptional (D4) drought conditions that encompassed much of the county to be relegated to only the NW and NE corners of the county, while the rest of the county improved to extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Significant rainfall of 1 to 3 inches fell across portions of Willacy County during the last week of April.  This rainfall allowed for improvement in drought conditions across the south central section of the county; exceptional (D4) drought conditions improved to extreme (D3) drought conditions, while the rest of the county remained entrenched in exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Significant rainfall of 1 to 2 inches fell across portions of Brooks County during the last week of April.  This rainfall allowed for slight improvement in drought conditions across the western central section of the county where exceptional (D4) drought conditions improved to extreme (D3) drought conditions, while the rest of the county remained entrenched in exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Significant rainfall of 1 to 2 inches fell across portions of Jim Hogg County during the last week of April.  This rainfall allowed for  improvement in drought conditions across much of the county. Extreme (D3) drought conditions returned to the county, except for a sliver of exceptional (D4) drought conditions along the far southern border.

Significant rainfall of 1 to 2 inches fell across portions of Zapata County during the last week of April.  This rainfall allowed for  improvement in drought conditions across much of the county. Extreme (D3) drought conditions returned to the northern two thirds of the county, while exceptional (D4) drought conditions remained over the southern third.
A communication tower knocked was knocked down by strong winds near La Paloma.

In North Los Fresnos, two tin roofs were lifted from old, poorly constructed trailers in a colonia neighborhood just east of the intersection of FM 510 and FM 1847 (Arroyo Blvd). Severe water and structural damage occurred at each residence; insulation was peeled from the roofs and some walls had cracked or collapsed. Both structures were uninhabitable. Nine persons were displaced.  Farther west along FM 510, a power pole was leaning at a 45 degree angle, and a mesquite tree was uprooted near the intersection of FM 803 and Henderson Road, about 4 miles to the southwest of the residential damage.

NWS employee reported tree limbs blown down in Rancho Viejo. Wind gusts were estimated at 50 to 60 mph.  A few minutes later, estimated gusts to 60 mph lifted a trampoline into and over a fence, and bent other fencing material in North Brownsville.
Broadcast media reported a tree blown down causing damage to a carport.  Nearby KMFE ASOS reported a 42 kt wind gust.

Observed rainfall from Automated Weather Observation System platforms, CoCoRaHS observers, cooperative observers, and Emergency Management personnel of 1.4 to 1.8 inches in Edinburg, and between 2 and 4 inches in Mercedes - much of the rain falling in less than one hour - created nuisance urban and field flooding due to rapid runoff after months of very dry weather.  Up to 2 feet of water accumulated in poor drainage locations of Edinburg and Mercedes.

Community Collaborative Rain, Hail, and Snow Network (CoCoRaHS), spotters, cooperative observers, and Automated Surface Observing Systems recorded between 2 and 3.5 inches of torrential rain in less than an hour, generally on a line from Santa Rosa to east of Cameron Park.  The torrents included much of Brownsville, Los Fresnos, and Harlingen.  At Brownsville (2.65 inches) and Harlingen/Valley Airport (2.37 inches), new daily records were set.  The heavy rainfall flooded previously parched farm and ranch fields with over a foot of water in some spots, particularly north of Los Fresnos, where the most rain (over 3 inches) fell.  Brief nuisance urban flooding was noted in Harlingen, portions of Brownsville, and Los Fresnos.

The lack of rainfall resulted in most of Brooks County being entrenched in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions the first week of May, except for an area of Extreme (D3) Drought conditions over the western central portion of the county. Periods of rain and scattered thunderstorms between May 10 and 15 would scour out the D4 area to just the eastern third of the county.  Torrential rains on May 24th would help improve conditions by the last few days of the month.

Little rainfall resulted in the great majority of Cameron County experiencing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions during the first week of May. Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions held firm across the NW and the NE corners of the county.
Little rainfall resulted in the northern half of coastal Cameron County continuing in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions, while the southern half held onto Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.
The general lack of rainfall during the first week of May allowed for all of coastal Willacy County was mired in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions.

A general lack of rainfall allowed for all of Hidalgo County to be mired in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions the first week of May, except for the SE corner which experienced Extreme (D3) drought conditions.  Locally heavy rains, generally between 1 and 3 inches from Mercedes to Weslaco between the 10th and 15th reduced the area of D4 to the western and northern portion of the county through May 21st.  Bands of heavy rain across the north third of the county on May 24th improved these areas from D4 to D3 by the 28th.  However, D4 remained across the western and central portions of the county - who missed the periodic heavy rainfall.
A lack of rainfall allowed for most of Jim Hogg County to continue in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, except for a sliver of Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions along the southern county border.

Little to no rain during the first week of May allowed for all of Kenedy County to remain entrenched in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions.  Patchy rainfall between the 10th and 13th near the coast helped trim a sliver of the D4 area to D3 (Extreme Drought) by May 14th.  Locally heavy rains estimated at 1 to 2 inches west of Highway 77 would further trim this area back from D4 to D3; however, the majority of the county held at D4 through the month.
Little to no rain during the first week of May allowed for all of Starr County to remain entrenched in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions.

Little to no rain during the first ten days of May allowed for the vast majority of Willacy County to be encompassed by Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, except for an area of Extreme (D3) Drought conditions in the south central portion of the county. Conditions would improve after locally heavy rainfall on the 11th, in time for the May 14th Drought Monitor update.

For the first ten days of May little to no rain fell, resulting in the northern two thirds of Zapata County experiencing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, except for the southern third, which was affected by Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions.  Locally heavy rain from strong thunderstorms late on the 10th, and again periodically through the 13th, would improve conditions rather dramatically by mid month.

Beneficial rainfall during the middle of May allowed for drought conditions to begin to improve. By the 14th of May, Cameron County began to see the improvements with the entire county immersed in extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Beneficial rainfall during the middle of May allowed for drought conditions to begin to improve. By May 14th, drought conditions had improved across the northern half of coastal Cameron County, where exceptional (D4) drought conditions improved to extreme (D3) drought conditions, resulting in all of coastal Cameron County in extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Beneficial rainfall during the middle of May allowed for drought conditions to begin to improve. By the middle of May, drought conditions began to improve across coastal Willacy County, with all of the area improving to extreme (D3) drought conditions from exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Beneficial rainfall during the middle of May allowed for drought conditions to begin to improve across Jim Hogg County. The county became split between Extreme (D3) |Drought conditions and Severe (D2) Drought conditions. The western two thirds of county improved to Severe (D2) Drought conditions and the eastern third was in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.

Beneficial rainfall during the middle of May allowed for drought conditions to begin to improve across Starr County. By the 14th of May, drought conditions improved across much of Starr County.  Most of the county saw improvement to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions from Exceptional (D4) conditions, except for the southeast corner which remained in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions and an area along the far western boundary which improved to Severe (D2) Drought conditions. ||By the 21st, the county was effectively split into thirds. The northwestern third of the county experienced Severe (D2) Drought conditions, the middle third Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, and the southeastern third Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions.

Beneficial rainfall during the middle of May allowed for drought conditions to begin to improve across Willacy County with improvements noticeable by the 14th of the month.  The vast majority of the county had improved to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions from Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions, except for the northwest corner of the county which remained in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions. By the end of the month, all of Willacy County was in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.

Beneficial rainfall during the middle of May allowed for drought conditions to begin to improve across Zapata County. Mid month totals were averaging 200 to 400 percent of normal; by the 14th of the month, the entire county improved from Extreme (D3) and Exceptional (D4) drought conditions to Severe (D2) drought conditions.

By the end of May, drought conditions continued to readily improve across Brooks County. Torrential rains estimated between 2 and more than 4 inches improved the northwestern half of the county improved from Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to Severe (D2) Drought conditions.  The southeastern half of the county improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions.

Drought conditions continued to improve through the end of the month of May across Jim Hogg County.  The western half of the county improved to Moderate (D1) Drought conditions, while the eastern half continued with Severe (D2) Drought conditions.

Drought conditions continued to improve in Starr County through the end of May. Primary improvements were across the northwest, where an estimated 2 to 3 inches of rain fell; the southeast corner continued to miss the action.  The county remained split, with the southeastern corner still in Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions, the middle third in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, the northern third in Severe (D2) Drought conditions, and an area of Moderate (D1) Drought conditions in the very far northwest corner of the county.

By the end of the month, drought conditions continued to improve across Zapata County, with much of the county improving to Moderate (D1) Drought conditions, except for a small sliver of Severe (D2) Drought conditions in the very far southern tip of the county. The full category improvement was the result of a large area of 1 to nearly 3 inches of rain across all but the northeast quarter of the county on May 24th.

Between 2.3 and 2.77 inches of rain fell in less than two hours on the west side of Harlingen, leaving ponded water in streets and fields and some nuisance urban flooding behind.  The event, which occurred very early on a Saturday morning, had little impact with few people out.

Around 2.5 inches of rain fell in less than two hours just southwest of Raymondville, leaving ponded water in streets and fields and some nuisance urban flooding behind.  The event, which occurred very early on a Saturday morning, had little impact with few people out.

While some areas of Cameron County received beneficial rains, totals were generally an inch or less and did little to alleviate drought conditions. Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through much of June.

While some areas of Coastal Cameron County received beneficial rains, totals were generally an inch or less and did little to alleviate drought conditions. Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through much of June.

While some areas of Coastal Willacy County received beneficial rains, totals were generally an inch or less and did little to alleviate drought conditions. Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through much of June.

While some areas of Willacy County received beneficial rains, totals were generally an inch or less and did little to alleviate drought conditions. Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through much of June.

Despite areas of Kenedy County receiving between an inch and two inches of rainfall during the first half of the month, the rainfall did little to improve drought conditions across Kenedy County. The majority of the county remained in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, with areas of Extreme (D3) drought conditions along the eastern and southern county borders.

While some areas of Hidalgo County received beneficial rains, totals were generally an inch or less and did little to alleviate drought conditions. Most of Hidalgo County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, except for an area of Exceptional (D4) drought conditions stretching from the southwest corner of the county into the center of the county.

Locally heavy rainfall of 2 to 4 inches fell across Zapata County during the first two weeks of June. This very beneficial rain allowed for Moderate (D1) drought conditions to continue across much of the county except for the very far southern tip of the county which  held onto Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Very isolated showers and thunderstorms across Brooks County during June dropped less than a quarter inch of rain. While any rain that fell was beneficial, it did little to improve drought conditions across Brooks County.  The northwestern half of the county remained affected by Severe (D2) drought conditions, while the southeastern half of Brooks County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

While most of Jim Hogg County saw little in the way of rainfall during much of June, isolated areas in extreme western Jim Hogg County received from two to four inches of rain during the first two weeks.  This rain allowed for the western half of Jim Hogg County to remain in Moderate (D1) drought conditions, while the eastern half of the county experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Areas of beneficial rain fell across Starr County throughout the first half of month. An estimated 2 to 4 inches fell across the western half of the county, with 3.75 inches reported at Falcon Dam.  Throughout the month of June, the county remained split, with Exceptional (D4) drought conditions in the southeastern corner, Extreme (D3) drought conditions in the middle third of the county, Severe (D2) drought conditions in the northern third of the county, with an area of Moderate (D1) drought conditions along the far north and western edges of the county.

At the Weslaco/Mid Valley Airport AWOS, a gust of 53 mph was recorded at 135 PM CDT. Further south, winds were estimated to be 60 to 65 mph based on the photos, descriptions, and prior experience with similar past events in the Rio Grande Valley. On the tarmac, the first damage occurred when one small plane flipped into another, causing damage to each. An empty trailer was flipped on its side at a local dealership just south of the airport. The most notable damage occurred at a warehouse at the intersection of Business 83 and S. Utah Avenue at approximately 139 PM CST, where much of the tin roof was torn from the building. Diagonally across the street, part of the metal roof at the Economy Inn and Suites was torn off. About one and one half miles south, part of a tin carport was blown into nearby trees and a house in Ranchero Village Mobile Home Park, most likely around 143-145 PM CST.A dilapidated house in Mercedes also lost part of its roof, though wind speed was likely somewhat lower than estimated and observed in Weslaco. Weslaco Police initially estimated at least $100 thousand in property damage.

Zapata County emergency manager and fire department reported floodwaters of 1 to 2 feet deep on Highway 83 in the vicinity of Falcon in the far southern portion of Zapata County. The emergency manager also reported that the Texas Department of Transportation had placed warning signs along portions of Highway 83, but closed no roads.
Starr County Sheriff���s Department reported floodwater covering the southbound lane of Highway 83 in the vicinity of Salineno.

Mission police department reported several car ports damaged or destroyed in the 800 block of East 21st Street in Mission. ASOS at KMFE, about 5 miles to the SE, reported peak wind gust of 39 knots during the thunderstorm.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: Strong thunderstorm wind gusts exceeding 40 knots affected the Laguna Madre Waters east of Kenedy County. Nearby TCOON buoy in Baffin Bay recorded gusts of 40.6 kts and 43 kts.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Zapata County saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. The eastern half of the county remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions, while the western half of the county remained in Moderate (D1) drought conditions.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Jim Hogg saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. The eastern two thirds of the county in remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, while the western third of the county remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Starr saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. Starr County remained split with the far southeastern corner of the county in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, the western third of the county in Severe (D2) drought conditions, and the remainder of the county in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Brooks County saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. The county remained primarily entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, except for a sliver of Severe (D2) drought along the far northern county border.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Hidalgo County saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. Exceptional (D4) drought remained draped across a huge swath of the county from the southwest corner of the county east to near Weslaco to just south of Linn-San Manuel, while the remainder of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Kenedy County saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. All of Kenedy County remained firmly planted in Extreme (D3) drought.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Willacy County saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. All of Willacy County remained firmly planted in Extreme (D3) drought.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Coastal Willacy County saw no improvements in drought conditions during. August. All of Coastal Willacy County remained firmly planted in Extreme (D3) drought.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Coastal Cameron County saw no improvements in drought conditions during August. All of Coastal Cameron County remained firmly planted in Extreme (D3) drought.

Hot, dry, and breezy conditions ensured that Cameron County saw no improvements in drought conditions during the first week of August. All of Cameron County remained firmly planted in Extreme (D3) drought.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve across Zapata County. Hot and breezy conditions combined with dry soils to allow drought conditions to worsen across the county. The eastern third of the county and the far northwestern corner of the county experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions. A sliver of Extreme (D3) drought conditions nudged in along the far eastern border, while a swath of Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained in the middle of the county.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall (the COOP site in Hebbronville recorded 0.69 inches) during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve across Jim Hogg County. Hot and breezy conditions combined with dry soils to allow drought conditions to worsen across the county. The southeast corner of the county slide into Exceptional (D4) drought, while a sliver of Severe (D2) drought clinged along the northern county border. The rest of the county remained entrenched firmly in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve across Starr County. Hot and breezy conditions combined with dry soils to allow drought conditions to worsen across the county. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions spread north, fully encompassing the eastern half of Starr County. The western half of the county continued to experience Extreme (D3) drought.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall (Brooks County Airport, in Falfurrias, recorded 1.43 inches of rain)  during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve across Brooks County. Hot and breezy conditions combined with dry soils to allow drought conditions to worsen across the county. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions pushed north to affect the southern third of the county. The rest of Brooks County remained in Extreme (D3) drought.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall across portions of Hidalgo County (McAllen Miller Airport recorded only 0.2 inches of rain) during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions engulfed the entire county.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall across portions of Kenedy County (a COOP site in Sarita reported 1.22 inches of rain) during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions encroached across the southwest corner of Kenedy County.  The remainder of the county continued to be entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall across portions of Willacy County during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions spread across the western half of the county, effectively splitting it in half.  The eastern half of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite isolated showers and thunderstorms dropping some much welcome rainfall (Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport received 1.38 inches of rain and Valley International Airport in Harlingen received 1.93 inches) across portions of Cameron County during the last two weeks of the month, drought conditions did not improve. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions spread across the western half of the county, effectively splitting it in half.  The eastern half of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Hot temperatures and a general lack of widespread and heavy rainfall led to drought conditions worsening across Zapata County during the first half of July. Severe (D2) drought conditions engulfed the county once again by the 16th, completely eliminating the Moderate (D1) drought conditions that had covered all but the northern third of the county beginning July 2nd.

Hot temperatures and a general lack of widespread and heavy rainfall led to drought conditions worsening across Jim Hogg County during the first half of July. Extreme (D3) drought conditions began to enter the picture once again for Jim Hogg County and Moderate (D1) drought conditions were eliminated from the county on July 2nd. ||Severe (D2) Drought conditions covered all but the northeast portion of the ocunty, where Extreme (D3) Drought returned.  The Extreme Drought conditions would spread across all but the western quarter of the county on July 23rd with hot dry conditions dominating most of the area to close out the month.

Hot temperatures and a general lack of widespread and heavy rainfall led to drought conditions gradually worsening across Starr County during July. The county remained split between Severe, Extreme, and Exceptional drought conditions. The far southeastern corner of the county experienced Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, the middle third of the county was entrenched in Extreme (D3) drought conditions early, which spread to all but the western quarter of the county by the 22nd, which remained in Severe (D2) drought - held up by periodic rain between the 16th and 20th.

Drought conditions across Brooks County worsened during the first half of July due to heat and a general lack of widespread and heavy rainfall. Extreme (D3) drought conditions spread further west across the county, to encompass almost the entire county, except for a sliver of Severe (D2) drought conditions along the far northern county border and a small area in the far southwestern corner of the county. Lack of rainfall and above normal temperatures toward month's end brought all areas of the county to Extreme (D3) conditions.

A general lack of rainfall allowed for Exceptional (D4) drought conditions to spread further east across Hidalgo County, resulting in a huge swath of the county from the southwest corner of the county east to near Weslaco to just south of Linn-San Manuel. The remainder of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Extreme to exceptional drought conditions spanned Kenedy County through the first half of July.  Exceptional (D4) drought conditions spread further south across eastern Kenedy County, resulting in the eastern half of the county experiencing Exceptional (D4) drought conditions, while the western half of the county remained ensconced in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite some rainfall during the first half of the month, drought conditions continued to plague inland Willacy County in July. Extreme (D3) Drought dominated the month, except a sliver of Exceptional (D4) developed toward the coastal regions on the 2nd and continued through the 22nd. Rainfall near the coast between the 16th and 20th returned Extreme (D3) Drought back to the areas toward the coast to finish the month.

Despite some rainfall during the first half of the month, drought conditions worsened across the eastern half of Cameron County. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions once again returned to the eastern half of inland Cameron County, while Extreme (D3) drought conditions remained draped across the western half of Cameron County. Scattered showers and storms between the 16th and 20th would improve conditions to close the month.

Despite some rainfall during the first half of the month, drought conditions worsened across Coastal Willacy County. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions once again returned to encompass the entire area on July 2nd and would continue until the 22nd.

Despite some rainfall during the first half of the month, drought conditions worsened across Coastal Cameron County through the 22nd of July. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions once again returned to encompass the entire area.

Drought conditions improved across all of Coastal Cameron County, as the effects from rain earlier in the month began to be felt. The entire area improved from Exceptional (D4) drought conditions to Extreme (D3) drought.

Drought conditions improved across all of Coastal Willacy County, as the effects from rain earlier in the month began to be felt. The entire area improved from Exceptional (D4) drought conditions to Extreme (D3) drought.

Thanks to rain earlier in the month, drought conditions improved across Cameron County, with the Exceptional (D4) drought conditions over the eastern half of the county, being replaced by Extreme (D3) drought conditions, resulting in the entire county experiencing Extreme (D3) drought.

Thanks to rain earlier in the month, drought conditions improved across Kenedy County, with the Exceptional (D4) drought conditions over the eastern half of the county, being replaced by Extreme (D3) drought conditions, resulting in the entire county experiencing Extreme (D3) drought.

Thanks to rain earlier in the month, drought conditions improved across the western half of Zapata County.  Moderate (D1) drought conditions replaced Severe (D2) drought conditions across the western half of the county, while the eastern half remained ensconced in Severe (D2) drought conditions.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: Several beachgoers and at least one fishing boat reported a waterspout 5 miles north of South Padre Island, roughly offshore just south of beach access number six. The waterspout was visible on the South Padre Island Beach Camera. The waterspout remained offshore for its duration and caused no damage, and meandered in the same area for more than an hour based on tracking by beach cameras and photos by the public.
Estimated downburst winds of around 65 mph damaged the roofs of homes and a small business, snapped tree limbs, and blew over a number of trailers at the San Ygnacio RV park.

Severe (D2) Drought would continue across all but the southeast third of Brooks County, which maintained Extreme (D3) Drought, from the end of June into the first day of July.  Dry, hot conditions to close June would worsen drought to Extreme Conditions in all but the southwest corner of the county beginning on July 2nd.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions would prevail across all but extreme western Jim Hogg county, where Moderate (D1) conditions remained to begin July.  Lack of rainfall to end June would soon contribute to worsening conditions by July 2nd.

Lack of rainfall during the latter half of June began to show its impact on drought in eastern Cameron County by early July, as Extreme (D3) Conditions which dominated the area in June would soon become Exceptional (D4) just after the start of July mainly along and east of Highway 77 and the coastal sand flats. Extreme Drought continued in all areas on July 1st.

Lack of rainfall during the latter half of June began to show its impact on drought in coastal Cameron County by early July, as Extreme (D3) Conditions which dominated the area in June would soon become Exceptional (D4) just after the start of July mainly from the coastal sand flats to the barrier island. Extreme Drought continued in these areas on July 1st.

Lack of rainfall during the latter half of June began to show its impact on drought in coastal Willacy County by early July, as Extreme (D3) Conditions which dominated the area in June would soon become Exceptional (D4) just after the start of July mainly from the coastal sand flats to the barrier island. Extreme Drought continued in these areas on July 1st.

Little change in drought conditions occurred during much of the month across Zapata County. The western two thirds of the county remained in Moderate (D1) drought, while the eastern third maintained Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Much of Jim Hogg County during the first week of September was encompassed by Exceptional (D4) drought conditions that were painted from the SE corner through much of the middle of the county. The Exceptional (D4) drought conditions were surrounded by Extreme (D3) drought conditions and small slivers of Severe (D2) drought conditions on the far northern and western borders.
Exceptional (D4) drought conditions reigned over much of Starr County during the first week of September, with only the western third of the county experiencing Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Despite some rain falling during the first week of September, little change was noticed in drought conditions across Brooks County. Much of the county remained engulfed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with southern quarter of the county covered in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Some rain fell almost every day from the 1st through the 16th across portions of Hidalgo County. During the time period, the ASOS at McAllen Miller International Airport recorded 5.45 inches. Benefits from this rain would not be felt until later in the month. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued to engulf the county.
Extreme (D3) drought conditions prevailed across much of Kenedy County during the first week of September. The SW corner of the county was engulfed in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

The benefits from showers and thunderstorms during the first half of September was felt little through the 16th of the month. Much of the county was engulfed by Extreme (D3) drought conditions. A swath of Exceptional (D4) drought conditions covered much of the western half of the county.

Rain fell nearly every day across portions of Willacy County during the first half of September. Despite this rainfall little change was noted in drought conditions across coastal Willacy County, with the entire area engulfed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Rain fell nearly every day during the first week of September across Cameron County.  Total accumulations varied across the county, the ASOS at the Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport recorded 3.9 inches of rain, while the ASOS at Valley International Airport in Harlingen measured only 1.61 inches. Regardless, this beneficial rainfall allowed for improvement in drought conditions. The entirety of Cameron County improved to Extreme (D3) drought conditions, wiping away Exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Rain fell almost every day across portions of coastal Cameron County. Despite this rainfall, little change was noted in drought conditions across coastal Cameron County, with the entire area engulfed in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Public reported quarter size hail at the intersection of Lincoln and 5th in downtown Zapata.  Also reported winds of 65 mph (estimated).

Drought conditions worsened across Starr County. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions spread west across the county, engulfing the eastern two thirds of the county, while the eastern third of the county experienced Extreme (D3) drought.

Drought conditions worsened across Jim Hogg County. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions surged northwest across the county, with Exceptional (D4) drought prevailing across most of the county. Extreme (D3) drought conditions surrounded the Exceptional (D4) drought conditions to the west , north and northeast, while small slivers of Severe (D2) drought conditions held on along far western and northern borders.

events.event_narrative: A thunderstorm moved west across the Gulf Waters and over South Padre Island. A marine thunderstorm gust of 35 knots was reported by the Coast Guard Station at South Padre Island.

After periods of significant rainfall during much of September, the benefits began to be felt as drought conditions began to improve. The county became divided up into thirds. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions were confined to the eastern third, while the middle of the county experienced Extreme (D3) drought conditions and the western third experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions.

After periods of rainfall during September, the benefits of the rainfall began to be felt as drought conditions began to improve across Jim Hogg County. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions were confined to the SE corner of the county, while much of the rest of the county was in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with small slivers of Severe (D2) drought conditions on the far western and northern borders.
Nearly daily rainfall dropped between 7 and 13 inches across parts of Cameron County. This significant rainfall allowed for all of Cameron County to improve to Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Rainfall during the first week of September was beneficial and allowed for drought conditions to improve across Kenedy County by the 10th of the month. While most of the county remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with a small area of Exceptional (D4) drought in the far SW corner, the NW corner of the county improved to Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Drought conditions did not improve greatly during the first few weeks of Brooks County as the heaviest rains stayed away from the county. However, some improvements were seen across the middle of the county where Exceptional (D4) drought conditions improved to Extreme (D3) drought conditions.  This resulted in most of the county in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with the far SE corner still in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions and a few slivers of Severe (D2) drought conditions along the western and northern county borders.
After nearly daily rainfall for much of the first half of the month, the benefits began to be felt across coastal Cameron County, with the entire area engulfed in Severe (D2) drought conditions.
After nearly daily rainfall for much of the first half of the month, the benefits began to be felt across coastal Willacy County, with the entire area engulfed in Severe (D2) drought conditions.

After significant rain during the month, with many locations seeing between 11 and 13 inches of rain during the month, drought conditions continued to improve greatly across Cameron County. Extreme (D3) drought conditions were eliminated as drought conditions improved. Moderate (D1) drought conditions prevailed across much of Cameron County, with an area of Severe (D2) drought conditions in the NW corner.

After a month of plentiful and beneficial rain, drought improvement continued across Kenedy County, with all of the Extreme (D3) drought conditions eliminated by the end of the month. The county was primarily covered by Severe (D2) drought conditions, with a swath of Moderate (D1) drought conditions along the northern border.

After nearly daily rainfall for much of the first half of the month, the beneficial rains allowed for drought conditions to improve across Willacy County. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions were eliminated from the county, with Extreme (D3) drought conditions confined west of Highway 281/I-69E. The rest of the county was covered in primarily Severe (D2) drought conditions, with a small area of Moderate (D1) drought conditions along the southern edge of the county.

Significant improvement in drought conditions occurred across Hidalgo County by the middle of the month.  Over 6 inches of rain was measured through the 23rd at McAllen Miller International Airport. Exceptional (D4) drought conditions were limited to a swath along the western county border, while much of the rest of the county was affected by Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with Severe (D2) drought conditions confined to the SE corner of the county.

After a wet month, drought conditions continued to improve across Willacy County, with Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailing, with only a small sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions along the southern boundary.

Drought conditions continued to improve throughout the last week of September as Exceptional (D4) drought became more scarce. The county was essentially divided in half, with the western half of the county experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions. The eastern half of the county was primarily covered in Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with small patches of Exceptional (D4) drought conditions in the NE and SE corners.

Drought conditions continued to improve throughout the last week of the  month, as Exceptional (D4) drought conditions became relegated to the far SE corner of the county. Extreme (D3) conditions were draped across the middle of the county from NW to SE and surrounding by Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Drought conditions continued to improve through the end of the month.  6.22 inches of rain were recorded during the month of September at McAllen Miller International Airport. By the end of the month, the county was split into two. The eastern half of the county was covered by Severe (D2) drought conditions, with the western half was primarily covered by Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with a few patches of Exceptional (D4) drought conditions in the NW and SW corners.

By the end of the month the benefits from some mid month rain showed with the improving drought conditions.  Exceptional (D4) drought conditions were confined to the far SE corner of the county, with a swath of Extreme (D3) drought conditions draped across the middle of the county from NW to SE. The remainder of the county was covered in Severe (D2) drought conditions.
Local law enforcement reported water approaching and entering homes in Rio Grande City.
Local law enforcement reported water approaching and entering homes in Rio Grande City.

After beneficial rains in September, most of Jim Hogg County was covered by Severe (D2) drought conditions by the first of October. An area of Extreme (D3) drought conditions held on in the SE corner of the county, while Moderate (D1) drought conditions spread across the western and northern county borders. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.

After beneficial rains in September, a variety of drought conditions were spread across Starr County during the month of October. The western half of the county was comprised primarily of Moderate (D1) drought conditions, but an area of Dry (D0) conditions emerged in the SW corner of the county.  The eastern half of the county was divided by a stripe of Severe (D2) drought conditions across the center of the county, a swath of Extreme (D3) drought conditions along the eastern county border, and an area of Exceptional (D4) drought conditions in the very far SE corner of the county. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.

After beneficial rains in September, the vast majority of Brooks County was draped in Severe (D2) drought conditions, with the exceptions of a sliver along the northern county border and the far SW corner of the county.  Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued to cling to the far SW corner of the county, while Moderate (D1) drought conditions spread south across the northern county border. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.

After beneficial rains in September, much of Hidalgo County was covered by Severe (D2) drought conditions. Along the far western edge of the county, a swath of Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted, with a patch of Exceptional (D4) drought conditions in the far SW corner of the county. Moderate (D1) drought conditions began to nudge into the far SE corner of the county.  Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.

After beneficial rains in September, the southern two thirds of Kenedy County was covered by Severe (D2) drought conditions, with the northern third covered by Moderate (D1) drought by the beginning of October. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.

After beneficial rains in September, the vast majority of Willacy County was engulfed by Severe (D2) drought conditions, except for a small sliver of Moderate (D1) drought across the southern county border. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.
After beneficial rains in September, all of coastal Willacy County was covered Severe (D2) drought conditions. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.
After beneficial rains in September, all of coastal Cameron County was covered Severe (D2) drought conditions. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.

After beneficial rains in September, most of Cameron County had improved to Moderate (D1) drought conditions by the beginning of October. Severe (D2) drought conditions still held tight in the far NW corner of Cameron County. Drought conditions held steady throughout the month.

Rainfall totals for the first half of November varied across Starr County. Totals generally range from one to inches, with isolated pockets of two to three inches. While the rainfall was welcome, it did little to alleviate drought conditions across the county. The western half of Starr County remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions, while the eastern half was covered primarily by Extreme (D3) drought conditions, with the SE corner of the county in Exceptional (D4) drought conditions.

Rainfall totals across Jim Hogg County generally ranged less than an inch during the first half of November across the eastern half of the county to two inches across the southwest corner.  While the rainfall was welcome, it did little to alleviate drought conditions across the county. The vast majority of the county was entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions. A sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions was draped across the far northern county border, while the SE corner of the county experienced Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Rainfall totals across Brooks County generally ranged less than an inch during the first half of November, with a few pockets of one to two inches across the eastern half of the county. While the rainfall was welcome, it did little to alleviate drought conditions across the county. The vast majority of the county was entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions. A sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions was draped across the northern county border, while the SW corner of the county experienced Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Rainfall totals across Hidalgo County generally varied greatly during the first half of November, with some locations in the southern third of the county receiving less than an inch and other locations further north receiving three and a quarter to five inches. While the rainfall was welcome, it did little to alleviate drought conditions across the county. Severe (D2) drought conditions claimed most of the county, with a sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions slipping in on the far SE corner of the county. Across the western third of the county Extreme (D3) drought conditions remained in control, with Exceptional (D4) drought conditions holding onto the far SW corner of the county.

Rainfall totals across Willacy County generally ranged from an inch to inches across the county. The welcome rainfall did allow for drought conditions to improve, especially along the southern county border. Severe (D2) drought conditions claimed most of the county, with a sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions slipping in on the far SE corner of the county. Across the western third of the county Extreme (D3) drought conditions remained in control, with Exceptional (D4) drought conditions holding onto the far SW corner of the county.

Rainfall totals across Kenedy County varied, but the vast majority of the county received between 2 and 4 inches of rainfall during early November. The welcome rainfall did allow for drought conditions to improve. Drought conditions divided Kenedy County into fairly equal thirds. Extreme (D3) drought conditions held onto the southern third of the county, while Severe (D2) drought conditions claimed the middle of the county, and Moderate (D1) drought conditions took the northern third.

Rainfall totals across coastal Willacy County generally ranged in the two to three inch range for the month of November, as most of the heaviest rainfall during the month fell further west. While the rainfall was welcome, it did little to alleviate the drought conditions across coastal Willacy County. The area remained entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions for the month.

Rainfall totals across coastal Cameron County generally ranged in the two to three inch range for the month of November, as most of the heaviest rainfall during the month fell further west. While the rainfall was welcome, it did little to alleviate the drought conditions across coastal Cameron County. The area remained entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions for the month.

Rainfall totals for the month of November varied greatly across Cameron County. Rainfall totals ranged from three to four inches on the eastern and western country borders to six to over seven inches across the interior and along the northern county broder. The rainfall was beneficial and allowed for drought conditions to improve across Cameron County. Most of Cameron County experienced Moderate (D1) drought conditions, with the far NW corner of the county still holding onto Severe (D2) drought conditions. Conditions improved by the end of the month to effectively eliminate Severe (D2) drought conditions from the county.

Benefits from rainfall throughout the month of November allowed for improvement in drought conditions across the county. Exceptional (D3) drought was eliminated from the county.  Moderate (D1) drought conditions replaced Severe (D2) drought conditions across the western border of Starr County, while much of the interior of the county was covered in Severe (D2) drought conditions, and the SE corner of the county improved to Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Benefits from rainfall throughout the month of November allowed for improvement in drought conditions across the county. Drought conditions improved to Moderate (D1) drought conditions along the western border and Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained draped across the northern boundary. The vast majority of the county was covered by Severe (D2) drought conditions, with the SE corner still mired in Extreme (D3) drought conditions.

Rainfall totals generally ranged from just below an inch of rain across portions of western Brooks County with the eastern half of the county slightly wetter, with totals of two to three inches. The benefits from rainfall throughout the month of November allowed for some improvement in drought conditions. Drought conditions improved in the SW corner of the county, where Extreme (D3) drought was shunted further west, but the vast majority of the county remained entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions. A sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained across the northern county border.

Rainfall totals varied greatly across Hidalgo County in November, with most of the county seeing rainfall totals between two and four inches. Some pockets of six to eight inches were noted across the northern half of the county. The benefits from rainfall throughout the month of November allowed for some improvement in drought conditions. Drought conditions improved in the SW corner of the county, where Extreme (D3) drought was shunted further west, but the vast majority of the county remained entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions. A sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained across the northern county border.

The benefits from rainfall throughout the month of November allowed for some improvement in drought conditions. Drought conditions improved in the SW corner of the county, where Extreme (D3) drought was shunted further west, but the vast majority of the county remained entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions. A sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained across the northern county border.

Improvements were seen across the southern third of the county, where Severe (D2) drought conditions spread further south and east, pushing the Extreme (D3) drought conditions to the SE corner of the county. The middle of the county remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions and the northern third of the county remained in Moderate (D1) drought conditions.

The western half of the county improved to Moderate (D1) and dry (D0) conditions, while the eastern half of the county experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions.

Severe (D2) drought conditions were relegated to the SW quarter of the county, with Extreme (D3) drought conditions clinging to a small sliver on the far SW corner.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions were eliminated from the county and the county was effectively split in half. The western half of the county was covered by Severe (D2) drought conditions, while Moderate (D1) drought conditions spread north and encompassed the eastern half of the county.

Moderate (D1) drought conditions spread north across the county. Extreme (D3) drought conditions were eliminated along the NE corner, with Severe (D2) drought conditions encompassing the eastern third.

Much of the county improved to Moderate (D1) drought conditions, with a stripe of Severe (D2) drought conditions surrounding the Extreme (D3) drought conditions, and a patch of Dry (D0) conditions along the northern border.

Two to four inches of rain fell in less than 90 minutes along the Highway 77 corridor in Brownsville. Reports were received from various sources including an offduty NWS employee. Several cars were reported stranded at the intersection of Pablo Kisel and Morrision road, where over a foot of water covered the road. A foot and a half of water was reported by a trained spotter covering the road in the 700 block of Paredes Line. A NWS employee reported flooding covering the frontage road along Hwy 77, near Sunrise Mall and 2 to 4 inches of water covering the road and water up to the top of the curb at the intersection of Boca Chica and Old Port Isabel Road.

Between 4.23 to 4.96 inches of rainfall fell in less than 90 minutes across western Brownsville, leading to flash flooding across that portion of the city. The Brownsville Emergency Operations Center reported several businesses with some water in them, numerous thoroughfares with several inches to nearly 2 feet of water on them acorss the area limiting travel. During the peak of the rains, 42 streets had flooding that reduced travel to one lane or less. Some resacas were also reported to have reached bankful or flooded low lying grassy areas.
Two to four inches of rain fell in less than 90 minutes across Brownsville. A NWS employee reported 8 inches of water covering the road at the FM 511 and Paredes Line Rd intersection.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: Strong thunderstorms over the Lower Texas Coastal Waters produced thunderstorm winds and gusts to gale force. KPIL reported a sustained wind of 37 kts with gusts to 46 kts 1203 am CST.  The South Padre Island Coast Guard Station reported maximum sustained wind of 38 kts with gusts to 48 kts at 1230 am CST.

Four mobile homes, in poor condition and not anchored, were damaged in Doolittle near the intersection of Ingle Road and Doolittle Road. Two mobile homes lost tin roofs, one was moved off of its foundation, and one rolled over on its side. Estimated winds of 55 to 60 mph.

More than 5 inches of rain fell across portions of Harlingen during a 5 hour period causing localized flooding of low lying and poor drainage spots. Local law enforcement reported water over a lower bridge on Breedlove Street, water over the road at the intersection of Polk Avenue and Highway 77, on Hayne, Tomas Lane and Marck Circle. There were numerous reports on social media reporting water over the road at the intersection of Ed Carey and Business 77/Sunshine Strip.

More than 5 inches of rain fell across portions of Harlingen during a 5 hour period causing localized flooding of low lying and poor drainage spots. Local law enforcement reported 5 to 6 inches of water in Primera and noted that water was approaching homes of residents.

Slow moving thunderstorms dropped over three inches of rain over the Raymondville area in the matter of a few hours, with a nearby COOP site reporting 3.2 inches. This rainfall caused water to rise rapidly in downton Raymondville. The Willacy County emergency manager reported several inches of water entering the Raymondville City Hall building.

Strong winds associated with the passage of a cold front surged across Harlingen during the early afternoon hours of November 22nd. The strong winds resulted in an older live oak tree crashing onto a home. The ASOS at nearby Valley International Airport reported sustained winds of 25 to 26 kts with gusts of 34 kts.

Strong winds associated with the passage of a cold front surged across South Padre Island during the afternoon hours of November 22nd. The strong winds resulted in palm trees falling on power lines and the loss of power to more than 3000 local utility customer. The South Padre Island Coast Guard station reported sustained winds of 26 kts with gusts to 33 kts on the Laguna Madre side of the island and KSPI reported sustained winds of 26 kts with gusts of 31 kts.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX OUT 20 NM
events.event_narrative: A 16 foot pleasure craft took on water during the early evening hours of November 22nd, in the Brownsville Ship Channel, near the Jaime J. Zapata Memorial Boat Ramp A Gale Warning was in effect and gale force wind gusts were recorded at nearby KSPL and the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station. Three men were rescued from the swamped boat with no injuries reported.

During the early morning hours of December 16th, temperatures dropped to or below freezing across large portions of Kenedy County.  The Sarita COOP site reported a low of 28 degrees and the Armstrong COOP site reported a low of 29 degrees.

After midnight, temperatures dropped below freezing across Zapata County for around 6 hours reaching a low of 29 degrees at the AWOS site in Zapata.

Significant rainfall during the last week of December allowed for the entirety of Willacy County to improve to Moderate (D1) drought conditions or better.

The remainder of the county was covered by Moderate (D1) drought conditions.

Much of the remainder of the county was covered by Moderate (D1) drought conditions, with a stripe of dry (D0) conditions across the northern county border.

A small sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions held on tightly across the northern border.
