A ice storm hit Cameron County where 1/8 to 1/2 inch of glaze accreted on trees, power lines, cars, and other exposed surfaces.  News reports indicated 9000 customers were without electricity during the peak of the storm early on the 29th, in Harlingen, San Benito, and other communities in Cameron County. There was likely some damage to tender tropical vegetation (such as banana plants, bougainvillea, etc.) but many of these plants should recover.

A ice storm hit coastal Cameron County where 1/8 to 1/2 inch of glaze accreted on trees, power lines, cars, and other exposed surfaces. News reports indicated nearly 9000 customers were without electricity during the peak of the storm early on the 29th  in Port Isabel, Bayview, and other communities across Cameron County. There was likely some damage to tender tropical vegetation (such as banana plants, bougainvillea, etc.) but many of these plants should recover.

A ice storm hit Hidalgo County where 1/8 to 1/2 inch of glaze accreted on trees, power lines, cars, and other exposed surfaces. Texas Department of Transportation noted ice accumulations on several roadways and overpasses. News reports indicated over 3000 customers were without electricity during the peak of the storm early on the 29th, across Hidalgo County. There was likely some damage to tender tropical vegetation (such as banana plants, bougainvillea, etc.) but many of these plants should recover.

Several 37 to 42 knots (43 to 48 mph) wind gusts were measured at the South Padre Island Coast Guard station. Peak winds at nearby Bayview/Cameron County Airport peaked at 35 knots (40 mph) at 353 AM CST. Approximately 8500 customers were without power across coastal Cameron County (Port Isabel, Laguna Vista, Bayview, South Padre Island) due to the strong and gusty winds disabling power lines.

A 43 kt wind gust was measured at the McAllen Miller International Airport ASOS site at 654 PM CST; gusts continued to gale force (39 to 44 mph) for about an hour. Approximately 9000 customers were without power across the mid Valley (Weslaco, McAllen) due to the strong and gusty winds disabling power lines.

Drought conditions across Brooks County held steady through the month of January.  Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across a swath of the western half of the county, while the remainder of the county experienced Moderate (D1) drought conditions, with a stripe of Abnormally Dry (D0) drought conditions along the northern county border. Periodic rain through the month would be enough to eliminate Severe (D2) drought conditions by the beginning of February.

Drought conditions across Jim Hogg County held steady through the month of January.  Severe (D2) drought conditions remain entrenched across much of the southern half of the county, while the remainder of the county was covered by Moderate (D1) drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions.  Periodic rain through the month would be enough to eliminate Severe (D2) drought conditions by the beginning of February.

Temperatures fell below freezing across Jim Hogg County for almost 6 hours. The Hebbronville RAWS site reported a low of 30 degrees, while the AWOS site at KHBV reported a low of 31 degrees.  During the morning, light freezing rain coated signs, fences, higher grass, etc. but caused no problems to roads or the electrical grid.

Temperatures fell to or below freezing for almost 3 hours on the morning of February 7th. The ASOS site in Zapata recorded a low of 32 degrees, while the COOP site in Escobas reported a low of 30 degrees.  Very light precipitation accompanied the cold during the early to mid morning, with a light coating on signs, fences, high grass, and trees/branches.  There was no impact to roads.
Temperatures fell to or below freezing for almost 3 hours on the morning of February 7th. The COOP site in Rio Grande City recorded a low of 31 degrees.

Temperatures fell to or below freezing for a number of hours across Jim Hogg County. The Hebbronville RAWS site reported a low of 30 degrees, while the ASOS site at KHBV reported a low of 31 degrees.  For a second straight day, very light precipitation accompanied the cold and froze on contact with elevated surfaces, including signs, fences, tall grass, and trees/branches.  None accumulated on roads, however.

Temperatures fell to or just below freezing for several hours on the morning of February 7th. The COOP observer in Sarita reported a low of 31 degrees, while further south in Armstrong, the COOP observer reported a low of 32 degrees.  Based on nearby observations in Kingsville, a little more than 20 miles north of Sarita, there was likely some very light precipitation that created a coating of ice on signs, fences, tall grass, and trees/branches.  There was no impact to roads, bridges, or the electrical grid.

Temperatures fell to freezing or just below across Brooks County during the early morning hours of February 7th. The COOP observer in Falfurrias reported a low of 32 degrees.  Based on surrounding observations and reports from officials in the region, very light precipitation accompanied the cold in some of the area, producing a light coating of ice on signs, fences, tall grass, and trees/branches.  There was no impact to roads or the electrical grid.

Temperatures fell below freezing during the early morning hours of February 12th. The RAWS site in Hebbronville reported a low of 32 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing across Zapata County during the early morning hours of February 12th. The ASOS site in Zapata recorded a low of 30 degrees and the COOP observer in Escobas reported a low of 29 degrees.
A billboard was damaged near Mile 2 East in Mercedes. The AWOS site in Weslaco, recorded sustained winds of 27.6 kts with gusts to 34.5 kts.

An 18-year-old male swimming near the Inverness Condominiums near the Good Hope Beach Access drowned in a rip current. Three other individuals were rescued, all of whom were brought to shore with injuries and were transported to local hospitals for medical treatment.
Trained spotter reported damage near the intersection of FM3073 and Highway 16, southwest of Hebbronville. Travel trailers, portable buildings and trees were blown over.
Sustained winds of over 30 mph along with gusts to 51 mph (measured by the KHRL ASOS) caused damage to a traffic light at the corner of Business 77 and Wilson Road in Harlingen.

Several hours of gusty winds caused minor damage to unfastened, light weight objects, such as lawn furniture, trampolines, trash cans. The strong winds also caused damage to several trees across the Mission and Edinburg area.
The AWOS at Brooks County Airport reported a 53 knot wind gust.
Golf ball sized hail was reported in Falfurrias by the public.

The Brooks County Emergency Manager and local law enforcement reported numerous trees down near the intersection of Lasater Street and Rice Street and along St. Mary's Street. Structural damage to business signs was also reported on Center Street.
The ASOS at the Port Isabel Airport in Bayview reported a 58 knot wind gust.
Public reported penny sized hail in Port Isabel.
NWS employee reported several one to two foot diameter trees snapped with estimated 60 mph wind gusts.
Trained spotter reported quarter size hail and provided a video that suggested hail up to half dollar size fell.

The far SE corner of the county experienced abnormally dry (D0) conditions, with the remainder of the county in Moderate (D1) drought conditions.

A general lack of rainfall and hot conditions allowed for Severe (D2) drought conditions to return to the eastern half of Starr County by the beginning of July. The remainder of the county continued to experience Moderate (D1) drought conditions.

Nearly all of Starr County was covered in Severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the first full week of July.  Only a tiny sliver of Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained along the far northern county border.   Drought conditions would hold steady through the remainder of the month.

Approximately 3.25 inches of rain fell near Lopeno in southern Zapata County. Zapata County Sheriff's Deputy reported 3 inches of water crossing US 83 near Lopeno. Nearby arroyos were also flowing but below bankfull and were still flowing at 7 am on August 13th.
CO-OP observer in Armstrong reported 5.12 inches of rainfall.
ASOS at McAllen Miller International Airport (KMFE) recorded 1.48 inches of rain in a little over an hour.
A trained spotter in Mission reported 1.5 inches of rain fell in 30 minutes.

Emergency manager reported two mobile homes with damage. One home had slid off the foundation and the second with part of roof torn off near the intersection of Mile 4 W and Mile 11 N road. Several tree limbs were knocked down onto power lines nearby along Mile 10 N road.
Severe (D2) drought conditions remained entrenched over most of Starr County, with the exception of a stripe of moderate (D1) drought conditions on the western and northern county borders.

Severe (D2) drought conditions remained over most of the western third of the county. The middle third of the county experienced moderate (D1) drought conditions and the eastern third remained abnormally dry (D0).

While far northern Kenedy County received between half to an inch of rain, the rest of the county was not as lucky.  Severe (D2) drought edged into the far SW corner of the county, while much of remainder of the county experienced moderate (D1) drought conditions. Abnormally dry conditions continued across the NW and SE corners of the county.

Little rain fell during the first week of August across Hidalgo County allowing drought conditions to worsen. Severe (D2) drought spread further north and east across Hidalgo County, with the western third of the county in Severe (D2) drought, the middle third of the county in moderate (D1) drought and the eastern third of the county abnormally dry (D0).  Beneficial rain during the second week of the month didn���t improve drought conditions, rather drought conditions held steady.

Beneficial rain fell across northern and eastern Brooks County during the first week of August. While this did not improve drought conditions across these areas, drought conditions did hold steady, with the much of the northern half of the county abnormally dry (D0).  Further south though, where less rain fell, severe (D2) drought conditions spread along the southern edge of the county.   Occasional rain during the remainder of the month allowed drought conditions to hold steady through the end of the month.

Periods of moderate to heavy rainfall fell across northern Jim Hogg County during the first week of the month. While the rainfall was beneficial it did not improve drought conditions where it fell, rather it allowed them to hold steady.  The northern quarter of the county remained drought free and the quarter below that remained abnormally dry (D0).  Less rain fell across the southern half of the county.  Severe (D2) drought conditions spread over the far SE corner of the county, while the remainder of the southern half of the county stayed in moderate (D1) drought conditions.

Spotty rain fell across Starr County during the first week of the month, but it did little to improve drought conditions. Severe (D2) drought spread further north and east across Starr County. The eastern three quarters of the county were engulfed in severe (D2) drought, while the other quarter held onto moderate (D1) drought conditions.

Although rain fell earlier in the month across portions of Kenedy County, little rain fell during the middle of the month and drought conditions worsened. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed over coastal Kenedy County, splitting the eastern half of the county between extreme (D3) drought conditions and severe (D2) drought conditions. Severe (D2) drought remained in the far SW corner of the county, while much of the remainder of the county continued to experience moderate (D1) drought conditions, with only the far NW corner of the county remaining abnormally dry (D0).

Little rain over coastal Cameron County through the month allowed drought conditions to worsen. The entirety of coastal Cameron County slide into severe (D2) drought conditions by the middle of the month.

The effects of rain earlier in August began to be felt across the western third of Starr County as drought conditions improved slightly from severe (D2) drought conditions to moderate (D1) drought conditions.  The remainder of the county remained entrenched in Severe (D2) drought conditions.

While periods of moderate to heavy rainfall fell during the last few days of the month, the effects would not be seen during the month of August.  The general lack of rainfall during the middle of the month allowed drought conditions to intensify across central Kenedy County as severe (D2) drought conditions spread further east and moderate (D1) drought conditions spread further north and eliminated the abnormally dry (D0) area in the far NW corner of the county.  Moderate (D1) drought conditions remained along the southern country border and extreme (D3) drought conditions remained across coastal Kenedy County.

While periods of moderate to heavy rainfall fell during the last few days of the month, the effects would not be felt during the month of August.  Severe (D2) drought conditions spread further east, fully encompassing the western half of the county, while moderate (D1) drought conditions increased in coverage taking over much of the eastern half of the county, with only a small sliver of abnormally dry (D0) conditions remaining on the eastern country border.

Little rainfall during the latter half of the month began to take its toll on drought conditions in Zapata County. A sliver of Severe (D2) drought conditions returned to the southeastern corner of the county. The remaining southern third of the county continued in moderate (D1) drought conditions, with the middle third continued to experience abnormally dry (D0) conditions.

Showers and thunderstorms associated with the seabreeze brought periods of rainfall to inland Kenedy County, little rain fell along the coast.  The rainfall maintained drought conditions where it fell.  Severe (D2) drought remained in the far SW corner of the county, with much of the remainder of the county in moderate (D1) drought conditions.  Severe (D2) drought conditions developed along the coast, where no rain fell.

Showers and thunderstorms associated with the seabreeze brought periods of rainfall to portions of Jim Hogg County.  This rainfall was beneficial but did not improve drought conditions. Rather drought conditions held steady where the rain fell.  Severe (D2) drought conditions spread over the far SW corner of the county to encompass a strip along the southern county border, while the remainder of the southern half of the county stayed in moderate (D1) drought conditions. The northern half of the county was split between no drought across the northern quarter of the county and abnormally dry (D0) conditions the second quarter.

Rainfall from spotty shower and thunderstorms did little to improve drought conditions. Severe (D2) drought conditions spread further west across Starr County engulfing almost the entirety of the county. The only remaining vestige of moderate (D1) drought conditions was in the far SW corner of the county.

Severe (D2) drought conditions spread across much of southern Zapata County by the middle of the month, despite rainfall earlier in the month. A stripe of moderate (D1) drought conditions surrounded the severe (D2) conditions and wrapped up the southern half of the county. The severe (D2) drought conditions were short lived and were replaced by moderate (D1) drought conditions by the 21st of August.
Dime to penny size hail was reported between Donna and Alamo.
Two poorly constructed mobile homes were destroyed. One home had the roof removed and walls were collapsed.
A large tree was uprooted.
Hidalgo County Sheriff's office reported several spots of trees and power lines down in and around Donna, Alamo, and San Juan.
A tree fell on a church near Lopezville and a mobile home had a roof overhang removed.
A tree, 8 inches in diameter, was uprooted in Pharr near the intersection of W. Bell and Dahlia, just south of Expressway 83 (IH-2).

Drought conditions improved across Kenedy County during the first week of September thanks to beneficial rainfall at the end of August.  Extreme (D3) drought conditions were eliminated from the county and replaced by severe (D2) drought conditions. The area covered by severe (D2) drought conditions shrank greatly, with only the far SW corner of the county and coastal portions of the county impacted.  Much of the remainder of the county was covered by moderate (D1) drought conditions, with a sliver of abnormally dry (D0) conditions across the far SE corner of the county. Rainfall during the first few days of September would allow drought conditions to improve with severe (D2) drought conditions eliminated by the 9th of the month.

Drought conditions improved across coastal Cameron County during the first week of September as the effects of beneficial rain at the end of August began to be felt.  Severe (D2) drought conditions were eliminated from the coastal Cameron County and replaced by moderate (D1) drought conditions.

While rain fell across Hidalgo County during the last few days of August, it was only enough to keep drought conditions from worsening during the first week of September. Severe (D2) drought conditions remained entrenched across the western half of Hidalgo County, while the most of the eastern half of the county continued to experienced moderate (D1) drought conditions, with a small sliver of abnormally dry (D0) conditions on the eastern county border. Rainfall during the first few days of September would allow drought conditions to improve with severe (D2) drought conditions eliminated by the 9th of the month.

While rain fell across Brooks County during the last few days of August, it was only enough to keep drought conditions from worsening during the first week of September. Severe (D2) drought conditions lingered along the southern border, while abnormally dry (D0) conditions continued across the NW corner of the county. The remainder of the county continued to experience moderate (D1) drought conditions. Rainfall during the first few days of September would allow drought conditions to improve with severe (D2) drought conditions eliminated by the 9th of the month.

Rainfall across Jim Hogg County the last few days of August was beneficial, but was not enough to improve drought conditions. Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across the southern third of the county, while moderate (D1) drought conditions encompassed the middle third and abnormally dry (D0) conditions covered the northern third of the county.

Rainfall across Starr County the last few days of August was beneficial, but was not enough to improve drought conditions. Severe (D2) drought conditions remained entrenched across the vast majority of Starr County. Moderate (D1) drought conditions covered the SW corner of the county.

Although rain fell across Zapata County the last few days of August, it was not enough to improve drought conditions. A sliver of severe (D2) drought remained along the SE corner of the county. The remainder of the eastern third of the county was covered by moderate (D1) drought conditions, while the rest of the county experienced abnormally dry (D0) conditions.  Rainfall during the first few weeks of September allowed drought conditions to improve and by the 16th of the month, all severe (D2) drought conditions were eliminated from the county.

Some rain fell during the first week of September, but it was not enough to allow drought conditions to improve across Starr County and a large area across northwestern and central Starr County remained in severe (D2) drought conditions through the first couple of weeks of September. The remainder of the county continued to experience moderate (D0) drought conditions. Significant rainfall on the 12th and 13th of the month would allow drought conditions to improve and by the 16th of the month, all severe (D2) drought conditions were eliminated from the county.

Although some rain fell during the first week of September, it was not enough for drought conditions to improve across Jim Hogg County during the first couple of weeks of September. A stripe of severe (D2) drought conditions remained across southern Jim Hogg County. Much of the county continued to experience moderate (D1) drought conditions, with the portions along the northern county border experiencing only abnormally dry (D0) conditions.  Significant rainfall on the 12th and 13th of the month would allow drought conditions to improve by the 16th of the month, all severe (D2) drought conditions were eliminated from the county.

The flooding included several roads with at least two feet of water across in poor drainage locations and where drainage ditches and canals were filled above capacity. Some resacas filled to bank full; running trails and playgrounds located some of them were covered in water during the peak of the flooding. The high waters forced road closures into the night, and several vehicles became stranded.

Generally less than 2 feet of water flooded typically poor drainage roads in the area during and just after the peak of the heavy rains.  In total, the band produced 2 to 3 inches of rain in a roughly 3 hour period.

The Arroyo Roma was reportedly in minor flood (bank full) after slow moving thunderstorms likely produced sufficient runoff into the waterway near Roma during the late morning and early afternoon of September 16th. Rainfall amounts in the area were unknown.

Microburst winds of 70 to 80 mph caused a large swath of damage across the Weslaco area. A newly constructed metal building had awning lifted, which helped tear off the front wall, the garage door was also blown in. Numerous softwood trees were blown down, some of which landed on homes, there were also numerous broken tree branches, power poles and lines were down as well. A survey team revealed peak winds ranging from 74 to 86 mph for the Los Coyotes Tornado. The 86 mph winds were measured by a property owner���s weather station, whose information was considered viable based on visual evidence of damage and radar depiction of velocity in the core of the circulation, which exceeded 60 knots (70 mph). Damage in Los Coyotes was to a few barns and outbuildings, as well as uprooted and snapped trees. Emergency Management noted seven power poles were leaning or down, but had been repaired by the time to survey was conducted on October 31.

The survey team estimated peak winds between 70 and 75 mph for the Willamar tornado. Primary damage was a cotton seed container/holder that was lifted from moorings into concrete block. The lack of material in the metal container allowed winds to get underneath and lift; pressures on the minimally anchored columns caused the damage. Other damage included a portion of roof peeled back from a mobile home, where a 12 year old child was injured by flying debris and taken to a local hospital in Harlingen for observation. The tin roof damage revealed poor connections to rotted wood. Minor damage to trees along Farm to Market Road 1420 was also noted.

Heavy and persistent rain fell across the City of Brownsville, mainly from downtown east towards the Port of Brownsville, and including all of the neighborhoods in Southmost, which took the brunt of the heavy rainfall. Four to seven inches of rain fell, with highest totals in the more densely populated sections of town where poor drainage is more of an issue as well. The heaviest rainfall, four to six inches, fell in a two to three hour window and flooding rapidly ensued, transitioning from nuisance to more life���threatening in less than an hour. Within an hour feet of water were inundating some roads and by three hours later up to 5 feet of water covered one of the most prone areas of town ��� the Four Corners area where State Road 4 (International Blvd.) intersects State Road 48 (Boca Chica Blvd./Padre Island Highway). Neighborhood roads in Southmost were inundated with two to three feet of water, and dozens of homes and businesses flooded due to a combination of high water that filtered into homes and vehicles that created waves of water which surged into them. At Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport, the 6.55 inches of rainfall was reported.

The downburst winds tore the roof and at least one wall from a poorly constructed trailer at a colonia of Pueblo de Palmas, east of La Joya. In Alton, winds downed two trees, one of which fell onto a recreational vehicle. Five to seven power poles were downed or snapped in the same area. At the peak of the storm, nearly 9,000 AEP customers in western Hidalgo County were without power.

After hours of rainfall the nuisance flooding became a flash flood. Several inches to at least a foot of water rose into homes in the Las Brisas subdivision on the east side of town, with three to five feet of water on neighborhood streets. At least three feet of water submerged vehicles along the frontage roads between the Westgate and Airport Road exits during the peak of the flash flooding. Additional high water closed portions of FM 1015 between Weslaco and Progresso (which also had flash flooding of unknown depth)and FM 493 near Donna. At least 26 separate boat rescues were made in flooded neighborhoods and more than 500 homes were impacted by some level of floodwater.

The estimated and measured ten to twelve plus inches of rain that fell in the Weslaco and Progresso area was far too much for drainage systems to handle, and even well after the rainfall stopped, numerous neighborhoods remained flooded and roads remained closed through the 26th.  Please see flash flood event for damage estimates.

Though homes are few and far between (mainly farm houses or workers homes), the majority likely had water inside them by late in the day. Hazardous, high water was found across nearly all of the County east of the expressway (and the larger communities).

Initial damage to tree limbs and some poorly built roofs in the Mission/Palmview area would intensify by the time the downburst reached the Madero and Granjeno communities, where more than 100 homes sustained varying levels of damage, dozens of power poles were felled, and hundreds of softwood trees were uprooted. Specific damage and associated impacts included the following: At least 150 homes and businesses sustained notable damage, and several dozen required significant repair. This included varied damage to nearly every building (RV, trailer, and fixed structure) in the Chimney Park RV and Mobile Home Park along the Rio Grande, as well as the adjacent neighborhood of Madero. The State Farm Arena lost a large part of its cladding (side wall) and up to 40% of its roof shingles and underneath decking allowing rainwater to leak into the facility. A several thousand foot community center in the town of Granejo was destroyed as free-standing reinforced cinderblock walls crumbled, and the wind destroyed ductwork/HVAC and an entire side wall on its way out of the building. A tractor trailer weighing 79,000 pounds, including freight, was moved and then tipped on its side in the community of Madero. Hundreds of softwood trees were uprooted and thousands of tree limbs were snapped, these included ash, mesquite, ebony, and palm. Dozens of wooden power poles were snapped, with more than 20,000 customers without power.

events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020 (LLNR 1330, Corpus Christi, TX 60 NM SSE) recorded moderate tropical storm force winds with at least one gust to hurricane force (64 knots).  The strong winds unmoored the buoy, which remained adrift into the autumn and eventually stopped recording completely in mid October.  The extent of the damage was unknown as of this writing.  A Texas A&M experimental research buoy, located very near or within the core eyewall, went offline prior to the arrival of the strongest winds whose value could only be estimated to be sustained hurricane force.  Damage to this buoy (56 nm east of the  northeast Kenedy County coast) was unknown as of this writing.

Tropical storm force sustained winds (39 to 51 mph with gusts to 63 mph) arrived along and up to 10 to 15 miles (estimated) from the shoreline of Kenedy County during the afternoon of August 25, and likely continued across the north half of this area through sunset or just beyond as Hurricane Harvey scooted by some 80 (south) to 60 (north) miles of the shoreline. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) sites at Rincon del San Jose and Baffin Bay - shoreline proxies to the coastline, reported sustained winds of 39 mph and 51 mph, respectively, with gusts to 47 and 63 mph, respectively.  No wind damage was reported over the largely unpopulated region.||While a storm surge estimated at up to 2 feet run up to and into the dunes along the barrier island, there were no indications from aerial photography of any new breaches or significant flooding or erosion.

Tennis ball sized hail was reported in the Los Villareales section of Rio Grande City, and Golfball sized hail at two nearby locations, by the public and local Sheriff's Office, between Midway Road and Hospital Drive, and along US 83 and FM 3167, all just a few miles east of Los Villareales in the west portion of Rio Grande City between 705 and 715 PM CDT.

Zapata County EM and US Customs and Border Protection reported high water out of the normal banks but within the berm area in and around San Ygnacio mainly on September 28th as a flood wave pushed south from Laredo toward Falcon International Reservoir. The high waters damaged U.S. Border Patrol equipment, including at least one generator, two light poles and one or two submerged vehicles. However, higher ground in San Ygnacio proper and above the river area was not impacted.  Visual evidence showed the high water surrounding the equipment during the morning through afternoon hours, though high waters likely continued through the 29th.

Several thunderstorms crossed southern Hidalgo County during the afternoon of October 10, 2017.  The most persistent band affected the McAllen/Metro area between 130 and 3 PM CST, dropping several inches of rain and resulting in numerous road closures due to high water from the west side of town (Nolana and 23rd to 29th Street) to the south side of town (10th and Wichita, just east of Miller Airport).  For the day, 5.07 inches of rain fell at Miller Airport, more than double the monthly average.  Additional heavy rainfall of 3.5 inches fell in La Joya and 3.79 inches in nearby Mission to the west.  Local minor flooding may have also occurred in these areas, but reports were unavailable as of this writing.

Bands of heavy rainfall associated with repeating thunderstorms eventually were too much for local drainage systems to handle in the south part of Weslaco to the north part of Progresso.  Bias corrected radar estimates of more than 5 inches of rain likely contributed to street flooding in the Quail Hollow neighborhood in south Weslaco, where 2 feet of standing water backed up and allowed minimal passage of vehicles through the neighborhood.  Water failed to flow through a nearby drain, worsening the situation.

Severe (D2) Drought returned to central Jim Hogg County on October 31, a result of prolonged hot and dry weather, with monthly rainfall just 10 to 25 percent of average (estimated at 0.25 to 0.75 inches having fallen) through the month, and following a relatively dry September and hot and dry summer.

Severe (D2) Drought Conditions persisted through mid November in south central Jim Hogg County.  A batch of showers and thunderstorms on November 11th would temporarily improve the conditions by the issuance of the November 14th, 2017 Drought Monitor.

Severe (D2) Drought returned to southern Jim Hogg County toward the end of November, following a two-week period with little to no rainfall, as well as a four days with afternoon humidity that fell to or below 25%, between the 18th and 25th.

Emergency management, social media, and other contacts reported between 2 and 3 inches of wet snow across most of Zapata County, with the heaviest amounts falling from the Rio Grande near Falcon, northeast across ranchlands along the Starr and Jim Hogg County line (south third of the county). The snow, falling overnight, created slushy accumulation along elevated bridges, including US 83, where there was at least one accident involving a sliding car and school bus (no injuries or deaths).

At least one ranch owner near Agua Nueva, as well as occasional reports from Jim Hogg County dispatch - with data blended from satellite observations, found snowfall ranging from around 0.5 near Hebbronville (close to the Duval County line) ranging to more than 4 inches across the southern third of the county. From radar estimates, the heaviest snow fell between 1 and 4 AM and again between 5 and 7 AM. In general, between 2 and 5 inches fell across the primary ranch areas with the least amount of snow near Hebbronville.  The snow, falling overnight, created slushy accumulation along elevated bridges and an inch or more on unimproved ranch roads.

Multiple snow bands between the pre-dawn hours and mid morning dropped  1 to 3 inches of snow across most of Starr County early on the 8th. Much of the heavier snow across the northwest half of the county fell between 1 and 4 AM, with more widespread coverage between 7 and 9 AM favoring the northeast portion of the county. A Rio Grande City Fire and Rescue worker, also a ranch owner, reported 2 inches near Santa Elena; another ranch owner reported 1.5 inches near El Sauz. Elevation may have made some difference in accumulation, as locations along the Rio Grande reported less snow, in some cases below heavy snow criteria (<1 inch).

A single moderate to heavy snow band between midnight and 3 AM, followed by lighter snows during the post-daybreak hours, dropped a whopping 3 to 6 inches of heavy wet snow across the northern half of Brooks County, with an estimated 2 to 3 inches across the southern half based on satellite, radar, and proxy observations on the King Ranch in neighboring western Kenedy County.  A fair measurement of 5.5 inches was received just southwest of Falfurrias, with 4.8 inches nearby. The snow, which fell at a rate of 1 to 2 inches per hour during the post midnight period, covered untreated rural roads with up to 3 inches of snow around the Falfurrias area. The snow also covered the US 281 bypass around Falfurrias, slowed traffic, and caused at least one tractor trailer to jackknife.  No injuries or fatalities were reported.

A single moderate to heavy snow band developed across the Kenedy County King Ranch around daybreak on December 8th, continuing in waves until 1030 AM before precipitation ended.  Cooperative observers 7 miles east of Sarita and 4 miles southeast of Armstrong (northern and central portions of the county) reported 2 inches each. County-wide, proxy data from Brooks and Willacy County suggested fairly widespread 2 inch totals, with the exception of the northwest corner between Sarita and Falfurrias, where 3 inches may have fallen. It was unknown whether slush accumulated on the elevated portion of US 77 around Sarita.

While several moderate to locally heavy snow bands persisted through the ranchlands of Brooks, Jim Hogg, Starr, and Zapata County, snow arrived late (mainly after sunrise) in most of Hidalgo County after periods of light rain overnight.  A sliver of the Brooks/Starr/Jim Hogg band covered the northern fifth of Hidalgo, where 2 inches likely accumulated.  Elsewhere, mainly from Alton to Edinburg and Elsa-Edcouch, around an inch fell in a fairly short period of time (8 AM to 1030 AM) with accumulation primarily on grassy surfaces and trees as surface temperatures largely remained above freezing -| and daylight was able to melt some of the snow on contact. There were no known reports of significant accidents from slick roads due to the snow.

While several moderate to locally heavy snow bands persisted through the ranchlands of Brooks, Jim Hogg, Starr, and Zapata County, snow arrived late (mainly after sunrise) in most of Willacy County after periods of light rain overnight.  Several reports of 1 inch of snow was reported across the northern half of the county, including the most populated city of Raymondville.  At one point between 9 and 10 AM, SR 186 west of Raymondville was covered with a coating of slush during the heaviest band. There were no known significant accidents despite the quick coating.

While several moderate to locally heavy snow bands persisted through the ranchlands of Brooks, Jim Hogg, Starr, and Zapata County, snow arrived late (mainly after sunrise) in coastal Willacy County after periods of light rain overnight.  A report of 1 inch of snow was reported across the northern coastal area, in Port Mansfield.

Light rain changed to snow latest in Cameron County, Texas, on December 8.  By 9 AM, light snow was falling across the county, with a small area of 1 inch accumulating over and north of Harlingen by 11 AM. Two thin bands of snow affected the county; the first band across the northern half between 8 and 10 AM, and a second across the southern half between 10 and 1230 PM.  Heaviest accumulations on grassy areas occurred during the early morning hours, but the official report at the NWS office in Brownsville (east side of the city) of 0.25 of snow occurred around noon during a short-lived band of moderate snow.

Severe (D2) Drought continued in central Jim Hogg through the December 12th Drought Monitor issuance, which followed a period of rainfall (December 7) and several inches of snow (December 8) that dropped a 7 day total of six times average.  Additional rains of more than an inch total fell on December 14 and 15, wiping out all traces of short and medium term drought.

Locally heavy wet snow falling at brief hourly rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour dropped temperatures to 32 degrees across much of Brooks County during the early morning of December 8th. Proxy observations included Linn/San Manuel (32 degrees) and both Armstrong (30 degrees) and Sarita (31 degrees) made the case for the winter of 2017/2018's first light freeze.

After rain changed to snow just before daybreak on December 8th, temperatures fell to or just below 32 degrees for several hours during the morning. Observations included both Armstrong (30 degrees) and Sarita (31 degrees), making the case for the winter of 2017/2018's first light freeze.

After rain changed to snow shortly before midnight on December 8th, temperatures fell to or just below 32 degrees soon after, as moderate to locally heavy snow dropped between 2 and 5 inches on most of the county. Temperatures remained there through an hour or two after daybreak, just after the snow tapered off. Hebbronville fell to 32 degrees at 135 AM and remained there until 815 AM.

After rain changed to snow shortly after midnight on December 8th, temperatures fell to or just below 32 degrees not to long after, as rain and snow developed across the south half of the county and moderate snow redeveloped across most of the county a few hours later.  Temperatures remained there until around daybreak. At Zapata County Airport, temperatures fell to 32 degrees at 335 AM and remained there until 655 AM.

Temperatures are assumed to have fallen to 32 degrees shortly before daybreak on December 8th as moderate snow developed over ranch country, and continued to fall steadily in bands until around 9 AM before tapering off, allowing temperatures to rise back above freezing. The Rio Grande City cooperative site carried a low temperature of 30 degrees at some point during the morning of the 8th.

US Border Patrol reported the death of an undocumented immigrant near Falfurrias, TX, during the afternoon of December 7, due to hypothermia, as indicated by medical staff who discovered the body. The sharp change of the season's first significant cold front after a record-shattering warm January through November likely contributed to the death by lack of acclimation.  Just two days earlier, temperatures had been in the mid 80s; on the 7th, wind chills in the lower 30s were too much for migrants with limited clothing and shelter.

US Border Patrol reported the death of two undocumented immigrants on the King Ranch in Kenedy County, TX, during the afternoon of December 7, due to hypothermia, as indicated by medical staff who discovered the bodies.  One death was to a 28 year old man who literally gave the clothes off his back to provide warmth for children. Two other migrant workers were given treatment for hypothermia and sent to regional hospitals. The sharp change of the season's first significant cold front after a record-shattering warm January through November likely contributed to the death by lack of acclimation.  Just two days earlier, temperatures had been in the mid 80s; on the 7th, wind chills in the lower 30s were too much for migrants with limited clothing and shelter.

US Border Patrol reported the death of one undocumented immigrant near the City of Hidalgo during the afternoon of December 7, due to hypothermia, as indicated by medical staff who discovered the bodies.  Border Patrol Search Trauma and Rescue (BORSTAR) agents and other medics from McAllen attempted to revive an unresponsive victim prior to rushing to a nearby hospital. Unfortunately, the victim was pronounced dead upon arrival at the hospital. The sharp change of the season's first significant cold front after a record-shattering warm January through November likely contributed to the death by lack of acclimation.  Just two days earlier, temperatures had been in the mid 80s; on the 7th, wind chills in the lower 30s were too much for migrants with limited clothing and shelter.
Cooperative observers 7 miles east of Sarita and 4 miles southeast of Armstrong recorded low temperatures of 32 and 31 degrees, respectively, for an estimated 2 hours early on New Year's Day 2018.

Temperatures fell steadily from the evening of December 31st through the morning of January 1st, reaching the freezing point (32) at Hebbronville/Jim Hogg County Airport a little after 230 AM, then falling further reaching 29 degrees just after 9 AM. Temperatures would fluctuate between 29 and 32 degrees through 10 AM on January 2nd. Light sleet and freezing drizzle joined the freezing temperatures at times between 230 and 1015 AM on the 1st, with minimal impact besides a light glaze on trees and grassy areas.

Temperatures fell steadily from the evening of December 31st through the morning of January 1st, reaching the freezing point (32) at Zapata County Airport just before 7 AM, and holding right around the freezing point through 1035 AM on January 2nd.  Light sleet and freezing drizzle joined the freezing temperatures at times between between 7 AM and 415 PM, most likely across the northern half of the county but with impact only to grassy areas and some brush.

After only rising a few degrees into the lower and mid 30s during the afternoon of New Year's Day, temperatures would bottom out once again overnight and during the early morning of January 2nd, reaching 31 degrees 7 miles east of Sarita, and 30 degrees 4 miles southeast of Armstrong.

After only rising a few degrees into the mid 30s during the afternoon of New Year's Day, temperatures would bottom out at or below 32 degrees in much of inland Willacy County early on January 2nd. Low temperatures fell to 30 degrees at Raymondville, and proxy observations in eastern Hidalgo and southern Kenedy County suggested nearly all of the county had 32 degree or lower temperatures for several hours. It was not known if light icing had occurred, which was the case in western Cameron and eastern Hidalgo County.

After only rising a few degrees into the mid and upper 30s during the afternoon of New Year's Day, temperatures would bottom out around 32 degrees across western Cameron County early on January 2nd. Low temperatures fell to 32 degrees in Harlingen, and there were several reports of light icing on trees and grasses with limited impact.  Temperatures would struggle to rise for a second day, reaching the upper 30s in most areas and setting the stage for another freezing morning on the 3rd.

After only rising a few degrees into the mid and upper 30s during the afternoon of New Year's Day, temperatures would bottom out around or just below 32 degrees across pocket of Hidalgo County, including all but the northern third and around urban McAllen, during the early morning of January 2nd. Weslaco/Mid Valley Airport fell to 31 degrees at around 830 AM; at this time, light freezing drizzle and perhaps some sleet resulted in a few reports of light icing on trees and grasses with limited impact.  Temperatures would struggle to rise for a second day, reaching the upper 30s in most areas and setting the stage for another freezing morning on the 3rd.

After only rising a few degrees into the low to mid 30s during the afternoon of New Year's Day, temperatures would bottom out around or just below 32 degrees across much of Starr County. Falcon Lake Mesowest would bottom out at 32 degrees shortly after 2 AM and continue at or near the freezing point through 730-8 AM. The cooperative observer in Rio Grande City recorded a minimum temperature of 30 degrees.  There did not appear to be any notable freezing precipitation in Starr on the 2nd, where drier air was present near the surface.

The cooperative observation station 3 miles west of Falfurrias recorded a low of 31 degrees toward daybreak on January 3rd. Based on proxy observations in western Kenedy County and northern Hidalgo County, low temperatures in some ranch areas likely dropped a bit lower.

The cooperative observation stations 7 miles east of Sarita and 4 miles southeast of Armstrong recorded minimum temperatures of 29 and 28 degrees, respectively, shortly after daybreak on January 3rd.  Kingsville Naval Air Station, about 22 miles north of Sarita, dipped to 26 degrees around 8 AM before the sun finally brought a relative warming trend. Times were estimated based on the Kingsville observations and those from northern Hidalgo County.

The cooperative observation station at Raymondville recorded a minimum temperature of 29 degrees shortly after daybreak on January 3rd.  Proxy observations at Port Mansfield (coastal Willacy, at 31 degrees) and San Manuel (northeast Hidalgo), as well as Armstrong, Kenedy County (28 degrees) made the case for all of the county to have reached 32 degrees or lower for at least two hours.

The mesowest/RAWS station at San Manuel dipped to 30 degrees around daybreak on January 3rd; Weslaco AWOS fell to 32 between midnight and 1230 AM, but other county sites (such as Edinburg AWOS) remained above freezing at that time. With the exception of the Rio Grande, county locations reached 32 degrees or slightly lower for a couple hours early on the 3rd, mainly between 6 and 8 AM.

The cooperative observation station at Rio Grande City fell to 30 degrees around or shortly after sunrise on January 3rd; the Mesowest/RAWS site at Falcon Lake touched 32 degrees. Proxy stations at Zapata County Airport and Hebbronville/Jim Hogg County suggest ranch communities in central and northern Starr County fell to around or just below freezing for several hours before and just after sunrise.||mesowest/RAWS station at San Manuel dipped to 30 degrees around daybreak on January 3rd; Weslaco AWOS fell to 32 between midnight and 1230 AM, but other county sites (such as Edinburg AWOS) remained above freezing at that time. With the exception of the Rio Grande, county locations reached 32 degrees or slightly lower for a couple hours early on the 3rd, mainly between 6 and 8 AM.

The AWOS station at Jim Hogg County Airport, as well as the nearby Mesowest site at the same location (4 miles northwest of Hebbronville) recorded another prolonged freeze that began a couple hours after sunset on the 2nd and continue until a couple hours after sunrise on the 3rd. Low temperatures bottomed out at 27 degrees, with proxy data farther south suggesting upper 20s to around 30 for minimum values. Duration of freezing temperatures likely ranged from 4 to 12 hours, with longest duration across the northern tier where the density of population is largest.

The AWOS station at Zapata County Airport dipped to 32 for six hours between 3 and 9 AM on the 3rd. Based on proxy observations in Jim Hogg County, eastern sections of  Zapata may have fallen a degree or two lower.

The AWOS at Falfurrias recorded a low temperature of 31 degrees.  However, wind protected ranchlands south and southwest likely fell into the mid and upper 20s, based on proxy observations from Kenedy, nothern Hidalgo, and western Willacy County. While frost was not recorded specifically, wind protected locations may have received some due to the clear, calm conditions that followed several days of cloudy and chilly conditions.

The cooperative observer 7 miles east of Sarita recorded 23 degrees, their coldest temperatures since January 7 and 8 (26 and 27) 2017 under clear skies and calm winds. Other nearby observations included 26 in Kingsville and San Manuel (northeast Hidalgo), and 28 in Raymondville. Duration of subfreezing temperatures is estimated from proxy observations at the RAWS/Mesowest location in San Manuel, adjusted to include both wind and non-wind protected locations.

The cooperative observer in Raymondville recorded a low temperature of 28 degrees.  Temperatures across the county were likely in the upper 20s, based on proxy observations at Linn/San Manuel RAWS (26) and Harlingen/Valley Int'l Airport ASOS (30). Duration of event was a blend between the colder ranching communities and slightly warmer farming communities closer to the more populated Lower Valley.

The cooperative observer in Port Mansfield recorded a low temperature of 32 degrees under clear and mainly calm conditions.  Temperatures in other nearby locations may have fallen a degree or two lower based on an observation from the RAWS/Mesowest site at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge in northeast Cameron County.

The RAWS/Mesowest location at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge fell to 29 degrees, and Bayview/Cameron County Airport fell to 31 degrees, under clear and calm conditions early on January 4th. cooperative observer in Port Mansfield recorded a low temperature of 32 degrees under clear and mainly calm conditions.  These were the coldest temperatures along the Lower Texas coast since January 7, 2017 - nearly one year earlier.

The ASOS at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport fell to 31 degrees early on the 4th, the coldest temperature recorded there since nearly a year ago (January 7, 2017, also 31 degrees).  Harlingen/Valley International Airport fell to 30 degrees, and a few locations may have touched into the upper 20s.  Light frost was fairly widespread across the county. Impact to agriculture from this particular day was unknown; multiple cold days in a row followed by another long-duration but minor freeze less than two weeks later may have aggregated the damage.

Most of Hidalgo County fell to or below freezing early on January 4th, with the sole exception of the City of McAllen. Across the ranch and farming communities north of the populated areas, temperatures fell into the mid and upper 20s, as did wind-protected Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge on the Rio Grande near Pharr (23 degrees). Weslaco and Edinburg fell to 32.  In general for the county, about 4 hours of freezing temperatures were observed under clear and calm conditions.

Minimum temperatures at Rio Grande City and Falcon Lake RAWS fell to 27 and 26 degrees respectively, the coldest since the same readings were recorded nearly a year earlier (January 8, 2017).  By proxy, much of Starr County likely fell to the upper 20s based on observations from Zapata to Jim Hogg and western Hidalgo County. Clear, calm  conditions aided the steady drop in temperatures after sunset on the 3rd.

Minimum temperatures at Zapata County Airport fell to 26 degrees, as did the low at Falcon Lake RAWS, just inside Starr County south of the Zapata/Starr County line. Based on observations in Starr County, low temperatures likely fell into the mid and upper 20s county-wide under clear and calm conditions.

Minimum temperatures at Jim Hogg County Airport 4 miles northwest of Hebbronville reached 30 degrees early on January 4th, but a pocket of mid to upper 20s temperatures likely was observed across most ranch areas based on proxy observations in Hidalgo, Starr, and Zapata County. Clear, calm conditions led to the coldest readings since January 8, 2017.

Temperatures fell to the freezing point around noon on January 16th, and dropped into the upper 20s by late afternoon then held through the night into the mid morning of the 17th before a slow rise above freezing with very low dew point temperatures (single numbers).  The cooperative location 3 miles west of Falfurrias fell to 27 overnight and early morning of the 17th. Duration of freezing temperatures ranged from 10 to more than 20 hours, with longest duration estimated to be in western portions of the county. |This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of rangelands for the remainder of winter.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.||Wind chill temperature fell into the upper teens during the peak of the combination of strong north wind and low temperatures during the afternoon and evening of the 16th.

Temperatures fell to the freezing point around noon on January 16th, and dropped into the upper 20s by late afternoon then held through the night into the mid morning of the 17th before a slow rise above freezing with very low dew point temperatures (single numbers).  The cooperative location 4 miles southeast of Armstrong fell to 25 by early morning of the 17th. Duration of freezing temperatures ranged from 10 to more than 20 hours, with the longest duration across the northern and eastern parts of the county. This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of range lands on the King Ranch for the next few weeks, before some helpful rains arrived in early to mid February.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.||Wind chill temperature fell into the upper teens during the peak of the combination of strong north wind and low temperatures during the afternoon and evening of the 16th.

Temperatures fell to the freezing point around 1 pm January 16th, and likely dropped into the upper 20s by late afternoon then held through the night into the mid morning of the 17th before a slow rise above freezing with very low dew point temperatures (single numbers).  The cooperative location at San Manuel fell to 29 by early morning of the 17th. Duration of freezing temperatures generally ranged from 15 to 19 hours. This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of range land for the next few weeks, with unknown pre-growing season damage to any crop land, before some helpful rains arrived in early to mid February.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.||Wind chill temperature fell into the mid to upper teens during the peak of the combination of strong north wind and low temperatures during the afternoon and evening of the 16th.

Temperatures fell to the freezing point around 4 pm January 16th, and dropped into the upper 20s early in the evening and held through the night into the mid morning of the 17th before a slow rise above freezing with relatively low dew point temperatures (teens, mostly).  Duration of freezing temperatures ranged from 12 to 18 hours. Brownsville/South Padre International Airport even dipped to 30 degrees for several hours overnight. This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of local farmland and impacts on tender tropical or subtropical vegetation for the next few weeks, with unknown pre-growing season damage to any crop land, before some helpful rains arrived in early to mid February.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.||Wind chill temperature fell into the mid to upper teens during the peak of the combination of strong north wind and low temperatures during the afternoon and overnight of the 16th into the pre-dawn hours of the 17th.

Temperatures fell to the freezing point around 4 pm January 16th, and dropped into the upper 20s to lower 30s early in the evening and held through the night into the mid morning of the 17th before a slow rise above freezing with relatively low dew point temperatures (teens to lower 20s, mostly).  The RAWS site at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge bottomed out at 28 degrees during the evening of the 16th. Duration of freezing temperatures varied widely, ranging from nearly 18 hours on the west side of Laguna Madre to less than 10 hours toward the beach, influenced by the relatively warm Bay and Gulf.||Wind chill temperature fell into the mid  teens during the peak of the combination of strong north wind, gusting to or above 30 mph, combined with low temperatures during the afternoon and overnight of the 16th into the pre-dawn hours of the 17th. There were likely some impacts to wildlife and some tropical vegetation at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge, but details were not known as of this writing.  There may have been additional cold stunning of Kemp's Ridley sea turtles in Laguna Madre Bay, but these details were also not known.

Temperatures fell to the freezing point around 3 pm January 16th based on proxy observations at nearby locations, and dropped into the upper 20s to lower 30s early in the evening and held through the night into the mid morning of the 17th before a slow rise above freezing with relatively low dew point temperatures (teens to lower 20s, mostly).  The RAWS site at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge bottomed out at 28 degrees during the evening of the 16th.  Duration of freezing temperatures ranged from 15 to nearly 20 hours.||Wind chill temperature fell into the mid to upper teens during the peak of the combination of strong north wind, likely gusting near 30 mph, combined with the  lowest temperatures during the afternoon and overnight of the 16th into the pre-dawn hours of the 17th.

Temperatures fell to the upper 20s to lower 30s across all of Hidalgo County during the mid to late afternoon of January 16th, and continued in similar ranges overnight before rising to the freezing during the mid to late morning and easing above 32 before noon. All locations, including downtown McAllen, fell below 32. Duration of freezing temperatures ranged from more than 20 hours in Weslaco to just two hours in McAllen (due to heat island concerns). Much of eastern and northern Hidalgo had 15 to 21 hours of freezing temperatures.||Lowest wind chill values ranged from the upper teens in breezier areas across the east half of the county to the low and mid 20s elsewhere.  This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of local farmland and impacts on tender tropical or subtropical vegetation for the next few weeks, with unknown pre-growing season damage to any crop land.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.

Temperatures fell to the upper 20s to around 30 across most of Starr County during the early to mid afternoon of January 16th, and continued in similar ranges overnight before rising to the freezing point during the mid to late morning and easing above 32 before noon. Durations of freezing temperatures varied from more than 20 hours across the northern third of the county in the ranches, to less than 10 hours along the Rio Grande. The coldest temperature was 29 at Rio Grande City, though some ranches may have dipped slightly lower near the Jim Hogg County line.||This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of grazing/range land and any cropland.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.

Temperatures fell to the upper 20s to lower 30s across most of Zapata County during the early to mid afternoon of January 16th, and continued in similar ranges overnight before rising to the freezing point toward or just after noon (depending on location). Durations of freezing temperatures varied from up to 24 hours across the eastern third of the county in the ranches, to less than 10 hours along the Rio Grande. The coldest temperature was 32 at Zapata County Airport, though ranch locations likely dipped into the upper 20s near the Jim Hogg County line.||This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of grazing/range land.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.

Temperatures fell to around 30 near Hebbronville soon after sunrise on the 16th, then eased back into the upper 20s during the afternoon of the 16th, continuing through mid morning of the 17th before finally edging over 32 during the afternoon of the 17th.   Duration of freezing temperatures was highest in Jim Hogg County among all locations in Deep South Texas, ranging from 21 to 30 hours based on proxy observations.||This particular event, coming on the heels of four consecutive freezing-point mornings to begin the New Year, likely was the final straw in full freeze-curing of grazing/range land.  Livestock impacts were unknown as of this writing.

Glaze ice accreted to 1/8 to 1/16 inch on trees and grasses beginning during the late afternoon of January 16th and continuing through just prior to midnight before precipitation tapered off. Temperatures, which fell to between 28 and 30 degrees in a pocket from San Benito through La Feria and toward the Willacy County line, allowed untreated elevated road surfaces to quickly glaze over.  This resulted in dozens of mostly minor accidents along elevated portions of IH-2 and IH-69E during the peak and for a few hours after the evening commute.  The elevated interchange between these highways was closed through the morning commute after at least two tractor-trailer trucks slid and blocked access. Other elevated portions of these and other roads, including FM-511 and SR 550 (toll) were closed due to the glaze. ||Power outages in the county exceeded 22 thousand (most likely in Cameron County), though the source may have been related more to intense usage on an early weeknight during the peak of the winter school and work season than to glaze icing alone, since accretion was light.

Glaze ice accreted to 1/8 to 1/16 inch on trees and grasses beginning during the late afternoon of January 16th and continuing through just prior to midnight before precipitation tapered off over the eastern half of Hidalgo County. Conversational light snow during the mid to late afternoon near McAllen ended, with freezing drizzle/light freezing rain developing soon after including parts of the McAllen/Edinburg metro area. Temperatures, which fell to the upper 20s in a pocket from Donna through Mercedes and north toward Elsa/Edcouch and the Willacy County line, allowed untreated elevated road surfaces particularly on IH-2 to quickly glaze over.  This resulted in dozens of accidents along elevated portions of IH-2 and IH-69C at the end and for a few hours after the evening commute, including a 15-vehicle pile-up on westbound IH-2 in McAllen.  Several elevated roads were closed through the morning commute, including the heavily traveled IH-2 and IH-69C junction in Pharr. ||There were unknown injuries from the pile-up, as well as other accidents along IH-69C between Pharr and Edinburg.||Power outages in Cameron and Hidalgo County combined exceeded 22 thousand (most were in Cameron County), though the outage source may have been related more to intense usage on an early weeknight during the peak of the winter school and work season than to glaze icing alone, since accretion was light.

The Jim Hogg County Sheriff's Office in Hebbronville reported a glaze of ice on elevated surfaces on some power outages from freezing rain and some sleet falling at air temperatures below 32 degrees, around noon.  Minimal additional impacts were reported.

The Emergency Management Coordinator of Zapata County, Texas, reported several large limbs blown down near a house in the city of Zapata, and the canopy of a gas station along US 83 was flipped off its moorings, causing minor damage to vehicles underneath but no injuries.  Peak gusts were estimated at 50 mph; the nearby Zapata County Airport which is a bit wind-protected, reached 40 mph.

Peak gusts ranged generally from 39 to 54 mph (peak 11 north of Edinburg at the South Texas International Airport) during the mid evening of January 11. Numerous small structural fires and other small grass fires were reported by Edinburg Fire, and multiple power lines were reported downed in Mission from the same post-frontal surge of northwest winds.

A surge of strong winds behind the dry front late on January 11th produced peak gusts between 44 and 54 mph during the mid evening.  Peak gusts of 53 mph at Harlingen/Valley International Airport (903 PM CT) and 54 mph at Bayview/Cameron County Airport (739 PM) partially contributed to patchy minor damage, including a tree down in Combes; the gusty winds at Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport (50 mph at 840 PM) sparked a brief fire on the airport grounds when a transformer blew near Iowa Avenue.

Facebook reports relayed to the NWS office in Brownsville reported two large hail reports east of Rio Grande City: Golfball sized hail 4.6 miles east, near La Puerta, and half-dollar sized hail (1.25) 4 miles east southeast of Rio Grande City near Los Velas road.

events.event_narrative: Two men were rescued by the U.S. Coast Guard after their 21-foot fishing boat capsized (as reported by local TV media). One man showed signs of hypothermia, and the other was face-down with no pulse but revived with CPR. Both were airlifted to a local hospital. The exact cause of the capsize was unknown, though combined seas had built to nearly 8 feet with a swell period from the east of 9 seconds. Note: Time of the incident was estimated.

Weeks of little to no rainfall, leaving departures from monthly averages (January and February through mid March) at 10 to 25 percent of the 3 inch or so average for the period, resulted in a brief period of Severe (D2) Drought in northeastern Hidalgo County during the final 10 days of March. A band of heavier rainfall from late evening on the 28th through early morning of the 29th would improve conditions for the start of April.

A band of heavier rainfall from late evening on the 28th through early morning of the 29th would improve conditions for the start of April.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: The NOAA/CO-OPS station at Brazos Santiago, just inshore from the Boca Chica Jetty, recorded a peak gust of 43 knots, with nearly two consecutive hours of gale force gusts between 35 and 43 knots, as a line of strong thunderstorms crossed through the waters along a late season cold front.  Location of the event listed here is a proxy to Brazos Santiago just north of the jetty, based on historical analogs of similar events with similar gusts in northerly flow along and behind significant cold fronts.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) location at Rincon del San Jose within the Kenedy County portion of the Laguna Madre near the Land Cut recorded a peak gust of 40 knots at 330 AM April 14th, during a one-hour period of gale force gusts as a line of strong thunderstorms crossed through the waters along a late season cold front. The gusts likely extended along the entire Laguna Madre to connect with similar observations a bit later at Realitos Peninsula, along Laguna Madre just south of Arroyo Colorado.

The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) location at the Realitos Peninsula (near the mouth of the Arroyo Colorado) recorded a peak gust of 36 knots at 642 AM CST.
