events.event_narrative: The NOAA/CO-OPS station at Brazos Santiago, just inshore from the Boca Chica Jetty, recorded a peak gust of 43 knots at 548 AM, with nearly two consecutive hours of gale force gusts between 35 and 43 knots, as a line of strong thunderstorms crossed through the waters along a late season cold front. The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) location at the Realitos Peninsula (near the mouth of the Arroyo Colorado) recorded a peak gust of 38 knots, also at 548 AM CST.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020, approximately 35 nm east-northeast of Port Mansfield, recorded a peak 3 second gust of 37 knots just before 4 AM CST April 14, as a late season cold front arrived with a line of thunderstorms that stretched from the Lower Texas coast through the Gulf up to 60 nm east. |||Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) location at Rincon del San Jose within the Kenedy County portion of the Laguna Madre near the Land Cut recorded a peak gust of 40 knots at 330 AM April 14th, during a one-hour period of gale force gusts as a line of strong thunderstorms crossed through the waters along a late season cold front. The gusts likely extended along the entire Laguna Madre to connect with similar observations a bit later at Realitos Peninsula, along Laguna Madre just south of Arroyo Colorado.

A newspaper report from Starr County indicated a large restaurant sign blew onto a vehicle and caused an unknown amount of damage to the vehicle during the passage of a thunderstorm in Rio Grande City a little after 8 PM on April 25th.

Severe (D2) Drought continued in extreme southeastern Brooks County until the April 3rd Drought Monitor update, which included 0.5 to 1.5 inches of rain that fell late on March 28th and early on March 29th.  Improvement to Moderate (D1) drought levels began on the 3rd.

Severe (D2) Drought continued in northeastern Hidalgo County until the April 3rd Drought Monitor update, which included 0.5 to 1.5 inches of rain that fell late on March 28th and early on March 29th.  Improvement to Moderate (D1) drought levels began on the 3rd.

Severe (D2) Drought continued in extreme southwestern Kenedy County until the April 3rd Drought Monitor update, which included 0.5 to 1.5 inches of rain that fell late on March 28th and early on March 29th.  Improvement to Moderate (D1) drought levels began on the 3rd.

Local emergency management, fire departments, and the US Fish and Wildlife Service reported a 300 acre wildfire developed rapidly during the afternoon of March 7th, when embers from a sugar cane burn in northern Tamaulipas, Mexico, just south of the Rio Grande drifted into the refuge and began the process of torching brush and grass. The wildfire, aided by dry fuels, gusty east winds, and near critical relative humidity levels, continued for nearly 48 hours before being 100 percent contained.  The refuge was closed to public operations through the following weekend for safety precautions and continued clean-up activities.
A grass wildfire covering over 300 acres occurred January 31, 2008 near La Gloria Texas in Starr County. The fire was reported by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service.

Slow moving thunderstorm clusters dumped torrential rains over and near Rio Grande City during the early to mid evening of May 4th, with storm totals likely between 4 and 5 inches across the area.  A combination of reports from law enforcement, emergency management, and social media indicated dangerous flooding in parts of the city, with several water rescues and minor flooding reaching into several homes on the east side of town.  Social media photos and discussion reported a yard with 1 to 2 feet of water flowing through it at around 8 PM CST; water rescues from stranded vehicles were reported along US 83 on the east side of town at around 8:55 PM CST, and another vehicle was reported stranded in floodwaters at the intersection of Flores and Monroe Street, also on the east side of town.  The NWS cooperative observer reported 4.28 inches with the event, most falling within two to three hours.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose near the Land Cut along Laguna Madre in southeast Kenedy County reported gusts to 35 knots between 1042 and around 1053 PM CST on May 20th, 2018.
A trained spotter reported an isolated thunderstorm produced hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter in an area approximately 9 miles North  Northeast of Raymondville.

The husband of a CO-OP observer reported hail fell at their residence near the center of town on Copano Road in Port Mansfield. The hail occurred when an isolated thunderstorm moved through the area. The thunderstorm was triggered by a cold front moving through Deep South Texas.

A trained spotter reported nickel to quarter size hail fell in Arroyo City with some of the hail measuring up to 1 inch in diameter. The hail was produced by an isolated thunderstorm which occurred along a cold front moving through Deep South Texas.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in northeast Brooks County by June 5th, and expanded to all the eastern third of Brooks County on June 12th.  Initial rains leading into the Great June Flood improved conditions to Moderate (D1) levels before the drought monitor update on June 19th.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in southeast Kennedy County by June 5th, and expanded to all but the northern tip of the county on June 12th.  D2 conditions continued until the week of June 18th, when  6 to 18 inches of rain fell and turned rainfall deficits into long term rainfall surpluses.  Until then, there was an unknown level of stress on livestock on the King Ranch and other Kenedy County ranches due to the harsh conditions.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in southeast Kennedy County by June 5th, and expanded to all but the northern tip of the county on June 12th.  D2 conditions continued until the week of June 18th, when  6 to 18 inches of rain fell and turned rainfall deficits into long term rainfall surpluses.  Until then, there was an unknown level of stress on livestock on the King Ranch and other Kenedy County ranches due to the harsh conditions.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in Willacy County by June 5th, and continued until the week of June 18th, when  6 to 14 inches of rain fell and turned rainfall deficits into long term rainfall surpluses.  Until then, there were a number of lost dryland row crops in un-irrigated fields, and stress on livestock as well.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in Coastal Willacy County by June 5th, and continued until the week of June 18th, when  10 to 14 inches of rain fell and turned rainfall deficits into long term rainfall surpluses.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in northern Cameron County by June 5th, and continued until the week of June 18th, when  6 to 18 inches of rain fell and turned rainfall deficits into long term rainfall surpluses.  An unknown number of dry land row crops sustained production loss or damage due to prolonged dry and above to much above average conditions between March and mid June.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in northeastern Cameron County by June 5th, and continued until the week of June 18th, when  5 to 12 inches of rain fell and turned rainfall deficits into long term rainfall surpluses.  An unknown number of dry land row crops sustained production loss or damage due to prolonged dry and above to much above average conditions between March and mid June.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in extreme northeastern Hidalgo County by June 12th, and continued until June 18th, as initial rainfall ahead of heavier rains associated with the Great June Flood improved conditions to Moderate (D1) Drought. The drought would be erased by generally 4 to 8 inches of rain during the week of June 18th.  An unknown number of dry land row crops sustained production loss or damage due to prolonged dry and above to much above average conditions between March and mid June.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions developed in extreme southeastern Hidalgo County by June 12th, and continued until the week of June 18th, when rainfall of 12 to 18 inches associated with the Great June Flood erased the drought.  An unknown number of dry land row crops sustained production loss or damage due to prolonged dry and above to much above average conditions between March and mid June.

Measured and estimated rainfall of between 7 and more than 12 inches in north central Brooks County from the pre-dawn hours through around noon on June 19th created high standing water in and around Falfurrias. More than a dozen roads in town were flooded, some with 2 to 3 feet of water depth, and a number of properties saw floodwater inside of them. Farther north, along US 281 but mainly in Jim Wells County, two to three feet of flowing water closed the highway for a time during the morning and early afternoon. Highest rainfall totals for the event included 12.1 inches at the NWS cooperative observing station 4 miles west of Falfurrias and 8 inches near the center of town.  Much of the flooding was the result of a combination of creeks, including Palo Blanco and Cibolo, overspilling their banks in nearby Jim Wells and Duval County, along with sheet flow from the same areas.  An unknown number of water rescues were conducted during the afternoon and evening of the 19th.

Heavy rains of 8 to more than 14 inches (estimated) across northern Brooks, northeastern Jim Hogg, eastern Duval, and much of Jim Wells County allowed substantial water flows into the riverine system of creeks, including Los Olmos, Palo Blanco, and Cibolo. Each creek flowed outside of its banks during and well after the heaviest rains fell, for much of June 19th and June 20th before waters receded below bank full. At Los Olmos Creek along the Brooks/Jim Wells County line, the gage reached flood stage (11 feet) around 4 PM CST on the 19th, and continued to moderate levels (12 feet) shortly after 6 PM. The creek would remain in moderate flood for a few hours, before dipping below 12 feet at around 9 PM CST.  Slower recession brought the stage below 11 feet by early evening on the 20th. ||The peak stage at 12.32 feet ended up being the third highest on record, with only values associated with locally heavy rainfall in late August 1967 and the remnants of Hurricane Fern in September 1971 at higher levels. ||Impacts included lowland flooding between 300 and 700 feet into the flood plain, as well as high enough flow to close several farm to market roads on the east side of Falfurrias. Flooding of the Cibolo/Palo Blanco system aggravated high water from the rainfall alone that created initial flash flooding in the area earlier on June 19th.

A band of thunderstorms, moving slowly from west to east, intersected the sea breeze and stalled between Brownsville and Los Fresnos, dumping 3 to 5 or more inches of rainfall in a 2 to 3 hour period, causing significant street flooding and some road closures. Flood prone roads, including Morrison Blvd. in north Brownsville was closed due to 3 feet of water; Dennet road nearby was also covered in 2 to 3 feet of water. Other roads between North Brownsville and Los Fresnos were flooded with an unknown amount of water depth.  Several to dozens of vehicles were flooded, with damage unknown as of this writing.

Monthly rainfall of about one half inch in northwest Zapata County - or between 10 and 25 percent of normal - combined with similar rains in June and very little in prior months - allowed drought conditions to worsen through July, with Severe (D2) Drought arriving in the northwest corner of the county by the 24th, continuing through the end of July and eventually worsening further by late August.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Automated Surface Observing System observation at Bayview (3 miles west of the Laguna Madre) recorded a wind gust of 41 knots between 2:43 and 2:55 PM CST.  The Texas Coastal and Ocean Observing Network location at Realitos Peninsula, where Arroyo Colorado intersects Laguna Madre, recorded an observation of 40 knots at 2:54 PM CST.

Thunderstorm winds of just over 45 mph knocked down several palm fronds and blew unfastened lawn furniture around portions of the City of Brownsville to Los Fresnos.  Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport recorded a wind gust of 46 mph at 2:17 PM CST.

Thunderstorm winds of between 45 and 52 mph knocked down several palm fronds and blew unfastened lawn furniture around portions of the City of Los Fresnos to Harlingen.  Harlingen/Valley International Airport recorded a wind gust of 52 mph at 2:46 PM CST.
Severe (D2) Drought maintained its grip on northern Zapata County through the 14th, and expanded slightly into central Zapata County through the 20th.

Continued dry and hotter than average weather through the end of August worsened drought across Zapata County.  Extreme (D3) conditions developed in northern portions of the county on the 21st, and spread into north central locations by the 28th.  Severe drought conditions spread into central Zapata County but no farther by month's end.

Continued dry and hotter than average weather through the end of August allowed Severe (D2) drought to develop across extreme western Jim Hogg County on August 28th, continuing through the end of the month. Impact on livestock was unknown as of this writing.

The Emergency Management Coordinator from Willacy County, Texas, reported a small tornado briefly touched down between Raymondville and San Perlita. There was no structural damage, but patches of sugar cane were blown down based on photo evidence, and a short video confirmed the brief touch down.

Temperatures fell below 32 degrees just before midnight on the 3rd, bottoming out in the lower to mid 20s county-wide by daybreak.  Duration of sub-freezing temperatures from AWOS and Co-operative observing sites was estimated to be 8 to 10 hours.

Temperatures fell below 32 degrees just before midnight, bottoming out in the 20s across most portions of the county by daybreak on the 3rd.  The cooperative observation at Falfurrias, TX, recorded a low of 21 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing between 2 and 4 AM, and bottomed out generally between 25 and 30 degrees by daybreak.  Duration of subfreezing temperatures in rural Starr, northern Hidalgo, and southeastern Zapata county ranged from 5 to 7 hours.

A fire, located on the Jones Ranch, near Agua Nueva, 20 miles south of Farm to Market Road 1017, or approximately 31 miles south of Hebbronville, burned approximately 6,400 acres. An incident command post was established at the site, and numerous local volunteer fire departments assisited in helping contain, and control, the blaze.  No structures were reported damaged, according to reports from the Texas Forest Service.

A grass fire near San Ygnacio, in northwestern Zapata County, burned approximately 500 acres and was contained. There were no structures threatened. Several local fire departments and Volunteer fire departments responded quickly to the blaze.

A sharp cold front quickly brought 50 to 54 mph wind gusts (10m level) to the Boca Chica Beach, Texas area just north of the Mouth of the Rio Grande, before daybreak on January 23, 2019. The near instantaneous increase in north winds caused a prototype rocket, known as the Starship Hopper, to loosen from its moorings.  The nose section toppled over in the winds. The following wind gusts were reported at  nearby NOAA and Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) platforms:||Brazos Santiago (BRZT2, NOAA/NOS/CO-OPS): 45 to 50 mph from 451 to 742 CT (intermittent after 548 AM).|South Padre Island CG Station (SPIT2,NOAA/NOS/CO-OPS):  47 to 52 from 451 to 748 CT. |Port Isabel (PTIT2, NOAA/NOS/CO-OPS): 45 to 51 mph from 451 to 536 AM.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 1 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through 8 AM.  Minimum measured temperatures in the Falfurrias area ranged from 30 to 33 degrees, but were likely between 28 and 32 elsewhere in the County.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 1 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through 8 AM.  Minimum measured temperatures ranged from 24/25 in rural Armstrong to 31 east of Sarita (closer to the coast).

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 1 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through 8 AM.  Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the mid to upper 20s (29 at Hebbronville).

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 1 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through 8 AM.  Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the mid and upper 20s (28 at Zapata airport) to around 32 just east of Falcon International Reservoir.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 1 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through 8 AM.  Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the mid and upper 20s (28 at Rio Grande City); Falcon Lake Mesowest (a protected area) briefly fell below 25 degrees.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 1 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through 8 AM.  Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the mid and upper 20s (27 at Linn/San Manuel) to around 30 degrees closer to Edinburg.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees during the pre-dawn areas, mainly in rural locations but also in suburbs around McAllen, Pharr, Mission, and in parts of Weslaco.   Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the mid and upper 20s in wind-protected areas to 30 to 33 degrees between Mercedes and Mission.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees during the pre-dawn areas, mainly in rural locations but also around Raymondville.   Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to around 30 degrees.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees during the pre-dawn hours, mainly in rural locations but also around Harlingen.   Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from around 30 along the Cameron/Willacy and eastern Hidalgo line, to the mid and upper 30s around Brownsville.

The Co-Ops location at Brazos Santiago peaked at a level of 1.96 feet above MHHW, which was approximately 1.5 feet above predicted levels and a good proxy for conditions on the beaches from Boca Chica to South Padre Island - at 948 PM CST the evening of October 12th.  The water levels translated to tidal run-up and overwash that flooded the beach and went well into the dunes, with water up to the stair cases of beachfront property not protected by sea walls. Some erosion was noted by local officials following the coastal flood, but damage was unknown.

Heavy rainfall measured and estimated between 4 and 7 inches in a general 3 to 4 hour period produced flash flooding, mainly in the east half of McAllen stretching east to the Donna area, mostly during the pre-dawn hours through a bit after daybreak on June 20th.  Between 2 and 4 feet of inundation was reported by law enforcement where the heaviest rains fell and combined with known poor drainage.  The frontage road between McAllen and Donna was closed in most spots during and just after the peak of the rainfall and during the early morning commute.  Several hundred homes and hundreds of vehicles received some level of flooding.

Heavy rainfall measured and estimated between 7 and 18 inches in a 3 to 5 hour period produced locally devastating flooding in Weslaco and Mercedes, just north of the expressway.  Measured rainfall at the Weslaco Cooperative station was 15.57 inches for the event, with 11.36 of it falling in a three hour period generally between 3 AM CST and 6 AM CST.  Radar estimates suggested higher amounts at the Las Brisas and other neighborhoods in northeast Weslaco, where nearly all homes had 18 inches of water depth or higher inside.  ||The rain flooded (at least 18 inches) 2500 homes in Weslaco, with an unknown number (but likely in the 1,000 range) in next-door Mercedes.  Video, photograph, and first response/law enforcement evidence showed widespread 2 to 4 feet of water depth, with a few poorly draining areas in east Weslaco and Mercedes of at least 5 feet of water depth.  An unknown number of vehicles were flooded throughout the area, and the Interstate 2 frontage road was closed through most of the morning.  Eighty-six of the eighty-nine school buses in the Weslaco Independent School District sustained significant flood damage. ||Publicly reported damage was estimated to be at least $12.5 million; standard doubling estimated the damage at $25 million though in reality, values could be much higher due to poor measurement due to the volume of uninsured properties that were impacted.  The rainfall in the east/north side of Weslaco was the highest on record (since 1910) for a single event, besting the Labor Day 1933 Hurricane (15 inches).

Multiple cells and clusters of thunderstorms during the pre-dawn hours into the morning commute on June 20th dropped measured and estimated rainfall between 5 and more than 8 inches in western Cameron County, which caused widespread flooding between La Feria, Harlingen, San Benito, and other locations. The flooding produced locally 2 to 4 feet of water depth, with Santa Rosa through La Feria particularly hard hit. Interstate 2 frontage road was closed from Harlingen to McAllen due to the intense rainfall, which fell at an estimated rate of 2 to 3 inches per hour in a few spots for 2 to 3 hours - and on top of prior rainfall earlier in the week.||Detailed damage for this particular event was not known, though total damage through multiple agencies along with standard doubling for uninsured properties, as well as significant damage to drainage canals, suggested event totals in Cameron County were over $60 million.  For this particular event, which included some of the highest rainfall rates, damage was estimated at around $35 million.  There were an unknown number of properties and vehicles damaged in this particular flood, though the numbers are likely above 1,000 for each case.  ||Full details will be available within 12 to 18 months of the event.

One day after 3 to more than 5 inches fell between Brownsville and Los Fresnos during the afternoon and early evening hours, a repeat event occurred, fed by deep tropical moisture and multiple boundaries left behind from devastating morning flooding across western Cameron and eastern Hidalgo County.  A persistent line of torrential rainfall dominated through the early evening commute, with another 3 to 6 inches having fallen for a two-day total of 6 to 11+ inches.  The second day rainfall produced more widespread flooding across locations in and east of Brownsville and Los Fresnos, with farm and subdivisions under 2 to 3+ feet of water when all was said and done. ||The additional flooding on saturated soils (pump priming from June 19) likely produced more damage this second go-round, including more erosion to drainage canals/ditches and mainly rural roads.  Doubling of the damage left a total of around $20 million.

The Roma Fire Department reported that Arroyo Roma exceeded its banks, flooding parts of town with 1 to 3 feet of standing and flowing water during the pre-dawn hours of June 21st, 2018.  The flooding was associated with the initiation of a thunderstorm system that would later cause significant flooding in western Hidalgo County, including the McAllen/Mission metropolitan region during the daylight hours later that morning. Measured and estimated rainfall was between 3 and 7 inches across southern and central Starr County.  Estimated public damage, along with a standard doubling, left nearly $3 million in property and other damage (estimated).

State and local emergency management officials, as well as ground truth rainfall totals, reported widespread flooding in south-central Hidalgo County, focused on the Mission/Alton/West McAllen area as a firehose of thunderstorms persisted for more than five hours through the morning commute until around noon before finally dissipating. Estimated and measured rainfall for the event ranged from 6 to 11 inches, with periods of 2 to 3 inches per hour embedded during the heart of the morning commute.  Numerous roads, thousands of homes and vehicles (specific number unknown) were under a range of water depth, ranging from 18 inches to 3 to 4 feet in either poorly draining neighborhoods from the west half of McAllen through Mission.||A peak total rainfall of 18.31 inches fell in Mission for the combined events of June 20-22.  Estimated damage, using a combination of county-reported damage and standard doubling, was an estimated $22 million for this particular event.  Actual values may be much higher as data continues to come in throughout 2019.

An additional 1 to 2.5 inches of rain fell over already flooded neighborhoods in the McAllen/Mission area early on June 22, exacerbating already dangerous conditions from prior flooding on June 20th and 21st.  Neighborhoods in the south and west side of McAllen that had a foot or more of water depth temporarily saw levels rise higher during the peak of the heavy rainfall, which fell for an hour or two during the pre-dawn hours.  Additional damage was unknown from the prior estimates.

The same clusters of thunderstorms that dropped between 12 and an estimated 18 inches in the Weslaco/Mercedes area early on June 20th dropped an estimated 5 to 10 inches on central through northeastern Willacy County (primary population areas), including a number of farm fields (agricultural damage unknown).  Final damage totals from initial emergency management surveys of public damage were nearly three-quarter of a million dollars, with standard doubling estimating the value at just over $1.5 million.

Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought persisted in northern Zapata County to begin September, before locally heavy tropical rainfall improved conditions to abnormally dry with pockets of moderate (D1) drought by September 11th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted in extreme northwestern Jim Hogg County before locally heavy tropical rainfall arrived and improved conditions to in northern Zapata County to begin September, before locally heavy tropical rainfall improved conditions to abnormally dry by September 11th.

Nearly four inches of rain fell in one hour in east Harlingen, causing varying amounts of flooding through the city.  2 to an estimated 3 feet of water piled up along some roads, including enough to flood an indoor garage at Harlingen/Valley International Airport.  Damage amounts were unknown as most of the flooding was high water on roads, though some vehicles were inundated.

Severe (D2) Drought continued briefly into the first day of April, based on the US Drought Monitor, over extreme southern Jim Hogg County.  Thunderstorms with heavy rainfall over this area on March 30th, 2019, would improve conditions by two categories (D2 to D0) on April 2nd.

Severe (D2) Drought continued briefly into the first day of April, based on the US Drought Monitor, over extreme northern Starr County.  Thunderstorms with heavy rainfall over this area on March 30th, 2019, would improve conditions by two categories (D2 to D0) on April 2nd.

A gust of 53 mph was recorded at McAllen/Miller airport at 735 AM CST. At around the same time (735 AM),  several power lines blown down in the south side of Pharr, just 2 to 4 miles east of the airport.

The squall line that originally developed in Starr and Zapata County weakened a bit over western and central Hidalgo County, still producing wind gusts up to 53 mph.  The central part of the line re-intensified over eastern Hidalgo County, and as it reached Cameron County began producing several reports of wind damage.  Along a 10 mile stretch from near Santa Rosa to San Benito, the following damage reports were received:|*Power lines down on the southeast side of Santa Rosa (820 AM CST)|*Tree blocking a road in West Harlingen (830 AM CST)|*Tree down on car with damage to vehicle on Diaz St. in San Benito (830 AM CST). ||Reports were received from Public and Law Enforcement.

The squall line that originally developed in Starr and Zapata County weakened a bit over western and central Hidalgo County, still producing wind gusts up to 53 mph.  The central part of the line re-intensified over eastern Hidalgo County, and as it reached Cameron County began producing several reports of wind damage as well as a peak wind gust to 74 mph at Valley International Airport in Harlingen (815 AM CST).  Additional damage reports received included:||*Multiple trees down between Harlingen and Combes on US Highway 77/Interstate 69E (815 AM CST)||Reports were received from ASOS and Law Enforcement.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Rincon del San Jose reported a peak gust of nearly 40 knots at 8 AM CST, part of a 30 minute stretch of Gale force gusts associated with a east-moving squall line.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula reported a peak gust of nearly 39 knots at 9 AM CST, part of a 24 minute stretch of Gale force gusts associated with a east-moving squall line.  The Cameron County Airport at Port Isabel, just three miles inland from the coast, reported a gust of 49 knots at 858 AM CST, and is used as a proxy for this report.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula reported a peak gust of nearly 38 knots at 10 AM CST, part of a 6 minute stretch of Gale force gusts associated with the back side of a squall line that had exited the coast about an hour earlier.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network (TCOON) site at Brazos Santiago reported a peak gust of 39 knots at 930 AM CST, part of a 6 minute stretch of Gale force gusts associated with an eastward moving squall line that had exited the coast about an hour earlier.  Note that Brazos Santiago is about 200 yards inshore, and used as a proxy for the Gulf waters just beyond the surf zone.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020 reported prolonged period of Gale force gusts associated with an eastward moving squall line and mesoscale effects, such as wake low and high pressure.  Peak gust was measured at 41 knots at 930 AM CST.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020 recorded a peak gust of 41 knots around sunrise, as a line of thunderstorms developed along a seasonally strong cold front racing through the Lower Texas Gulf waters.
A report of nickel sized hail was received from the public, at the intersection of New Hampshire Ave. and I-69E in Harlingen.

Falfurrias Police Department reported downed power lines in Falfurrias.  Nearby observations from Hebbronville and Alice showed gusts with the storms to be near 30 mph, but it was likely that stronger gusts caused the damage in this case.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020, 45 nm northeast of Port Mansfield, reported a brief gust to 35 knots as the first in a series of strong thunderstorms passed across the Lower Texas Gulf waters beyond 20 nautical miles offshore.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020, 45 nm northeast of Port Mansfield, reported a brief gust to 35 knots as the second in a series of strong thunderstorms passed across the Lower Texas Gulf waters beyond 20 nautical miles offshore.

events.cz_name: WATERS FROM BAFFIN BAY TO PT MANSFIELD TX EXT FROM 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: NOAA Buoy 42020, 45 nm northeast of Port Mansfield, reported about 40 minutes of gale-force gusts as a cluster of thunderstorms moved across the Lower Texas Gulf waters beyond 20 nautical miles offshore.  Peak gusts reached 39 knots at 830 AM CST.

The Zapata County Sheriff's Office reported estimated nickel-sized hail, wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph, and low visibility from heavy rainfall along US Highway 83 about 5 miles north-northeast of San Ygnacio.

One large live oak tree was blown down at the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge along the Rio Grande, taking down several power lines and blocking an access road before removal.  Another large tree was reported down a bit farther north in South Alamo, ten minutes later.

The pulse-severe thunderstorm that felled trees just north of the Rio Grande minutes earlier produced its strongest gusts in North Alamo.  In and near the Red Barn Colonia, at least two poorly homes sustained full destruction, and several downed trees and fences were also reported in the area.

Quarter to golf ball sized hail was reported in Alamo with the core of a severe thunderstorm that also produced damaging winds.  Golf ball hail was reported at 5 AM approximately 3 miles south of Alamo city center, and quarter-sized hail was reported at 514 AM (CDT) in Alamo, from social media reports. No damage was reported with either event.
Nickel-sized hail was reported via Facebook in the El Monte Colonia near Monte Alto during the pre-dawn hours of May 14, 2019.

Street flooding of some poor drainage neighborhoods and urban areas was reported in Pharr when a steadily moving thunderstorm with heavy rainfall passed through the area. Near the intersection of Jackson Road and West Sam Houston Boulevard, one call was stalled in the road in water depth of approximately 2 feet.  Other areas had one foot or more of water, with some diversion of traffic around the flood. No non-vehicle property damage was reported.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: Reported in Port Mansfield of Laguna Madre. One half inch diameter hail was also reported at the Harbormaster's office in town.

The Valley Morning Star newspaper reported electrical lines downed by strong winds on West moran Court and 23rd Street. At least two trees were blown down between Harlingen and La Feria, with one across the intersection of Parker and Ebony in La Feria.  Numerous customers were without power during the peak of the storm.  Sustained winds reached 44 mph, with gusts to 52 mph, at the Valley International Airport east of Harlingen at 2:53 PM CST; at Brownsville International Airport, sustained winds reached 41 mph at 2:26 PM CST.

A roof was blown off of a mobile home in Mercedes, in extreme eastern Hidalgo County, sometime between Noon and 2:00 PM CST, from strong sustained winds with higher gusts.  Based on corroborating observations in Brownsville, and Harlingen, which is only about 10 miles away.

A fire, located on Jones Ranch, 20 miles south of Farm to Market Road 1017 burned approximately 6,400 acres between January 31st and February 1st, but was contained. An incident command post was established at the site on the 31st, and numerous local Volunteer Fire Departments, county emergency management personnel, the Texas Forest Service, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, responded to requests for aid.

A 1,400 acre fire located at US Highway 281 and Farm to Market Road 1017 was contained sometime late on February 1st, it is believed. Ten homes were threatened and saved. The Texas Civil Air Patrol (TXCAP) provided air reconnaissance; several local Fire Departments responded.  Illegal burning by a landowner started the fire.

A 2,300-acre wildfire erupted at the San Rafael Ranch, located along the Jim Hogg/Brooks County line, along Farm to Market (FM) Road 755 by the Kelsy Curve, 10 miles north of FM 1017, threatened 3 structures, all of which were saved. Numerous Fire Departments, Jim Hogg Sheriff���s Office, Texas Forest Service, and the Hidalgo County Emergency Management Coordinator (EMC) responded. Civil Air Patrol aircraft performed two smoke detection reconnaissance runs, which were able to help contain the fire quickly.

A 2,300-acre wildfire erupted at the San Rafael Ranch, located along the Jim Hogg/Brooks County line, along Farm to Market (FM) Road 755 by the Kelsy Curve, 10 miles north of FM 1017, threatened 3 structures, all of which were saved. Numerous Fire Departments, Jim Hogg Sheriff���s Office, Texas Forest Service, and the Hidalgo County Emergency Management Coordinator (EMC) responded. Civil Air Patrol aircraft performed two smoke detection reconnaissance runs, which were able to help contain the fire quickly.

A wildfire rapidly grew to 1200 acres, located between Farm to Market (FM)Road 1017, and FM 755, west of Alaniz Road, near La Gloria in south central Starr County. Four homes were threatened and saved. Blackhawk helicopters responded with suppressants. The Texas Forest Service and numerous local fire departments also responded, as did the City of McAllen Public Works Department. The fire was contained with no injuries.

A plot of pallets burned on a one acre tract of land bordering a residential community, located at the intersection of South|Tower Road and Rancho Blanco. Gusty southeast winds up to 40 mph quickly spread the embers toward up to 500 homes in the area.  Eight hundred residents were evacuated, and a shelter was established at the Alamo Community Center located nearby.  Unfortunately, despite saving many of the homes, three of the homes affected were damaged.  ||In addition to the damage, 350 homes lost power. The fire was contained and residents were allowed to return to their homes late in the day.  A large number of local and regional fire departments, as well as the Texas Department of Public Safety and the U.S. Border Patrol aerial reconnaissance unit, also assisted in response and relief efforts.

A 400 acre fire, likely spread by gusty southeast winds between 25 and 35 mph, located at the intersection of Farm to Market Road (FM) 649 and Sanchez Road, in western Starr County, was contained. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, along with several local Fire Departments, responded.

A fire quickly spread to 400 acres at the Vela Martinez Ranch along the Zapata/Webb County line, driven by sustained southeast winds 20 to 25 mph with gusts of 30 mph or more, combined with falling humidity values below 30 percent, and perhaps down to 25 percent.  Slowly diminishing winds late in the day, as well as ample help from local fire departments and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, helped contain the blaze.

Severe drought conditions progressed into Zapata County by the end of February, exacerbating the threat for wild fire growth and posing a few difficulties to the local feed supply for livestock in the area.

events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network platform at Realitos Peninsula recorded a peak gust near 37 knots at 1138 AM CST, associated with a thunderstorm downburst signature. Gale force gusts prevailed from 1142 through 1154 AM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: The Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network site at Baffin Bay, just a couple miles north of the northern Laguna Madre, recorded wind gusts just shy of 50 knots as a slowly decaying mini-supercell thunderstorm passed over the site. Values used here are proxy to the nearby location in the entrance of Baffin Bay. Gusts in excess of 40 knots were recorded for 12 minutes.

The cooperative observer in McCook reported a measured wind gust to 58 mph, which blew down several large tree limbs and streen signs in the town, as well as blew down power lines four miles southeast of the town about four minutes later.

Broadcast media reported structural damage to a mobile home in the La Homa Five Colonia just north of Alton. Damage included a torn off roof and partial wall collapse.  Wind speed estimated from similar radar depiction from the same storm which caused minor damage about 10 miles northwest in McCook.

The Emergency Management Coordinator for Willacy County reported damage to eight utility poles and 20 to 30 mesquite trees on the I-69E Frontage Road near the intersection with Conley Road, north of Raymondville. The utility pole damage was a combination of those uprooted from the ground and others broken in half. Bark was peeled from some of the mesquite trees.  Damage width of poles and trees was about one-half mile long.  In addition, grass of one and one-half foot tall was blown down in circular fashion in nearby locations.
Police briefly closed the Solis Road exit along westbound Interstate Highway 2 (frontage) due to minor nuisance flooding.
The Roma Police Department reported several roads with minor flooding. Time of overall flooding is estimated based on report received at 1930 CDT.

Spotters and local law enforcement reported sporadic street flooding in southeast and east Harlingen after torrential thunderstorm rains dumped 2 to 3 inches in about an hour. Minor street flooding was most common along Ed Carey Blvd. (FM Loop 499) and U.S. Highway 77 (business) between Hale Avenue and Sam Houston Drive. No significant property damage was reported.

A severe thunderstorm produced sporadic straight line wind damage|from Monte alto to portions of north Elsa during the evening of|June 24th. Storm motion was from northeast to southwest out of western Willacy County, and several large tree limbs were snapped, and a few trees were uprooted, on the east side of Monte Alto. Winds also caused a free standing metal tower to collapse in Monte Alto. As the storm moved southwestward, large swaths of sugar cane were|noticeably bent towards the ground. Farther west, two poorly |constructed mobile homes were completely destroyed and another was|rolled on its side in a colonia about 2 miles west of Monte Alto. Near Elsa, just off of  Monte Cristo Road, over a dozen wooden power poles were snapped across N. Mile Five and One-Half Road. Some metal sheet roofing was torn from a nearby home, and a storage shed had considerable damage to walls and roofing. Based on the construction quality of the buildings and the transmission tower, and the type of trees damaged, peak wind speeds were estimated at 65 to 75 mph.

Numerous large mesquite and a few large ash tree limbs, including some uprooted trees, were seen on an NWS Storm Survey in western Willacy County from State Highway 186 about 8 miles west of Raymondville through and just south of Lasara along FM-1015. A few power lines were also felled. Wind speed estimated from the damage indicators and radar estimates.

An off-duty NWS employee, along with local news media, reported a tractor trailer jack-knifed with the cab dangling on the side of Interstate 69C on the overpass above FM 490 just north of the South Texas International Airport.  It was not determined if the jack-knife was caused by wind, slick roads, or both, but wind gusts over 40 mph had begun as persistent outflows from a developing mesoscale convective system over eastern Hidalgo and western Willacy County.
One tree was blown down along Cummings Road in Donna. Time estimated from radar and from nearby gust to 41 mph at McAllen/Miller Airport at 734 PM CDT.
Penny sized hail was reported in Alamo as a strong thunderstorm passed through just before sunset.

In addition to damaging winds that were surging through the area, the County Emergency Management staff reported estimated nickel-sized hail with the same severe thunderstorm in eastern Hidalgo County. Torrential, sideways-moving rain was also reported.

A large tree was blown down on the road near the Edinburg/McAllen line 5 miles southwest of Edinburg. Large branches were also blown down nearby.  Peak wind gusts at McAllen/Miller International Airport reached 41 mph (36 knots) but reached 52 mph (45 knots) at South Texas International Airport (about 11 miles north of Edinburg) during the same time period.

Measured and estimated rainfall between 6 and 15 inches that fell predominantly from early evening June 24th through a bit after midnight on June 25th produced widespread flash flooding across southeastern Hidalgo County.  Hardest hit locations were near the Cameron and Willacy County line, including locations just west of Santa Rosa through Monte Alto, and between Sebastian and Elsa. ||In the tri-county area (western Willacy, northwestern Cameron, and southeastern Hidalgo), 1188 homes were considered destroyed or with major damage, with an additional 182 homes with minor damage. Hundreds of streets flooded, including 30 Texas-managed highways. This included the frontage roads of Interstate 2 and Interstate 69E.  More than 100 persons were evacuated to higher ground when dozens of homes were threatened by 2 to 4 feet of water in each county; Monte Alto was hardest hit in Hidalgo County.  Individual Assistance costs were estimated at $27.6 million as of early August 2019; Public Assistance values were unknown but likely to add to the damage, which will be estimated at $75 million in all three counties. Daily rainfall records were set in the flood area, including 6.95 inches in Weslaco, more than 3 inches above the prior record for the date set in 1951. ||Despite the flooding and damage, much which occurred in the dark, there were no know deaths of injuries directly attributed to the flood.

Measured and estimated rainfall between 8 and 12 or more inches that fell predominantly from early evening June 24th through a bit after midnight on June 25th produced widespread flash flooding across western Willacy County.  Hardest hit locations were Sebastian, Lyford, Raymondville, and La Sara. ||In the tri-county area (western Willacy, northwestern Cameron, and southeastern Hidalgo), 1188 homes were considered destroyed or with major damage, with an additional 182 homes with minor damage. Hundreds of streets flooded, including 30 Texas-managed highways. This included the frontage roads of Interstate 2 and Interstate 69E.  ||More than 100 persons were evacuated to higher ground when dozens of homes were threatened by 2 to 4 feet of water in each county; the entire western two thirds of Raymondville was under 1 to 3 feet of water; up to 4 feet was noted in LaSara during the peak of the heavy rain just before midnight on June 24th, and poor drainage flow in canals and ditches backed up water into Sebastian well after the rain had ended.   |Individual Assistance costs for the affected area in the three counties was estimated at $27.6 million as of early August 2019; Public Assistance values were unknown but likely to add to the damage, which will be estimated at $75 million in all three counties. Daily rainfall records were set in the flood area, including 9.7 inches in Raymondville which shattered the prior daily record by nearly 8 inches on the date (prior was 1.83 inches in 1923) and set a new daily record for the month of June (prior was 6.23 in 1993), with records going back to 1910. ||Despite the flooding and damage, much which occurred in the dark, there were no know deaths of injuries directly attributed to the flood.

Measured and estimated rainfall between 8 and 15.2 inches that fell predominantly from early evening June 24th through a bit after midnight on June 25th produced widespread flash flooding across northwestern Cameron County.  Hardest hit locations were the west side of Harlingen through La Feria, north to Santa Rosa, and back east to near Combes. ||In the tri-county area (western Willacy, northwestern Cameron, and southeastern Hidalgo), 1188 homes were considered destroyed or with major damage, with an additional 182 homes with minor damage. Hundreds of streets flooded, including 30 Texas-managed highways. This included the frontage roads of Interstate 2 and Interstate 69E (with up to four feet of water in Cameron County).  ||More than 100 persons were evacuated to higher ground when dozens of homes were threatened by 2 to 4 feet of water in each county.  In northwestern Cameron County, total neighborhoods were inundated with 1 to 3 feet of water in northwest Harlingen, Santa Rosa (where some reports noted 4 feet of water depth), and Combes. |   |Individual Assistance costs for the affected area in the three counties was estimated at $27.6 million as of early August 2019; Public Assistance values were unknown but likely to add to the damage, which will be estimated at $75 million in all three counties. Daily rainfall records were set in the flood area, including 6.29 inches in Harlingen, more than four inches above the prior calendar day record (2.23 inches in 1926).  The total was also a new daily record for the month (5.89 on June 20, 2018); records date back to 1912 at the site.||Despite the flooding and damage, much which occurred in the dark, there were no know deaths of injuries directly attributed to the flood.

Slow drainage of torrential rains of 6 to 15 inches in just six hours during the evening of June 24th through just after midnight on June 25th maintained widespread flooding of 1 to as much as 3 feet of water depth across many neighborhoods and roads in the eastern portion of the Rio Grande Valley. Hundreds of roads remained closed or impassible, and hundreds to more than a thousand homes continued to have some water in them for several (mainly fair weather days) following the causative event. Water did not recede completely in some neighborhoods until up to 2 weeks following the rains, much due to the interconnected drainage system which was unable to handle the rainfall rate, which was a 1 in 500 probability event occurring in locations only built to sustain 1 in 5 or 1 in 10 probability events. ||Please note: Damage listed here is only a fraction of the total damage which is shown in the flash flood entries for these locations.

Estimated total damage for this event is listed in the flash flood entries for these locations.

Estimated total damage for this event is listed in the flash flood entries for these locations.

A strong cloud to ground lightning bolt struck and set ablaze a wind turbine and tower at the Willacy County Los Vientos wind farm during the initial severe thunderstorm that impacted the county during the early evening of June 24, 2019.  Another strike destroyed a small grain silo just to the west of Lyford and Raymondville.  Time of the strike is estimated from peak lightning frequency, which exceeded 300 cloud to ground strikes in 15 minutes.

A New York Times article described potential heat-related deaths, as provided by United States Border Patrol (USBP), during the afternoon of June 23, 2019, in the brush inside the levee along the Rio Grande south of McAllen. One woman (age unknown but assumed to be in her 20s) and three children (two infants and a toddler) were pronounced dead when found that evening. Between 3 and 4 PM CDT, the heat index at McAllen/Miller Airport, less than 10 miles north of the location of the bodies and the most relevant proxy location, reported more than an hour of heat index of 118 degrees.  Excessive heat is defined as values 116 or higher in the region.

United States Border Patrol reported 29 hospitalizations from potential heat-related illnesses between June 7 and June 9, when afternoon heat index across the Rio Grande Valley and Deep South Texas ranged, generally, from 111 to 124 degrees.  Of the 29 hospitalizations, four were directly related to heat exhaustion, on Friday June 7th.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A rare afternoon band of showers, some rotating, from South Padre Island into the Gulf waters out to 60 nautical miles out. One cell produced a brief waterspout just east of the middle of the City beaches that moved onshore before dissipating.

Beach Patrol and Emergency Management from the City of South Padre Island, as well as public video, showed a brief waterspout moved onshore near Gulf Boulevard City Beach Access #10.  Before dissipating, the waterspout displaced beach umbrellas and tents, with minimal damage.  Time estimated from video, reports, and radar.

Zapata County authorities and the Zapata County News (via the Emergency Management Coordinator) reported several instances of minor damage from a microburst during the late afternoon of August 24. In Falcon Heights (2 miles south-southeast of Zapata City), two anchored deer blinds were blown onto U.S. 83 from a nearby store display.  In the city of Zapata, minor roof damage was reported to homes, several trees and large limbs were blown down, and power outages covered a large part of the city for 8 to 24 hours.
The daughter of a former NWS Brownsville/Rio Grande Valley employee reported quarter sized hail along N. 17th Street in McAllen.
Several portions of a fence were blown down at Chabad RGV in north McAllen.
One roof was blown off a residence in Raymondville, and there were several calls to dispatch of trees and power poles down between Raymondville and Lyford.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions continued across nearly all of Brooks County through September 9th.  Locally heavy rains from the outer bands of Tropical Storm Fernand (September 3-5) would improve conditions thereafter.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions continued across southern Jim Hogg County through September 9th, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) conditions near Hebbronville.  Locally heavy rains from the outer bands of Tropical Storm Fernand (September 3-5) would improve conditions thereafter.  A state disaster declaration for livestock and other agricultural impacts included Jim Hogg County.

Severe (D2) Drought conditions continued across central and southern Zapata County through September 9th, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) conditions near San Ygnacio.  Locally heavy rains from the outer bands of Tropical Storm Fernand (September 3-5) would improve conditions thereafter.  A state disaster declaration for livestock and other agricultural impacts included Zapata County.
Severe (D2) Drought persisted in a small band near Hebbronville from September 10 through the 30th.
Severe (D2) Drought persisted in a small band near San Ygnacio east through the northern Zapata ranchlands from September 10 through the 30th.
The automated surface observing system at Harlingen/Valley International Airport reported a wind gust to 54 mph.  A few power outages and minor tree damage was noted in the area.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: Boaters reported a brief, small waterspout northeast of South Padre Island.  No damage was noted.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted across northern Jim Hogg County into early October, and would expand southward across all but the eastern and southern third of the county from the 8th through the 14th as rain-free conditions continued at the tail end of the summer rainy season.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted across northern Zapata County into early October, and would expand southward across all but the southern tip of the county from the 8th through the 14th as rain-free conditions continued at the tail end of the summer rainy season.

Severe (D2) drought expanded to cover all but the eastern quarter of Jim Hogg County on October 15, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) returning to northwest portions as well.  A bit of rain after the 15th would slightly improve conditions toward the end of the month.

Severe (D2) drought expanded to cover all but extreme southern Zapataq County on October 15, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) returning to areas along the Webb County line north of San Ygnacio.  A bit of rain after the 15th would slightly improve conditions toward the end of the month.
Severe (D2) drought expanded into northwest Starr County on October 15th, a trend that would continue with limited rainfall through the end of the month.

Paltry rainfall and modest humidity allowed Severe (D2) Drought to persist across all but the eastern quarter of Jim Hogg County through the end of October.  A sliver of Extreme (D3) Drought that appeared on the 15th was eliminated by rain that grazed the border of Webb County on the 17th.

Paltry rainfall and modest humidity allowed Severe (D2) Drought to expand across all but a sliver of southern Zapata County through the end of October.  A sliver of Extreme (D3) Drought that appeared on the 15th was eliminated by rain that grazed the border of Webb County on the 17th.
Paltry rainfall and modest humidity allowed Severe (D2) Drought to expand across the northern half of Starr County for the last week of October.

A cluster of potent thunderstorms developed in northeastern Mexico and moved north into Cameron County early Sunday morning. Within this cluster of storms, a strong linear downburst crossed South Padre Island from 1:24 AM CST to 1:40 AM CST. The South Padre Island Police Department reported downed power lines in between the paralleling Padre Blvd and Laguna Blvd on South Padre Island, and at one point all of South Padre Island had lost power due to 31 transmission poles that were taken down by the wind.

A line of strong thunderstorms developed over the lower Rio Grande Valley and quickly became severe as it progressed eastward across Cameron County. Within the line, a very notable downburst developed just ahead of Bayview and caused destructive straight-line winds. Widespread tree damage was surveyed, in addition to the destruction of a sunroom on the south side of Bayview. Also, several large trees were uprooted with numerous large tree branches down.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: Peak winds of 49 knots (Storm Force) were recorded at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station at 142 AM CST (242 AM CDT).  A period of Gale to Storm Force gusts was observed from a rapidly developing squall line between 136 AM and 2 AM CST (236 and 3 AM CDT). No damage was reported, so far, to any water craft at the station or in Laguna Madre.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: Peak winds of 45 knots (Gale Force) were recorded at the Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) site at Realitos Peninsula at 130 AM CST (230 AM CDT), associated with a rapidly developing squall line between Bayview and Boca Chica Beach early on the 21st.  No known damage to watercraft was noted.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: Peak winds of 56 knots (Storm Force) was recorded at the Brazos Santiago monitoring station along the South Padre Island jetty at 142 AM CST (242 AM CDT).  Gale to Storm Force gusts were recorded between 136 AM and 206 AM CST (236 and 306  AM CDT), associated with a rapidly developing squall line between Bayview and Boca Chica Beach early on the 21st.  No known damage to watercraft was noted, but the near 70 mph gusts produced damage to power poles on South Padre Island during the same time.

A tight pressure gradient between a surface high pressure over the Mississippi River Valley and a low pressure system over southeastern Colorado resulted in strong breezy to windy conditions across the Rio Grande Valley throughout the day on November 20th. A strong gust of 41 mph (36 knots) early in the afternoon knocked down a large shopping center sign that fell on a vehicle at the intersection of East Ridge Road and South M Street in the city of McAllen.

Severe (D2) drought persisted across the majority of Jim Hogg County on November 5, and a sliver of Extreme Drought (D3) developed across the southwestern portion as well. The Severe area would shrink to the western half of the county after scattered showers and thunderstorms affected mainly the eastern half on the 7th and 8th.
Severe (D2) drought persisted across the northern half of Starr County on November 5, and a sliver of Extreme Drought (D3) developed along northwestern portions as well.

Severe (D2) drought persisted across the majority of Zapata County on November 5, and an area of Extreme Drought (D3) developed across central and eastern portions as well.  That area would shrink to just a sliver on November 12th, courtesy of scattered showers and thunderstorms on the 7th and 8th.
Rain-free conditions along with modest relative humidity maintained Severe Drought (D2) across the eastern third of Jim Hogg County through the end of November.
Rain-free conditions along with modest relative humidity maintained Severe Drought (D2) across northwestern Starr County through the end of November.
Rain-free conditions along with modest relative humidity maintained Severe Drought (D2) across most of Zapata County through the end of November.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across all but the eastern sliver of Jim Hogg County through November 4th.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across northern Starr County through November 4th.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across all but extreme southwest Zapata County through November 4th.

Strong and gusty winds cranked up just before noon along the Federal Highway 77 corridor, extending across the Lower Rio Grande Valley on into Hidalgo and Brooks County. Sustained winds of 25 to 38 mph, with frequent gusts above 40 mph, were common between 9 AM and sunset. Peak sustained winds of 38 mph occurred between 1:30 and 2:00 PM CST; a peak gust of 48 mph was observed at McAllen/Miller Airport at 1:49 PM CST.||Numerous power lines were knocked down across the populated portions of the county from McAllen and Pharr east to the Cameron County line; at least 2000 customers were without power during the peak of the winds in the afternoon. Hidalgo County emergency management reported receiving several phone calls of utility poles on fire due to strong winds whipping the power lines.

The Texas Forest service reported a wildfire burned approximately 800 acres 6 miles Southeast of La Gloria in Starr County, not too far from the initiation point of the Burns Ranch Fire near the four corner border of Brooks, Hidalgo, and Jim Hogg County. Additional data on this particular fire was unavailable at the time of this writing.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the western third of Jim Hogg County through the end of December.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the north-central third of Starr County through the end of December.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the majority of Zapata County through the end of December.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 3 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through about 8 AM. Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the mid and upper 20s (27 at Zapata airport) to around 32 just east of Falcon International Reservoir.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 3 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through about 8 AM. Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from the mid and upper 20s (24 at Armstrong) to around 32.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees around 3 AM (later in unprotected areas and small cities) and continued through about 8 AM. Minimum measured and estimated temperatures ranged from about 30 to around 32 (30 at Rio Grande City).

The cooperative observer at the Hollywood Hunting Camp about 3 miles west of Falfurrias recorded a minimum temperature of 26 degrees, while the Automated Weather Observing Station at Brooks County Airport  recorded a low temperature of 32 degrees for about 30 minutes around daybreak on December 18th.  The cooperative site at Linn/San Manuel in northern Hidalgo County recorded a low of 30 degrees.  Given these proxy observations and the likelihood of rural ranchland seeing temperatures between the two values for at least two hours implies a minor freeze occurred on the morning of December 18.

The Automated Weather Observing Station at South Texas International Airport (11 miles north of Edinburg) recorded a low temperature of 31 degrees, with temperaturest between 31 and 32 degrees for nearly two and one half hours around daybreak on December 18th . The cooperative site at Linn/San Manuel in northern Hidalgo County recorded a low of 30 degrees, which likely lasted more than 2 hours given the proximity to the Airport.

The Automated Weather Observing Station at Jim Hogg County Airport recorded several hours with temperatures at 32 degrees, and the on-site RAWS observation nearby recorded a couple of hours at 32, all during the pre-dawn through just after sunset hours.

The automated weather observing station at Zapata County Airport reached 27 degrees during the predawn hours of December 19th, with proxy observations at Jim Hogg County Airport northwest of Hebbronville (reaching 28 degrees) and Rio Grande City (Starr County, 30 degrees estimated) both falling to or below freezing for at several hours.

The automated weather observing station and the RAWS station onsite at the Jim Hogg County Airport northwest of Hebbronville both fell to around 28 or 29 degrees during the pre-dawn through daybreak hours of December 19th. Duration of the freezing temperatures lasted around four hours.

The cooperative observer at Rio Grande City reached either 29 or 30 degrees early on the morning of December 19, and nearby Falcon Dam coop reached 32 degrees.  The RAWS station near Falcon Lake reached 29 degrees as well.  General duration of hte freeze was around four hours, though some pockets may have reached five hours in wind protected locations.

The cooperative observer in Raymondville (Willacy County) touched 32 degrees on December 19th (duration unknown).  The Automated Weather Observing System in Brooks County Airport was 33 degrees for around 4 hours, and it was likely that typical wind protected locations in Kenedy County fell below 32 degrees and potentially into the upper 20s for several hours early on the 19th. Therefore, it is assumed that several hours of freezing conditions occurred in Brooks County early on the 19th.

The cooperative observer in Raymondville (Willacy County) touched 32 degrees on December 19th (duration unknown).  The Automated Weather Observing System in Brooks County Airport was 33 degrees for around 4 hours, and it was likely that typical wind protected locations in Kenedy County fell below 32 degrees and potentially into the upper 20s for several hours early on the 19th. Therefore, it is assumed that several hours of freezing conditions occurred across inland Kenedy County (King Ranch area).

events.event_narrative: A thunderstorm passed over the offshore Gulf of Mexico coastal waters east of Port Isabel producing high winds. The Port Isabel Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network site recorded winds up to 37 knots as the thunderstorm moved into the Gulf waters.

events.event_narrative: A thunderstorm moving across the offshore Gulf coastal waters produced high winds over the coastal waters. Buoy 42020 recorded winds up to 39 knots as the initial outflow from the thunderstorm passed by.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A thunderstorm moved over the Laguna Madre and the offshore Gulf of Mexico coastal waters producing high winds. Winds up to 36 knots were recorded at the Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network Station located northeast of Port Isabel as the thunderstorm and associated outflow moved through.

A tight pressure gradient between a surface high pressure off the Carolina coast and a low pressure system over West Texas resulted in strong windy conditions across the Rio Grande Valley throughout the day on January 10th. A strong gust of 47 mph late in the morning knocked down a large restaurant sign that fell and blocked traffic on University Drive in the city of Edinburg.

events.event_narrative: A thunderstorm moved across the Laguna Madre and Gulf of Mexico coastal waters producing strong and gusty winds. The Harbor Master reported winds gusts to 49 knots as the thunderstorm moved through Port Mansfield and the Laguna Madre.
