events.event_narrative: An outflow from strong thunderstorms over the coastal waters south and east of Baffin Bay moved across Port Isabel, the Laguna Madre and the Gulf of Mexico coastal waters producing strong winds over these areas. |The Automated Surface Observing System at Port Isabel,just 4 miles from Laguna Madre and less than 10 miles from the nearshore Gulf waters, reported winds of 35 knots as the thunderstorm moved through the area, and similar winds likely crossed into the Laguna Madre and the adjacent Gulf waters near South Padre Island.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
events.event_narrative: A cold front moved through Deep South Texas and the adjacent coastal waters producing isolated thunderstorms. One thunderstorm moved through Port Mansfield and the Laguna Madre producing strong and gusty winds.  Wind speeds of 34 knots were recorded at the Rincon Del San Jose Texas Coastal Ocean Observing Network C-MAN station.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across central Starr County through January 20th.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the majority of Zapata County through January 20th.
Severe (D2) Drought conditions prevailed across the western portion of Jim Hogg County through January 20th.
Severe (D2) drought persisted across the central portion of Starr County on January 21st and then expanded slightly into early February.

Severe (D2) drought persisted across the majority of Zapata County and a small area of Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the western portion of the county on January 21st. These drought areas persisted through the end of January and into early February.
Severe (D2) drought persisted across the western portion portion of Jim Hogg County on January 21st and then expanded slightly into early February.

A sliver of Extreme Drought (D3) persisted across western Zapata County, with the remainder of the County in Severe Drought (D2), through the 10th of February, as rain-free and low humidity conditions continued.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted across all but northeast and southwest Starr County through February 10th, due to a combination of little to no rainfall and dry conditions with warm days and cool nights.
Severe (D2) Drought persisted across western Jim Hogg County through February 10th, due to a combination of little to no rainfall and dry conditions with warm days and cool nights.
Severe (D2) Drought persisted across a slice of southwestern Hidalgo County through February 10th, due to a combination of little to no rainfall and dry conditions with warm days and cool nights.

Severe (D2) drought conditions nosed into southwestern Brooks County on February 11th, and would expand to cover the western two-thirds of the county by the 18th, and continue through month's end. Lack of rainfall and low humidity, along with a number of crisp/chilly mornings and warm afternoons, helped worsen the conditions.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions arrived in southwestern Jim Hogg County on February 11th, as Severe (D2) conditions spread across all but the northeastern corner of the county on the 11th, then expanded to cover the remainder of the county by the 18th.  These conditions then continued through month's end.  The drought expansion was due a combination of little to no rainfall, low humidity, and a combination of warm afternoons and crisp cool mornings.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions arrived in northwestern Starr County on February 11th, as Severe (D2) conditions spread across all but the southwestern corner due to prior rainfall impacts.  Those impacts would be erased by a series of dry cold fronts, and by month's end D2 conditions covered all of Starr outside of the D3 region. Pasture managers noted that Conservation Reserve Program land needed to be grazed or hayed due to the drought and keep it idle from any crop growth due to the drought impacts, by late February.

Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to cover all but the northeast and southwest corner of Zapata County on February 11th, with Severe (D2) prevailing in these areas. These conditions remained through month's end. The culprit for the expansion and worsening drought was a combination of little to no rainfall, low to very low humidity, and warm afternoons and cool/crisp mornings.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded into the western third or northern Hidalgo County on February 11th, eventually covering all of northern Hidalgo County by the 18th and continuing through month's end. According to the USDA Farm Service Extension Agent in Edinburg, pasture/crop managers were considering grazing/haying and taking a penalty, rather than planting dryland crops with the high threat of failure.

Severe (D2) Drought continued in the western half of southern Hidalgo County on February 11th, continuing through month's end. According to the USDA Farm Service Extension Agent in Edinburg, pasture/crop managers were considering grazing/haying and taking a penalty, rather than planting dryland crops with the high threat of failure.

A collection of observations between Encino and Falfurrias indicated a freeze, likely with frost in some locations.  Minimum temperatures fell to between 26 and 33, with times estimated through proxy observation at mesonet/remote automated weather station (RAWS) sites, as well as NWS Cooperative sites.  The cooperative site just west of Falfurrias recorded the lowest value of 26 at around 7 AM.

A collection of mesonet and cooperative observations between Armstrong and Sarita reached freezing temperatures around sunrise on February 27.  Minimum temperatures fell to between 28 and 33, with times estimated through proxy observation at mesonet/remote automated weather station (RAWS) sites. The cooperative site 4 miles southeast of Armstrong recorded a low of 28 degrees at around 7 AM.

Proxy observations based on sheltered/wind protected locations in neighboring Brooks, Starr, and Zapata Counties suggested a light freeze in much of ranch-owned Jim Hogg County around sunrise on February 27th. Low temperatures in these areas likely ranged from 28 to 33 degrees.  At the Jim Hogg County Airport, low temperatures reached 33 degrees.

In rural northern Hidalgo County, minimum temperatures fell to between 29 and 32 degrees around sunrise on February 27th.  Duration of the freezing temperatures was gleaned from the mesowest/remote automated weather station (RAWS) location at Linn/San Manuel. The cooperative observer in San Manuel reported a low of 30 degrees.

In much of Starr County, based on observations from multiple sites along the Rio Grande and other proxy locations in Zapata, Brooks, and northern Hidalgo County, minimum temperatures fell to between 28 and 32 degrees around sunrise on the 27th. At the cooperative observing station in Rio Grande City, the minimum temperature reached the freezing point right around sunrise.

In much of Zapata County, based on observations from multiple sites along the Rio Grande and other proxy locations in southwest Starr County, minimum temperatures fell to or just below freezing around sunrise on the 27th. Zapata County Airport dropped to 31 degrees, while the remote automated weather station (RAWS) at Falcon Lake, just south of the county line, dropped to 28 degrees.

Severe (D2) Drought continued in western Brooks County to begin March 2020. D2 conditions would creep eastward to cover all bu a small pocket of eastern Brooks County by March 10th, continuing through March 16th. A very small areas of Extreme (D3) conditions would touch southwest Brooks County by March 10th.
Severe (D2) Drought continued in most of northern Hidalgo County to begin March 2020. The D2 conditions would expand to cover all of the area on March 3rd, and continue through March 16th.
Severe (D2) Drought continued in the western half of southern Hidalgo County, mainly west of Mission, to begin March 2020.
Extreme (D3) Drought continued in northern Starr County, with Severe (D2) Drought elsewhere in the county, to begin March 2020.
Extreme (D3) Drought continued in southwestern Jim Hogg County, with Severe (D2) Drought elsewhere in the county, to begin March 2020.
Extreme (D3) Drought continued across much of Zapata County, with Severe (D2) conditions at the northeast and southwest corner of the county to begin March.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in Willacy County on March 3rd, and would continue through month's end.  Just enough rainfall fell at various times during the period to keep this condition as status quo, despite near record monthly heat.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in southern Kenedy County on March 3rd, and would develop in northern Kenedy County on March 17th. Central Kenedy County would remain in moderate (D1) Drought, courtesy of showers that moved through the region, keeping status quo while rain missed the northern third of the county.  Just enough rainfall fell at various times during the period in southern Kenedy County to keep Severe Drought as status quo, despite near record monthly heat.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in southern Kenedy County on March 3rd, and would develop in northern Kenedy County on March 17th. Central Kenedy County would remain in moderate (D1) Drought, courtesy of showers that moved through the region, keeping status quo while rain missed the northern third of the county.  Just enough rainfall fell at various times during the period in southern Kenedy County to keep Severe Drought as status quo, despite near record monthly heat. This included coastal sections of the county.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in Willacy County on March 3rd, and would continue through month's end.  Just enough rainfall fell at various times during the period to keep this condition as status quo, despite near record monthly heat.  Conditions were similar along the coast.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in Cameron County on March 3rd, and would continue through March 30th due to a combination of mainly much above average temperatures and limited rainfall - all which contributed to high evaporation rates for this time of year.

Severe (D2) Drought arrived in Cameron County on March 3rd, and would continue through March 30th due to a combination of mainly much above average temperatures and limited rainfall - all which contributed to high evaporation rates for this time of year. Similar conditions prevailed along the coast.

Severe (D2) drought expanded into southern Hidalgo County on March 3rd, and would continue through March 16th. Impacts on dryland crops (not planted) and cattle (additional water hauling) became more acute by mid-month with the lack of rain and near record heat overall.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions expanded to cover all of Starr County on March 3rd, and would continue through March 16th. Reports from the USDA Farm Service Extension office in Edinburg mentioned an increase in water hauling for cattle on ranches across the county by the end of the period.

Extreme (D3) Drought conditions expanded to cover all but the northeast corner of Jim Hogg County (which remained at Severe (D2) levels) on March 3rd; these conditions would continue through March 16th.
Extreme (D3) Drought conditions expanded to cover all of Zapata County on March 3rd; these conditions would continue through March 16th.

Extreme (D3) Drought would expand to cover all but the eastern sliver of northern Hidalgo County on March 17th.  A local heavy rain event  of more than 4 inches near McCook (southwestern portion) late on March 20th would briefly reduce drought by one category (to Severe, or D2) in the southwest corner of the area on March 24th, which would continue through the end of the month.  The worsening conditions overall forced many dryland crops to a delayed spring planting.

Extreme (D3) Drought would expand to cover the western half of southern Hidalgo County on March 17th.  A local heavy rain event  of more than 4 inches near McCook (northwestern corner) late on March 20th would briefly reduce drought by one category (to Severe, or D2) in the northwest corner of the area on March 24th, which would continue through the end of the month.  The worsening conditions overall forced many dryland crops to a delayed spring planting.

Extreme (D3) Drought would expand into southwestern Brooks County on March 17th, and continue through the end of the month.  The rest of the county would remain at Extreme (D2) Drought, with the exception of a small sliver in the east-center portion of the county, which held at Moderate (D1) drought due to just enough rainfall from occasional rains that stretched into Kenedy County.

Exceptional (D4) Drought developed in extreme western Jim Hogg County, with Extreme (D3) Drought expanding into all but the northeast sliver of the county on March 17th.  D3 would cover that area as well - all courtesy of much above average temperatures, little to no rainfall, and periods of low afternoon humidity. Anecdotal evidence from the USDA Farm Services Extension office in Edinburg suggested continue water hauling for cattle ranches in the county.

Exceptional (D4) Drought developed in all but the extreme southern corner of Zapata County and northwest section (north of San Ygnacio) on March 17th, and would continue through month's end, expanding to all but the northwest corner which remained at Extreme (D3) levels.

Exceptional (D4) Drought developed in the northwest corner of the county on March 24th, and continued through the end of the month.  The remainder of the county remained at Extreme (D3) levels, with a sliver of Severe (D2) along the Hidalgo County line north of US 83.

Extreme (D3) level drought developed in southeast Cameron County, from west of Brownsville to Rio Hondo and points east, on March 31st due to continued lack of rainfall and record to near-record warm to hot temperatures.  Grasslands turned to straw while trees filled out as spring continued.

Extreme (D3) level drought developed in southeast Cameron County, including all populated coastal communities (South Padre, Port Isabel, and Laguna Vista) on March 31st due to continued lack of rainfall and record to near-record warm to hot temperatures.  Grasslands turned to straw while trees filled out as spring continued.
Three inches of rain fell in about 2 hours from a slow moving thunderstorm in McCook.  Radar estimated 3 to 5 inches in the area from McCook northwest to the Hidalgo/Starr County line.

As a strong supercell moved through the southwestern corner of the county on the morning of April 4th, rainfall amounts where sufficient to reduce Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to Severe (D2) Drought conditions along that area, allowing Severe (D2) Drought conditions to prevail through most of the county starting on April 7th. Additional rains on April 9/10 helped care a bit more of the Severe Drought away in the southern and northwestern part of the county by April 14th, with a combination of Moderate (D1) to Severe Drought prevailing until month's end.

A strong supercell along with scattered showers on the morning of April 4th brought some much needed relief to much of Jim Hogg County. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions were confined to the southwestern third of the county with a tiny sliver of Exceptional (D4) Drought remaining at the far southwestern corner starting on April 7th. The remaining two thirds of the county was generally characterized by Severe (D2) Drought.

A strong, long-lasting supercell cut across the northern portion of Hidalgo county early in the morning on April 4th, bringing some much needed rain to the area. Rainfall amounts were sufficient to drop the Extreme (D3) Drought conditions in Northern Hidalgo County to Severe (D2) Drought conditions starting on April 7th.  Slight improvements to Moderate (D1) Drought developed after additional rainfall on April 10th, but most of the area remained in Severe conditions through the end of the month.

A long-lasting, strong supercell moved through Willacy County on the morning of April 4th, bringing much needed rainfall along with some hail and damaging winds. Rainfall was sufficient to drop the Severe (D2) Drought conditions across the northern half of the county, leaving only the bottom half in Severe (D2) Drought through the end of the month into May.

A long-lasting, strong supercell skirted along the southern edge of Kenedy County on the morning of April 4th, bringing much needed rainfall to the area. Rainfall was sufficient to drop the Severe (D2) Drought conditions across the southern half of the county, leaving only the top third in Severe (D2) Drought through the end of the month into May.

The supercell that moved through the northern portion of Zapata County on the night of April 9th brought sufficient rainfall to reduce the drought severity to Severe (D2) Drought and even Moderate (D1) Drought conditions beginning April 14th. However, the lower half of the county received very little rain and remained in Extreme (D3) and mostly Exceptional (D4) Drought.

A supercell moved into Starr County on the night of April 9th, bringing sufficient rainfall to reduce the severity of the drought to mostly Severe (D2) conditions across most of the county. Slivers of Exceptional (D4) and Extreme (D3) Drought persisted along the border of Zapata County and a small section of Extreme (D3) Drought persisted along the Rio Grande where little to no rainfall fell.

A supercell that moved into Jim Hogg County from the west on the night of April 9th along with some trailing showers and thunderstorms on April 10th brought some beneficial rainfall to most of the county. On April 14th, Severe (D2) Drought was reduced to only the southwestern third of the county with the remainder of the county in Moderate (D1) Drought.  These conditions held through the remainder of the month.

Rainfall during mid April was sufficient to improve drought conditions in Zapata County, dropping the area of Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought starting April 21st and continuing through the end of the month.

Rainfall during mid April was sufficient to improve drought conditions in Starr County, dropping the area of Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought starting April 21st and continuing through the end of the month.

A mini-supercell thunderstorm rolled through central and southeastern Willacy County a little more than an hour after sunrise, and produced damaging winds near San Perlita and on nearby ranches around 830 AM CDT. One residence in San Perlita, fully exposed to the northwest, sustained significant damage when its poorly constructed roof lifted off.  The residence was a mobile home with a separate addition on a pier/block foundation. Nearby damage was noted along an 5.28 mile stretch of State Highway 186, with more than a dozen wooden power poles broken, uprooted, or leaning. Nearly all of the broken poles showed notable rot at the breakpoint, and others were only anchored in shallow soil. In total, county Emergency Management mentioned a total of 26 poles were damaged.  The survey revealed a range of estimated wind speeds from 61 to 70 mph.

events.event_narrative: As the long track supercell pushed off the coastline of northeastern Cameron County, the Realitos platform reported a wind gust of 41 knots.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted in northern Cameron County, with a slice of Extreme (D3) Drought from Brownsville to Los Fresnos in southern Cameron County, through the month of April 2020, as welcome rainfall for other parts of the Rio Grande Valley and Deep S. Texas missed most of the county - though just enough fell to preclude any worsening until May.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted in northeastern Cameron County, including the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge through Arroyo City, with Extreme (D3) Drought at points south, including Port Isabel and South Padre Island, through the month of April 2020, as welcome rainfall for other parts of the Rio Grande Valley and Deep S. Texas missed most of the county - though just enough fell to preclude any worsening until May.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted in Willacy County into early April, before a single thunderstorm dropped more than 2 inches in and around Raymondville to San Perlita on the 4th, which would help improve conditions across the northern half of the county by April 7th.

Severe (D2) Drought persisted in Coastal Willacy County into early April, before a single thunderstorm dropped more than 2 inches in and around Raymondville to San Perlita on the 4th. This system would continue and affect all of Coastal Willacy County, which would be removed from D2 drought on April 7th and continue for the rest of the month.

Severe (D2) Drought would continue across northern and southern Kenedy County into the first few days of April, before a fast moving thunderstorm dropped more than 1 inch of rainfall over the southern half of the county, which would improve drought conditions there by April 7th.

Severe (D2) Drought would continue across northern and southern Coastal Kenedy County into the first few days of April, before a fast moving thunderstorm dropped more than 1 inch of rainfall over the southern half of the area, which would improve drought conditions there by April 7th.

Extreme (D3) Drought would persist in most of northern Hidalgo County until showers and thunderstorms tracked across the area on April 3rd and 4th, dropping an estimated 1 to 2 inches and improving the D3 drought by one category by April 7th.

Extreme (D3) Drought would persist across southwestern Hidalgo County, with Severe (D2) drought elsewhere in populated southern Hidalgo County, for most of the first half of April 2020.  Rainfall of around an inch on April 9th would remove the sliver of Extreme (D3) drought for the April 14th monitor.

Severe (D2) Drought covered most of Brooks County, with a sliver of Extreme (D3) Drought in the southwestern part of the county to begin April. This sliver would be eliminated by April 7th, courtesy of early morning thunderstorms on April 4th that dropped over an inch of welcome rainfall.

Extreme (D3) Drought covered nearly all of Jim Hogg County, with a sliver of Exceptional (D4) Drought in the westernmost portion against Zapata County, and a very small area of Severe (D2) conditions in the far northeast corner of the county, through April 3rd.  On the 3rd and 4th, enough rain fell from strong thunderstorms (mainly on the morning of the 4th) to remove the D4 area (except for a very small corner of the southwest portion) and reduce the coverage of D3 to just the southwest half of the county.

Extreme (D3) Drought covered all but a pocket of the eastern/northeastern sliver of the county (D2, or Severe Drought there), and the far western part of the county (Exceptional, or D4 Drought) through most of the first half of April, as the heaviest rainfall associated with thunderstorms on April 4th generally stayed north of the county.

Exceptional (D4) Drought covered all but the northwestern quarter of Zapata County into early April, before torrential rains associated with thunderstorms overnight on April 3rd into the early morning of April 4th dropped between 1.5 and more than 5 inches in a slice of the northern part of the county, bringing a one category improvement in these areas.  Southern Zapata would remain Exceptional a bit longer into April as those rains missed this region.

A long-lasting, strong supercell moved through Willacy County on the morning of April 4th, bringing much needed rainfall along with some hail and damaging winds. Rainfall was sufficient to drop the Severe (D2) Drought conditions across the northern half of the coastal sections, leaving only the bottom half in Severe (D2) Drought through the end of the month into May.

Rainfall from a fast-moving supercell thunderstorm in the southern half of coastal Kenedy County dropped 1.5 to 2 inches of rainfall early on April 4th, improving drought from Severe (D2) to Moderate (D1) while leaving the northern half of the coastline unchanged.  These conditions would remain through the remainder of April.

Additional pockets of rainfall on April 9th and 10th in southern Hidalgo County removed the small area of Extreme Drought in the southwest corner of the county, with Severe (D2) Drought continuing for the remainder of April beginning on the 14th.

The Deputy Emergency Management Coordinator, along with the public, reported several instances of minor wind damage in Zapata and Siesta Shores just to the south during the mid evening of April 28, 2020. Damage included several felled limbs of mesquite trees in Zapata City park, a poorly constructed awning blown down to an recreational vehicle on the west side of the city, and a power pole leaning along Swope Lane in Siesta Shores. Based on other recent wind events in the City, wind speeds were estimated to be just below severe (58 mph) levels.

The observation platform at Brazos Santiago, just inshore of the entrance to the Brownsville Ship Channel and along the south side of the Isla Blanca jetty, recorded a wind gusts of 50.54 knots at 1136 AM local time.  No damage was reported on the southern tip of South Padre Island.

Rainfall mostly associated with the supercell event during the morning of April 4th brought some minor drought relief to Zapata County at the beginning of April. However, the bottom third of the county remained in Exceptional (D4) Drought, with the middle third in Extreme (D3) Drought, and the top third in Severe (D2) Drought starting on April 7th. Zapata County reported poor pasture and rangeland conditions at the beginning of April, with some bare pastures. Producers in Zapata continued to sell off cattle or feed hay and cubes.

With April temperatures remaining well above normal and limited rainfall the last week of April, the southeastern half of Cameron County remained in Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, while the rest of the county remained in Severe (D2) Drought conditions.  These conditions would expand a bit soon after the start of the month, then prevail deep into May.
With April temperatures remaining well above normal and limited rainfall the last week of April, the southwestern half of Willacy County remained in Severe (D2) Drought conditions.

A rapidly developing severe thunderstorm crossed the Rio Grande into Zapata County shortly after midnight on May 26. Widespread damage was surveyed across the city with more than two dozen single wide mobile and manufactured homes having partial or total roof damage. Nearly all of the critically damaged infrastructure was of poor and older construction. More than a dozen wooden utility poles were leaning or broken, most of which had wet or rotting bases. A quick-developing severe thunderstorm formed in the farm and ranchlands of extreme southwestern Hidalgo County along the Starr County line around 530 PM on June 18th, then raced through Sullivan City before crossing the Rio Grande into northern Tamaulipas, Mexico. The storm produced damaging straight-line winds at a colonia in unincorporated Hidalgo County just north of the city limits.  Nine residences had partial or total roof damage, three recreational vehicles were flipped, and at least three dozen mesquite trees had a combination of large limbs blown down or were broken/cracked at the base.  All damage was facing to the south or south-southwest, in the direction of the storm motion.  Each residence was a manufactured home or mobile trailer; one was uninhabited, and one was tilted after being blown off of its pier/block foundation with no visible anchorage. All of the damaged buildings had poor to very poor roof connections.||Each of the recreational vehicles was not anchored properly to the ground. Two were older and rusted, but a third was newer but only sitting on jack pallets.  The third vehicle weighed more than three tons, and was a key reason for the top wind speed estimate of 70 mph.  A nearby older construction manufactured single-wide home was undamaged, and nearby power lines/poles and mesquite trees had no visible damage.

events.event_narrative: As Hurricane Hanna passed over the Lower Texas coastal waters on July 25th, buoy 42020 reported sustained winds and frequent gusts to hurricane strength for a period of a little more than 2 hours, with the max reported gust recorded at 73 knots. Tropical storm force winds preceded and followed this period of hurricane-force winds. The first onset of tropical storm force winds started at 4:50 CST on July 25th and then persisted for almost 6 hours, before a brief lull and then the onset of hurricane force winds. Following the hurricane-force winds, tropical storm-force persisted for almost 4 more hours, ending at 20:00 CST.

Hurricane Hanna moved across the western Gulf of Mexico and made landfall on the mid-Kenedy County coastline at around 5 PM Central Time Saturday, July 25th, carrying sustained 90 mph winds with gusts over 100 mph in a small portion of the inner eye wall. While there aren't many observations in Kenedy County during this event, Buoy RSJT2 is just off the coastline in the Laguna Madre that borders this county and can be used as a reasonable proxy. Peak winds reached 71 mph with a gust to 103 mph. With observations from RSJT2, along with radar analysis, it is reasonable to assume that Kenedy County experienced hurricane-force winds around 14:00 CST to 16:30 CST. At this time, sustained property and crop damage costs are unknown for this area.

Hurricane Hanna moved across the western Gulf of Mexico and made landfall on the mid-Kenedy County coastline at around 5 PM Central Time Saturday, July 25th, carrying sustained 90 mph winds with gusts over 100 mph in a small portion of the inner eye wall. Based on the proxy observations, sustained winds likely reached near hurricane force (71 mph). With observations from RSJT2, along with radar analysis, it is reasonable to assume that portions of Willacy County experienced hurricane-force winds around 14:30 CST to 16:30 CST. ||Damage surveys revealed significant property and flora damage in Port Mansfield. |Poorly built or poorly anchored structures sustained the heaviest damage, including several flipped recreational vehicles and several partially or totally destroyed mobile trailer homes.  Near Laguna Madre, all moderately constructed homes in one neighborhood had varying damage to roofs/shingles, fences, siding, and outbuildings.  A few boat garage doors were blown out along bayside entries.  Dozens of tree limbs were blown down and several uprooted, and at least a dozen power poles were snapped or leaning along SR 186 in and near Port Mansfield.||NCEI's new report as of the end of 2020, totaled Hanna as a 1.1 billion dollar damage event, so total property damage was updated in early 2021.  Public Assistance property damage estimates, mainly due to wind, were around $127.6 thousand, and NCEI's estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts) was $59.85 million for coastal Willacy County.

Hurricane Hanna moved across the western Gulf of Mexico and made landfall on the mid-Kenedy County coastline at around 5 PM Central Time Saturday, July 25th, carrying sustained 90 mph winds with gusts over 100 mph in a small portion of the inner eye wall. While there aren't many observations in Willacy County during this event, Buoy RSJT2 is just off the coastline in the Laguna Madre just north of Willacy County and can be used as a reasonable proxy. Based on the proxy observations, sustained winds likely reached near hurricane force (71 mph).With observations from RSJT2, along with radar analysis, it is reasonable to assume that portions of Willacy County experienced hurricane-force winds around 14:30 CST to 16:30 CST. ||Substantial and widespread wind damage was noted in and near Raymondville.  A damage survey estimated wind gusts in Raymondville to have reached 75 to 80 mph during the period of eyewall passage, though strong tropical storm force gusts continued well into the evening and overnight of July 25/26 as the back side feeder bands continued to pummel the county from Raymondville to Lyford to Lasara and Sebastian. A peak gust of 80 mph was recorded in neighboring Hidalgo County, a few miles southwest of the Hidalgo/Willacy County line, at 1005 PM CST July 25. ||Damage included roof, shingle, and some wall damage to several dozen homes in Raymondville, as well as damage to farm buildings on the east side of town.  100 percent of the county was without power during the peak of the storm, due to dozens of snapped or leaning power poles and downed lines.  Thousands of trees/limbs were snapped and dozens uprooted. A stadium light stanchion was ripped out of the ground by an eddy wind at Raymondville High School. Similar but lesser damage was seen in Lyford and Sebastian, where peak winds may have been closer to tropical storm force.   Final individual assistance and insured property damage estimates for inland Willacy County were provided at the end of 2020 by NCEI. Local storm data experts partitioned the total damage estimate between the affected counties, and the portion for inland Willacy was $139.65 million. Public assistance damage estimates were $2.59 million. ||Sustained crop damage costs associated with these damaging winds is estimated to be 34.6 million - a combination of citrus and sugar cane.

Tropical Storm-force winds ravaged northern Cameron County from mid afternoon on July 25th until just after midnight on July 26th.  Strongest winds occurred during the evening of July 25th, when the southern and eastern eyewall clipped the region along and north of Interstate 2 between Harlingen/Rio Hondo and La Feria north to the Willacy County line.  Measured and estimated wind gusts in these areas were near hurricane force (65 mph) with sustained winds peaking between 40 and 50 mph.  Harlingen/Rio Grande Valley International Airport reported a peak gust to 63 mph before taking a power loss. ||The slow movement of the inner core of Hanna allowed minor wind damage to occur in this area, with at least one hundred trees losing large limbs along with power lines and several power poles snapped or bent. Minor damage also occurred to poorly built structures along the IH-2 corridor as well as along the IH-69E corridor from Harlingen/San Benito northward.  This included a number of fences blown down and a roof blown off a shed near La Feria. At the storm's peak, an estimated 50 thousand electric customers were without power.  NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts) was $99.75 million for inland Cameron County. Public Assistance dollar values were estimated to be $1.88 million.||Crop damage was also significant, with sugar cane snapped in many fields and young fruit being blown off citrus trees, which also sustained damage.  Estimated dollar value loss based on reports from Texas Agrilife in late summer was $25.9 million in Cameron County.

Intermittent Tropical Storm-force winds affected coastal Cameron County from late afternoon on July 25th until the pre-dawn hours of July 26th.  Strongest winds occurred in two segments: First, during the initial approach of the southwestern edge of the eyewall between mid afternoon and early evening on the 25th, then again overnight to just before daybreak on the 26th in strong southeasterly feeder bands that pushed gusts  to 55 mph. Peak sustained winds reached 46 mph at 252 AM CST with a peak gust of 55 mph occurring at 253 AM CST. Gusts over 50 mph also occurred during the afternoon in the southwest eyewall.||Crop damage in the coastal portion of Cameron County was included with the total for Cameron County overall, listed in the Cameron entry.  Property damage was limited in coastal Cameron County as strongest winds favored the northern portion, where population is much less and infrastructure tends to be better built. Details were not available as of this writing.

The slowly weakening inner eyewall of Hurricane Hanna slid across southern and central Brooks County during the evening of July 25th, producing peak sustained winds (though incomplete) of 34 mph with a peak gust of 53 mph at the Brooks County Airport east of Falfurrias. Stronger winds, likely sustained at 40 to 45 mph with estimated gusts to 55 or 60 mph, were likely over the southern third of the county which experienced the more persistent rains and wind in the eyewall.  A storm survey conducted in southern Brooks County found dozens of large tree limbs down, but no significant structural damage, near Encino.

The slowly weakening inner eyewall of Hurricane Hanna eased into northern Hidalgo County during the early evening of July 25th and would exit a few hours after midnight on the 26th.  The Automated Weather Observing System 11 miles north of Edinburg reported a peak sustained wind of 45 mph with a peak gust of 54 mph soon after 6 PM CST on the 25th before the sensor stopped reporting.  Farther east, near the Willacy County line, a sensor reported a peak gust to 80 mph (Texas Agriscience Center, just a few miles from the Willacy County line) as the southern inner eyewall crossed at 1005 PM CST - just on the edge of the Northern Hidalgo zone area.||A NWS Storm Survey team investigated some of the area and found dozens of large tree limbs blown down along IH 69C/US 281. No significant structural damage was reported along the route, though not all areas were surveyed and it's likely that there may have been additional rural damage between San Manuel and Raymondville along and near SR 186. Based on NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts) there was likely $33.25 million in damage for Northern Hidalgo.

The slowly weakening inner eyewall of Hurricane Hanna eased into southern Hidalgo County along the Willacy County line during the evening of July 25th and would exit the southwest corner of the county just before daybreak on the 26th.  Widespread wind damage was noted in more than a dozen colonias from near Elsa/Edcouch to north of Edinburg (San Carlos to Doolittle), including damage to roofs, walls, shingles, and windows to dozens of poorly constructed/anchored homes severely damaged and at least a dozen (that were seen on survey) were demolished. Hundreds of trees and dozens of power poles were damaged (leaning or snapped), and power outages across this area were likely to be around 150 thousand in total. NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts) was $299.25 million for Southern Hidalgo County, and public assistance dollars due to wind were estimated at $5.7 million. ||An automated sensor several miles northeast of Elsa (Texas AgriScience Center platform) reported a peak gust to 80 mph as the southern inner eyewall crossed at 1005 PM CST. Peak winds at McAllen/Miller Airport were 39 mph (at 245 CST on the 26th), but a peak gust of 60 mph was recorded at 928 PM CST on the 25th.  Additional gusts between 40 and 50 mph occurred through the night as the eastern eyewall of the weakened system (a tropical storm) oozed through southwest Hidalgo County. In general, peak winds were measured/estimated at 65 to 80 mph in the area near the Willacy County line, and 60 to 65 mph in the McAllen/Mission/Sullivan City area.||Wind damaged crops was also common in the Rio Grande Valley's breadbasket with an estimated $29.2 million in citrus and snapped sugar cane alone, based on an initial report from Texas Agrilife.||While there were no direct fatalities with Hanna in southern Hidalgo County, there were five indirect deaths in the recovery days following Hanna. Four in one family from carbon monoxide poisoning on July 27th, and one elderly man who fell from a ladder while attempting roof repairs on July 28th.

Hurricane Hanna weakened to a Tropical Storm as it moved into Hidalgo and Starr County before exiting the US into northwest Tamaulipas and northern Nuevo Leon, Mexico, during the post-daybreak hours of July 26th.  Though weakening, the well-organized and large cyclone maintained tropical storm force wind gusts measured as high as 64 mph in northeast Starr County during the pre-dawn hours of the 26th. The Remote Automated Weather Station at Falcon Lake in southwestern Starr reported a peak gust to 52 mph at 111 AM CST, also on the 26th.||Local ranchers reported an unknown number of large limbs blown down, along with a few barns pushed off their moorings and an unknown number of buildings with shingle damage, in the eastern half of the county.  A tin roof was blown off a service station in Roma. NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts) was $32.5 million for Starr County.

A second round of rainfall dropped an estimated 2 to 5 inches of rain in about two hours between la Feria and Santa Rosa, exacerbating ongoing flooding in western Cameron County and leaving pockets of 2 to 4 feet of water in roads, neighborhoods, and ditches.  Public assistance property damage is listed in the episode for Hurricane Hanna, as it was the trigger event for the continuation of the flooding. Crop damage (Cotton, other dryland crops) due to the heavy rain is listed in the episode for Hurricane Hanna.

Storm surge generated by Hurricane Hanna pushed tide levels above ground in excess of 3 feet along coastal Kenedy County beginning by mid afternoon of July 25th and likely continuing through landfall at approximately 4 PM local standard time on the mid-Kenedy County coast along the Padre Island National Seashore (PINS). Though high water marks had not been specifically provided on PINS at the time of this writing, ground and aerial surveys suggested water levels above ground may have exceeded 4 feet above normally dry ground on portions of PINS in Kenedy County.  Levels up to 5.48 feet above normally dry ground at the shoreline (Mean Higher High Water) were noted along the Coastal Bend just north of Kenedy County at the north entrance to PINS. Though Hanna did not create any known new cuts into the Barrier Island of Kenedy County, visual evidence from ground and aerial post-storm surveys indicated eight rearranged washover channels from the combination of storm surge and breaking waves.  Most dunes were eroded to varying levels on the Kenedy portion of PINS.||Along Laguna Madre, tides ran out on northwest flow ahead of landfall, but rose sharply on strong southeast to south flow post-landfall. At the Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network platform at Rincon del San Jose, near the land cut about one-third the distance north of Port Mansfield, return flow pushed water levels to an estimated 3.43 feet above Mean Sea Level (MSL; note:  an equivalent value based on the MHHW datum was not available) at 418 AM CST July 26th.  The high water levels - based on 2.5 feet or greater MSL as proxy, began at 8 PM CST July 25th and continued through 11 PM CST July 26th before slowly receding. ||Other than severe beach erosion, there was little known property damage due to Storm Surge in largely unpopulated coastal Kenedy County. However, damage estimates to fishing huts and other coastal properties as calculated from NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts) was $11,866 for coastal Kenedy County.

Storm surge generated by Hurricane Hanna pushed water and breaking waves deep into the dunes in the Willacy County portion of the Padre Island National Seashore (PINS), mainly between mile marker 55 and 60 to the Mansfield cut.  There was likely water deep into the dunes farther south in coastal Willacy County, but levels are unknown.  A sharp cutoff to significant surge/coastal flooding was likely near the Cameron County line, where strengthening westerly flow held sea water from reaching into the dunes after the morning high tide on July 25th.  Though high water marks had not been specifically provided on the Willacy County section of PINS at the time of this writing, ground and aerial surveys along with video taken just prior to landfall in Kenedy County suggested water levels above ground may have exceeded 3 feet above normally dry ground in this area. Dunes were severely eroded north of the Mansfield Cut.||Along Laguna Madre, tides ran out on northwest flow ahead of landfall, but rose sharply on strong southeast to south flow post-landfall. This produced another surge event on the 26th...see the second event listing for Coastal Willacy for details. ||Other than severe beach erosion, there was little known property damage due to Storm Surge in largely unpopulated coastal Willacy County north of the Mansfield cut. However, damage estimates for fishing huts and other coastal properties was calculated by local storm data experts using NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts) and was $11,866 for coastal Willacy County.

Along Laguna Madre in northern coastal Willacy County, the approach of Hurricane Hanna just 15 miles north of the county line produced strong outbound tide on strong northwest winds. As the eye moved onshore and passed the longitude of Laguna Madre, winds quickly shifted to the south with strong tropical storm force gusts, and waters rose rapidly.  Peak tide (2.62 feet above Mean Sea Level) occurred at Port Mansfield at 1136 AM CST July 26th.  Based on these conditions, as well as survey results that showed return water about 25 yards into marsh grass along Laguna Madre in Port Mansfield, it was possible that 3 feet of water above normally high ground occurred at some point between 10 AM CST and 6 PM CST on July 26th, all associated with the backside circulation around Hanna, which had weakened to a tropical storm (but still with a large envelope) in northeast Mexico. ||Other than flattened marsh grass, no visible property damage was seen due to surge water in the town of Port Mansfield based on an NWS storm survey conducted on July 27th.

Hurricane Hanna made landfall along the Kenedy county|coast on the evening of July 25, 2020. As Hanna pushed inland, its|eastern outer rain bands produced several areas of rotation. The Brownsville radar briefly detected|a debris signature as it moved northward toward the Brownsville|airport. Here, an|empty tractor trailer was moved on an angle into a stand of trees, |an unanchored travel trailer was flipped, a storage shed was flattened,|and several mesquite trees lost large limbs. Reports of high flowing water blocking passage along SR-186 just west of Port Mansfield were received during the evening of July 25th, when feeder bands into the eastern semicircle of then-Tropical Storm Hanna dropped an additional 4 to 8 inches of rainfall into central and eastern Willacy County. Other flooding was noted in poor drainage locations of Raymondville, and there was an unknown amount of field flooding in eastern Willacy County due to an estimated 11 to 13 inches of rainfall through the duration of the event, which began during the mid afternoon of July 25th. ||Water depths of 2 to 3 feet were likely in some areas, though specifics were unknown.  A known poor drainage location at an apartment complex in south Raymondville had up to 3 feet of water depth in parking areas, blocking access to the facility.  Other flood related damage in central Willacy County was minimal. In Port Mansfield, where nearly 15 inches of rain fell, including 9 inches in initial inner eyewall bands on July 25th, sandy soil and antecedent dry conditions kept flooding to a minimum. ||Crop damage from flooding rain was significant in Willacy County, including a heavy loss of cotton lint (or bolls) which were destroyed by the flood.  Estimates suggest that $36 million in cotton crop was lost from Hanna's flooding rains.||Property damage from flood waters was calculated using NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts). Afternoon and early evening rains of 2 to 3 inches fell across the IH-2 corridor of Cameron County, from La Feria to east of Harlingen, and saturated soils ahead of the torrential rains that were to come later in the evening as the southern and eastern eyewall pulled copious tropical moisture into northern Cameron County after sunset.  Estimated rainfall of 4 to 6+ inches by mid evening began to produce known flash flooding in La Feria and Harlingen, with two water rescues conducted in La Feria just after 10 PM CST.  Despite lighter rains, flash flooding would continue due to poor drainage situations, especially in the La Feria/Santa Rosa area.  A broad south to north feeder band added another 2 to 4+ inches of rainfall to the storm totals during the pre-dawn hours, and light rains would continue to around noon in western Cameron County before ending.  Note:  Estimated flood-related public assistance property damage is provided in this episode.  However, the total damage would also include another 3 to 5 inches that would fall in an unrelated tropical band of torrential rain during the evening of July 27th.||Flooding would decimate the cotton (lint) crop and other unharvested dryland crops to an estimated value of $27.1 million.  Public assistance property damage as of this writing from flooding rainfall was estimated to be at $3.3 million. Additional public and individual assistance dollar damages, as well as insured damages, from flood waters was calculated using NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts). Total property damage from flood waters for Cameron County was $9.968 million.

Trusted reports from Facebook indicated 1 to 2 feet of standing water in some neighborhood streets in Los Fresnos during a period of outer south to north moving feeder bands well east of the center of Tropical Storm Hanna which was moving into northern Mexico south of Starr County at around the same time.  An estimated 3 to 5 inches additional rainfall fell during this period, with measured and estimated storm totals of 6 to 9 inches in southeastern Cameron County.  No significant flooding was reported, and any property damage was unknown. ||Some of the cotton crop (lint, or bolls) and perhaps other crop was flattened by the torrential rains in fields between San Benito and Bayview.  Exact dollar damage estimates for these fields was unknown; an estimated total is provided in the Flash Flood Entry for this episode in Cameron County.

Torrential rains associated with both the eastern and southern eyewall (late evening of July 25th) and persistent southeast to northwest feeder bands that followed (after midnight through late afternoon of July 26th) created widespread flash and areal flooding across many portions of populated Hidalgo County as then-Tropical Storm Hanna slowly moved from Hidalgo County into Starr County, Texas, and eventually into northern Mexico on July 26th.  Heaviest rainfall directly associated with Hanna and the feeder bands fell in the Mission-South McAllen-Pharr region, where measured and estimated rainfall of 10 to 15 inches produced 18 inches to 4 feet of water depth and required a number of water rescues during the prolonged period of flooding.  A few specific reports included:|*Numerous water rescues in the City of Mission (pre-dawn hours, July 26)|*Numerous streets with up to 2 feet of water depth in Weslaco (8 AM July 26 report)|*Canal overtopping banks and flooding roads in South McAllen on S. 23rd Street (830 AM July 26th)|*3 feet of water, rising, in Mission (830 AM report)|*Water entering homes in southeast Edinburg, estimated just after sunrise July 26||An unknown number of properties were damaged by floodwaters, but dozens if not hundreds of vehicles had varying levels of floodwater inside them. In total, there were at least 200 persons and several dozen pets rescued/evacuated by State of Texas rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, to name two.  ||Public and individual assistance dollar damages, as well as insured damages, from flood waters was calculated using NCEI's total dollar damage estimate (divided among the affected counties by local storm data experts). Total property damage from flood waters for Cameron County was $9.968 million. In addition, an initial public assistance value was available - subject to further updates - and was estimated to be $7.99 million.  Please note that a second round of flooding rain on July 27th exacerbated the ongoing conditions but that value is folded into this episode for brevity.  Crop damage due to the flooding was estimated to be 27.1 million, heavily weighted by damage to cotton but also some damage to other dryland crops. ||Final public,  individual assistance, and insured damage was likely to range somewhere from $200 to $500 million when all data are counted later in 2020 and beyond.

High standing water due to a total of 7 to 10 inches of rainfall that fell directly from Hurricane/Tropical Storm Hanna from late on July 25th through early afternoon on July 26th continued to close roads and stand in neighborhoods, fields, and ditches through the end of July. An additional 2 to 3 inches fell during the late afternoon and early evening of July 27th from an unrelated tropical rain band, leaving total rainfall of 10 to 15 inches in the area.||A combination of the heavy rain with known drainage capacity issues in the form of pumps, pipes, and retention kept water levels ranging from one to three feet deep on several Farm-to-Market and County Roads in the southwest corner of Willacy County from near Sebastian to north of Lyford to the eastern Hidalgo County line.  Fields saw similar water levels, and low lying neighborhoods had high water near homes, with spot-built farm homes seeing some water inside. ||Note:  Public Assistance (which includes damage to roads and bridges) and Crop damage is listed on the Flash Flood event in southwestern Willacy County for brevity. High standing water due to a total of 7 to 10 inches of rainfall that fell directly from Hurricane/Tropical Storm Hanna from late on July 25th through early afternoon on July 26th continue to close roads and stand in neighborhoods, fields, and ditches through the end of July between the east side of Edinburg and the Cameron/Willacy/Hidalgo County line. An additional 3 to 5 inches fell during the late afternoon and early evening of July 27th from an unrelated tropical rain band, leaving total rainfall of 10 to 15 inches in the area.  Conditions began to improve on the west end of the flood area by July 30th, including areas west of North Donna.||A combination of the heavy rain with known drainage capacity issues in the form of pumps, pipes, and retention kept water levels ranging from 18 inches to four feet deep on at least a dozen roads, including portions of SR 107 into La Villa as well as neighborhoods along and east of Veterans Blvd. from Pharr to east of Edinburg out to Elsa/Edcouch and near Monte Alto.   Fields saw similar water levels, and low lying neighborhoods had high water near homes, with spot-built farm homes seeing some water inside. This included a number of colonias where streets remained flooded with 1 to 3 feet of water for days after the rain ended.  For a third straight summer, the Las Brisas neighborhood in northeast Weslaco had 1 to 3 feet of water in streets and curbsides, with at least two homes with 6 inches to a foot of water inside. | |Another round of torrential rains on August 1st would keep the high waters going a bit longer  mainly in areas along and east of FM 1015 (Weslaco to Elsa and points east) before dry weather allowed all water to recede. ||Note:  Public Assistance (which includes damage to roads and bridges) and Crop damage is listed on the Flash Flood event in western Cameron County for brevity. Individual assistance and insured damage from flooding in this area was likely to be in the millions of dollars.  A value of nearly $23 million was added for privately insured damage, as reported through the National Flood Insurance Program through FEMA, to the flash flood entry in Hidalgo County.

Strong and gusty winds along the Federal Highway 77 corridor developed during the late morning of March 2nd, and continued periodically through the night and into the afternoon of March 3rd.  The strongest winds, occurring shortly after noon on the 2nd, reached toward the coast, with peak sustained wind of 37 mph, gusting to 48 mph, at Bayview/Laguna Heights.

Strong winds developed along the Federal Highway 77 corridor during the late morning and afternoon of March 2nd, and extended west into central Hidalgo County.  These winds continued overnight and into the early morning of the 3rd, and were followed by another round of gusty winds behind the cold front later on the 3rd. The strongest winds, occurring just after noon on the 2nd, likely caused power outages to thousands of customers across the populated Lower Rio Grande Valley, including southern and central Hidalgo County. A wind gust of 46 mph was recorded at McAllen/Miller Airport, with sustained winds of 37 mph.

The Burns Ranch Fire, which began along the four county line of Jim Hogg, Starr, Brooks, and Hidalgo County, rapidly spread through an estimated 25,600 acres of extreme southern and southwestern Brooks County within hours of onset, becoming what would be the most significant wild fire for Deep South Texas of the 2008 season. Severe damage to a summer mansion on the ranch was noted in follow-up reports. The fire forced closure of Federal Highway 281 between Farm-to-Market (FM) Road 490 and FM 755 through most of the night of the 18th.

The Burns Ranch Fire, with origins in extreme southwest Brooks County, spread rapidly southeast into extreme northern Hidalgo County by late afternoon on March 18th, eventually crossing Federal Highway 281 and continuing toward Willacy County.  The fire threatened residences in rural northern Hidalgo County, resulting in the evacuation of at least 200 persons.  In addition, four buildings were destroyed in these areas.  ||Livestock damage was also noted, in the form of 50 head of cattle killed by the blaze, with perhaps hundreds others sustaining injuries. Dozens of volunteer fire departments aided the containment effort, which continued into the 19th and 20th as some locations rekindled briefly.

The Sordito Fire, another large fire ignited during the mid afternoon on March 18th, burned an unknown number of acreage in northern Brooks County near State Highway 285 and Brooks County Road 214 west of Falfurrias. The fire was contained, but not without threatening five structures, which were saved by the rapid response teams.

An explosively developing wild fire just northwest of Hebbronville, along State Highway 359, quickly blossomed to 10,000 acres, fed by strong wind gusts which may have exceeded 60 mph in some spots according to some accounts. Five homes were threatened and saved, but one barn was damaged.  The Dana Fire was eventually contained during the evening. Local ranchers evacuated livestock and the Jim Hogg Sheriff���s Office issued a voluntary evacuation order. Numerous fire departments from Jim Hogg, Kleberg, Jim Wells, and Webb County, among others, responded.

A 1500 acre fire on State Highway 281 developed as a possible offshoot of the Burns Ranch Fire and threatened ten homes and numerous outbuildings, resulting in some self evacuation. The Texas Department of Transportation responded with three maintainers, and the fire was assumed to be contained late in the evening.

The Encino Fire, which began during the morning of the 19th when north winds ratcheted up above 25 mph and humidity remained near or just below 35 percent, quickly grew to 2525 acres during the day in an area located near Lucero Rd on the east side of Federal Highway 281.  The fire destroyed one outbuilding. Resources worked a back burn to control the fire, and two helicopter tankers provided air support. Numerous fire departments from Brooks, Hidalgo, and neighboring counties aided the containment and control effort. One firefighter was treated for minor injuries due to smoke inhalation at the scene, but soon was released.

Strong to high winds developed along the Federal Highway 77 corridor during the late morning and afternoon of March 2nd, continuing overnight and into the late morning of the 3rd. The strongest winds, occurring just after noon on the 2nd, blew an awning off of a western wear store at 1606 77 Sunset Strip (Business Federal Highway 77) in Harlingen; a sign was also blown down at Valley Vista Mall. Sporadic power outages were also reported in some areas. A wind gust of 55 mph was recorded at Valley International Airport in northeast Harlingen at 1:37 PM CT, and sustained 1 minute winds of 45 mph were also reported at time to be determined.||Sustained winds of 36 mph, with gusts to 42 mph, were reported at the Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport during the early afternoon as well.

The Alta Vista Fire, located near Farm-to-Market (FM) road 1017 20 miles north of La Gloria (Starr County) burned 3000 acres in the Alta Vista Ranch during at least the afternoon and evening of March 3rd.  |No homes or structures were threatened. Several local fire departments and other agencies from Hidalgo, Starr and Jim Hogg County responded.

The La Perla Fire developed rapidly and spread to 1011 acres on the   La Perla Ranch, just 5 miles from the town of San Ygnacio. Mandatory evacuations were ordered for the town by Emergency Management officials. The evacuees went to the Zapata Community Center. Six homes were threatened; one outbuilding was destroyed. The evacuation order was lifted by the 4th as the winds subsided and the fire was contained. Responders included personnel from Zapata County and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Very strong and gusty winds cranked up just before noon along the Federal Highway 77 corridor, reaching near or at 40 mph between Noon and 3:30 PM, along with a peak gust to 54 mph at Valley International Airport at 12:27 PM.  The highest sustained wind was recorded at approximately 2:52 PM CT.  Several power lines were knocked down from Brownsville to Harlingen, and a tree fell onto power lines at 112 Dew Street in Harlingen. It is likely that at least one thousand residents were temporarily without power during the peak wind period.

Strong and gusty winds blew through coastal Cameron and Willacy County during the late morning and afternoon of March 17th.  Winds were just a bit less near the coast, owing to the presence of a marine layer.  However, peak sustained winds of 36 mph were recorded at Bayview/Port Isabel airport at around 1:53 PM CST.

Very strong and gusty winds cranked up just before noon along the Federal Highway 77 corridor, reaching near or at 40 mph between Noon and 3:30 PM, along with a peak gust to 54 mph at Valley International Airport in Harlingen, only about 6 miles south of the Willacy County line, at 12:27 PM.  The highest sustained wind was recorded at approximately 2:52 PM CT.  It is likely that hundreds of residents were temporarily without power during the peak wind period in the county.

Strong and gusty winds blew through coastal Cameron and Willacy County during the late morning and afternoon of March 17th.  Winds were just a bit less near the coast, owing to the presence of a marine layer.  However, peak sustained winds of 36 mph were recorded at Bayview/Port Isabel airport at around 1:53 PM CST, and these winds were likely similar up along the coast of Willacy County as well.
Severe (D2) drought conditions stretched into Brooks County, TX, by March 25th, and continued to worsen through the end of the month.
Severe (D2) drought conditions stretched into Hidalgo County, TX, by March 25th, and continued to worsen through the end of the month.

Severe (D2) drought conditions spread into Jim Hogg and Starr Counties just before mid month, with the drought gradually worsening as the month progressed and rainfall remained virtually nil, along with many windy days with low to moderate humidity.

Severe drought (D2) continued to intensify in Zapata County through March, with extreme drought (D3) conditions edging to the Webb/Zapata County Line by the end of the month. No rainfall and repeated intrusions of windy dry weather exacerbated the conditions heading into April.
Heat indices around McAllen, TX exceeded 111 degrees for a couple of hours starting at 1:50 PM CDT and the MFE ASOS even exceeded 116 degrees for a period of time around 4 PM CDT.

Heat indices in Cameron County exceeded 111 degrees for a couple of hours starting at 1:50 PM CDT and the BRO ASOS even exceeded 114 degrees for a period of time around 3 PM CDT, and HRL topped at 112 degrees around 2 PM CDT.
Heat indices around Zapata, TX exceeded 111 degrees for a couple of hours starting around 4 PM CDT and the APY ASOS even exceeded 115 degrees for a period of time around 5 PM CDT.
Heat indices around McAllen, TX exceeded 111 degrees for a couple of hours starting at 1:50 PM CDT and hovered around 112 degrees for a couple of hours during the afternoon of August 28th.
Hidalgo County Emergency Manager reported flooding into homes in Monte Alto as well as in homes near the intersection of FM2812 and FM493 due to heavy rain.
Cameron County Emergency Manager reported extensive flooding along HWY 107 west of FM2556 due to heavy rain.
Yard and street flooding due to heavy rain with approximately 1 foot of water depth was reported via social media.
Several inches of water covered a resident street in Edinburg. This was reported via social media.

A large metal awning from a local convenient gas station severely damaged and partially blown off. Wind gusts of at least 60 mph were estimated to have occurred at the intersection of Bass Blvd and Business 83 at 8:30 PM CDT when a strong thunderstorm moved through the area.

As swell from Hurricane Laura reached the lower Texas coast late on August 26th, the wave energy from this swell combined with high tide at 2:36 AM CDT on the 27th, allowed water levels to remain above 1.25 feet MHHW at the Brazos Santiago NDBC buoy from 11 PM on the 26th through noon on the 27th. The peak water level of 1.87 feet MHHW occurred at 3:06 AM CDT on the 27th. This activity caused some coastal erosion along the beaches of South Padre Island as high waves (up to 10+ feet in some cases) set-up and ran up into gaps in the dunes, into the dunes, or calved more robust dunes by erosion. Erosion began several hours prior to high tide due to wave action as Laura propagated its peak swell four to six hours prior to landfall.

Emergency management continued to report road closures across portions of northwest Cameron County due to ongoing flooding from rainfall from Hurricane Hanna, along with additional rainfall at the end of July and then the rainfall on August 1st. Road closures from standing water were reported through the afternoon of August 8th, with gradual improvement over the course of the first week of August as no additional significant rainfall fell.  Note:  Estimated flood damage from this event is included in the Hanna episode as part of July 2020 Storm Data.

Strong and gusty southeast winds persisted through the night of the 17th and into the morning of the 18th, where they pulsed up once again along the Federal Highway 77 corridor between Brownsville and Harlingen.  Sustained winds of 40 mph were recorded at Valley International Airport at 952 AM CST, with a peak gust to 52 mph at 1044 CST; sustained winds of 43 mph were recorded at the Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport sometime between  830 and 10 AM CST, with a peak gust of 52 mph at 929 AM CST. Additional power outages from fallen lines, and/or tree limbs having fallen on them, were noted during the morning of the 18th from Brownsville to Harlingen.

Strong and gusty southeast winds persisted through the night of the 17th and into the morning of the 18th, where they pulsed up once again along the Federal Highway 77 corridor and likely reaching into Willacy County between Sebastian and Raymondville.  Sustained winds of 40 mph were recorded at Valley International Airport in northeast Harlingen, just 6 miles south of the county line, at 952 AM CST, with a peak gust to 52 mph at 1044 CST. Some power outages from fallen lines, and/or tree limbs having fallen on them, may have occurred during the morning of the 18th between Sebastian and Raymondville.

Notable damage occurred during the middle of the afternoon in portions of Hidalgo County, as a surge of sustained winds near 40 mph with gusts of at least 52 mph produced minor structural damage at industrial buildings, more downed power lines, and some tree damage, mainly between Pharr, McAllen, Edinburg, and Weslaco. ||Two minor injuries were reported near McAllen from a partial roof or wall collapse at an old building. As of this writing, an estimated 7000 customers had lost power in portions of the area, primarily the populated portions of Hidalgo County, due to the winds. McAllen/Miller airport had a peak sustained wind of 39 mph at around 3:03 PM CST, with a gust to 51 mph at around 3:09 PM CST.

As swell from Hurricane Laura reached the lower Texas coast late on August 26th, the wave energy from this swell combined with high tide (Port Mansfield Channel Entrance) at approximately 2:11 AM CDT  on the 27th, likely produced minor coastal flooding in the form of run-up to and just into the dunes at narrow beaches of Willacy County, both south and north of the Mansfield cut. Unknown is the degree of erosion; assumed is erosion similar to what was observed at South Padre Island. A peak water level of 1.8 feet above Mean Higher-High Water (MHHW, or above normally dry ground on the shoreline) occurred at 10:12 AM CST on the 27th at the Realitos Peninsula tide guage, inshore (Laguna Madre) about 11 miles southwest of the Willacy County barrier island line.

As swell from Hurricane Laura reached the lower Texas coast late on August 26th and early on August 27th, the wave energy from this swell combined with high tide (Port Mansfield Channel Entrance and Malaquite Beach) at approximately 2:11 AM CDT  on the 27th, likely produced minor coastal flooding in the form of run-up to and just into the dunes at narrow beaches of Willacy County, both south and north of the Mansfield cut. Unknown is the degree of erosion; assumed is erosion similar to what was observed at South Padre Island. Unfortunately, due to heavy erosion from Hurricane Hanna a month earlier, as well as the difficult-to-reach location on Padre Island National Seashore, it is unknown how much additional erosion occurred along the Kenedy County barrier island.

A surge of sustained winds near 40 mph with estimated gusts perhaps up to 61 mph knocked down several trees or large limbs across the northern half of the county, including Hebbronville. Local power outages likely occurred in the area as well; the sharp wind gusts also caused a wild fire just northwest of town to explosively spread.  Measured sustained winds at the Jim Hogg County/Hebbronville Airport were 38 mph, with gusts to 53 mph, at 6:05 CST.

A surge of sustained winds near 40 mph with estimated gusts perhaps near 60 mph likely carried into western Brooks County on a few occasions from mid afternoon through early evening. Data were extrapolated for southwestern portions of the county between 3 and 4 PM CST based on observations near McAllen and the onset of an explosively developing wild fire at the Burns Ranch. ||Data were extrapolated for northwestern portions of the county based on measured wind gusts over 50 mph, with estimated gusts to 61 mph, along with damage to trees, in northeastern Jim Hogg County during the early evening.

A surge of sustained winds near 40 mph with estimated gusts perhaps near 60 mph likely affected portions of Zapata County during the late afternoon and early evening. While specific damage was not reported, emergency management noted pockets of minor damage with the high winds in Zapata, and perhaps farther north toward San Ygnacio.  Measured winds of 34 mph with gusts to 48 mph were recorded at Laredo between 6 and 7 PM CST; extrapolation of sustained winds of 38 mph, gusting to 53 mph, at Hebbronville at 6:05 PM CST may be representative of similar winds in Zapata County at those times.

A surge of sustained winds near 40 mph with estimated gusts perhaps nearing 55 to 60 mph likely occurred in northern Starr County during the mid and late afternoon. Data were extrapolated for northern and northeastern portions of the county between 2:30 and 4:30 PM CST based on observations near McAllen, and the onset of an explosively developing wild fire at the Burns Ranch (just north of the Starr and Hidalgo line with Brooks County), as well as another wild fire southeast of La Gloria.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: As a strong tropical thunderstorm/shower associated with a mid-level inverted trough and a surplus of tropical moisture moved over the Laguna Madre near Port Isabel early on September 5th, the TCOON site recorded a gust to 43.74 knots.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: As a strong tropical thunderstorm/shower associated with a mid-level inverted trough and a surplus of tropical moisture moved over the Laguna Madre near the Laguna Atascosa Wildlife Refuge early on September 5th, the Realitos Peninsula TCOON site recorded a gust of 40.8 knots.

An NWS survey of tidal run-up and overwash on South Padre Island found significant dune erosion at many of City and County beach access points between Isla Blanca Park and Clayton's Beach Bar.  Beta's water eroded more dunes that began with run-up associated with Hurricane Laura in late August. Though water levels during the time of the run-up (through the high tide cycle) were above 1.5 feet above Mean Higher High Water (MHHW), the strongest push of wave energy occurred at this time (high combined seas and long period swell from the east).

An NWS survey of tidal run-up and overwash on South Padre Island found a second day of significant dune erosion at many of City and County beach access points between Isla Blanca Park and Clayton's Beach Bar.  Beta's water eroded more dunes that began with run-up associated with Hurricane Laura in late August. Water levels on this day peaked just below the highest for the event, reaching 2.42 feet above Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) at 218-224 AM CST on the 21st. Run-up was similar to that from late on the 19th/early on the 20th as landward push of sea water was slightly less.

The NOAA tide gage at Brazos Santiago recorded a peak value  of 2.54 feet above Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) at 10:24 PM CST on September 21st.  However, notably less landward push of sea water caused only minimal erosion and run-up toward the dunes during this particularly high tide.  Nearby gages at Port Isabel and South Padre Island Coast Guard Station, along the western bay shore and eastern bay shore of Laguna Madre, recorded 2.59 feet (11 PM CST) and 2.5 feet (10:36 PM CST) above MHHW; the Realitos Peninsula location at the mouth of the Arroyo Colorado in Laguna Madre recorded 2.52 feet (12:42 AM, September 21). within an hour or two of the report at Port Isabel.

A tide gage at Port Mansfield (inside Laguna Madre) recorded a peak value of 1.61 feet above Mean Sea Level (MSL) at 10:06 PM CST on September 20th.  This mini-high tide corresponded closely to high tide times along the coast farther south, and it is assumed that minor coastal flooding in the form of tidal run-up slightly into the dunes of the Willacy County Beaches near Port Mansfield occurred at this time. It is unknown exactly how much water moved into, or calved, the dunes (which had been previously eroded from Hanna in late July and Laura in late August).

A tide gage at Port Mansfield (inside Laguna Madre) recorded a peak value of 1.39 feet above Mean Sea Level (MSL) at 7 AM CST on September 20th.  However, the location inside Laguna Madre was likely unrepresentative of conditions along the barrier island farther south, down to the Cameron County line.  An NWS survey on South Padre Island found significant beach erosion during the high tide cycle during the evening of the 19th, a result of strong landward push of high seas and swell. Therefore, times listed here are a proxy to similar impacts just 10 to 20 miles farther south on September 19th.

A tide gage at Port Mansfield (inside Laguna Madre) rose above 1.5 feet above Mean Sea Level (MSL) around 6:30 PM September 21, and continued well above 1.5 feet through the 23rd, peaking at 1.80 MSL at 3:24 PM on the 22nd. Though tide levels inside Laguna Madre remained high through the 23rd, the lack of landward push of water from Beta that day as the cyclone had already made landfall on the 22nd along the central Texas coast, well north of Port Mansfield, suggested that landward push of water had ended much earlier.  An NWS survey on South Padre Island found significant beach erosion during the high tide cycle during the evening of the 20th, a result of continuing strong landward push of high seas and swell. It was likely that additional minor erosion affected the northern coast of Willacy County into the high tide over September 21/22.

A tide gage at Baffin Bay, just north of the Kenedy/Kleberg County line, peaked at 2.34 feet above Mean Sea Level (MSL) around 8 PM CST September 21, and continued above 2 feet above MSL through 5 PM CST on the 23rd. Though tide levels inside Laguna Madre remained high through the 23rd, the lack of landward push of water from Beta that day as the cyclone had already made landfall on the 22nd along the central Texas coast, well north of Port Mansfield, suggested that the push may have ended earlier. However, since northern Kenedy County was much closer to the outswell from slow-moving Beta for several days, it's possible that additional run-up to or just into the dunes occurred for two or more day period.

Continued high seas and swells propagating to the west from the long-departed Hurricane Delta (which made landfall at around 6 PM CDT on October 9th) produced another, though lesser, round of tidal run/up and overwash that may have produced a bit more beach erosion following the larger impacts a day earlier.  Seas at NOAA Buoy 42002, 200 miles east of South Padre Island, were still between 8 and 10 feet with swell continuing at 10 to 11 seconds.||The NOAA tide gauge at Brazos Santiago recorded a peak value of 2.38 feet above Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) at 3:42 am CDT on October 10th. Nearby gauges at Port Isabel and the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station recorded 2.44 ft (from 1:42-1:48 AM CST) and 2.41 ft (3:42 AM CDT) above MHHW respectively. The Realitos Peninsula gauge slowly peaked several hours later, recording 2.35 ft above MHHW from 9:18-9:24 AM CDT. The Realitos location was still in minor flooding stage and slowly rising while the previous 3 locations were reaching peak levels.

Peak levels of 1.77 ft above MSL from 11:36-11:54 PM CST. Water levels were then slow to fall, not falling back below 1.5 ft above MSL until around noon CST on October 12th.
