The passage of Hurricane Delta about 200 miles east of South Padre Island at around midnight on October 9th produce peak sea heights of 35 feet just prior to the eye's arrival at 1140 PM CDT on the 8th. Swell periods of more than 12 seconds began during the late afternoon at the site, and propagated quickly to the Cameron County Beaches. Soon after the time of high tide (around 1:30 AM), tide levels reached 2.12 feet above normally dry ground at the foam/sand line (2:48 AM).  The combination of strong wave push with these above predicted tides produced significant beach erosion and some likely property damage at public beach access point 5 (north of the City), unprotected by dunes or the sea wall.  Visual inspection did show water had risen above previously calved dunes from Hurricane Laura and Tropical Storm Beta in late August and late September, respectively.  Renourishment costs were unknown as of this writing, but likely to run above $5 million based on data from earlier erosion from Hurricane Laura.

The passage of Hurricane Delta about 200 miles east of the Willacy County coast around 2 AM on October 9th produced peak sea heights of 35 feet just prior to the eye's arrival at 1140 PM CDT on the 8th. Swell periods of more than 12 seconds began during the late afternoon at the site, and propagated quickly to the Willacy County Beaches. Soon after the time of high tide (likely close to 2:30 AM based on proxy with Brazos Santiago on South Padre Island), the combination of strong wave push with these above predicted tides likely produced significant beach erosion on the beach-facing barrier island.

The passage of Hurricane Delta about 200 to 225 miles east of the Kenedy County coast around 4 AM on October 9th produced estimated peak sea heights of 35 feet just prior to the eye's arrival at 1140 PM CDT on the 8th. Swell periods of more than 12 seconds began during the late afternoon at the site, and propagated quickly to the Kenedy County barrier island. Soon after the time of high tide (likely between 2:30 and 3:30 AM), the combination of strong wave push with these above predicted tides likely produced significant beach erosion on the beach-facing barrier island.

The subtropical mid level ridge of high pressure has continued near to well above normal temperatures and dry conditions across Zapata County for most of November. This helped to develop Severe (D2) Drought conditions across the southwest corner of the county. These conditions persisted through the end of the month, before expanding into the beginning into December.

The subtropical mid level ridge of high pressure has continued near to well above normal temperatures and dry conditions across Starr County for most of November. This helped to develop Severe (D2) Drought conditions across the western half of the county. These conditions persisted through the end of the month, before expanding into the beginning into December.

Even while a couple of cold fronts moved through the region at the end of November, these frontal passages were generally dry, with any rainfall generally confined to the coastal areas and offshore. These dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to expand across all of Zapata County into mid December.

Even while a couple of cold fronts moved through the region at the end of November, these frontal passages were generally dry, with any rainfall generally confined to the coastal areas and offshore. These dry conditions allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to expand across the southwestern half of Starr County into mid December.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across Zapata County. Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the southern fourth of the county, with the rest of the county remaining in Severe (D2) Drought.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across Starr County. Extreme (D3) Drought developed across the western fourth of the county, with Severe (D2) Drought conditions expanding across the middle half of the county.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across Jim Hogg County. Severe (D2) Drought developed across the western two-thirds of the county.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several generally dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across Brooks County. Severe (D2) Drought developed across the extreme southeast corner of the county.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several generally dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across inland Kenedy County. Severe (D2) Drought developed across a sliver of the west and southern portion of the county.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several generally dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across Hidalgo County. Severe (D2) Drought developed across a sliver along the eastern border of the county.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several generally dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across Hidalgo County. Severe (D2) Drought developed across the northeast corner of southern Hidalgo county.

With a fairly active synoptic pattern bringing several generally dry cold fronts through the region during the first half of December, drought conditions worsened across Hidalgo County. Severe (D2) Drought developed across the western fourth of the county.

With little to no rainfall through mid December across much of the Lower Rio Grande Valley, drought conditions continued to worsen. Extreme (D3) Drought expanded southeastward across Starr County to include the southwestern half of the county, while Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include the entire other half.

With little to no rainfall through mid December across much the Deep South Texas Brush Country, drought conditions continued to worsen. Severe (D2) Drought expanded across Jim Hogg County to include the entire county, except for the northeast corner, which remained in Moderate (D1) Drought.
With little to no rainfall through mid December across much of the Lower Rio Grande Valley, drought conditions continued to worsen. Severe (D2) Drought expanded across all of Northern Hidalgo County.

With little to no rainfall through mid December across the Lower Rio Grande Valley, drought conditions continued to worsen. Severe (D2) Drought expanded across Southern Hidalgo County to include the northeast portion, along with a sliver along the western border of Southern Hidalgo County.

With little to no rainfall through mid December across much of the Deep South Texas Brush Country, drought conditions continued to worsen. Severe (D2) Drought expanded across Brooks County to include the southern three-fourths of the county.

With little to no rainfall through mid December across the King Ranch region of Deep South Texas, drought conditions continued to worsen. Severe (D2) Drought expanded across almost all of Inland Kenedy County, excluding the northwest corner.

With little to no rainfall through mid December across much of the Lower Rio Grande Valley, drought conditions continued to worsen. Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include the western half of Willacy County.

With little to no rainfall across the Rio Grande Plains through the end of December, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to include the majority of Zapata County, while a sliver along the eastern border remained in Severe (D2) Drought.

With little to no rainfall across much of the Lower Rio Grande Valley through the end of December, Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include the eastern third of Southern Hidalgo County, along with maintaining a portion along the western border.
With little to no rainfall across much of the Lower Rio Grande Valley through the end of December, Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include the western third of Cameron County..

With little to no rainfall across the Rio Grande Plains through January, Extreme (D3) Drought continued across all but a very small sliver of extreme eastern Zapata County to begin 2021, and would cover all of the county by mid month.

Just enough rainfall fell at times from late December 2020 through January 2021 to maintain a pocket of Moderate (D1) Drought across central and western Hidalgo County through mid January.  However, a pocket of little to no rain that extended west to IH-69C, including the populated McAllen metropolitan area, would slide Severe (D2) levels westward to include these areas and the nearby farmland by the 19th.

With modest rainfall countered by a number of dry cold fronts in January, Severe (D2) Drought held firm in western Cameron County through January.  Just enough rainfall fell along and east of IH-69E in early January to nudge to D2 area to west of a Harlingen-Los Indios line on the 12th, which would hold through month's end.
Rain and thunderstorms acted to improve Severe (D2) Drought conditions across central and southern portions of Brooks County.

A band of rain and thunderstorms at the turn of the calendar year would help improve drought conditions from Severe (D2) to Moderate (D1) across eastern portions of Starr County. Severe to Extreme (D3) Conditions would continue elsewhere through the 18th.

Rain and thunderstorms in a band from eastern Starr through northwest Hidalgo, western Brooks, and eastern Jim Hogg County helped improve Severe (D2) Drought to Moderate (D1) conditions across western portions of Northern Hidalgo County.

Due to a lack of precipitation across the area, Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed in southwestern portions of Inland Kenedy County. Severe (D2) Drought conditions also expanded slightly northward across northwestern portions of Inland Kenedy.  The Extreme conditions would expand slightly toward the end of the month, covering more of the King Ranch and other ranches in western Kenedy. ||Severe (D2) Drought conditions improved slightly across central portions of Inland Kenedy County as a result of shower activity closer to the coast from a few days earlier.
Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across northeastern portions of Northern Hidalgo County.

Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, drought conditions worsened in Brooks County. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed in far southeastern Brooks County. Severe (D2) Drought conditions also expanded across eastern portions of Brooks County.

Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, drought conditions worsened in Jim Hogg County. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across the western third of Jim Hogg County. Severe (D2) Drought conditions also expanded across central and eastern Jim Hogg County.

Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, drought conditions worsened in Jim Hogg County.  Extreme (D3) Drought conditions expanded into central Jim Hogg County. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded eastward across the remainder of Jim Hogg County. These conditions would prevail into early February.

Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, drought conditions worsened in Starr County. Extreme (D3) Drought conditions expanded slightly across far northern portions of Starr County. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded eastward across the remainder of Starr County. These conditions would continue into early February.

Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, drought conditions worsened in Brooks County. Severe (D2) Drought expanded across the vast majority of Brooks County, with the exception of far northern areas. Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place over southeastern Brooks County.  The extreme area would nudge a bit farther north and west, covering the entire Brooks County King Ranch area by the 26th, with no changes elsewhere.

Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, drought conditions worsened in Northern Hidalgo County. Severe (D2) Drought expanded across the vast majority of Northern Hidalgo County, with the exception of far southwestern areas. Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place over far northeastern portions of Northern Hidalgo County.  These conditions would prevail into early February.

Due to a lack of rainfall across the area, drought conditions worsened in Southern Hidalgo County. Severe (D2) Drought conditions continued to fill in across far western and central portions of Southern Hidalgo County, including the McAllen metropolitan region as well as nearby farmland.  These conditions would prevail into early February.
Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 1:00 AM and continued through 8:00 AM. Minimum temperatures fell to the upper 20s, with 28 degrees as the measured low at Zapata airport.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 12:00 AM and continued through 9:00 AM. Minimum temperatures fell to the middle and upper 20s, with 29 degrees measured at the Falcon Lake RAWS site and 26 degrees at the Rancho Los Comitas COOP site.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 12:00 AM and continued through 8:30 AM. Minimum temperatures fell to the middle and upper 20s, ranging from 25 degrees measured at the La Rucia Mesonet to 28 degrees at Brooks County Airport.

While the Hebbronville airport only measured a minimum temperature of 33 degrees, several other COOP/Mesonet/RAWS sites in surrounding counties measured minimum temperatures in the upper 20s (28 at Zapata Airport, 26 at the Rancho Los Comitas COOP site in Starr County, and 25 at the La Rucia Mesonet in Brooks County). Given the observed temperatures at these proxy sites and the likelihood of rural ranchland seeing temperatures falling below freezing, it is implied that much of central and southern Jim Hogg county experienced a light freeze on the morning of December 1st. The estimated timing of freezing temperatures is from 1:00 AM to 8:30 AM.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 12:00 AM and continued through 9:00 AM. Minimum temperatures fell to the middle and upper 20s, with 25 degrees as the measured low at the Linn-San Manuel RAWS site. The San Manuel COOP site also recorded a minimum temperature of 28 degrees.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 2:30 AM and continued through 8:00 AM. Edinburg International Airport recorded a minimum temperature of 32 degrees. Given the minimum temperatures simultaneously recorded in adjacent Starr County, it can be implied that additional northwestern portions of Southern Hidalgo also experienced temperatures below freezing.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 12:00 AM and continued through 9:00 AM. Minimum temperatures ranged from the middle 20s to lower 30s across Inland Kenedy County. Readings of 26 degrees were recorded at the Sarita Union Pacific Railroad (UPR) Mesonet, 28 at the Armstrong COOP site, and 31 degrees at the ARMSTR UPR Mesonet.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 2:30 AM and continued through 8:30 AM. Minimum temperatures fell to the upper 20s, with 27 degrees recorded as the minimum temperature at the YTURIA Union Pacific Railroad Mesonet site. The Raymondville COOP site also recorded a minimum temperature of 32 degrees.

Low temperatures fell to or below 32 degrees at 1:00 AM and continued through 8:30 AM. Damage from the microburst was first surveyed about 2 miles west of the center of town along and near Farm to Market (FM) Highway 496. In the neighborhood of Falcon Mesa, along FM 3074, numerous barrel tiles were torn from the roof; in the same neighborhood, numerous large limbs from ebony and live oak trees were blown down, and minor damage to roofs was noted at other homes.  Similar tree and roof damage was noted at another neighborhood along Oak Street, just south of the Zapata Cemetary.||Farther east along FM 496, several large fiberglass storage tanks were rolled, and damaged beyond repair, at a facility between FM 3074 and the Zapata County cemetary. On the same property, a manufactured home had numerous holes in its west facing wall, from wind driven pebbles and stones. The same home had fairly significant asphalt shingle damage to its roof. A nearby low metal tower was bent in half.||The worst-looking damage was seen just west of the center of town, along FM 496 only 1/3 mile west of the intersection of Federal Highway 83.  Here, significant damage was incurred to many units at the Highway 496 Storage facility. ||The microburst slammed into the west facing wall of the first of two long, cinderblock structures, and lifted most of the roof up and over the first building, slamming it into the second building about 50 feet to the east. While the truss and bracing of the roof appeared sound, only long nails were found at the connections of the eaves. Missiles generated by the broken roof drove into both cinderblock, and an individual metal garage, in the second building. Another light metal structure, housing another set of individual storage units, separated and collapsed on the leeward side of the second building. ||The microburst continued moving steadily southeast, causing notable damage to neighborhoods in the southwest part of town. Dozens of homes and other structures with poorly anchored roofing material sustained significant damage; a large portion of tin roof was removed from a two story church a few blocks from the center of town. Another barrel-tile roof was damaged at a motel, and the water leak caused at least one unit to be uninhabitable.||In all neighborhoods, hundreds of mesquite and ebony tree limbs of many shapes and sizes were snapped off, some onto roofs, including the town's public library.  As the storm finally edged south, additional tree damage was noted in the Falcon Lake Estates subdivision, just south of the bridge, where a report of a blown down roof of a two story house was also received as the storm weakened slightly.||The Zapata County Emergency Manager reported power lines and several trees were down in Zapata and approximately 200 to 300 people were without power at 9 pm. ||Wind speeds were estimated to be between 70 and 75 mph area wide, with the strongest speeds generally along and just south of FM 496 from just west of the cemetary to highway 83.  Total path length was estimated to be a little more than 3.5 miles long; width was estimated to be about 1.5 miles.

Severe (D2) Drought continued across all but northern Brooks County through the first few days of January.  A stripe of rainfall as the calendar turned from 2020 to 2021 was enough to improve conditions in northern and western Brooks County with the next Drought Monitor on January 5th.

Severe (D2) Drought covered all but a sliver of northeastern Jim Hogg County to begin 2021, but a band of heavy rain at the turn of the calendar would produce improvement, though brief, in eastern Jim Hogg County for the monitor on the 5th. Worsening drought would arrive a week later, however, toward the Rio Grande Plains section of the county.

Extreme (D3) Drought would cover the western two-thirds of Starr County, with Severe (D2) Drought elswhere, to begin 2021.  A band of moderate rain at the turn of the calendar year would cause brief but minor improvements over eastern Starr by January 5th.

Severe (D2) Drought would cover northern Hidalgo County to begin 2021, though a welcome band of moderate rainfall at the turn of the calendar would improve conditions mainly west of US 281/IH-60C by the January 5th monitor.

Severe (D2) Drought would prevail across western Willacy County through January.  Some beneficial rains along and east of US 77/IH 69E on the 9th/10th would slightly shrink the area to west of the highway from central Willacy, and occasionally light rains thereafter would maintain the status quo thereafter.

Spotty rain near the northeast Kenedy County coast was enough to improve conditions there; otherwise, Severe (D2) Drought maintained its grip on the western two-thirds of the county through January 11th.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought remained in place across Brooks County. Severe (D2) Drought covered much of the county except the northeastern sliver, while Extreme (D3) Drought continued across southeastern Brooks County.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought remained in place across much of central and western Kenedy County. Severe (D2) Drought covered most of these areas, while Extreme (D3) Drought continued across portions of western Kenedy County.  The D2 and D3 areas would expand slightly eastward during the final week of the month.
Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) drought remained in place across western Willacy County. The area would nudge into central Willacy County by mid month.
Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) drought remained in place across western Cameron County through February.  The area would nudge eastward toward Harlingen on February 9th.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) drought remained in place across much of Southern Hidalgo County away from some western areas including McAllen, which held in moderate (D1) drought due to a stripe of prior rainfall in January.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought remained in place across much of Northern Hidalgo County. Severe (D2) Drought covered most of the area, while Extreme (D3) Drought continued across northeastern portions of Northern Hidalgo.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought remained in place across much of Jim Hogg County. Extreme (D3) Drought covered much of western and central Jim Hogg, while the eastern third of the county remained in Severe (D2) Drought).

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought remained in place across much of Starr County. Extreme (D3) Drought covered approximately the western half of the county, while the eastern half remained in Severe (D2) Drought.
Due to a persistent lack of rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought remained in place across all of Zapata County through the end of the month.

Due to a lack of substantial rainfall, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought continued across Jim Hogg County. Extreme drought overtook the vast majority of the county, with a small sliver of eastern Jim Hogg remaining in Severe drought until February 23rd, when it too was overtaken by D3 conditions.

Due to a lack of substantial rainfall, wind, and frequent low humidity, Extreme (D3) Drought overtook all but the eastern eighth of Starr County on February 9th, with Severe (D2) Drought otherwise.  D3 would expand a bit farther east on the 23rd, leaving just a sliver of eastern Starr in D2 by month's end.
A lack of substantial rainfall allowed for Severe (D2) Drought to expand into Coastal Kenedy County.

A lack of substantial rainfall allowed for Severe (D2) Drought to expand slightly farther eastward across more of far northern Willacy County, while Extreme (D3) Drought slipped from the border with Hidalgo and Kenedy on the 16th to the northwestern eighth of the county from the 23rd through the 28th.

A lack of substantial rainfall combined with sufficient days with low humidity allowed for Extreme (D3) Drought to expand and cover all but far northeastern portions of the county, while Severe (D2) Drought covered the remaining fifth of northeast Brooks County.
A lack of substantial rainfall allowed for Extreme (D3) Drought to expand and cover all but a sliver of Northern Hidalgo along between FM 490 and SR-186; Severe (D2) Drought covered this area.
A lack of substantial rainfall allowed for Severe (D2) Drought to expand across all of Southern Hidalgo County.
