Temperatures fell below freezing around 11:30 PM on the 19th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 8:30 AM on the 20th. A low temperature of 23 degrees was recorded at the Linn-San Manuel RAWS site, and a low of 28 degrees was recorded at the San Manuel COOP site.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 12:30 AM on the 20th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 8:30 AM. A low temperature of 28 degrees was recorded at the Hebbronville Airport.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 1:30 AM on the 20th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 8:30 AM. A low temperature of 27 degrees was recorded at the YTURIA Union Pacific Railroad Mesonet site.  Widespread frost joined the cold temperatures for most of the time when temperatures were below freezing.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 2:30 AM on the 20th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 9:00 AM. Lows fell into the lower 30s and upper 20s across the county. Widespread frost joined the cold temperatures, forming on roofs and vehicles under the clear skies prior to air temperatures falling below freezing, and as early as midnight; grass frost formed soon after.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 3:30 AM on the 20th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 7:30 AM. Lows fell into the lower 30s and upper 20s across northern portions of Southern Hidalgo County.||Widespread frost joined the freezing temperatures for the entire event, likely beginning as early as midnight on vehicles, roofs, and grass.
Temperatures fell below freezing around 5:30 AM on the 20th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 8:30 AM. A low of 27 degrees was recorded at the Zapata Airport.

Despite sparse observation coverage, based off of observations from Inland Kenedy County and adjacent Kleberg County, it is estimated that temperatures fell below freezing across portions of Coastal Kenedy County around 4:00 AM and did not exceed 32 degrees again until 9:00 AM on the 19th. The nearby SARITA and ARMSTR Union Pacific Mesonet sites both recorded a low of 25 degrees.

Despite sparse observation coverage in the area and based off of observations from Inland Willacy as well as other adjacent counties, it is estimated that temperatures fell below freezing around 2:00 AM on the 20th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 8:00 AM. A low temperature of 27 degrees was recorded at the nearby YTURIA Union Pacific Railroad Mesonet site.  Widespread frost likely joined the cold temperatures for nearly all of this event.

Temperatures fell below freezing across portions of Coastal Cameron County around 3:30 AM on the 20th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 7:30 AM. A low of 30 degrees was recorded at the Laguna Atascosa RAWS site.  Widespread frost joined the freezing temperatures, likely beginning as soon as midnight on vehicles and roofs, with grass frost soon after.
Temperatures fell to or below freezing around 3 AM on Saturday, February 13th and lasted through about 3 PM. A low of 32 degrees was observed at the SARITA Union Pacific Mesonet site.
Temperatures fell to or below freezing around 4:30 AM on Saturday, February 13th and lasted through about 3 PM. A low of 31 degrees was observed at the Hebbronville Airport.

Temperatures fell to or below freezing around 4:30 AM on Saturday, February 13th, remained at or below freezing through the afternoon. Temperatures did not rise above freezing until around 2 PM on the 14th. A low of 31 degrees was observed at the Brooks County Airport on the morning of the 13th, and a low of 30 degrees occurred on the 14th.

Despite a data outage from the Brooks County Airport, it is implied that temperatures fell below freezing across northern portions of Brooks County around 4:30 AM on the 18th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 10:30 AM. This is based off of observations from adjacent Jim Hogg, Kenedy, and Kleberg counties.

Temperatures fell below freezing across portions of Inland Kenedy County around 4:30 AM on the 18th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 10:30 AM. The SARITA Union Pacific Mesonet site recorded a low of 32 degrees on the morning of the 18th.

Temperatures fell below freezing across portions of Jim Hogg County around 4:30 AM on the 18th and did not rise back above 32 degrees until around 10:30 AM. The Hebbronville Airport recorded a low of 32 degrees, as did the Hebbronville RAWS site.

Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought persisted across Brooks County. Much of the county experienced Extreme (D3) Drought, with the exception of far northeastern Brooks which experienced Severe (D2) Drought to begin March. D3 conditions would gradually spread toward the northeast corner of the county through the 22nd.

Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought persisted across Starr County. The vast majority of Starr was in Extreme (D3) Drought, with the exception of extreme eastern Starr County which experienced Severe (D2) Drought for the first eight days of the month.

Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought persisted across all but a sliver of Northern Hidalgo County on the 1st (mainly near FM 490 near the South Texas International Airport, and including the Linn/San Manuel and McCook areas).  By the 2nd, all of Northern Hidalgo was in D3 conditions, which would continue through the 22nd.
Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Severe (D2) Drought persisted across all of Southern Hidalgo County on the 1st day of March.

Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought persisted across Inland Kenedy County. West-central and southwestern areas near the King Ranch remained under Extreme (D3) Drought to begin March. Severe (D2) Drought persisted across much of Inland Kenedy away from northeastern portions of the county. D3 conditions would ooze eastward across the midsection of the county, expanding into Coastal Kenedy County by March 9th.
Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Severe (D2) Drought persisted across central portions of Coastal Kenedy County.

Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought persisted across much of Willacy County. Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place for far western Willacy, while much of central Willacy saw Severe (D2) Drought to begin the month of March. D3 conditions would spread gradually eastward by mid month, while D2 conditions held on in the eastern half of Inland Willacy County.
Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place across all of Zapata County to begin March.
Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place across all of Jim Hogg County for the first full week of March.
Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across all of Inland Cameron County to begin the month of March.

Due to a lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded into a sliver of Southern Hidalgo county from the north, to include Hargill and areas around the South Texas International Airport 11 miles north of Edinburg. Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across the remainder of Southern Hidalgo, from McCook to Monte Alto to the Rio Grande.

Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed across far northeastern portions of Zapata County. Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place across the remainder of the county.

Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed across the western half of Jim Hogg County. Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place across the eastern half. These conditions would remain unchanged through the end of March.

Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, a stripe of Exceptional (D4) Drought developed across western and central portions of Starr County on March 9th, with a portion of Extreme Drought remaining near Roma and the eastern half of the county, with a sliver of Severe Drought (D2) remaining on the border of Hidalgo County.

Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded into central portions of Coastal Kenedy County, with D2 continuing near the Wind Farms and toward the Willacy County line.  By the 16th, the area of D3 would expand a bit farther north and south.

Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought expanded across much of Zapata County, with the exception of the northwestern portions of the county where long term rainfall departures remained sufficient to hold onto Extreme (D3) conditions.

Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought expanded across western Starr County to include the Roma/Falcon Lake region. Extreme (D3) Drought also expanded slightly along portions of the Starr-Hidalgo County border, though a sliver of Severe (D2) Drought would hold near Sullivan City (on the border of Hidalgo).

Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded significantly across southern and eastern portions of Southern Hidalgo County. Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across southwestern portions of Southern Hidalgo, from Mission to La Joya and Sullivan City.
Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Severe (D2) Drought expanded into and included the vast majority of Coastal Willacy County on March 16th and would hold through month's end.
Due to a persistent lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought developed across far western portions of Cameron County. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded into more of central Cameron County.
Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed and covered all of Zapata County beginning on March 23rd and continuing through the end of the month.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall and dry fronts, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed in extreme northeastern Starr County, continued in western portions. Extreme (D3) Drought continued elsewhere and finally overtook the southeastern portion of the county. Cattle ranchers reported the need for additional water hauling due to the lack of available water supplies.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed in southern and eastern portions of Brooks county while Extreme (D3) Drought overtook the northeastern sliver of the county that had been in Severe (D2) conditions.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed across the majority of Northern Hidalgo county, with the exception of southwestern portions of the area near McCook. Dryland crops were unable to be planted due to the dry soil, causing a delay in the start of certain crops' growing season, and water hauling increased for cattle ranchers in the area.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed across northern portions of Southern Hidalgo County while Extreme (D3) Drought overtook the remainder of the county. The increased D4 area included the area north of Edinburg, including Faysville and Hargill.  Dryland crops could not be planted at their usual time due to the lack of soil moisture.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed across southwestern portions of Inland Kenedy County. Extreme (D3) Drought also pushed eastward across the remainder of Inland Kenedy.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded eastward across the majority of Coastal Kenedy County, with the exception of far southern areas and the barrier island over the southeast portion.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed across far western portions of Willacy County. Extreme (D3) Drought also expanded eastward across central and eastern Willacy with a sliver of Severe (D2) Drought across the southeast portion of Inland Willacy County.

Due to persistent lack of significant rainfall, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded eastward across more of western and central Cameron County, to include the Harlingen area and many of the crop field surrounding it. Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across central Cameron County.

The King Fire burned thousands of acres across Brooks County near Encino. A power line was found to the cause of the fire, which ignited during the mid afternoon of March 17th and exploded to more than 10,000 acres in just a few hours (late afternoon), then continued until March 20th, when it was 100% contained. The fire consumed 11,728 acres and 1 residential building.  Several other buildings were affected, but were not damaged.  Damage value listed is an estimate.

The North Jones Fire ignited on February 9th and continued until February 10th when it was 100% contained. The fire consumed around 4,000 acres through its duration.  There were no reports of structural damage despite the large acreage.

Time of initiation of the St. Carlos Wildfire in Kenedy County was estimated to be around 5:30 PM CDT and it continued to burn until around 8:00 PM CDT on March 24th when it was 100% contained. The fire consumed a total of 745 acres. A Spot Request was submitted for a wildfire that initiated just south of Armstrong, TX off of Highway 77 around 5:45 PM CDT, soon after ignition. The cause of the wildfire was an escape of a prescribed burn.

The event known as the Baffin Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 3:00 PM CDT just south of Sarita, TX near Highway 77 and burned until the early morning hours on the 21st, when it was announced to be 100% contained by 8:00 AM CDT. This wildfire consumed a total of 4,800 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Fire Service on March 20th was used as a guide for the earlier ignition and the very rapid spread that followed.

The Butterfly Fire (also known as Butterfly 1 Fire, since a second larger wildfire initiated nearby a few days later) was estimated to have initiated around 9:30 AM CDT on March 12th and continued until 7:30 PM CDT on the 13th when it was reported to be 100% contained. This wildfire consumed a total of 387 acres.  This fire was determined to have started by faulty equipment/use of equipment (potentially by humans).

The Butterfly 2 Fire ignited on March 17th around 3:30 PM and continued through around 6:00 PM on March 18th when it was 100% contained. The fire consumed a total of 413 acres.  The cause of this fire was not known as of this writing, but was suspected not to be by humans.
Law enforcement reported dime-sized hail in the city of Raymondville as thunderstorms moved through the area. Time frame is estimated.
The Willacy County Sheriff's Department reported hail up to the size of nickels in Raymondville as storms moved through the area. Time frame is estimated.

The Tecolote Fire, likely ignited by a lightning strike, began on the afternoon of April 1st and continued through the afternoon on April 10th, when it was 100% contained. It consumed 818.7 acres through its duration.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across Zapata County. Exceptional Drought would continue across the county through the end of the month as well.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across the western half of Jim Hogg County, while Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place out east. These conditions would remain largely unchanged through late April.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across the western half of Starr County, while Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place out east. A small portion of far northeastern Starr County also saw Exceptional Drought continue. These conditions would remain unchanged through mid-April.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across much of south-central and southeastern Brooks County, while Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place across the remainder of the county. An area of showers and thunderstorms in extreme northeast Brooks/northern Kenedy County would improve conditions to Severe (D2) near the county line on the 20th. Otherwise, conditions would remain unchanged through late April.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across much of Northern Hidalgo county, while some far southwestern portions of Northern Hidalgo remained under Extreme (D3) Drought. These conditions would remain unchanged through mid-April.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across northern portions of Southern Hidalgo County, while the remainder of the county saw Extreme (D3) Drought continue.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across western portions of Inland Kenedy County, while the remainder of the county saw Extreme (D3) Drought continue. These conditions would remain unchanged through mid-April.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across far western portions of Inland Willacy County, while the majority of the county saw Extreme (D3) Drought continue to begin April.
Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Extreme (D3) Drought continued across much of Coastal Kenedy County. These conditions would remain unchanged through mid-April.

Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Severe (D2) Drought covered nearly all of Coastal Willacy County, with a sliver of the northwestern section in Extreme (D3) Drought through mid April.
Due to a persistent lack of rainfall across the area, Extreme (D3) Drought continued across western portions of Cameron County, and Severe (D2) Drought continued across central portions.

Rainfall late March 31/early April 1st finally caused coverage of Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to shrink, with portions of southeastern Hidalgo (mainly from Donna and points east) returning to Severe (D2) Drought on the 6th.
Rainfall late March 31st/early April 1st finally caused coverage of Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to shrink, with much of central and western Cameron County returning to Severe (D2) Drought.
Rainfall finally caused coverage of Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to shrink, with portions of central Willacy County returning to Severe (D2) Drought.

Beneficial rainfall occurred across populated southern Starr County on April 16th/17th, providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. Exceptional (D4) Drought was removed from southern Starr County, which returned to Extreme (D3) Drought.

Beneficial rainfall occurred across the southeast portion Northern Hidalgo County early on April 18th, providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. Exceptional (D4) Drought was removed from southeastern portions of Northern Hidalgo County, which returned to Extreme (D3) Drought.  On April 27th, a sliver of D3 conditions near the Starr County line with degrade to D4, as this area missed out on earlier rainfall and combined with a several day period of warmth and low humidity to push into the Exceptional category.

Beneficial rainfall of 1.5 to 2.5 inches occurred across eastern Hidalgo County (between Edinburg and Monte Alto) early on April 18th, providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. Exceptional (D4) Drought was completely removed from Southern Hidalgo County, and Extreme (D3) Drought was also trimmed away from more of far Southern Hidalgo County.

Beneficial rainfall occurred across Inland Kenedy County (north and south) on late April 17th/early April 18th - generally one half to on inch, providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. Exceptional (D4) Drought was removed from far southwestern Kenedy County, and Extreme (D3) Drought was also trimmed away from far northern as well as southeastern portions of Kenedy County, returning those areas to Severe (D2) Drought.

Beneficial rainfall of 0.5 to 1.5 inches occurred across southern and northern Coastal Kenedy County in mid-April (late 17th/early 18th), providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. Extreme (D3) Drought was trimmed out of far northern and far southern portions of Coastal Kenedy.

Beneficial rainfall estimated between 1 and 2.5 inches occurred across Willacy County during the pre-dawn hours on April 18th, providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. The small area of Exceptional (D4) Drought was removed, and Extreme (D3) Drought was removed from western and central portions of Willacy County.

Beneficial rainfall, generally 1.5 to 2.5 inches, fell across Coastal Willacy County during the pre-dawn hours of  April 18th, providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. All but a sliver of  Severe (D2) Drought, in the northwest corner of the zone, was removed.

A couple of pockets of beneficial rainfall occurred across southern Cameron County near the Rio Grande, and northern Cameron County near the Willacy County line early on April 18th, providing some relief to drought conditions in the area. Extreme (D3) Drought was removed from Cameron County and Severe (D2) Drought was trimmed slightly.
A combination of hot and dry weather led to the expansion of drought conditions in Starr County. Exceptional (D4) Drought expanded across northern and northeastern Starr County.
A combination of hot and dry weather led to the expansion of drought conditions in Jim Hogg County. Exceptional (D4) Drought expanded across the remainder of eastern Jim Hogg County.
A combination of hot and dry weather led to the expansion of drought conditions in Brooks County. Exceptional (D4) Drought expanded across much of western Brooks County.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Zapata County through the first half of May before the season's first squall line crossed the area late on May 11th, which would help improve conditions by the 18th. Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across all of the county.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Jim Hogg County. Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across all of the county to begin May, with a small pocket of rain on April 30th in extreme southeastern portions of the county knocking down levels to Extreme (D3) by May 7th. A pronounced line of showers and storms late on May 11th would allow further reductions by the May 18th drought monitor.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Starr County. Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across the northern half of Starr County, while Extreme (D3) Drought covered the southern half.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Brooks County. Exceptional (D4) Drought continued across much of the area. Northeastern portions of Brooks County remained under Extreme (D3) Drought, while extreme northeastern areas remained under Severe (D2) Drought.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Northern Hidalgo County. Exceptional (D4) drought continued across the majority of the area, while southeastern portions of Northern Hidalgo remained under Extreme (D3) Drought.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Southern Hidalgo County. Northern and western portions of Southern Hidalgo remained under Extreme (D3) Drought, while the remainder stayed at Severe (D2) Drought.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Kenedy County. Drought conditions ranged from Severe (D2) across far southeastern and far northern areas, to Extreme (D3) across central and western areas, and Exeptional (D4) across portions of southwestern Kenedy.

Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Willacy County. Extreme (D3) Drought continued across the western Willacy County, while Severe (D2) continued across central portions.
Warm and mainly rain-free weather allowed for drought conditions to persist across Cameron County. Severe (D2) Drought continued across central and western portions of Cameron County.

Warm and mainly rain-free conditions allowed for drought to persist across Coastal Kenedy County. Central areas remained under Extreme (D3) Drought while the remainder of northern and southern Coastal Kenedy remained under Severe (D2) Drought. Rainfall in late April and early May would then bring an end to Severe drought conditions in Coastal Kenedy County.

Starr County saw some improvement in drought conditions owing to rainfall early in the month. Coverage of Exceptional (D4) Drought was reduced to northwestern areas, but Extreme (D3) Drought remained in place across the majority of the county. A small portion of southeastern Starr was reduced to Severe (D2) Drought.

Brooks County saw some improvement in drought conditions owing to rainfall early in the month. Exceptional (D4) Drought was removed from the county, with Extreme (D3) Drought occupying most of the county. Far northeastern areas including Falfurrias remained under Severe (D2) Drought.

Northern Hidalgo County saw some improvement in drought conditions owing to rainfall early in the month. Exceptional (D4) Drought was removed from the county, with Extreme (D3) Drought occupying most of the county. Far southeastern areas remained under Severe (D2) Drought.

Southern Hidalgo County saw some improvement in drought conditions owing to rainfall early in the month. Extreme (D3) Drought was removed from much of the county aside from far northwestern portions. The vast majority remained at Severe (D2) Drought. Rainfall of generally 3 to 6 inches in mid-May from multiple events would then bring an end to Severe (D2) Drought conditions with the Drought Monitor update on May 18.

Inland Kenedy County saw improvement in drought conditions owing to rainfall early in the month. Exceptional (D4) Drought was removed from the county. Severe (D2) Drought covered the western half of the county, with a slightly smaller area in southwestern Kenedy County falling under Extreme (D3) Drought.

Inland Willacy County saw improvement in drought conditions owing to rainfall early in the month. Extreme (D3) Drought was removed from the county, and Severe (D2) Drought covered the western half of the county. Rainfall of generally 1 to 4 inches from multiple events in mid-May would then bring an end to Severe (D2) Drought conditions with the Drought Monitor update on May 18.

Cameron County saw improvement in drought conditions owing to rainfall early in the month. Severe (D2) Drought coverage reduced slightly, but mostly remained in place across western Cameron County. Rainfall of generally 2 to 5 inches from multiple events in mid-May would then bring an end to Severe (D2) Drought conditions with the Drought Monitor update on May 18.
Rain and thunderstorms finally brought some drought relief to Zapata County, which saw Exceptional (D4) Drought removed from the area and replaced by Extreme (D3) Drought.

Rain and thunderstorms finally brought some significant drought relief to Jim Hogg County, which saw Exceptional (D4) Drought removed from the area and replaced by Extreme (D3) Drought. The sliver of eastern Jim Hogg originally under Extreme (D3) Drought was replaced by Severe (D2) Drought.

Rain and thunderstorms brought some additional drought relief to Starr County, which saw Exceptional (D4) Drought removed from northwestern Starr and replaced by Extreme (D3) Drought. Central and eastern Starr County remained under Severe (D2) Drought.

Rain and thunderstorms brought some additional drought relief to Brooks County, which saw Extreme (D3) Drought removed from the area. Southern and western portions of Brooks County remained under Severe (D2) Drought. Rainfall of 2 to 5 inches from a squall line of May 19th would provide additional relief, and Severe (D2) Drought would be removed with the May 25 Drought Monitor update.

Rain and thunderstorms brought some additional drought relief to Northern Hidalgo County, which saw Extreme (D3) Drought removed from the area. Much of Northern Hidalgo remained under Severe (D2) Drought with the exceptions of far southeastern areas. Additional rainfall of 1 to 2.5 inches on May 19th would lead to Severe (D2) Drought being removed with the May 25 Drought Monitor update.

Rain and thunderstorms brought some additional drought relief to Inland Kenedy County, which saw Extreme (D3) Drought removed from the area. Portions of southwestern Kenedy remained under Severe (D2) Drought. Rainfall of 2 to 5 inches on May 19th would provide additional relief, and Severe (D2) Drought would be removed with the May 25 Drought Monitor update.

Beneficial rainfall allowed for drought conditions to improve significantly across Zapata County through the end of May. Extreme (D3) Drought was reduced back to mainly northwestern portions of Zapata, while Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across much of the remainder of Zapata County.

Beneficial rainfall allowed for drought conditions to improve significantly across Jim Hogg County through the end of May. Extreme (D3) Drought was completely removed from the county, while Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across western portions of the county. Additional rainfall would lead to Severe (D2) Drought being removed from the county with the June 1 Drought Monitor update.

Beneficial rainfall allowed for drought conditions to improve significantly across Starr County through the end of May. Extreme (D3) Drought was completely removed from the county, while Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across northern portions of the county. Additional rainfall would lead to Severe (D2) Drought being removed from the county with the June 1 Drought Monitor update.

Severe (D2) Drought remained in place across northwestern portions of Zapata County. This would persist through the first week of the month, with some beneficial rain events finally ending Severe (D2) Drought in the area with the June 8 Drought Monitor Update.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM ARROYO COLORADO TO 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TX
events.event_narrative: Video received from KRGV Weather Social Media Page of waterspout over Laguna Madre. Timing estimated from report.
As thunderstorms moved through the area, the RAWS site at Linn-San Manuel measured a wind gust to 60 mph or 52 knots.

As thunderstorms moved through the area, an anemometer at the Pharr Emergency Operations Center measured a wind gust to 73 mph, or 63 knots.  The anemometer is situated 90 feet (27 meters) above the ground, nearly three times higher than standard NWS measuring equipment and more than four times higher than eye level; wind speed listed here (56 knots) was reduced to account for near-ground friction.

As thunderstorms moved through the area, the ASOS station at the McAllen airport measured a gust to 63 mph, or 55 knots. Gusts of 54 knots or higher lasted for about 20 minutes, based on the station reports.

High northerly winds, associated with a wake low developing behind a thunderstorm complex, contributed to enhanced northerly swell which led to coastal flooding across portions of Coastal Cameron County on the morning of May 19th. Water levels topped out at 2.51ft above normally dry ground around noon in the Port Isabel area. Other high water levels measured included 2.45ft above normally dry ground at SPI Brazos Santiago, and 2.45ft above normally high ground at the South Padre Island Coast Guard Station. These highest levels occurred generally between 11:30am and 12:15pm.  Several docks, signs, and boats sustained damage from the Storm-Force wind gusts and pounding waves associated with the event.  Dollar damages for boats are estimated and provided in a separate episode for Marine High Wind.

High northerly winds, associated with a wake low developing behind a thunderstorm complex, contributed to enhanced northerly swell which led to coastal flooding across portions of Coastal Willacy County on the morning of May 19th. Water levels topped out at 2.25ft above mean sea level (an estimated for water levels above normally dry ground) around 1:00pm in the Port Mansfield area.

Cameron County Beach Patrol responded to a call regarding a drowning victim which came in at 6:47 PM that evening. Witnesses suggested/confirmed the fatality was rip current related, and an off-duty NWS employee vouched for the dangerous rip current potential during the entire weekend (May 22-23).
Social media report received of a truck trapped in high water in the Harlingen area. Water depth was estimated to be around 3 feet.
Social media report received of several flooded streets with 2 to 3 feet of water depth near Miller Jordan Middle School in San Benito.
Social media report received of streets flooded in the San Cristobal Subdivision in Edinburg. Water depth was estimated to be 2 to 3 feet in some spots.

Public report received of flood waters reaching up over the top of car wheel wells in the Weslaco area. Emergency managers also reported water depth of up to 3 feet in spots during this event, mostly in the area just south of Interstate Highway 2 between Westgate and Airport Boulevard.
Off-duty NWS Employee reported several tree limbs up to 5 inches in diameter snapped off of trees nearby. Time and duration was estimated via radar.
Numerous reports on social media of trees damaged or uprooted near the Linn-San Manuel area.

Numerous reports received via social media of tree damage and tree branches down on vehicles near Mercedes. Time was estimated via radar and based on NWS Storm Survey on damage from Donna to just east of Weslaco.
Social media report of a damaged carport and a barn roof torn off in the Linn area. Time was estimated via radar.

More than two dozen structures sustained varying damage to|poorly constructed wood, asphalt, and aluminum/tin roofs,|roof decking, and shingles in the Siesta Shores and Falcon|Heights neighborhoods in south Zapata, Texas. A poorly seated|cinder block knee wall and attached fence was blown down, and|a 100-foot tall thin metal tower was twisted. A few power poles|were knocked down by by flying aluminum roof pieces. Dozens of|medium mesquite limbs were blown down by flying aluminum roof|pieces.

An NWS Storm Survey team on the way out to the City of Zapata noted at least a dozen mainly mesquite, live oak, and ebony trees large limbs blown down between Rio Grande City and Roma.  A social media report also noted an uprooted tree in the Escobares area. Time was estimated via radar.
The AWOS at Edinburg International Airport measured a gust to 52 knots/60 mph as storms moved through the area during the early afternoon hours.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: Coast Guard reported 3 unmanned fishing boats breaking loose, then capsizing and sinking in the Laguna Madre due to high marine thunderstorm winds. Damage was also observed at the Dolphin Docks location in Port Isabel, which was quoted as being between $25-30k based on similar damage instances in the past. Time was estimated based on wind observations nearby. Damage costs are estimated as well.
Severe (D2) drought conditions continued in Zapata County, TX, from late March into the first full week of April, as increasing sun angle and lack of rainfall maintained very dry soils.
Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across Jim Hogg County, TX, into the first full week of April, as increasing sun angle and lack of rainfall maintained very dry soils.
Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted in Starr County, TX, into the first full week of April, as increasing sun angle and lack of rainfall maintained very dry soil.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across the western portions of Hidalgo County, TX into the first full week of April, as increasing sun angle combined with lack of rainfall to maintain very dry soils.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted in the western portions of Brooks County, TX, into the first full week of April, as increasing sun angle combined with lack of rainfall maintained very dry soils.

At least a half dozen manufactured homes sustained|damage, mainly from peeled-back or blown off tin roofs, and car ports|knocked down, in portions of Donna and Weslaco along and near the |Interstate 2 corridor. One home slid off its foundation midway between|the cities. Several mesquite and ash trees were uprooted,|split, or lost large limbs. One uprooted large tree damaged a car|in Donna.  Several parts of fences were blown down, and unanchored road|signs were also blown down.
An off-duty NWS Employee noted five large limbs blown down from mesquite trees in west-central San Benito. Wind speed estimated based on similar accounts of tree damage with the same squall line.

Local emergency management coordinator and on-site law enforcement/fire and rescue reported water entering properties on the east side of Los Fresnos in poorly draining locations where 3 inches fell in a 2 to 3 hour period.
Social media report received of water rising up to the doorsteps of homes in San Benito near the intersection of Oscar Williams Road and I69E.  Depth of water unknown, but likely 2 feet or less.
Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed in Zapata County by the second week of April, with the drought gradually worsening by the middle of the month.
Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed in Jim Hogg County by the second week of April, with the drought gradually worsening by the middle of the month.
Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed in Starr County by the second week of April, with the drought gradually worsening by the middle of the month.
Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed in western Hidalgo County by the second week of April, with conditions continuing, and worsening slightly, through the end of the month and into May.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed in western Brooks County by the second week of April, with the drought worsening by the middle of the month as very dry weather prevailed with virtually no rainfall.

Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded into Kenedy County, TX, during the second week of April, and continued through the remainder of the month.  Unlike locations much farther inland in Deep South Texas and the Lower Rio Grande Valley, a bit more humidity, followed by locally heavy rainfall during the last full weekend of the month, held conditions at severe levels until the 30th.

Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded into Willacy County, TX, during the second week of April, and continued through the remainder of the month.  Unlike locations much farther inland in Deep South Texas and the Lower Rio Grande Valley, a bit more humidity, followed by locally heavy rainfall during the last full weekend of the month, held conditions at severe levels until the 30th.

Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded into Cameron County, TX, during the second week of April, and continued through the remainder of the month.  Unlike locations much farther inland in Deep South Texas and the Lower Rio Grande Valley, a bit more humidity, followed by locally heavy rainfall during the last full weekend of the month, held conditions at severe levels until the 30th.
Severe (D2) drought conditions developed over eastern Brooks County, TX, by April 8th, and continued through the middle of the month, before worsening further.
Severe (D2) drought conditions developed over eastern hidalgo County, TX, by the second week of April, and would further worsen by the middle of the month.

Exceptional (D4) drought conditions developed over Zapata County by the middle of April and continued through the end of the month, as persistent winds, increasing sun angle, and lack of rainfall brought the highest level of drought into the Rio Grande Plains and middle Rio Grande Valley.

Exceptional (D4) drought conditions developed in Jim Hogg County by the middle of April and continued through the end of the month, as persistent winds, increasing sun angle, and lack of rainfall brought the highest level of drought into the Rio Grande Plains.

Exceptional (D4) drought conditions developed in northern Starr County by the middle of April and continued through the end of the month, as persistent winds, increasing sun angle, and lack of rainfall brought the highest level of drought into the Rio Grande Plains and middle Rio Grande Valley.

Exceptional (D4) drought conditions developed across western Brooks County by the middle of April and continued through the end of the month, as persistent winds, increasing sun angle, and lack of rainfall brought the highest level of drought from the Rio Grande Plains farther east into Deep South Texas.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions expanded into eastern Brooks County by the middle of April, and remained through the end of the month. Locally heavy rains in the county's midsection on April 27th helped ease conditions a bit, but only enough to hold the drought at D3.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed over extreme western Cameron County, which includes some water sensitive crops, by the middle of April, continuing through the end of the month.  Some welcome rains on the 27th and 28th helped keep the extreme conditions from expanding farther east.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed over extreme western Willacy County, by the middle of April, continuing through the end of the month.  Some welcome rains on the 27th and 28th helped keep the extreme conditions from expanding farther east.

Local emergency managers reported street flooding on the south side of McAllen, between 23rd Street and Ware Avenue southwest of McAllen/Miller International Airport, in the neighborhood east of Los Encinos Park, with water covering the entire road at their location.
Per reports from social media, heavy rain led to street flooding on Olga Avenue in south McAllen.
Local emergency managers reported street closures along South 29th Street between Elmira and Daytona Avenues in south McAllen due to heavy rain.
Local emergency managers reported street closures south of Nolana and east of Bicentennial due to flooding in central McAllen.
Reports received of street flooding in Weslaco, with standing water at the intersection of Westgate Drive and W Pike Boulevard.
Reports received of minor street flooding in Donna near Salinas Road, just southwest of Donna High School.
The Starr County Sheriff's Office reported that San Juan Drive in Garceno, west of Rio Grande City, was flooded with at least 2 feet of water, causing traffic to divert away from the area.

Report received from the public, via the MPing app but confirmed with social media reports, of streets flooded with some vehicles stranded as well along Griffin Parkway north of the center of Mission.

The City of Mission's social media page shared multiple reports of street closures due to minor flooding, mainly in the southeast portion of the center of Mission near Keralum Avenue, which is east of Conway, south of 9th, and west of Bryan Road.
Pictures and videos were received via social media of multiple funnel clouds observed between Progreso and Weslaco. Timing is estimated.
Per public reports, numerous portions of a Frontage Road in Mercedes were flooded.
Public reports received of water covering North Border Avenue near Weslaco High School.
Local emergency managers reported standing water at the Intersection of Wilson Road and Frontage Road in Harlingen.

Report received via Broadcast Media of water completely covering lanes and shoulder on I-2/US-83 Eastbound near Mercedes. Lanes were closed as a result. Multiple water rescues eventually were needed. Video was also received via social media of water rising up to homes in the Mercedes area.
An NWS Employee reported water up to two feet deep resulting in stalled vehicles on the westbound Frontage Road near Rio Grande Valley Premium Outlets near Mercedes.
A Co-Op Observer reported 5.8 inches of rain occurring between 10:30 AM and 2:00 PM, along with minor flooding in the Port Mansfield area. One house also experienced flooding.
The Los Fresnos Police Department reported more than 10 streets in the city were experiencing flooding. Floodwaters were rising over curbs and spilling into sidewalks at the time of the report.
Brownsville Police reported that about 30 streets in the city were experiencing flooding. Floodwaters were deep enough to prevent cars from traveling through.

Reports received via social media of flooding along Frontage Road near the Sunrise Mall in Brownsville, with floodwaters reaching up to the headlights of cars. Additional flooding was also noted on FM 802/Ruben Torres Boulevard.
Reports received via public of resacas (oxbow lakes) near Valley International Country Club were overflowing onto parts of FM 802.
Public reports received via social media showed several streets near UTRGV Brownsville Campus were flooded, and portions of the campus were without power due to lightning strikes and/or flooding.
Reports received via social media of water rising halfway up wheels on vehicles as well as a few stalled cars in Olmito Estates.

Pictures received via social media of flooding estimated at 2 to 3 feet of water depth at Old Alice Road and Price Road in Brownsville, with water nearing gas pumps and buildings. This location is a flood-prone area which has seen several similar events since 2010.
A Co-Op observer in McCook recorded a wind gust to 53 knots, or 61 mph. Hail between the size of peas and dimes was also noted at the time.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued over northern Zapata County during the third week of May.  These conditions would improve by the last week of the month after rainfall from the 14th through 17th was fully incorporated into the Drought Monitor.

Drought conditions improved from Extreme(D3) to Severe(D2)across southern Zapata County the middle of May, helped by some effects of heavy rains in the middle of the month.  Additional improvement would be noted to end the month as these rains were incorporated into the Drought Monitor.

Scattered thunderstorms, some with torrential rains, falling between May 14th and 17th, helped temporarily alleviate the drought conditions, dropping extreme (D3) back to severe (D2) across all of Jim Hogg County toward the last week of May.  Unfortunately, hot and dry weather would return extreme conditions to portions of the county to close out the month.

Courtesy of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms, some with locally heavy rainfall, between May 14th and 17th, drought conditions eased to severe(D2) across all of Starr County during the latter third of May. Extreme(D3) conditions would return, however, to the northern tip of the county by the end of the month.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms pushing across western Brooks County between May 14th and 17th would relieve drought conditions a shade, with values dropping to Severe (D2) across the entire county by the 20th.  Unfortunately, dry and hot weather returning to close the month would bring conditions back to extreme in western portions of the county.

Severe (D2) drought conditions would continue across western and central Hidalgo County through the end of the month.  However, effects from additional rains between the 14th and 17th would filter into southeastern portions of the county, dropping the index back to moderate(D1) from May 27th through the 31st.
Extreme (D3) drought conditions redeveloped over eastern Jim Hogg County by the end of May as very hot and dry conditions returned to Deep South Texas between May 22nd and the end of the month.
Extreme (D3) drought conditions returned to most of Brooks County by the end of May, as very hot and dry weather prevailed over Deep South Texas from May 22nd until the end of the month.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions returned to extreme northern Starr County by the end of May, courtesy of very hot and drier weather from May 22nd through the end of the month in the Rio Grande Valley.
Severe (D2) drought conditions prevailed over western Kenedy County by the end of May as drier and hotter conditions developed over Deep South Texas after the 22nd.

A microburst descending from a potent severe thunderstorm first produced damage just north of Alton, at a mobile home park near the intersection of Moorefield (Farm to Market Road 681) and Monte Cristo (Farm to Market Road 1925).  In this neighborhood, at least six mobile homes were overturned by the winds, generally along and near the intersecion of 9 1/2 Mile Road and Inspiration Road. Just to the northeast, in the Las Ca��as colonia along and north of Monte Cristo, the combination of a pulse microburst striking a number of very poorly constructed homes led to the destruction of 14 mainly trailer-type residences, near the intersection of Monte Cristo (Farm to Market Road 1925) and Farm to Market (FM) 681. ||In a number of cases, the residences were completely demolished. A total of 13 persons sustained minor injuries requiring transport to local hospitals. By mid afternoon on the 16th, all were released. While the majority of injuries were minor, in one instance, a 3 year old girl had to be rescued from a pile of rubble that was once an unanchored trailer home. In addition to the building damage, at least eight wooden telephone poles were pulled down.||The damage track continued to the east southeast, generally along and north of FM 1925, at least to the intersection of FM 1925 and Federal Highway 281, twelve miles away. The vast majority of damage beyond the Las Ca��as neighborhood was hundreds of downed limbs from mesquite trees. Based on assessment from an NWS survey team, peak winds were between 65 and 70 mph, with the highest values likely where the telephone poles were pulled down in the Las Canas colonia, and again in the mesquite stand about two miles east. ||Based on radar signatures, it is possible that winds of 60 mph or greater continued into rural locations of eastern Hidalgo County, north of Edcouch and Elsa.

The same severe thunderstorm that rolled a number of trailer homes, ripped a roof off of an industrial building, and blew down hundreds of trees and limbs in central Hidalgo County continued to maintain strength while racing into northwest Cameron County. Wind gusts estimated near 80 mph damaged homes in Santa Rosa, and flipped two vehicles along Farm to Market Road 506, including a pickup truck on a driveway near the intersection of Orphanage and Louisiana. A number of power lines were also down in the area.

The severe thunderstorm which caused structure, vehicle, and power line damage moments earlier in Santa Rosa roared into the northern portion of Harlingen, eventually producing an 86 mph wind gust at Valley International Airport (KHRL) at exactly 405 AM, which blew off portions of three hangar roofs on the airport grounds. Pieces from one of these roofs, made of heavier asphalt underlines, knocked out at least two large windows in the control tower! In a nearby neighborhood just west of the airport, generally well constructed buildings fared well; however, dozens of large tree limbs were snapped and some fences were partially blown down.||The storm continued to produce damage farther east, with a 25 square foot portion of one residence's roof ripped away by the winds in Las Yescas.  The storm gradually weakened as it headed through largely uninhabited eastern Cameron County, on its way to dissipation in the Gulf.
The Zapata County Airport Automated Weather Observing System reported a little over 2 hours of heat indices meeting or exceeding 111 degrees. There were no illnesses or fatalities reported.

The Zapata County Automated Weather Observing System reported just over 2 hours of heat indices meeting or exceeding 111 degrees, and by proxy, it is reasonable that Starr County near the Rio Grande also received 2 hours of these conditions. The Mesowest locations near Falcon Dam reported several hours between 111 and 116, but these raw data are considered several degrees too high (in both temperature and dew point). A reduction supports two to three hours of 111. There were no illnesses or fatalities reported.

The Automated Weather Observing System at Zapata County Airport, 4 miles northeast of the city, reported 3 hours of heat indices exceeding 115 degrees starting at 3 PM CDT. There were no known heat related illnesses or casualties as of this writing.

The Automated Weather Observing System at the Zapata County Airport reported 3 hours of heat indices exceeding 115 degrees starting at 3 PM CDT, and by proxy, it's safe to assume that Starr County received similar conditions for this time period. The Mesowest location at Falcon Lake reported excessive heat values of 119 to 123, but these are considered several degrees too high based on comparative observations in past events. ||There were no known heat related casualties in these areas as of this writing.

The Automated Weather Observing System at the South Texas International Airport 11 miles north of Edinburg, along FM 490, reported 3 hours of heat indices reaching or exceeding 111 degrees beginning at 3 PM CDT. There was about a 30 minute period of heat indices exceeding 115 degrees beginning around 3:30 PM, but it was not long enough to meet Excessive Heat Criteria.

The Automated Weather Observing System at the South Texas International Airport 11 miles north of Edinburg, along FM 490, reported 3 hours of heat indices reaching or exceeding 111 degrees beginning at 3 PM CDT. There was about a 30 minute period of heat indices exceeding 115 degrees beginning around 3:30 PM, but it was not long enough to meet Excessive Heat Criteria.  The sensor location straddles the NWS forecast zones of northern and southern Hidalgo County.

The McAllen Airport ASOS site first recorded heat index values reaching or exceeding 111 degrees around 2:30 PM CDT. Heat index values then remained above 111 degrees through 5:30 PM, topping out around 112 degrees during this time. Edinburg International Airport also observed heat index values of 111 degrees at least intermittently during this time. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

This event is based largely on observed heat index values across Southern Hidalgo county and also across Zapata County, the latter of which saw heat indices top out at 112 degrees but only lasting for about an hour. Given the higher heat index values in Hidalgo/Zapata counties, it is inferred that Starr County also experienced heat index values in excess of 111 degrees for at least two hours. The Falcon Lake RAWS site recorded values technically reaching Excessive Heat criteria, but this observation site has a history of running notably higher than surrounding areas. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.
The Cameron County Sheriff's Department reported FM 2480 between Bayview and Los Fresnos was flooded, with up to 1 foot of water covering the westbound lane.
Reports received via social media of Marina Drive in Port Isabel covered with several inches of water.
Video received via social media of water covering several streets and intersections in the Arroyo Colorado Estates area. Water depth was estimated at 12 to 18 inches.
Video received via social media showing several portions of Padre Island Boulevard covered with water along with numerous side streets also experiencing flooding.

An off-duty NWS employee reported  2 to 3 feet of water flooding multiple roads in north Brownsville, including Morrison at Stagecoach; a neighborhood between Alton Gloor and east Morrison Blvd.; and a section along Dennet Road east of the Woods' End neighborhood.  Several cars had water above their wheels, stalled in the floodwaters.  This area had last seen similar flooding on June 19 and 20, 2018.

An official with the local Council of Government reported several feet of water on property next to her house, with over six inches of water inside her home north of La Joya. Total event rainfall exceeded 10 inches in this area over the course of several hours; additional flooding was also experienced in the area.

A 23-acre fire at Tom Gill and 5 Mile Line Road, approximately 8 miles northwest of Alton, TX, threatened 5 Homes and several horses. The horses were moved to a safe area. Despite saving the structures and horses, one firefighter was transported to the hospital for smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion injuries. Responding agencies included several from western Hidalgo County, as well as the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Department and the Texas Department of Public Safety.  Hot spots continued to burn late into the night of the 16th and likely into the 17th before being extinguished.

A 450 acre fire developed during strong winds during the afternoon of April 16th along Farm-to-Market (FM) Road 1017, near Hebbronville.|Six homes and six structures were threatened and saved. Numerous local Volunteer and county Fire Departments assisted with fire fighting efforts, as well as the Texas Forest Service and the Texas Department of Public Safety.

A wildfire, known as the Las Cuatas Fire,located along Farm-to-Market Road (FM) 755 at the intersection with Federal Highway 281 near the|Community of Rachal, quickly grew to 1900 acres, driven by gusty southeast winds and excellent low level dispersion. The fire destroyed two residences, one which was not being lived in, as well as one outbuilding.  Ten other homes were threatened and saved; an estimated 150 persons self-evacuated as the fire neared their homes.||Numerous Volunteer Fire Departments and Emergency Management responders helped in the firefighting effort, from Brooks, Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County. The Texas Department of Public Safety provided aircraft and dozers to fight the blaze. The fire was contained later that night into the morning of May 1st.

A second wildfire, known as the Mestena Fire, located 10 miles west of Federal Highway 281 on Farm to Market (FM) Road 755, along the Brooks/Jim Hogg County line, rapidly spread to 697 acres at roughly the same time as the nearby Las Cuatas Fire near Rachal.  This wildfire, also spread by gusty southeast winds and occurring with excellent dispersion, threatened three homes, and destroyed one outbuilding.||The Texas Department of Public Safety provided aircraft to the scene, and Volunteer Fire Departments and other local emergency management support assisted from nearby counties and cities, including Brooks, Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County. The fire was contained later that night into the morning of May 1st.

Torrential thunderstorm rains fell generally between 430 and 7 PM across much of the Brownsville area, then were followed by steadier, locally heavy rains during the mid evening.  Another round of lighter rains developed overnight.  Storm totals ranged from 3 to 5 inches across the area, with the highest totals along a line from Rancho Viejo through Brownsville Airport, extending southeast to the Sabal Palm Audubon Center near the Rio Grande. Minor nuisance flooding was reported in poor drainage areas during the initial torrential rains, but, overall, the rain was welcome relief from drought conditions which had been dominant through most of the spring.

Several reports of significant flooding along FM 802/Ruben Torres Blvd in Brownsville. This includes multiple reports of stranded vehicles near the WalMart, as well as between Robindale Blvd and Central Ave.

Many portions of FM 802/Ruben Torres Blvd in Brownsville remained under several feet of water through the morning hours on the 2nd due to overwhelmed drainage systems in the area. It was not until around 9:00-9:30 AM local time on October 2nd that flood waters finally began to recede to the point of roads being traversable by mid-size cars.  Other high water of 2 to 3 feet along the sides of roads in a subdivision along Dana Avenue north of Ruben Torres Blvd. continued through the afternoon of October 2nd.  Damage to vehicles and property was not known as of this writing.
Brownsville Police Dept reported road closures due to flooding on East Washington St in downtown Brownsville.
A video was received from the public of water entering a home near the intersection of Jamie Zapata Ave and Robindale Blvd in Brownsville.
Picture received from the public of a vehicle partially submerged in flood waters near the intersection of FM 511 and State Hwy 48.
TXDOT reports standing water on I-69E/US-77 near and north of the business 77 split roughly 4 miles north of Raymondville.
Picture received from the public of portions of the I-2 Frontage Road under several inches of water. Exact depth unknown at this time.
The Weslaco Chief of Police reported 2.19 of rain, with 1.5 falling in one hour. Several reports of street flooding were passed on with water starting to top curbs.
Report received from public of several inches of water topping the curbs at the intersection of Business 77 and Harrison Road in Harlingen.
Picture received from public of Madison Ave in Harlingen under several inches of water. Exact depth unknown at this time.
Video received from public of water reaching up to car bumpers along Washington Ave between Commerce and 1st Streets in Harlingen.
Video received from the public of water covering US-77/Sunshine Strip near the VA Health Center in Harlingen. Water was reaching up to the bumpers of some sedans.
Picture received from the public of water halfway up the wheel wells of several cars in Los Fresnos near the library.
Public report of several inches of water flooding the intersection of Boca Chica Blvd and Central Ave.
The Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport recorded a wind gust to 52 knots/60 mph as severe thunderstorms moved through the area.
Video received from public of a tropical funnel cloud near Exit 23A on I-69E in Harlingen.
NWS Employee reports tree down on North Indiana Ave just north of Boca Chica Blvd near Rick's Auto Service.

Flooding along Ruben Torres Blvd. during the peak of the evening commute, and the result of an estimated 3 to 4 inches of rain per hour for two hours, stranded dozens of vehicles under up to 3 feet of water. A report of 4+ feet of water was obtained from a worker at the Circle K gas/convenience store at the intersection of Ruben Torres and N. Central Avenue during the peak of the flood shortly after 9 PM on the 1st.  Other structures had some flooding, including homes just south and north of Ruben Torres.  Damage values were unknown as of this writing.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across southern portions of Jim Hogg County, generally south of TX-16 and west of Farm to Market 1017, due to a lack of significant rainfall and temperatures above seasonal average.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across southern portions of Zapata County, generally between Morales-Sanchez and south along US-83 to the border of Starr County, due to a lack of significant rainfall and temperatures above seasonal average.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across southwestern portions of Starr County, generally from the border of Zapata County and along US-83 to near Roma, due to a lack of significant rainfall and temperatures above seasonal average.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across southern portions of Jim Hogg County due to a lack of significant rainfall, above normal temperatures, and a dry cold front in late October. A cold front on the evening of November 3rd brought beneficial rain to the region and ended the Severe (D2) drought.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded across the western half of Starr County due to a lack of significant rainfall, above normal temperatures, and a dry cold front in late October. Another cold front on the evening of November 3rd brought beneficial rain to the region and ended the Severe (D2) drought.

Severe (D2) Drought expanded across southern Zapata County due to a lack of significant rainfall, above normal temperatures, and a dry cold front in late October. Another cold front on the evening of November 3rd brought beneficial rain to the region and ended the Severe (D2) drought.
Severe (D2) Drought continued across southwestern portions of Starr County due to a lack of significant rainfall and temperatures above seasonal average.
Severe (D2) Drought continued across southern portions of Zapata County due to a lack of significant rainfall and temperatures above seasonal average.

The La Gloria Fire was estimated to have initiated around 3:00 PM CDT on October 27th and continued until 3:30 PM CDT on the 28th when it was reported to be 100% contained. This wildfire consumed a total of 208 acres. Three unoccupied (at the time of the fire reaching the location) and one hunting trailer were lost. Dollar damages are estimated.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across a tiny sliver of northern Starr County, generally along the border with Jim Hogg County between Farm to Market 649 and Farm to Market 1017, due to a lack of significant rainfall and temperatures above seasonal average.

Thunderstorm winds estimated at 50 knots downed several large tree limbs and felled at least one large mesquite when its base snapped, ripped 3 to 4 pieces of roofing off of a carport on Hoy Street, and lofted a trampoline into powerlines. Damage value is estimated.||Note: The estimated wind gust of 50 knots is equivalent to 58 mph.

Torrential rains of 1.5 to 2 inches in one hour reported, and more than 2 inches in less than 2 hours,  at Brownsville/South Padre International Airport and nearby neighborhoods in Cameron County caused flooding at the intersection of Boca Chica and Highway 48. Local Emergency Manager reported waters flowing over the curb and the intersection becoming impassable at 1:28 PM.

There were several gusts of 34 knots (39 mph) between 11:54 AM CST and 12:42 PM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: The Port Isabel Water Level Observation Network (PTIT2) reported a 34 knot (39 mph) wind gust associated with the strong thunderstorms moving eastward across the region at 1:00 PM and 1:24 PM CST.

events.cz_name: COASTAL WATERS FROM PT MANSFIELD TO RIO GRANDE RIVER TX OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: The SPI Brazos Santiago TCOON (BZST2) reported a 38 knot (44 mph) wind gust associated with the strong thunderstorms moving eastward across the region between 1:12 PM and 1:24 PM CST. Several gusts of 34 knots (39 mph) or greater were reported between 12:42 PM CST and 2:00 PM CST.

events.cz_name: LAGUNA MADRE FROM PORT OF BROWNSVILLE TO ARROYO COLORADO
events.event_narrative: A strong thunderstorm associated with a cold front developed between Port Mansfield and the Laguna Atascosa Wildlife Refuge late in the afternoon on December 18th. The Realitos Peninsula TCOON site recorded gusts of 34 knots between 6:54 PM CST and 7:18 PM CST.

A resaca overflowed its banks along Vermillion Avenue, from 1 to 1.5 miles north of the intersection with Boca Chica Blvd. (State Road 4).  At least three feet of water likely occurred toward the end of the heavy rainfall, where an estimated 3 to 4 inches fell per hour for two hours between 5 and 6 PM CST on the 1st.  A CoCoRaHS observer along Vermillion Avenue reported more than 10 inches on the 1st, with most falling during this period; the two-day total was 13.53 inches.

A resaca continued to overflow its banks along Vermillion Avenue, from 1 to 1.5 miles north of the intersection with Boca Chica Blvd. (State Road 4), well into October 2nd with the road remaining closed. At 18 inches to two feet of water covered the center of the road, with up to four feet on the normal road edges. A CoCoRaHS observer along Vermillion Avenue reported more than 10 inches on the 1st, with most falling during this period; the two-day total was 13.53 inches. End time of the significant flooding is estimated.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 12:35 AM on January 3rd and remained below freezing until 8:55 AM. Low temperatures fell into the lower to middle 20s across the area. A minimum temperature of 23 degrees was observed at the Brooks County Airport.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 12:00AM and remained below freezing until 8:30AM. Low temperatures fell into the lower to middle 20s with a NWS cooperative observer in Armstrong reporting a low of 25 degrees. A minimum temperature of 21 degrees was reported at the Sarita Union Pacific Railroad (UPR) mesonet site.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 12:05AM and remained below freezing until 8:30AM. The Hebbronville airport recorded a low of 25 degrees. The Hebbronville Remote Automated Weather Station observed a minimum temperature of 24 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 1:30AM and remained below freezing until 8:30AM. Low temperatures fell into the upper 20s to around 32 degrees away from urban areas in southern Hidalgo County. A minimum temperature of 27 was observed at the South Texas International Airport 11 miles north-northeast of Edinburg. The RAWS site at Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge along the Rio Grande observed a low of 26 degrees. Meanwhile, the ASOS station at McAllen International Airport only reported a low of 35 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 10:11 PM on January 2nd and remained below freezing through 8:11 AM on the 3rd. Low temperatures fell into the lower to middle 20s across the area. A minimum temperature of 23 degrees was observed at the Falcon Lake RAWS site. The mesonet site six miles northwest of La Gloria recorded a low of 22 degrees.

Temperatures fell below freezing around 12:05AM and remained below freezing until 8:30AM. The Yturria Union Pacific Railroad mesonet site (UR295) in northern Willacy County recorded a minimum temperature of 26 degrees. Given low temperatures in the middle to upper 20s observed in adjacent northern Hidalgo County and Inland Kenedy County, it is implied that temperatures across much of Inland Willacy County were also in the middle to upper 20s.

Severe (D2) Drought developed across western portions of Zapata County, between the Rio Grande River and roughly 6 miles east of US-83 from just northwest of Zapata to the Webb/Zapata County line, on February 8th and expanded ever so slightly on February 15th, due to a lack of significant rainfall.

The event known as the Polo Fire was estimated to have initiated around 3:00PM CST just south of Armstrong, TX east of Highway 77 and burned until the middle of the afternoon on the 13th, when it was announced to be 100% contained by 5:19PM CST. This wildfire consumed a total of 3,628.8 acres. A spot request submitted by the Texas A&M Fire Service and an NWS Employee���s report at 4:45PM CST about smelling smoke in the Harlingen area on February 12th were used as a guide for the earlier ignition and the very rapid spread that followed.

The event known as the 755 Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 2:00PM CST south of Encino, TX near the intersection of US-281 and FM 755. It burned until the afternoon of the 18th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 2:00PM CST. This wildfire consumed a total of 2,000 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Fire Service on February 16th and the GOES-16 Day Land Cloud Fire RGB channel were used as a guide for the ignition time and very rapid spread that followed.

A tight pressure gradient between a surface high pressure off the Carolina Coast and a low pressure system over the Panhandle of Texas resulted in very windy conditions across the Rio Grande Valley throughout the day on February 16th. An estimated gust of 45 knots early in the afternoon damaged the metal roof of the Boys and Girls Club in San Benito. This caused an estimated $10,000 worth of damage and kept them to closed for the remainder of the week. Sporadic power outages were also reported across portions of Cameron County. |Note: 45 knots is equivalent to 52 mph.
